New Zealand's electoral authority distinguishes these arrangements from parties joining government. The distinction shows that keeping a government functioning need not mean sharing its entire program.

evidence.locator: Parties negotiate to form a government
evidence.note: The Electoral Commission's Parties negotiate section differentiates coalition membership from support on certain issues/laws; the card does not claim all agreements have identical terms or require support on every bill.

original_record.label: Confidence and supply agreement
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish supporting a government on specified matters from joining its coalition.

relations.note: The New Zealand MMP explanation discusses confidence and supply as one arrangement parties may negotiate when no party can govern alone, not an inevitable consequence of MMP.

original_record.card: Connecting concrete and abstract representations means explicitly showing how familiar examples correspond to symbols or general concepts. Without that bridge, learners may manipulate a formula yet struggle to apply it elsewhere. Comparing several representations can direct attention away from surface details toward the underlying relation.

evidence.note: Checked explicit mappings and risk of inert knowledge; transfer is a goal of the method, not an automatic outcome in every setting.

original_record.label: Connecting concrete and abstract representations
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explicitly map familiar objects or examples onto abstract symbols so knowledge can transfer beyond surface features.

relations.note: The guide's mapping between examples and abstract symbols complements, but is not identical to, coordinating words and pictures.

original_record.card: Constituency tests investigate which words behave together as a unit inside a sentence. Replacing a group with a pronoun or moving it can supply evidence for a phrase. Different tests offer complementary clues, so a sentence's visible sequence alone need not reveal its internal structure.

evidence.note: Checked replacement and movement methods and unit interpretation; no single test is presented as infallible or every sequence as a constituent.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Constituency tests supply evidence about phrase units, while structural ambiguity shows how different arrangements of those units can change interpretation.

original_record.label: Constituency tests
original_record.learning_takeaway: Combine replacement and movement evidence to identify word groups that behave as sentence units.

relations.note: Constituency tests supply evidence about phrase units, while structural ambiguity shows how different arrangements of those units can change interpretation.

original_record.card: Constitutive moral luck concerns traits and dispositions shaped partly by factors people did not choose, including inheritance and upbringing. If those traits influence action, judging someone's character also raises a question about control. The issue is responsibility for who one has become, not merely what happens afterward.

evidence.note: SEP's constitutive-luck paragraphs identify genes, caregivers and peers, and connect dispositions with action; partly avoids a deterministic claim that character or conduct is wholly unchosen.

original_record.label: Constitutive moral luck
original_record.learning_takeaway: Examine responsibility for dispositions shaped partly by unchosen development and inheritance.

relations.note: The source explicitly classifies luck in character and dispositions as constitutive moral luck, extending the control problem to agents as well as actions.

original_record.card: Construct validity asks whether a measure actually captures the concept it is intended to represent. A procedure can produce consistent scores yet miss its intended target. The challenge is therefore more than repeatability: it is connecting an observable measurement to the psychological idea being studied.

evidence.note: Section 2.3 defines construct validity and separates validity from reliability; the card does not assert that surface plausibility or one correlation settles the question.

original_record.label: Construct validity
original_record.learning_takeaway: Ask whether an operational measure captures the intended psychological concept.

relations.note: The source explicitly contrasts measuring the intended construct with merely obtaining consistent results; observer agreement is one specified form of that consistency.

original_record.card: A constructed treatment wetland uses wetland plants, soils and associated microorganisms as part of an engineered water-treatment system. Water-quality improvement depends on these natural processes working within a designed setting. The vegetation is therefore part of the treatment approach, not merely decoration around a pond.

evidence.note: EPA’s opening definition identifies treatment systems using vegetation, soils and microbial communities to improve water quality.

original_record.label: Constructed treatment wetland
original_record.learning_takeaway: Treat wastewater with deliberately arranged vegetation, soils and microbial processes.

relations.note: Both approaches use vegetation and surrounding ecological processes for water-quality goals, but a treatment wetland and a streamside buffer have different layouts and roles.

original_record.card: Germany's constructive vote of no confidence requires the Bundestag to elect a successor Chancellor by a majority of its members while seeking the incumbent's dismissal. Opposition must therefore agree on a replacement, not merely on rejection. Article 67 also requires forty-eight hours between motion and election.

evidence.note: Basic Law Article 67 supplies majority membership, successor election, dismissal request and waiting period; the institutional consequence follows those express conditions and is bounded to Germany.

original_record.label: Constructive vote of no confidence
original_record.learning_takeaway: Understand why Germany requires choosing a successor while removing the Chancellor.

relations.note: Compare Germany's constitutional replacement requirement with New Zealand's negotiated support arrangements. Both concern parliamentary support for government, but one is a removal procedure and the other an interparty agreement.

original_record.card: Convergent evolution produces similar features in separate evolutionary lineages. Bird and bat wings both serve flight, but their wing structures arose independently. Their underlying forelimbs still share ancestry, showing that the answer depends on which feature and evolutionary level a comparison is examining.

evidence.note: Berkeley connects analogous wings with convergent evolution while distinguishing homologous forelimbs.

original_record.label: Convergent evolution
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explain similar functions that evolved separately rather than being inherited from a shared ancestor.

relations.note: Contrasting wing function with forelimb ancestry makes convergence and biological homology distinguishable without making them mutually exclusive at every level.

original_record.card: A conversational acknowledgment gives brief evidence that a listener is following or understanding, often without taking the speaking turn. Responses such as yeah or a head nod can serve this function. Their role is feedback within coordination, rather than necessarily endorsing the truth of everything the speaker says.

evidence.note: Checked brief verbal/gestural evidence and turn status; understanding is not equated with agreement or complete comprehension of every detail.

original_record.label: Conversational acknowledgment
original_record.learning_takeaway: Provide brief verbal or gestural evidence of understanding, often without taking over the speaking turn.

relations.note: The grounding chapter explicitly lists acknowledgments and head nods as positive evidence of understanding, generally without taking a turn.

original_record.card: A conversational implicature is an interpretation suggested by context rather than guaranteed by the sentence's truth. Hearing that a customer sighed might suggest annoyance, yet the speaker can add that the customer was relieved. This cancellability helps distinguish an implicature from a necessary entailment.

evidence.note: Checked context dependence and cancellation without contradiction; the card does not say a sigh always implies annoyance.

original_record.label: Conversational implicature
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a contextually suggested conclusion from a necessary implication by checking whether it can be cancelled.

relations.note: The source directly contrasts the cancellable anger interpretation with the necessary breath entailment of sighing.

original_record.card: Conversational turn-taking coordinates who speaks and when. Experiments with conversation fragments show that listeners can anticipate turn endings, supporting accounts that involve preparation before silence arrives. Such laboratory tasks isolate useful cues, but do not establish how every transition is managed in natural conversation.

evidence.note: The abstract and experiments report button-press anticipation with conversation fragments; the introduction distinguishes anticipation ability from proof of use in every natural exchange. The card now states the observed ability and the limited inference, while retaining the turn-completion framework.

original_record.label: Conversational turn-taking
original_record.learning_takeaway: Coordinate alternating speakers partly by anticipating possible turn endings rather than waiting only to react after silence.

relations.note: The research paper explicitly relates turn anticipation to possible completion points called transition-relevance places.

original_record.card: Coordinating graphics with verbal explanations helps learners connect what an image shows with the process being described. Relevant labels can sit close to the visual elements they explain. Decorative or overly detailed pictures may distract instead, so the principle concerns meaningful integration rather than adding images indiscriminately.

evidence.note: Checked near-element labels, relevant graphics, and distracting-detail caveat; no visual/verbal learning-style categories are implied.

original_record.label: Coordinating graphics and verbal explanations
original_record.learning_takeaway: Place relevant verbal explanations alongside the visual elements they explain so learners can connect representations.

relations.note: The guide links visual/verbal integration with connections between representations, while the second method specifically connects concrete examples to abstract ideas.

original_record.card: Stressed corals can lose the symbiotic algae living in their tissues, leaving them pale or white. This bleaching also removes an important food source. A bleached coral is not necessarily dead, but prolonged stress makes recovery harder and can ultimately lead to death.

evidence.note: NOAA explains stress-driven expulsion of symbiotic algae, loss of color and food, possible recovery and death if stress persists.

original_record.label: Coral bleaching
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish stress-driven loss of symbiotic algae from immediate coral death.

relations.note: Bleaching shows what can happen when a coral’s beneficial partnership with algae is disrupted.

original_record.card: The Coriolis force appears when motion is described from a rotating reference frame. A path can seem to bend sideways because the observer’s coordinate system is turning. An inertial-frame description accounts for the same motion without assigning this apparent force a separate physical interaction.

evidence.locator: 6.3 Centripetal Force; inspected passage indices 44, 50 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1165039268847; fs-id1165039316978
evidence.note: A rotating frame describes apparent trajectory bending through an inertial force absent from the inertial-frame account.

original_record.label: Coriolis force
original_record.learning_takeaway: A rotating frame describes apparent trajectory bending through an inertial force absent from the inertial-frame account.

relations.note: The source explicitly contrasts rotating-frame Coriolis descriptions with inertial-frame accounts.

original_record.card: A countersubject is recurring counterpoint that accompanies a fugue's subject. Its identity matters: the composer brings back recognizable accompanying material when the subject returns, rather than inventing completely different counterpoint each time. The same countersubject can appear in different voices as the texture changes.

evidence.note: Fugue Analysis defines consistent accompaniment and identifies one countersubject in alto and soprano; no requirement that every fugue have one is imposed.

original_record.label: Countersubject
original_record.learning_takeaway: Identify recurring counterpoint accompanying successive subject entries.

relations.note: The source defines countersubject specifically within its fugue analysis and contrasts it with nonrecurring accompaniment.

original_record.card: A covalent network solid contains atoms joined in an extended web of covalent bonds. Disrupting that network requires breaking bonds, rather than merely separating intact molecules. Such solids often have high melting temperatures; diamond illustrates the hardness that extensive covalent bonding can produce.

evidence.locator: 10.5 The Solid State of Matter; inspected passage indices 14 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm59353248
evidence.note: A continuous covalent-bond network helps explain the hardness and high melting temperatures of diamond-like solids.

original_record.label: Covalent network solid
original_record.learning_takeaway: A continuous covalent-bond network helps explain the hardness and high melting temperatures of diamond-like solids.

relations.note: The passage explicitly attributes network-solid properties to the connected covalent bonds between its atoms.

original_record.card: Cover crops are grown primarily to keep living vegetation on the soil and provide conservation benefits, rather than as the main harvested crop. Their roots and residues can reduce erosion and add organic matter. Timing and management determine how those functions fit around the farm’s other crops.

evidence.note: NRCS defines seasonal vegetative cover rather than cash crops and identifies erosion reduction, organic matter and soil-structure benefits.

original_record.label: Cover crops
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a crop grown for soil cover and ecosystem functions from one grown primarily for harvest.

relations.note: Cover crops supply living cover, while no-till changes soil disturbance and residue handling; they can serve complementary but distinct soil-management functions.

original_record.card: A covering index contains every column a particular query needs, including its output columns. The database can answer that query from the index without looking up matching rows in the original table. Whether an index covers a query therefore depends on that query's requested information.

evidence.note: Checked search-plus-output coverage and eliminated table lookup; an index can cover one query without covering every query.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: This index design changes how a database retrieves selected columns; it is an implementation facet rather than a synonym for the database itself.

original_record.label: Covering index
original_record.learning_takeaway: Include search and output columns in an index so a query need not consult the original table.

relations.note: This index design changes how a database retrieves selected columns; it is an implementation facet rather than a synonym for the database itself.

original_record.card: Creep is deformation that accumulates under sustained loading over time. In metals and ceramics at elevated temperatures, it can become important even below the usual yield stress. Components such as turbine blades must therefore be assessed for service duration and temperature, not only their initial deformation.

evidence.locator: Chapter 10: Creep, Fracture, and Fatigue; inspected passage indices 68, 69, 71 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-69; paragraph-70; paragraph-72
evidence.note: Time-dependent deformation can accumulate at elevated temperature even below a material’s usual yield stress.

original_record.label: Creep (materials)
original_record.learning_takeaway: Time-dependent deformation can accumulate at elevated temperature even below a material’s usual yield stress.

relations.note: Creep emphasizes sustained load and time, while fatigue emphasizes repeated loading; the sources treat these as different failure concerns.

original_record.card: For a displaced linear spring–mass system released from rest, critical damping returns it toward equilibrium as quickly as possible without oscillation. It marks the threshold between oscillatory and nonoscillatory response; simply adding more damping makes the return slower rather than always improving the result.

evidence.locator: 15.5 Damped Oscillations; inspected passage indices 18, 19 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1167131215180; fs-id1167131503759
evidence.note: Tune the linear damping threshold for rapid nonoscillatory return to equilibrium.

original_record.label: Critical damping
original_record.learning_takeaway: Tune the linear damping threshold for rapid nonoscillatory return to equilibrium.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies critical damping as the threshold regime within damped harmonic motion.

original_record.card: A fluid’s critical point marks the end of the liquid–vapor coexistence boundary. As it is approached, the distinction between the two phases disappears. Above the critical temperature, applying more pressure cannot produce a separate liquid phase, although the fluid can become dense.

evidence.locator: 10.4 Phase Diagrams; inspected passage indices 40 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm114606944
evidence.note: At the end of liquid-vapor coexistence, the liquid-gas boundary disappears and pressure alone cannot liquefy hotter gas.

original_record.label: Critical point of a fluid
original_record.learning_takeaway: At the end of liquid-vapor coexistence, the liquid-gas boundary disappears and pressure alone cannot liquefy hotter gas.

relations.note: The source explains the disappearance of the liquid–vapor boundary as the transition to supercritical fluid behavior.

original_record.card: Crop rotation changes the crops grown in a field through a planned sequence over time. This can interrupt recurring pest associations and diversify how the field is used. It is a preventive management practice, rather than simply moving an existing pest after it has become a problem.

evidence.note: Identifies crop rotation as a way to prevent pest problems within IPM.
Defines planned crop sequence over time on the same field and reduced pest pressure as a possible benefit.

original_record.label: Crop rotation
original_record.learning_takeaway: Disrupt recurring crop-pest associations by changing the crop grown in a field over time.

relations.note: EPA explicitly includes rotation among preventive practices within integrated pest management.

original_record.card: A crystal vacancy is an unoccupied position where an atom or ion normally belongs in a lattice. It differs from an interstitial defect, where a particle occupies a gap between regular positions. Both disturb an otherwise repeating internal arrangement of particles.

evidence.locator: 10.5 The Solid State of Matter; inspected passage indices 24 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm62566768
evidence.note: A missing atom at a regular lattice site is a structural defect distinct from an interstitial impurity.

original_record.label: Crystal vacancy
original_record.learning_takeaway: A missing atom at a regular lattice site is a structural defect distinct from an interstitial impurity.

relations.note: The solid-state section explicitly describes vacancies as defects in a crystalline solid’s repeating pattern.

original_record.card: A spinning baseball can experience a sideways aerodynamic force that bends its path. NASA's simplified curveball model links the curvature to spin, speed and air density. It treats the path as a circular arc when drag and the resulting changes in the force are neglected.

evidence.note: NASA Aerodynamic Force gives the spinning-ball force and explicitly states the approximation; retain model qualification rather than declaring every real pitch a circular arc.

original_record.label: Curveball aerodynamics
original_record.learning_takeaway: Connect spin-generated sideways force with a curved pitch trajectory.

relations.note: NASA explicitly explains the curveball through aerodynamic force acting on a spinning baseball.

original_record.card: Cyanotype uses light-sensitive iron salts to produce a characteristic blue image. Exposure and washing make the image visible on a prepared surface. Because the process can record objects placed directly on paper, it can join photographic chemistry with close observation of a specimen’s shape.

evidence.note: Iron-salt chemistry and washing are in a05; Atkins supplies the contact-specimen application.
Directly arranged algae establish the specimen application.

original_record.label: Cyanotype
original_record.learning_takeaway: Light acts on iron-salt-coated paper, and washing develops the characteristic blue image.

relations.note: Atkins used cyanotype contact images to record algae specimens.

original_record.card: In a weakly damped spring–mass system, oscillations lose energy and their amplitude declines. A common low-speed model makes the damping force proportional to velocity and opposite to motion. Under that model, the oscillating displacement fits inside a shrinking exponential envelope.

evidence.locator: 15.5 Damped Oscillations; inspected passage indices 7, 9, 10, 12 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1167131080334; fs-id1167131181569; fs-id1167129966801; fs-id1167131498071
evidence.note: Dissipation removes oscillator energy so its amplitude declines rather than continuing indefinitely.

original_record.label: Damped harmonic motion
original_record.learning_takeaway: Dissipation removes oscillator energy so its amplitude declines rather than continuing indefinitely.

relations.note: The source contrasts weakly damped oscillation with critical and overdamped responses as damping increases.

original_record.card: Darshan concerns the devotional encounter of seeing a deity, commonly through an image. The visual interaction can be central to puja rather than merely decorative. Debates about internet worship make this emphasis especially visible by asking how an encounter changes when the image is mediated online.

evidence.locator: Opening; online shrine discussion, lines 56 and 82
evidence.note: The case study identifies visual interaction and internet-mediated puja.

original_record.label: Darshan
original_record.learning_takeaway: Seeing a deity’s image can be a devotional encounter; visual presence matters in temples and in debates over online worship.

relations.note: Darshan is presented as a common visual dimension of puja.
The case study identifies devotional visual encounter within Hindu practice.

original_record.card: Dasymetric mapping uses additional information to redistribute an aggregate quantity within reporting areas. Population can be allocated away from places identified as uninhabited. The method replaces a uniform-density assumption with a distribution informed by ancillary data, so the result depends on that information.

evidence.note: Ancillary data refine within-zone population allocation.

original_record.label: Dasymetric mapping
original_record.learning_takeaway: Ancillary information reallocates aggregate population away from uninhabited areas instead of assuming uniform density within census boundaries.

relations.note: Compare uniform reporting-area shading with redistribution informed by supplementary spatial information.

original_record.card: The de Broglie wavelength associates a wave with a particle’s momentum: larger momentum means shorter wavelength. Electrons as well as photons obey this relationship. It provides a bridge between particle motion and wave behavior, helping explain why matter can produce diffraction patterns.

evidence.locator: 6.5 De Broglie’s Matter Waves; inspected passage indices 6, 7, 8, 9 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: list-00001; fs-id1163711990811; fs-id1163712336118; fs-id1163712430653
evidence.note: The matter-wave discussion and Equation 6.54 give wavelength as Planck’s constant divided by momentum and connect matter waves with diffraction.

original_record.label: de Broglie wavelength
original_record.learning_takeaway: Relate particle momentum to matter-wave wavelength, extending wave behavior beyond photons.

relations.note: The two subjects approach wave-particle behavior from complementary directions: light transfers energy discretely, and matter exhibits wavelength-dependent behavior.

original_record.card: A dead position ends a chess game because neither player could checkmate through any possible sequence of legal moves. This is stronger than saying that checkmate seems unlikely or cannot be forced: even cooperative play by the opponent would not make mate possible.

evidence.note: FIDE 5.2.2 quantifies over any legal sequence; the cooperative-play explanation unpacks that condition rather than adding a material-count rule.

original_record.label: Dead position in chess
original_record.learning_takeaway: Recognize a draw where neither side can ever deliver legal checkmate.

relations.note: Both end the game as a draw, but stalemate concerns present legal moves while dead position concerns impossibility of future mate.

original_record.card: Psychological studies sometimes conceal their precise purpose because knowing it could change participants' responses. That creates an ethical tension between informative behavior and informed participation. The cited ethics account limits deceptive procedures and requires a later explanation of the purpose, data use and reasons for concealment.

evidence.note: Section 2.4 explains response distortion and debriefing, with ethical limits; the card attributes this account and does not treat scientific convenience as sufficient permission for harmful deception.

original_record.label: Deception in psychological research
original_record.learning_takeaway: Examine the tension between realistic responses and participants' knowledge of a study's purpose.

relations.note: The source directly connects permissible use of deception with a subsequent full debriefing rather than treating concealment as an unrestricted research tool.

original_record.card: DEFLATE is a lossless compressed-data format combining two techniques. Repeated byte strings become LZ77-style length-and-distance references, while literals and references are represented with Huffman codes. Data is organized into blocks, which can use fixed codes, transmitted code tables, or no compression.

evidence.note: Checked the combination and three valid block types; not described as an Internet standard because RFC 1951 is informational.

original_record.label: DEFLATE
original_record.learning_takeaway: Combine LZ77 references and Huffman-coded symbols inside a lossless block format.

relations.note: The RFC abstract and section 2 expressly state that DEFLATE combines the LZ77 algorithm with Huffman coding.

original_record.card: A deformation retract continuously moves a space onto one of its subspaces, ending with that subspace’s points fixed. A stronger version keeps those points fixed throughout the movement. This distinction separates the final result of the deformation from what happens during every intermediate stage.

evidence.locator: Deformation Retract -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-4; paragraph-5; paragraph-6; paragraph-7
evidence.note: A continuous deformation moves a space onto a subspace, with a stronger version fixing that subspace throughout.

original_record.label: Deformation retract
original_record.learning_takeaway: A continuous deformation moves a space onto a subspace, with a stronger version fixing that subspace throughout.

relations.note: The definition constructs a deformation retract using a homotopy.

original_record.card: A cue-only delayed judgment of learning asks someone to estimate future recall after time away from the material, using a cue without the answer visible. The delay reduces reliance on immediate familiarity. The cited guide treats this as promising for allocating study, while noting limited classroom evidence.

evidence.note: Recommendation 6a, printed pp. 23–24, describes the cue-only delayed judgment procedure: delay after study, target answer absent and prospective recall judgment. The guide rates classroom evidence as limited; the narrower label retains the same selected facet and reserved ID.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Both approaches use information to guide subsequent learning, but a learner's delayed recall estimate is distinct from the broader formative use of assessment evidence.

original_record.label: Cue-only delayed judgments of learning
original_record.learning_takeaway: After a delay, use only a cue to judge future recall so immediate familiarity is less misleading.

relations.note: Both approaches use information to guide subsequent learning, but a learner's delayed recall estimate is distinct from the broader formative use of assessment evidence.

original_record.card: The Ottoman devshirme forcibly recruited Christian boys for conversion, education and state service. Some entered military units, while others pursued administrative roles. The system linked coercive removal from families with the state’s attempt to train personnel whose careers depended on the ruler.

evidence.note: Recruitment, conversion, schooling and military/administrative destinations are explicit.

original_record.label: Devshirme
original_record.learning_takeaway: The Ottoman state forcibly gathered Christian boys, converted and educated them, and assigned them to military or administrative service.

relations.note: Devshirme supplied some recruits to the Janissaries while also serving other state roles.

original_record.card: Diagnostic sensitivity asks: among people who have the target condition, how often is the test positive? A highly sensitive test misses fewer affected people. This is different from asking whether a particular positive result means disease, which requires a probability conditioned on the test result.

evidence.note: NCI defines sensitivity as positive-test probability given cancer and separately defines predictive value in the reverse conditional direction.

original_record.label: Diagnostic sensitivity
original_record.learning_takeaway: Read sensitivity as the chance of a positive test among people who have the target condition.

relations.note: Sensitivity conditions on disease status, while positive predictive value conditions on a positive test.

original_record.card: Diagnostic specificity asks: among people without the target condition, how often is the test negative? Higher specificity means fewer false positives in that group. It complements sensitivity, but neither quantity alone tells a patient the probability of disease after receiving a positive result.

evidence.note: NCI defines specificity as negative-test probability without cancer and distinguishes it from sensitivity and positive predictive value.

original_record.label: Diagnostic specificity
original_record.learning_takeaway: Read specificity as the chance of a negative test among people without the target condition.

relations.note: Sensitivity and specificity describe test behavior in different disease-status groups; they are complementary rates, not interchangeable names.

original_record.card: Dick Fosbury's lasting influence came from the high-jump technique bearing his name. He won Olympic gold in 1968, but his legacy extended beyond that result: the Fosbury Flop transformed how the event was approached. Olympedia distinguishes this technical influence from his relatively brief competitive prominence.

evidence.note: Olympedia biography supports 1968 gold, technique and enduring influence; the card does not invent biomechanical details absent from this source.

original_record.label: Dick Fosbury
original_record.learning_takeaway: Examine an athlete whose enduring influence came from a new jumping style.

relations.note: The biography identifies Fosbury's innovation and Olympic result specifically with the high-jump event.

original_record.card: A diffraction grating uses many regularly spaced lines or openings to combine light waves by interference. Their contributions reinforce at selected angles, producing narrow bright maxima. Different wavelengths reinforce at different angles, allowing a grating to separate light into a spectrum for analysis.

evidence.locator: 4.4 Diffraction Gratings; inspected passage indices 5, 7, 8 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1172100770948; fs-id1172100664530; fs-id1172100887164
evidence.note: Many regularly spaced slits produce narrow interference maxima that separate light by wavelength.

evidence.locator: 4.5 Circular Apertures and Resolution; inspected passage indices 5 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1172102062471
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected passage establishes the alternate example, field identity, or alias used in the takeaway.

original_record.label: Diffraction grating
original_record.learning_takeaway: Many regularly spaced slits produce narrow interference maxima that separate light by wavelength.

relations.note: The grating is an optical instrument exploiting interference to reveal wavelength composition.

original_record.card: Aquatic organisms use oxygen dissolved in water, which is different from the oxygen chemically bound inside water molecules. Microorganisms decomposing organic matter can consume this available oxygen. If consumption outpaces replenishment, oxygen levels fall and conditions can become difficult for other aquatic life.

evidence.note: USGS’s BOD account distinguishes dissolved available oxygen and describes microbial decomposition consuming it with ecological consequences.

original_record.label: Dissolved oxygen in water
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish biologically available dissolved oxygen from the oxygen bound inside water molecules.

relations.note: Biochemical oxygen demand measures an oxygen-consuming process that can lower the dissolved-oxygen concentration.

original_record.card: Replicated-log consensus lets machines agree on an ordered command history despite crash failures and unreliable communication. Raft-style protocols preserve safety under delays and partitions, but remain available only while a suitable majority can communicate. Agreement here concerns replicated commands, not every form of collective decision-making.

evidence.note: Sections 2 and 5 distinguish safety under non-Byzantine communication failures from availability requiring an operational communicating majority. The card gives a Raft-style example, not a theorem about every consensus protocol.

original_record.label: Replicated-log consensus under crash faults
original_record.learning_takeaway: Make non-Byzantine replicas agree on ordered commands, with availability requiring a communicating majority.

relations.note: The bounded crash-fault replicated-log problem is a specific coordination problem within distributed systems, with the failure model made explicit.

original_record.card: Dante’s Divine Comedy uses terza rima to link successive three-line stanzas. A rhyme introduced in the middle of one tercet becomes the surrounding rhyme in the next, with a final line completing the sequence at a canto’s close. Form carries continuity across local divisions.

evidence.note: The glossary explains Dante’s interlocking tercets and closing line.

original_record.label: Divine Comedy
original_record.learning_takeaway: Dante’s interlocking terza rima connects successive tercets, while a final line completes each canto’s rhyme sequence.

relations.note: The glossary explicitly identifies Dante’s use of the interlocking rhyme scheme.

original_record.card: A divisional structure places several functions together around a product, market, service, or region. Each division can coordinate its own activities and take clearer responsibility for its segment. The tradeoff is that divisions may become isolated, with duplicated systems and weaker coordination across the whole organization.

evidence.note: Checked grouping basis and divisional isolation; did not claim that geographic and product divisions must use identical arrangements.

original_record.label: Divisional organizational structure
original_record.learning_takeaway: Place several functions together within product, market, or regional divisions to concentrate accountability locally.

relations.note: OpenStax explicitly describes divisions as groupings of functional departments and contrasts their local coordination with functional silos.

original_record.card: DNA metabarcoding examines a mixed sample for traces of multiple species. Broadly targeted primers amplify DNA fragments, and high-throughput sequencing reads the resulting mixture. The approach turns one pooled sample into a multispecies assessment rather than a test focused on only one organism.

evidence.note: USGS defines metabarcoding through nonspecific primers, PCR, high-throughput sequencing and identifying multiple species in a pooled sample.

original_record.label: DNA metabarcoding
original_record.learning_takeaway: Identify multiple species from a pooled DNA sample using broad primers and sequencing.

relations.note: The glossary presents metabarcoding as a multispecies analysis of a pooled DNA sample, making it an editorial application link to environmental-DNA investigation.

original_record.card: DNA methylation adds small chemical tags to particular places on DNA. These marks can change how proteins interact with the molecule and whether nearby genes are used. The underlying DNA sequence stays the same, while its activity can change.

evidence.note: The epigenomics explanation describes methyl groups attached to DNA bases, changed DNA–protein interactions and altered gene use without sequence rewriting.

original_record.label: DNA methylation
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explain how methyl tags influence DNA–protein interactions without rewriting the DNA sequence.

relations.note: Both are epigenomic marks, but methylation tags DNA directly while histone modification tags its packaging proteins.

original_record.card: The doctrine of double effect distinguishes harm intended as a means from harm foreseen as a side effect of pursuing a good end. Its defenders also require proportionality and attention to avoiding harm. Merely saying a bad result was unintended does not make it permissible.

evidence.note: SEP sections 1 and 3 support the intention/foresight distinction, proportionality and harm minimization; attribution to defenders avoids presenting a contested doctrine as settled morality.

original_record.label: Doctrine of double effect
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish intending harm as a means from foreseeing it as a side effect.

relations.note: The entry explicitly warns that intended versus foreseen harm is a different distinction from doing versus allowing harm; neither distinction should be substituted for the other.

original_record.card: Doing harm and allowing harm distinguish bringing about a harmful outcome from failing to prevent it. Philosophers dispute their moral significance. Rachels's paired cases compare deliberate drowning with deliberately withholding rescue, testing whether the distinction alone can explain a difference in blame.

evidence.note: SEP sections 1–2 present Rachels's cases and objections to both their comparability and generalization; the card treats the cases as a test, not proof that killing and letting die are always equivalent.

original_record.label: Doing versus allowing harm
original_record.learning_takeaway: Separate causing versus permitting harm from intention and from moral verdicts.

relations.note: The entry uses driver and bystander trolley variants to examine whether doing/allowing explains moral judgments, and records challenges to that explanation.

original_record.card: In a double-blind study, participants and the relevant researchers do not know which group each participant belongs to. Concealing assignments helps limit both participant expectations and experimenter expectations. It is a protection against those influences, not a substitute for sound sampling, measurement or comparison groups.

evidence.note: Section 2.3 defines concealed assignment for researchers and participants; the final limitation follows the chapter's separate design requirements and avoids claiming that blinding alone demonstrates causation.

original_record.label: Double-blind study
original_record.learning_takeaway: Compare controlling participant expectations with controlling researcher expectations.

relations.note: Double blinding is directly introduced as controlling both experimenter and participant expectations, so its relation to expectancy bias is stated rather than inferred.

original_record.card: When doubling is allowed in backgammon, a player offers it at the start of their own turn, before rolling. The opponent can decline and lose at the old value, or accept. Acceptance gives that player the cube and the exclusive right to offer the next redouble.

evidence.note: USBGF Doubling supports own-turn timing, before rolling, refusal cost and ownership. When allowed preserves format exceptions such as the separately discussed Crawford game; this is descriptive scoring, not advice to gamble.

original_record.label: Doubling cube
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how accepting a double transfers the right to offer the next redouble.

relations.note: The federation presents the cube as the game's mechanism for offering and accepting increased stakes.

original_record.card: A cyclist riding in another rider's wake can encounter less aerodynamic resistance and use less energy to maintain speed. The leading rider can also gain a smaller benefit. Road-racing groups exploit this shared airflow, although position and spacing affect how much shelter each rider receives.

evidence.note: Exploratorium explains follower and leader advantages and spacing dependence; avoid exporting its numerical savings to all speeds, terrains or formations.

original_record.label: Drafting in cycling
original_record.learning_takeaway: Connect riding in another cyclist's wake with reduced aerodynamic effort.

relations.note: The museum's Aerodynamics and Drafting explanation explicitly applies wake airflow to road cycling.

original_record.card: Drawboring deliberately offsets peg holes in a mortise-and-tenon joint. Driving a wooden peg through them pulls the pieces tightly together. A tapered metal drawbore pin can first test the fit, but the temporary pin and the wooden peg securing the finished joint have different roles.

evidence.note: Lee Valley explains offset holes drawing the joint tight and distinguishes temporary tapered test pins from final wooden pegs.

original_record.label: Drawboring
original_record.learning_takeaway: Pull a mortise-and-tenon joint tight by driving a peg through intentionally offset holes.

relations.note: Drawboring is a specific way to tighten and secure a mortise-and-tenon assembly.

original_record.card: Drip irrigation delivers water through small outlets placed near individual plants. In the inspected hydroponic example, a hose system supplies nutrient solution at plant bases instead of sending a continuous stream down a channel. The delivery arrangement targets the root area rather than wetting an entire surface uniformly.

evidence.note: UMN’s drip-system passage describes hoses and small holes/outlets located at each plant base, contrasted with nutrient-film channels.

original_record.label: Drip irrigation
original_record.learning_takeaway: Deliver water or nutrient solution near individual plants through controlled small outlets.

relations.note: Localized delivery through outlets is a particular irrigation method within the broader application of water to plants.

original_record.card: After contract bridge's opening lead, the declarer's partner lays their hand face up as dummy. The declarer chooses which cards to play from both partnership hands. This creates a distinctive information pattern: defenders can see one opposing hand, but not the declarer's concealed cards.

evidence.note: ACBL Play supports timing, exposed dummy and declarer's control; the information consequence is directly entailed, without claiming defenders see each other's hands.

original_record.label: Dummy in bridge
original_record.learning_takeaway: Understand why one partnership hand becomes visible and is played by declarer's instructions.

relations.note: The play instructions define dummy as a specific role within the declaring partnership.

original_record.card: Duplicate bridge compares results from players holding the same deal of cards. A weak hand is therefore judged against what others achieved with that weak hand, rather than against opponents lucky enough to receive stronger cards. The format reduces the influence of the deal's initial luck.

evidence.note: ACBL Duplicate Bridge supports identical deals and comparison against the field; reduces rather than eliminates chance, without claiming every duplicate scoring system is identical.

original_record.label: Duplicate bridge
original_record.learning_takeaway: Understand comparison against other players holding the same cards.

relations.note: ACBL presents duplicate as a bridge format in which the same deals are played at multiple tables.

original_record.card: A dyad is a two-person social group. Its existence depends directly on both participants: when one leaves, no two-person group remains. This gives the relationship a different structure from a larger group, where some members can continue interacting after another person withdraws.

evidence.note: Checked two-member dependence; not claimed that all social consequences or obligations disappear when a dyad ends.

original_record.label: Dyad (social group)
original_record.learning_takeaway: See why a two-person group depends on both members' continued participation and cannot outlast either member's departure.

relations.note: OpenStax explicitly contrasts Simmel's two-member and three-member groups by withdrawal and the continuing relationships available.

original_record.card: A dynamic Huffman block in DEFLATE carries descriptions of its own coding tables before the compressed data. The descriptions encode code lengths, including repeated lengths. Fixed-code blocks avoid that table description, creating a format-level choice between predetermined codes and block-specific ones.

evidence.note: Checked transmitted lengths and repeated-length symbols; no unsupported claim that dynamic blocks always compress better.

original_record.label: Dynamic Huffman blocks in DEFLATE
original_record.learning_takeaway: Transmit block-specific code lengths rather than always using the format's fixed Huffman tables.

relations.note: RFC 1951 sections 3.2.6–3.2.7 define fixed and dynamic Huffman block types within DEFLATE.

original_record.card: In the E. coli Long-Term Evolution Experiment, researchers replayed evolution using bacteria from different points in one population’s history. Later samples were more likely to evolve aerobic citrate use. The result showed how earlier genetic changes could enable a later innovation, making evolutionary history experimentally testable.

evidence.note: The 2008 primary abstract reports replay experiments from different generations and a higher probability of aerobic citrate use in later clones, supporting historical contingency under the experiment’s oxic conditions.

original_record.label: E. coli Long-Term Evolution Experiment
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how revived archived populations let researchers test whether prior mutations enabled a later innovation.

relations.note: Replaying different inherited genetic backgrounds links this experiment to genetics through the effect of prior changes on a later trait.

original_record.card: The Eads Bridge relied on deep pneumatic caissons to place mid-river piers on solid rock. This enabled a major Mississippi rail crossing, but construction brought serious human costs, including deaths from caisson disease. The case joins structural innovation with the hazards of working below a river’s surface.

evidence.locator:
Eads Bridge | ASCE
; inspected passage indices 4, 5, 6 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-5; paragraph-6; paragraph-7
evidence.note: Pneumatic caissons established deep river foundations for a major rail crossing, with serious construction hazards.

original_record.label: Eads Bridge
original_record.learning_takeaway: Pneumatic caissons established deep river foundations for a major rail crossing, with serious construction hazards.

relations.note: ASCE explicitly describes the Eads Bridge as a major railroad crossing and explains its foundations.

original_record.card: An ecofact is a natural remain that provides archaeological evidence, such as an animal bone or plant seed associated with human activity. Its importance comes from what it can reveal about past lives, even though people did not manufacture it as an artifact.

evidence.locator: What is an Archeologist?, ecofacts definition
evidence.note: Natural remains and seed/bone examples distinguish ecofacts from manufactured artifacts.

original_record.label: Ecofact
original_record.learning_takeaway: Unmanufactured remains such as seeds and animal bones can be archaeological evidence of human resource use.

relations.note: Associations establish why an unmanufactured remain is evidence of human activity.
The NPS explicitly includes ecofacts among the evidence archaeologists study.

original_record.card: In this research-methods sense, ecological validity concerns how well findings apply to ordinary settings. Unobtrusive observation of people in their usual surroundings can improve realism, but sacrifices experimental control. A realistic setting helps the applicability question without automatically answering every question about cause and effect.

evidence.note: Section 2.2's naturalistic-observation discussion supports realism, generalization and control tradeoffs; retain this cited sense rather than treating all uses of ecological validity as interchangeable.

original_record.label: Ecological validity
original_record.learning_takeaway: Assess how closely a research setting represents real-world behavior.

relations.note: Real-world applicability and accurate measurement of an intended construct are different validity questions; the comparison is a learning bridge, not a claim that one guarantees the other.

original_record.card: Economic signaling uses observable actions or credentials to convey information about less visible qualities. A prospective worker's qualifications may help an employer infer preparation or persistence. The signal does not remove all uncertainty; it offers evidence about something the employer cannot fully observe before hiring.

evidence.note: Checked credential-as-signal example and remaining uncertainty; not claimed that a credential perfectly measures ability or always forms a separating equilibrium.

original_record.label: Signaling in economics
original_record.learning_takeaway: Use observable credentials or actions to convey information about otherwise hidden qualities.

relations.note: The source's credential and employer-investigation examples support distinguishing information supplied by the informed party from screening initiated by the less-informed party.

original_record.card: Economy of mechanism asks security designers to keep protection mechanisms small and simple. Hidden access paths may escape notice during normal use, so extra complexity makes careful examination harder. The aim is a design whose safeguards can be understood and checked, rather than complexity mistaken for protection.

evidence.note: Checked the simplicity and unnoticed-access-path rationale; not a claim that the shortest possible system is always safest.

original_record.label: Economy of mechanism
original_record.learning_takeaway: Keep protection mechanisms small and simple to make hidden access paths easier to examine.

relations.note: Saltzer and Schroeder directly identify economy of mechanism as a foundational protection-design principle and explain its error-detection rationale.

original_record.card: Organisms can alter the physical environment that other species use. Beavers, for example, build dams that create aquatic habitats and change local living conditions. Ecosystem engineering draws attention to these habitat modifications, extending the study of species interactions beyond who eats whom.

evidence.note: The NPS Wolves and Beaver passage explicitly calls beavers ecosystem engineers and describes dams creating aquatic habitat.

original_record.label: Ecosystem engineering
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explain how organisms change physical habitat for other species, using beaver dams.

relations.note: Physical habitat modification by organisms is an ecological interaction connecting species with the environment they create.

original_record.card: Edge embeddedness counts how many common neighbors the two ends of a tie share. Mutual contacts create a social setting around the relationship and may make misconduct more visible. A local bridge has zero embeddedness, connecting people without that immediate shared-neighbor context.

evidence.note: Checked shared-neighbor count and zero case; mutual friends are not claimed to ensure trust or prevent all misconduct.

original_record.label: Edge embeddedness
original_record.learning_takeaway: Count the mutual neighbors of a connected pair to describe the social context surrounding their tie.

relations.note: The chapter directly equates zero embeddedness with the local-bridge condition and discusses mutual neighbors' reputational role.

original_record.card: An efficiency wage can exceed the worker's reservation wage because pay changes behavior as well as cost. In the labor-discipline model, a more valuable job encourages effort and makes departure less attractive. A firm weighs the wage bill against the amount of effective work it obtains.

evidence.locator: Section 6.7 Wages, effort, and profits in the labour discipline model, Figure 6.6 and efficiency wages definition; Section 6.4 Employment rents
evidence.note: Checked explicitly as a model, not a universal wage law; distinct from a statutory minimum wage or a claim that raising any wage always pays for itself.

original_record.label: Efficiency wage
original_record.learning_takeaway: Pay above the reservation wage when the induced effort and reduced turnover can justify the extra wage cost.

relations.note: The model uses the value at risk from losing a job to connect wages with effort; this applies the employment-rent mechanism to wage setting.

original_record.card: Heating egg white unfolds proteins and allows them to connect with one another. The resulting network traps water, changing a flowing liquid into a firmer structure. Too much heating can make that network rubbery, showing how the same molecular process can produce very different cooking textures.

evidence.note: Exploratorium describes heat unfolding egg-white proteins, intermolecular bonds, trapped water and rubberiness after excessive heating.

original_record.label: Egg protein coagulation
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explain why a liquid egg becomes a network that traps water as it is heated.

relations.note: Eggs can stabilize food in different ways: heat-linked protein networks versus yolk emulsifiers separating fat droplets.

original_record.card: The Eiffel Tower was originally intended to last only twenty years after its exhibition role. Scientific experiments, especially radio transmission, gave it a continuing technical purpose and helped preserve it. The structure’s history shows how repurposing infrastructure can change the value and lifetime of an engineering project.

evidence.locator: Eiffel Tower information : facts, height in feet, weight, ...; inspected passage indices 3, 7, 8 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-4; paragraph-8; paragraph-9
evidence.note: Radio experiments gave an originally temporary exhibition structure a continuing technical role.

original_record.label: Eiffel Tower
original_record.learning_takeaway: Radio experiments gave an originally temporary exhibition structure a continuing technical role.

relations.note: The official monument reference identifies the structure as a tower and documents its later communications use.

original_record.card: The Train scene in Philip Glass's Einstein on the Beach provides a concrete example of additive process. A five-chord progression gradually lengthens as each chord receives more subdivisions. Musical change comes from stretching the allotted duration of recurring harmonies rather than continuously introducing new chords.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 35.1 describes the named scene, five chords and added subdivisions; the claim is limited to that example, not the entire opera.

original_record.label: Einstein on the Beach
original_record.learning_takeaway: Observe a five-chord progression expanding through added subdivisions.

relations.note: The source explicitly recommends the Train scene as an example of additive growth in chord duration.

original_record.card: Wind sets surface water in motion, and friction passes some movement into deeper layers. Earth’s rotation deflects those layers as their speeds decrease, producing the turning pattern called an Ekman spiral. It describes changing current direction with depth, rather than a single uniform flow beneath the wind.

evidence.note: NOAA explains downward momentum transfer through friction, decreasing speed and successive Coriolis deflection.

original_record.label: Ekman spiral
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explain why a wind-driven current changes direction and weakens with depth.

relations.note: The Ekman spiral is a specific physical-oceanography pattern linking wind, friction and rotation.

original_record.card: The elaboration likelihood model distinguishes persuasion through evaluating a message's arguments from persuasion through peripheral cues. A buyer might compare safety evidence or respond to a celebrity endorsement. The model connects these routes with the audience's motivation and effort in processing the message.

evidence.note: Section 12.3, Figure 12.15 and central/peripheral route paragraphs, support argument evaluation, endorsement cues and processing effort; the card identifies a model rather than an exhaustive settled binary for all persuasion.

original_record.label: Elaboration likelihood model
original_record.learning_takeaway: Compare evaluating an argument with responding to peripheral cues.

relations.note: The model concerns how a persuasive message is processed; foot-in-the-door concerns the sequence of requests. Their comparison distinguishes explanatory route from influence procedure.

original_record.card: A material’s elastic limit marks the stress beyond which unloading leaves permanent deformation. It is different from elastic modulus, which measures stiffness within the elastic range. A material can therefore deform easily yet recover substantially, or be stiff while tolerating less recoverable strain.

evidence.locator: 12.4 Elasticity and Plasticity; inspected passage indices 7, 8, 9 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1163709757929; fs-id1163709667701; fs-id1163713071188
evidence.note: Distinguish recoverable deformation from permanent shape change when stress exceeds a material’s elastic limit.

original_record.label: Elastic limit
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish recoverable deformation from permanent shape change when stress exceeds a material’s elastic limit.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies elastic modulus and elastic limit as different parameters governing elastic behavior.

original_record.card: Rocks beside a locked fault can deform as plate movement continues. When the fault slips, stored elastic strain is released and the rocks rebound toward a less-deformed shape. Elastic rebound theory connects gradual stress buildup with the sudden energy release of many earthquakes.

evidence.note: USGS’s Reid account describes progressive deformation, locked-fault strain and sudden release/rebound inferred from the 1906 earthquake.

original_record.label: Elastic rebound theory
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explain earthquakes as sudden release of strain accumulated while rocks deform elastically.

relations.note: Slow-slip events provide a contrast to the abrupt strain-release picture, showing that fault displacement can unfold over different timescales.

original_record.card: Electrolysis uses an external electrical supply to drive a redox reaction that would not proceed spontaneously in that direction. Recharging a battery is one example: electrical work pushes its discharge chemistry backward, restoring some of the chemical state that can later deliver energy.

evidence.locator: 17.7 Electrolysis; inspected passage indices 6, 9, 12 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm133590080; fs-idm174200080; fs-idp152393360
evidence.note: An imposed voltage drives an otherwise nonspontaneous redox transformation.

original_record.label: Electrolysis
original_record.learning_takeaway: An imposed voltage drives an otherwise nonspontaneous redox transformation.

relations.note: The electrolysis section explicitly lists electroplating as a use of externally driven electrolytic cells.

original_record.card: Electrons possess intrinsic angular momentum called spin. Measuring its projection along a chosen axis gives two possible values, conventionally called spin up and spin down. These labels refer to the measurement axis; they do not describe a continuous range of classical orientations within the atom.

evidence.locator: 8.3 Electron Spin; inspected passage indices 6, 7, 8, 11 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1170902277768; fs-id1170902065387; fs-id1170903866542; fs-id1170903793199
evidence.note: Electrons have intrinsic half-integer angular momentum with two measured projections along a chosen axis.

original_record.label: Electron spin
original_record.learning_takeaway: Electrons have intrinsic half-integer angular momentum with two measured projections along a chosen axis.

relations.note: The source uses the Stern–Gerlach silver-atom result as evidence of the two electron-spin projections.

original_record.card: Electroplating deposits metal onto a conducting object by reducing dissolved metal ions at its surface. In one silver-plating setup, the object serves as cathode while a silver anode supplies metal. Current, voltage, and solution composition influence the coating’s quality.

evidence.locator: 17.7 Electrolysis; inspected passage indices 21, 22, 23, 24 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm182126896; fs-idm52313424; fs-idm104543584; fs-idm28358112
evidence.note: Reduction deposits a metal coating on a conducting cathode while process conditions control coating quality.

original_record.label: Electroplating
original_record.learning_takeaway: Reduction deposits a metal coating on a conducting cathode while process conditions control coating quality.

relations.note: The source explicitly describes electroplating as a use of electrolytic cells.

original_record.card: Elizabeth Peyton compares the immediacy of monotype with the dense revisions possible in her paintings. A plate’s workable pigment gives the print process a limited window for adjustment. Her account shows how choosing a medium also changes the time and manner in which an image can be developed.

evidence.locator: Peyton’s comparison of painting and monotype, lines 26–28
evidence.note: The interview discussion contrasts revised paintings with the monotype working window.

original_record.label: Elizabeth Peyton
original_record.learning_takeaway: Peyton contrasts densely revised paintings with the time-limited immediacy of monotype, where a plate can be manipulated only while its pigment remains workable.

relations.note: Peyton’s account explicitly discusses how this process affects her work.

original_record.card: Removing dams from the Elwha River restored connections between upstream habitat and the sea. The project reopened routes used by migrating fish and allowed sediment to move again. It demonstrates that river restoration can involve reconnecting processes across a whole watershed, not only repairing one riverbank.

evidence.note: NPS describes the dams’ barriers to fish and sediment and the restoration through dam removal.

original_record.label: Elwha River restoration
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explore how removing dams reconnects fish migration and sediment movement.

relations.note: Reconnecting fish movement and sediment transport makes the Elwha project an ecological case linking organisms with physical processes.

original_record.card: Emergent norm theory explains crowd behavior through guidelines that participants develop in unfamiliar situations. People bring prior expectations, interact, and may accept new ways of acting as circumstances change. The theory treats crowds as more than irrational masses, while leaving questions about how norms spread and gain acceptance.

evidence.note: Checked explanatory status and the source's unresolved acceptance/spread questions; the theory is not presented as a universally established causal law.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source explicitly makes changing and newly established norms central to the emergent-norm account of crowds.

original_record.label: Emergent norm theory
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explain crowd conduct through locally developing guidelines in unfamiliar situations rather than assuming all crowds act irrationally.

relations.note: The source explicitly makes changing and newly established norms central to the emergent-norm account of crowds.

original_record.card: Employment rent is the value of keeping a job above the worker's next-best alternative, after considering its benefits and costs. Losing that surplus makes dismissal consequential. In the labor-discipline model, this can influence effort and retention, connecting wage setting to something beyond the minimum pay a worker would accept.

evidence.locator: Section 6.4 Employment rents; Section 6.7 Wages, effort, and profits in the labour discipline model
evidence.note: Checked job-versus-alternative surplus and model-based effort/retention channels; no blanket claim that fear of dismissal explains all work motivation.

original_record.label: Employment rent
original_record.learning_takeaway: Measure the value of holding a job above the worker's next-best alternative, making job loss consequential.

relations.note: CORE explicitly links employment rents to staying with a firm and incentives to provide effort, then develops the efficiency-wage model.

original_record.card: ENCODE, the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements, investigates the working parts of the genome. Its research includes epigenomic maps from different cell types, helping distinguish the DNA sequence a cell carries from the regions it uses. A shared genome can support different cellular patterns of activity.

evidence.locator: How are researchers exploring the epigenome?
evidence.note: NHGRI states that ENCODE catalogs working genomic parts and includes cell-type epigenomic maps; the same fact sheet explains differentiated cells and altered marks.

original_record.label: ENCODE
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish identifying functional genomic elements from merely obtaining a DNA sequence.

relations.note: Histone marks are one kind of epigenomic information that makes ENCODE’s cell-type maps useful for studying differential genome use.

original_record.card: The open cells exposed at wood’s end grain can draw adhesive away from a joint’s interface. Excessive penetration leaves voids and helps explain why a simple end-to-end butt bond can be weak. Joint geometry matters because increasing useful bonded area can change how loads pass between pieces.

evidence.locator: Density and Porosity, p. 10–6; End-Grain Joints, pp. 10–16 to 10–17
evidence.note: USDA describes end-grain porosity, overpenetration/bond-line voids and the increased area achieved by scarf/finger arrangements.

original_record.label: End-grain gluing
original_record.learning_takeaway: Connect end-grain porosity with adhesive overpenetration and weak butt-joint behavior.

relations.note: Adhesive penetration at end grain is a specific material-and-joint problem within woodworking.

original_record.card: Mitochondria retain their own genetic material, divide in a bacteria-like way and have surrounding membranes consistent with an engulfed ancestor. These clues support endosymbiotic origins from once-independent cells. The broad ancestry is well supported even while details of the earliest host–partner sequence remain debated.

evidence.note: OpenStax discusses mitochondrial genomes, fission-like division, membranes and unresolved ordering relative to the host nucleus.

original_record.label: Endosymbiotic theory
original_record.learning_takeaway: Use organelle genomes, division and membranes as evidence of ancestry from once-independent cells.

relations.note: Organelle similarities and shared ancestry offer a molecular/cellular setting for the ancestry reasoning introduced by biological homology.

original_record.card: Organisms leave genetic traces in water, sediment and other surroundings through shed cells and biological material. Environmental DNA sampling uses those traces to investigate which organisms may be present. It can reveal a species without requiring researchers to catch or directly observe that organism.

evidence.note: The USGS EDNA definition lists environmental samples and genetic material shed by organisms; this supports indirect detection.

original_record.label: Environmental DNA
original_record.learning_takeaway: Detect organisms through genetic traces in environmental samples without having to capture them.

relations.note: Metabarcoding is one way to analyze mixed environmental DNA for multiple species.

original_record.card: Cutting an apple exposes its tissues to oxygen, allowing enzymes to drive browning reactions. Changing conditions such as acidity can slow the process. The color change therefore connects damage to plant cells with chemical activity, rather than being explained solely by the fruit drying out.

evidence.note: ACS’s explanatory section connects exposed apple tissue, oxygen, enzymes and the slowing effect of acidity.

original_record.label: Enzymatic browning
original_record.learning_takeaway: Connect a cut fruit surface, oxygen and enzyme activity with a change in color.

relations.note: Both topics concern food-quality changes mediated by enzymes, while acidifying an exposed surface and heat-blanching before freezing are different interventions.

original_record.card: Epistemic closure asks whether competent deduction preserves knowledge. On a common formulation, someone who retains knowledge of a premise and comes to believe its consequence by competent deduction knows that consequence. This is not a claim that people automatically know every implication of everything they know.

evidence.note: SEP section 1 rejects unqualified entailment closure and gives the competent-deduction principle with continued premise knowledge; the card presents a formulation within a disputed debate.

original_record.label: Epistemic closure
original_record.learning_takeaway: Investigate whether competent deduction from known premises preserves knowledge.

relations.note: Knowledge preservation under inference is a specific epistemological question; the closure entry and the broad account of cognitive success support this placement without implying universal acceptance of closure.

original_record.card: A safe belief would not easily have been false: in nearby possible circumstances where the person holds it, it remains true. This proposed condition on knowledge differs from asking what the person would believe if the claim were false. What counts as nearby is itself contested.

evidence.note: SEP section 5.2 gives the nearby-worlds formulation and discusses vagueness of nearness; the card avoids treating safety as a settled necessary or sufficient condition.

original_record.label: Epistemic safety
original_record.learning_takeaway: Ask whether a belief could easily have been false in nearby circumstances.

relations.note: The source explicitly distinguishes safety's nearby true beliefs from sensitivity's response to falsity, noting that the two modal conditions are not equivalent.

original_record.card: A sensitive belief tracks a counterfactual question: if the claim were false, would the person stop believing it? A mirage-based belief may fail because the same appearance would persuade without water. Sensitivity has been proposed as a condition on knowledge, but its adequacy is disputed.

evidence.note: SEP section 5.1 states the counterfactual and desert-water example, then discusses limitations; the card does not equate sensitivity with safety or endorse it as sufficient for knowledge.

original_record.label: Epistemic sensitivity
original_record.learning_takeaway: Ask whether someone would stop believing a claim if it were false.

relations.note: Section 5.2 explicitly contrasts sensitivity with safety and explains why counterfactual contraposition does not make them equivalent.

original_record.card: Epistemicism treats vagueness as a limit of knowledge rather than an absence of precise boundaries. There is, on this view, an exact cutoff between a heap and a non-heap, although we cannot identify it. Statements remain true or false even when their status is inaccessible.

evidence.note: SEP section 3.2 describes hidden sharp boundaries and preservation of bivalence; on this view makes the controversial account explicit rather than reporting it as a discovered linguistic fact.

original_record.label: Epistemicism about vagueness
original_record.learning_takeaway: Consider the view that vague categories have sharp boundaries we cannot know.

relations.note: The article presents epistemicism among responses to sorites, preserving classical bivalence while denying that every adjacent pair must share the same status.

original_record.card: Epistrophe repeats a word or phrase at the ends of successive units. Different statements arrive at the same verbal destination, giving their sequence a recurring point of emphasis. Its placement distinguishes it from anaphora, where the repetition appears at the beginning instead.

evidence.note: End repetition is contrasted with anaphora in the glossary.

original_record.label: Epistrophe
original_record.learning_takeaway: Repeating words at successive phrase or stanza endings gives the sequence a recurring point of arrival.

relations.note: The two devices distinguish where repeated wording occurs.

original_record.card: Equal-interval classification divides an attribute’s numeric range into classes of the same width. It emphasizes comparable steps in value, but does not guarantee equal numbers of places in each class. A strongly uneven dataset may therefore leave some map classes sparsely populated.

evidence.note: Equal-width intervals and uneven class occupancy follow the stated method.

original_record.label: Equal-interval map classification
original_record.learning_takeaway: Dividing an attribute’s numeric range into equal-width intervals emphasizes value differences rather than equalizing the number of mapped places.

relations.note: Equal-width values and equal-count classes solve different classification problems.
Equal-width numerical classes are a specific decision in representing attributes on maps.

original_record.card: Wood exchanges moisture with the air around it. Its equilibrium moisture content is the point at which it is neither gaining nor losing moisture under those conditions. Because temperature and relative humidity matter, wood does not have one universally correct moisture level for every room or season.

evidence.note: USDA Chapter 4 defines EMC by no net gain/loss and relates it to surrounding temperature and relative humidity.

original_record.label: Equilibrium moisture content of wood
original_record.learning_takeaway: Relate a wood component’s stable moisture level to its surrounding air rather than one universally dry state.

relations.note: Sorption hysteresis adds moisture-history dependence to the environmental conditions that determine a wood specimen’s EMC.

original_record.card: Eric Mazur's work on Peer Instruction helped redesign introductory physics lectures around students' reasoning. In the reported courses, learners answered conceptual questions individually, discussed their explanations, and voted again. The case makes a teaching method inspectable through its sequence of activities rather than a lecturer's reputation alone.

evidence.note: Checked coauthorship and course design; did not attribute every result solely to discussion because other course elements also changed.

original_record.label: Eric Mazur
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explore how a physicist's course redesign made individual commitments and peer reasoning part of lectures.

relations.note: The coauthored paper directly documents Mazur's implementation of Peer Instruction and describes its question/discussion/revote sequence.

original_record.card: For a small object launched outward from an isolated spherical body, escape velocity is the minimum initial speed that permits escape without further thrust. Ignoring atmospheric drag, it depends on the body’s mass and starting distance, not the projectile’s mass in this ideal model.

evidence.locator: 13.3 Gravitational Potential Energy and Total Energy; inspected passage indices 27, 30, 42, 46 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1168326809119; fs-id1168329319252; fs-id1168329151238; fs-id1168329060634
evidence.note: Under ideal gravitational assumptions, sufficient initial speed permits escape without further propulsion.

original_record.label: Escape velocity
original_record.learning_takeaway: Under ideal gravitational assumptions, sufficient initial speed permits escape without further propulsion.

relations.note: The source derives escape speed by comparing kinetic energy with gravitational potential energy.
