Increasing rhoticity in New York English is a textbook example. Above refers to awareness of the change, rather than simply locating its speakers at the top of society.

evidence.note: Checked awareness-based definition and rhoticity example; the wording avoids confusing awareness with a universal top-down social-class origin.

original_record.label: Linguistic change from above
original_record.learning_takeaway: Trace consciously noticed adoption of a prestigious outside variant, illustrated by New York City's rhoticity shift.

relations.note: The source classifies this as a kind of language change; it is placed within historical linguistic inquiry without making prestige the explanation for every change.

original_record.card: A linguistic change from below develops largely outside speakers' conscious awareness. The textbook illustrates it with the goose vowel moving forward in Canadian English. Speakers can participate in a shifting pronunciation pattern without noticing it, unlike consciously adopting a prestigious form recognized as different.

evidence.note: Checked Canadian vowel example and conscious-awareness distinction; no claim that every unrecognized pronunciation difference is historical change.

original_record.label: Linguistic change from below
original_record.learning_takeaway: Trace language-system changes that spread below conscious social awareness, such as gradual vowel fronting.

relations.note: The source explicitly contrasts below-awareness system changes with socially noticed changes from above.

original_record.card: Litotes makes an understated assertion by denying its opposite. Calling something not unwelcome, for example, can express acceptance with restraint. The wording leaves room for context and tone to determine how much emphasis the speaker intends, rather than stating the positive claim directly.

evidence.note: Denial of an opposite and understatement are defined.

original_record.label: Litotes
original_record.learning_takeaway: Denying an opposite can make an understated assertion, sometimes giving a speaker an appearance of modesty.

relations.note: Understatement through negation is a rhetorical strategy for shaping an assertion.

original_record.card: Living shorelines use plants and other natural materials, sometimes with low structural elements, to stabilize estuarine coasts. They can buffer waves while preserving habitat and allowing marsh processes to continue. The approach connects erosion protection with ecological functions rather than treating the shoreline only as a rigid boundary.

evidence.note: NOAA describes vegetation/natural materials with optional low sills, estuarine settings, wave buffering, habitat and marsh processes.

original_record.label: Living shoreline
original_record.learning_takeaway: Stabilize sheltered coasts using vegetation and natural materials while retaining habitat functions.

relations.note: A living shoreline and a riparian buffer both connect protective vegetation with aquatic habitat, while addressing different boundary conditions.

original_record.card: A local bridge connects two nodes that have no common neighbor. Removing it leaves no two-step alternative route between its endpoints; reaching the other side takes a longer path, if one exists. This precise edge property helps distinguish network-spanning connections from ties embedded among mutual friends.

evidence.note: Checked no-common-neighbor definition and possible disconnection; a local bridge need not disconnect the entire graph when removed.

original_record.label: Local bridge in a network
original_record.learning_takeaway: Identify a tie whose endpoints have no mutual neighbor and whose removal makes their shortest connecting path longer.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly states that local bridges have zero edge embeddedness because their endpoints share no neighbors.

original_record.card: Water-saving basins capture part of the water used by navigation locks so it can be reused. Panama’s 2016 expanded-lock design provided three basins per chamber and specified sixty-percent reuse per lockage. Such storage reduces demand on lake water that also serves surrounding communities.

evidence.locator: First Panama Canal Water-Saving Basin Filled, Testing Process Begins; inspected passage indices 0, 1, 3, 4 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-1; paragraph-2; paragraph-4; paragraph-5
evidence.note: Documents the 2016 basin system, three basins per chamber, designed reuse fraction, and shared lake-water resource.

original_record.label: Lock water-saving basin
original_record.learning_takeaway: Side basins permit part of a lockage’s water to be reused instead of discharged.

relations.note: The Canal Authority explicitly describes the basins as water-reuse components of the new lock chambers.

original_record.card: If high probability licenses belief, each ticket in a large fair lottery may reasonably be treated as a loser. Combining all those beliefs yields that every ticket loses, although one must win. The lottery paradox challenges combining individually plausible beliefs without restriction.

evidence.note: SEP section 3 presents Kyburg's acceptance rule and agglomeration conflict; the conditional opening avoids asserting that probability alone actually suffices for rational belief or knowledge.

original_record.label: Lottery paradox
original_record.learning_takeaway: Compare rational acceptance of each likely loser with certainty that one ticket wins.

relations.note: The article introduces the preface paradox as a companion challenge to agglomeration, while noting that it does not require the same probabilistic acceptance rule.

original_record.card: LZ77-style compression replaces repeated strings with references to earlier input. In DEFLATE, a reference gives a backward distance and a length, telling the decoder what earlier bytes to copy. Literal bytes handle material without a suitable match in the available history.

evidence.note: Checked literals, distance-length pairs, and earlier-history copying; wording identifies the DEFLATE implementation rather than imposing its limits on every LZ77 variant.

original_record.label: LZ77
original_record.learning_takeaway: Replace repeated byte strings with backward distance and length references within a sliding history.

relations.note: RFC 1951 section 2 identifies LZ77 as a compression technique used to represent repeated strings with backward references.

original_record.card: Ma Huan was a Muslim translator and chronicler who joined Zheng He’s fourth voyage. His role puts written observation alongside travel through foreign ports. As a learning case, it invites attention to the people who recorded and interpreted encounters during imperial expeditions.

evidence.locator: The Seven Voyages, fourth voyage paragraph, line 96
evidence.note: The fourth-voyage paragraph identifies Ma Huan as a Muslim translator and the voyages’ main chronicler.

original_record.label: Ma Huan
original_record.learning_takeaway: A Muslim translator accompanied Zheng He’s fourth voyage, illustrating the role of linguistic and cultural expertise in imperial travel records.

relations.note: The source explicitly places Ma Huan on the fourth voyage.

original_record.card: Magna Carta began as a 1215 settlement between King John and rebellious barons, and its first version failed to secure lasting peace. Later reissues gave it a different career. Its constitutional reputation grew from that subsequent history, rather than arriving fully formed in 1215.

evidence.note: Failed initial settlement, later reissues and subsequent influence are described.

original_record.label: Magna Carta
original_record.learning_takeaway: The failed settlement of 1215 was reissued in later versions; its later constitutional influence should be distinguished from its baronial setting.

relations.note: Distinguishing the original political setting from later interpretations is a contextual reading exercise.

original_record.card: Malus’s law describes linearly polarized light passing through an ideal polarizer. The transmitted intensity equals the incoming intensity multiplied by the squared cosine of the angle between polarization and the filter’s axis. Parallel alignment transmits maximally; perpendicular alignment blocks the light in this ideal model.

evidence.locator: 1.7 Polarization; inspected passage indices 12, 13, 14 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1172100922102; fs-id1172098448775; fs-id1172098377558
evidence.note: A polarizer transmits an intensity proportional to the squared cosine of its angle to incoming polarization.

original_record.label: Malus’s law
original_record.learning_takeaway: A polarizer transmits an intensity proportional to the squared cosine of its angle to incoming polarization.

relations.note: Brewster reflection produces a polarized component whose transmission through an ideal filter can be analyzed using Malus’s law.

original_record.card: Managed aquifer recharge deliberately adds water to underground storage. At Sand Hollow, water spread in a reservoir seeps into the underlying sandstone aquifer. Monitoring water levels, infiltration rates and chemistry helps determine where that water goes and how effectively the recharge system is working.

evidence.note: The USGS case documents intentional reservoir infiltration and monitoring of levels, recharge rates and chemical signals tracking recharge movement.

original_record.label: Managed aquifer recharge
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish deliberate underground replenishment from simply storing surface water.

relations.note: The general recharge practice is illustrated by the specifically monitored Sand Hollow Reservoir.

original_record.card: Manchester's experimental Baby computer tested a way to store data electronically in cathode-ray tubes. Patterns of dots represented binary information, including a program held in memory. Its successful run in 1948 demonstrated a stored-program approach that made changing a task different from rewiring a machine.

evidence.locator: Historical description paragraphs 1–6 (original Baby, 1948); paragraph 8 and object details (1998 replica, YS23/1998)
evidence.note: This collection record identifies a 1998 working replica; the historical description at paragraphs 1–6 supplies the facts about the original 1948 Manchester Baby. The URL remains an explanatory subject link, not a canonical assertion that the original and replica are the same physical object.

evidence.locator: ENIAC being set up; ENIAC tube change
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The museum's stored-program explanation and ENIAC's documented cable-and-switch setup support a historical comparison of how programs were configured.

original_record.label: Manchester Baby
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how cathode-ray-tube storage let an experimental 1948 machine hold and run its own program.

relations.note: The museum's stored-program explanation and ENIAC's documented cable-and-switch setup support a historical comparison of how programs were configured.

original_record.card: The Manila galleon trade connected Asian commerce with Spanish America across the Pacific. Silver traveled west, while Asian goods passed through Manila toward Mexico. Imported textiles and other objects also influenced local artistic production, making the route a channel of cultural as well as commercial exchange.

evidence.note: Silver, Asian goods and artistic influence are stated in the essay.

original_record.label: Manila galleon trade
original_record.learning_takeaway: American silver moved west across the Pacific while Asian goods traveled through Manila to Mexico, where imports influenced local artistic production.

relations.note: Imported objects provide a material record of commercial and artistic exchange.

original_record.card: Under Akbar, mansabdars held ranks that connected administrative service with responsibility for supplying cavalry. Revenue from assigned land supported them, and allocations could be shifted as their rank or position changed. This tied officeholders’ resources to imperial appointment rather than secure hereditary possession.

evidence.note: Rank, cavalry recruitment and reassigned revenue support the mechanism.

original_record.label: Mansabdari system
original_record.learning_takeaway: Under Akbar, administrators’ ranks combined civil service and cavalry responsibilities with revenue allocations that could be reassigned.

relations.note: Both cases connect service and revenue, but belong to different imperial arrangements.

original_record.card: A marine heatwave is unusually warm ocean water measured against the normal conditions for that place and season. A common definition requires temperatures above the seasonal ninetieth percentile for at least five consecutive days. The comparison is local and time-specific, not one temperature threshold for every sea.

evidence.note: NOAA NCEI gives a local seasonal 90th-percentile threshold and persistence of at least five consecutive days.

original_record.label: Marine heatwave
original_record.learning_takeaway: Identify unusual ocean warmth relative to local seasonal history rather than one worldwide temperature threshold.

relations.note: Unusual ocean warmth can be a coral stressor, but a heatwave definition and the biological bleaching response are different subjects.

original_record.card: Marine stratus forms a low cloud layer associated with coastal ocean air. Winds can carry it inland, while daytime warming and mixing with drier air can make it evaporate. Its changing extent reflects both movement of the cloudy air and changes in temperature and humidity.

evidence.locator: What are Marine Layer Clouds?; Advection; Dissipation
evidence.note: NWS’s marine-layer account describes formation over ocean, advection inland and dissipation through heating or drier-air mixing.

original_record.label: Marine stratus
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explain coastal low-cloud sheets through ocean formation, inland advection and daytime evaporation.

relations.note: Comparing stable marine-layer structure with temperature inversions connects the cloud’s persistence to vertical mixing conditions without asserting identity.

original_record.card: Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland connected chlorofluorocarbon use with damage to stratospheric ozone. Sunlight can release chlorine atoms that repeatedly participate in ozone-destroying reactions. Their work illustrates why a small amount of a regenerated reactive species can have a much larger chemical effect.

evidence.locator: 12.7 Catalysis; inspected passage indices 24, 25, 27 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm242073328; fs-idm4297296; fs-idm225343040
evidence.note: Molina and Rowland showed how chlorine derived from human-made compounds catalyzes ozone destruction.

original_record.label: Mario J. Molina
original_record.learning_takeaway: Molina and Rowland showed how chlorine derived from human-made compounds catalyzes ozone destruction.

relations.note: The source explicitly presents Molina and Rowland’s chlorine mechanism as catalytic ozone destruction.

original_record.card: Marker-assisted selection chooses breeding material using DNA markers associated with traits of interest. A breeder reads the marker pattern rather than relying only on the trait’s visible expression. The method depends on an established marker–trait relationship, so detecting a genetic difference alone is not enough.

evidence.locator: Plant breeding and marker-assisted selection introduction
evidence.note: UNL defines genotype-based selection and explicitly requires marker patterns known to be associated with the target traits.

original_record.label: Marker-assisted selection
original_record.learning_takeaway: Select breeding candidates using genetic markers associated with a useful trait.

relations.note: Linked markers can track a trait during breeding, applying the co-inheritance relationship introduced by genetic linkage.

original_record.card: Markov’s inequality bounds the chance that a nonnegative random quantity exceeds a positive threshold using only its finite mean. Divide the mean by the threshold to obtain the bound. No specific distribution shape is required, but dropping nonnegativity would invalidate this argument.

evidence.locator: Markov's Inequality -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 3 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-4
evidence.note: Bound the probability of a nonnegative quantity exceeding a positive threshold using its mean.

original_record.label: Markov’s inequality
original_record.learning_takeaway: Bound the probability of a nonnegative quantity exceeding a positive threshold using its mean.

relations.note: The Chebyshev reference derives its variance bound by applying Markov’s inequality to a squared deviation.

original_record.card: A martingale is a random process with finite expectations whose expected next value, given its history, equals its current value. It can still fluctuate substantially. A symmetric one-dimensional random walk illustrates this: either step is possible, but their conditional average produces no expected change.

evidence.locator: Martingale -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 3 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-4
evidence.note: A process’s conditional expected next value equals its present value despite its random future.

original_record.label: Martingale
original_record.learning_takeaway: A process’s conditional expected next value equals its present value despite its random future.

relations.note: The source defines a martingale through conditional expectation given the previous process values.

original_record.card: Mastery learning holds intended outcomes steady while allowing time and support to vary. Learners work through units, demonstrate sufficient understanding, and receive additional help when needed before progressing. Approaches differ in their thresholds and organization, so aiming for mastery is not itself one uniform teaching procedure.

evidence.locator: What is it?; distinction from teaching for mastery
evidence.note: Checked fixed goals, variable time/support and variation among implementations; avoided conflating mastery learning with every approach called teaching for mastery.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Using unit-test evidence to provide corrective support before progression applies the formative feedback idea within a particular instructional model.

original_record.label: Mastery learning
original_record.learning_takeaway: Hold learning goals steady while varying time and corrective support before progression to new units.

relations.note: Using unit-test evidence to provide corrective support before progression applies the formative feedback idea within a particular instructional model.

original_record.card: A clay statue raises a puzzle: the clay seems able to survive squashing, while the statue does not. Does that show two coincident objects, or should their relationship be understood differently? Material constitution investigates this disputed relationship between an object and the matter that constitutes it.

evidence.note: SEP opening and section 1 present the statue/lump persistence argument alongside identity and revisionary views; seems and the question explicitly avoid settling the dispute in favor of two objects.

original_record.label: Material constitution
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a statue from the material constituting it through their possible persistence conditions.

relations.note: The statue-and-clay argument explicitly invokes Leibniz's Law: if their persistence properties differ, identity is threatened. The entry presents rival responses rather than endorsing that inference without qualification.

original_record.card: A matrix organization gives people reporting relationships along two dimensions, commonly a function and a project. This can connect specialist departments to shared project goals. It also creates potential conflict when two managers make competing demands, so coordination depends on more than drawing intersecting lines on a chart.

evidence.note: Checked simultaneous functional/project reporting and conflict risk; matrix work is not simply any cross-functional conversation.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The organizational-design chapter explicitly identifies matrix structure as one of the principal designs and explains its dual authority.

original_record.label: Matrix organization
original_record.learning_takeaway: Combine functional and project authority, gaining cross-functional coordination while creating potential dual-boss conflicts.

relations.note: The organizational-design chapter explicitly identifies matrix structure as one of the principal designs and explains its dual authority.

original_record.card: The matrix-tree theorem turns counting into a determinant. Form a graph’s Laplacian from vertex degrees and adjacency, then remove the same row and column. For a finite, simple, unweighted, undirected graph, the resulting determinant counts spanning trees, avoiding an explicit listing of every tree.

evidence.locator: Matrix Tree Theorem -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2
evidence.note: A Laplacian cofactor equals the number of spanning trees.

evidence.locator: Laplacian Matrix -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3
evidence.note: Defines the undirected graph Laplacian by degrees and adjacency.

original_record.label: Matrix-tree theorem
original_record.learning_takeaway: Count a graph’s spanning trees by evaluating a cofactor of its Laplacian.

relations.note: The theorem’s explicit conclusion is the number of spanning trees.

original_record.card: Mauna Loa Observatory’s carbon-dioxide record depends on more than taking repeated readings. Air samples are assessed for background conditions, and the analyzer is frequently checked against reference gases. Reporting carbon dioxide in dry air helps prevent changing water vapor from masquerading as a change in carbon dioxide.

evidence.note: NOAA explains background selection, frequent calibration and why dry-air mole fraction removes dilution effects of variable water vapor.

original_record.label: Mauna Loa Observatory
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how representative air sampling and repeated calibration support an atmospheric CO2 record.

relations.note: Mauna Loa and Landsat offer different long-term environmental records whose comparability depends on calibration, an editorial measurement-practice bridge.

original_record.card: Maydianne Andrade investigated why male redback spiders sometimes risk being eaten during mating. Her observations and experiments compared nutritional, remating and paternity explanations. The case shows how an apparently self-defeating behavior can be studied by separating competing hypotheses and measuring reproductive consequences.

evidence.note: Berkeley’s teaching case names Andrade, lays out the three hypotheses and describes observations and laboratory experiments.

original_record.label: Maydianne Andrade
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how competing explanations for redback mating behavior can be tested with observations and experiments.

relations.note: Andrade’s named research program supplies the experiments used to study the redback sexual-cannibalism case.

original_record.card: Mean ceramic dating estimates occupation timing from an assemblage of pottery whose production periods are known. Combining the ceramics gives a date estimate for the group. It does not turn every sherd into an exact timestamp for the deposit containing it.

evidence.note: Assemblage production dates supply occupation estimates.

original_record.label: Mean ceramic dating
original_record.learning_takeaway: An assemblage’s production periods can estimate occupation timing; the method uses multiple ceramics rather than a single object.

relations.note: Compare an assemblage estimate with a lower chronological bound from associated finds.
The NPS describes mean ceramic dating as a method archaeologists use to estimate occupation.

original_record.card: Meantone temperament narrows fifths to improve the tuning of major thirds. The discrepancy is distributed across a chain of fifths rather than left entirely in the resulting third. This can suit particular keys well, while movement into other keys exposes the compromise's limits.

evidence.locator: What is all the fuss about temperament?
evidence.note: UNSW's worked example describes thirds improved by narrowing four fifths and worsening problems in other keys; no relation is made to personality temperament Q80157.

original_record.label: Meantone temperament
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how slightly narrowed fifths improve thirds but constrain modulation.

relations.note: The cited tuning comparison presents meantone as a different way to reconcile pure-interval demands on fixed-pitch instruments.

original_record.card: Mechanical strain describes deformation relative to an object’s original dimensions. Stretching a short bar by a millimeter produces more axial strain than stretching a much longer bar by the same amount. This dimensionless measure separates proportional deformation from absolute displacement or the applied force.

evidence.locator: 12.3 Stress, Strain, and Elastic Modulus; inspected passage indices 10, 11 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1163709749578; fs-id1163713006766
evidence.note: Describe deformation as a dimensionless change relative to original size or shape.

original_record.label: Mechanical strain
original_record.learning_takeaway: Describe deformation as a dimensionless change relative to original size or shape.

relations.note: The source defines Young’s modulus as the ratio of axial stress to axial strain in the linear regime.

original_record.card: A mechanistic organizational structure emphasizes hierarchy, defined roles, and standardized routines. These features make control and consistency central to coordination. It is one end of a design continuum, not a description of every organization with rules; real structures can combine mechanistic and more flexible features.

evidence.note: Checked hierarchy, formal routines and continuum qualification; no universal claim that this structure is either best or obsolete.

original_record.label: Mechanistic organizational structure
original_record.learning_takeaway: Coordinate work through hierarchy, standardized procedures, and defined roles where consistency is important.

relations.note: The source explicitly places mechanistic and organic forms at opposite ends of a continuum and allows combinations of their features.

original_record.card: Melodic inversion turns an idea's interval directions upside down. A rising movement becomes a falling one. Real inversion preserves the precise sizes and qualities of intervals, while tonal inversion adjusts them to fit the scale or key, allowing the transformed melody to remain within its tonal setting.

evidence.note: Section 11.2.1 explicitly distinguishes real and tonal inversion; the tonal-setting consequence restates its scale/key qualification rather than claiming every interval is unchanged.

original_record.label: Melodic inversion
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish interval-preserving real inversion from key-preserving tonal inversion.

relations.note: Inversion changes interval direction; retrograde changes note order, so their labels should not be treated as aliases.

original_record.card: A melodic retrograde presents notes in the reverse order. It differs from melodic inversion, which reverses the direction of intervals rather than the sequence itself. Reading a tune backward and turning its upward leaps into downward leaps are therefore two distinct ways to transform musical material.

evidence.note: Sections 11.2.7 and 11.2.1 support order reversal versus interval-direction reversal; no claim that retrograde necessarily reverses every performance parameter.

original_record.label: Melodic retrograde
original_record.learning_takeaway: Hear how reversing note order differs from inverting intervals.

relations.note: Comparing the two definitions separates reversal of event order from reversal of melodic direction.

original_record.card: A waiting-time distribution is memoryless when waiting beyond one point leaves the same distribution for the additional wait. Exponential and geometric laws provide continuous and discrete examples. The condition concerns remaining waiting time given survival so far, rather than an absence of all information about a process.

evidence.locator: Memoryless -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3
evidence.note: Gives the conditional waiting-probability definition.

evidence.locator: Exponential Distribution -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 4 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-5
evidence.note: Identifies the continuous exponential memoryless law.

evidence.locator: Geometric Distribution -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 3, 4 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-4; paragraph-5
evidence.note: Identifies the discrete geometric counterpart and its indexing conventions.

original_record.label: Memoryless property
original_record.learning_takeaway: Elapsed waiting does not alter the remaining-wait distribution; exponential and geometric laws provide continuous and discrete examples.

relations.note: The exponential-distribution source explicitly identifies its memoryless property.

original_record.card: Meno's paradox asks how inquiry can work: if you already know the answer, inquiry seems unnecessary; if you do not, how could you recognize it? One response distinguishes partial knowledge from total ignorance. A searcher may know enough to recognize an answer without already possessing it.

evidence.note: SEP section 6.1 states the dilemma and partial-knowledge response; one response avoids presenting it as the only interpretation of Plato or the final resolution of all inquiry puzzles.

original_record.label: Meno's paradox of inquiry
original_record.learning_takeaway: Question how inquiry can recognize an answer it does not already know.

relations.note: A puzzle about gaining and recognizing knowledge belongs within epistemology's study of cognitive success; the bridge uses the inquiry passage and the field's inspected overview.

original_record.card: A mental set is persistence with a problem-solving approach that worked before but is ineffective now. Familiarity can keep a solver repeating the same strategy instead of reconsidering the problem. Functional fixedness is a particular case involving an object's expected use.

evidence.note: Section 7.3 defines persistence with an earlier successful approach and explicitly calls functional fixedness a type of mental set; no claim that all learned routines are harmful.

original_record.label: Mental set
original_record.learning_takeaway: Recognize persistence with a formerly useful approach after circumstances change.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies functional fixedness as a type of mental set, narrowing a habitual strategy to assumptions about object use.

original_record.card: Morris’s Merton Abbey workshops used a site with river water and grounds suitable for washing and drying fabrics. Textile production depended on these practical conditions as well as on design. The workshops show how making patterned cloth joined artistic choices with the resources and layout of a place.

evidence.note: Water, washing/drying grounds and textile workshop functions are documented.

original_record.label: Merton Abbey workshops
original_record.learning_takeaway: Morris’s workshop site offered river water and grounds for washing and drying fabrics, tying textile production to the practical properties of its location.

relations.note: Compare the workshop’s material resources with the named design’s documented printing method.

original_record.card: Metafiction draws attention to a narrative’s own fictional or constructed status. A work can make readers notice that its world has been invented and arranged. Such reflection concerns fictionality, which differs from a narrator merely commenting on the practical act of telling a story.

evidence.note: Fictionality and constructedness distinguish metafiction from metanarration.

original_record.label: Metafiction
original_record.learning_takeaway: Fiction can call attention to its own invented or constructed status, making the reader notice how the work is made.

relations.note: The handbook explicitly distinguishes comments on fictionality from comments on narrating.

original_record.card: Metanarration occurs when a narrator comments on the act or process of telling. These remarks may organize the account or draw attention to its communication. They need not announce that events are fictional, so metanarration can also appear in nonfictional narratives.

evidence.note: Narrating-process commentary and nonfictional use are explicit.

original_record.label: Metanarration
original_record.learning_takeaway: A narrator can comment on the act of telling without claiming that the story is fictional.

relations.note: The source contrasts reflection on telling with reflection on fictional construction.

original_record.card: The method of initial rates compares reaction speeds measured soon after mixing different starting concentrations under otherwise matched conditions. Holding one concentration fixed while changing another isolates its influence. Rate ratios reveal reaction orders before the resulting rate law is used to find the constant.

evidence.locator: 12.3 Rate Laws; inspected passage indices 29, 37, 39 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm147402384; fs-idp221247360; fs-idm59663552
evidence.note: Change initial reactant concentrations across trials to infer reaction orders and the rate constant.

original_record.label: Method of initial rates
original_record.learning_takeaway: Change initial reactant concentrations across trials to infer reaction orders and the rate constant.

relations.note: The source explicitly uses initial-rate experiments to determine reaction orders.

original_record.card: For an ideal statically determinate planar truss, the method of joints isolates connections and balances forces in each direction. Start at a joint with no more than two unknown member forces. Working through the joints identifies which members carry tension and which carry compression.

evidence.locator: 5.6: Methods of Truss Analysis; inspected passage indices 71, 73, 76, 77, 78, 79 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-72; paragraph-74; paragraph-77; paragraph-78; paragraph-79; paragraph-80
evidence.note: Resolve axial truss-member forces by applying equilibrium to one pin joint at a time.

original_record.label: Method of joints
original_record.learning_takeaway: Resolve axial truss-member forces by applying equilibrium to one pin joint at a time.

relations.note: The method’s stated procedure explicitly calls for finding zero-force members before continuing the joint calculations.

original_record.card: Metonymy refers to something through an associated attribute or object. The substitution works through a recognizable connection rather than literal identity. An institution, for instance, may be evoked through an object linked with its authority, letting a compact expression stand for a wider social relationship.

evidence.note: Association-based substitution is defined and illustrated.

original_record.label: Metonymy
original_record.learning_takeaway: An associated attribute can stand for the person or thing meant, as an institution may be named through a symbolic object.

relations.note: Associated naming is a rhetorical means of creating meaning through a substitute expression.

original_record.card: A mezuzah places a parchment inscribed with Torah verses at a doorway, usually within a protective case. The practice brings scriptural words into domestic thresholds. Its meaning depends on the written scroll, not simply on treating the visible container as an ornament.

evidence.note: Torah text, parchment, protective case and doorpost placement are explicit.

original_record.label: Mezuzah
original_record.learning_takeaway: A parchment text enclosed on a doorpost brings scriptural words into the threshold of everyday domestic space.

relations.note: The collection label identifies the scroll’s inscription as verses from the Torah.

original_record.card: Midrash can draw moral or theological teaching from biblical wording through interpretive stories and associations. Such readings need not follow only the immediate narrative situation. Comparing them with contextual readings reveals different questions a commentator may bring to the same scriptural passage.

evidence.note: Sefaria contrasts instructive interpretation with narrative-context reading.

original_record.label: Midrash
original_record.learning_takeaway: Interpretive stories can draw moral or theological meaning from biblical words beyond the immediate narrative setting.

relations.note: The lesson explicitly compares midrashic and contextual approaches to the same passages.

original_record.card: A mikveh is a Jewish ritual bath. Cologne’s medieval example descends about sixteen meters to groundwater and stood within a Jewish quarter. This named case offers a way to examine religious practice, access to water and communal architecture together without assuming every bath has the same design.

evidence.note: Cologne bath depth, groundwater and Jewish-quarter setting are documented.

original_record.label: Mikveh
original_record.learning_takeaway: A Jewish ritual bath can be studied through its built setting; Cologne’s medieval mikveh reaches groundwater deep beneath the former Jewish quarter.

relations.note: The museum identifies the bath as a material feature of Jewish communal religious life.
The museum identifies the mikveh as a Jewish ritual bath.

original_record.card: Milgram's participants believed they were administering increasingly strong shocks when an experimenter instructed them to continue; the learner actually received none. In the original setting, many continued to the highest level. Changing the setting or bringing the learner closer reduced obedience, limiting any simple universal conclusion.

evidence.note: Section 12.4 describes the deceptive shock setup and lower continuation rates in office/proximity variants; no claim that all participants obeyed or that this settles explanations of historical atrocities.

original_record.label: Milgram's obedience experiments
original_record.learning_takeaway: Compare obedience in the original setup with changes produced by proximity and setting.

relations.note: Milgram tests responses to an experimenter's commands, whereas Asch tests responses to a group's judgments. The comparison distinguishes authority-directed obedience from peer conformity.

original_record.card: Miner’s rule estimates cumulative fatigue damage by adding the fraction of expected lifetime consumed at each load level. Failure is predicted when the sum reaches one. The linear accumulation assumption is only an approximation; changing crack behavior or strengthening can make actual damage evolve differently.

evidence.locator: 6.5: Fatigue; inspected passage indices 85, 86, 89, 91 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: section_4; paragraph-90
evidence.note: Approximate cumulative fatigue damage by adding consumed lifetime fractions while recognizing nonlinear-damage limitations.

original_record.label: Miner’s rule
original_record.learning_takeaway: Approximate cumulative fatigue damage by adding consumed lifetime fractions while recognizing nonlinear-damage limitations.

relations.note: The reference uses lifetimes obtained from S–N behavior to calculate the consumed fractions in Miner’s rule.

original_record.card: In spoken language, a minimal pair consists of words differing in one sound position. English pill versus kill provides evidence that the contrasting sounds belong to different phonemes, since the words have different meanings. Failing to find such a pair does not establish equivalence.

evidence.note: The chapter first notes signed-language parameter contrasts, then adapts minimal pairs to spoken-language sounds using pill/kill. The card now explicitly describes the spoken case and does not exclude signed minimal pairs from the broader identity.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The phonology chapter explicitly presents minimal pairs as evidence for contrastive distribution and phoneme analysis.

original_record.label: Minimal pair
original_record.learning_takeaway: Use a spoken-language word pair differing in one sound as evidence of contrastive phonemes, without treating failure to find a pair as proof of equivalence.

relations.note: The phonology chapter explicitly presents minimal pairs as evidence for contrastive distribution and phoneme analysis.

original_record.card: The Mishnah is a compilation of Jewish legal traditions that forms a foundational layer of the Talmud. Later discussion comments on and works through this material. Distinguishing the earlier collection from its commentary helps readers see how a composite religious text carries different layers of teaching.

evidence.note: The Talmud definition distinguishes Mishnah legal traditions from commentary.

original_record.label: Mishnah
original_record.learning_takeaway: An early compilation of Jewish legal traditions forms a textual layer on which later Talmudic discussion comments.

relations.note: The source explicitly situates the Mishnah within the Talmud’s textual composition.

original_record.card: Later information can alter how an earlier event is remembered. In Loftus and Palmer's car-crash studies, wording in questions affected speed estimates and later reports of broken glass. The finding shows how post-event suggestions can shape reports, rather than proving that every eyewitness memory is inaccurate.

evidence.note: OpenStax describes both question wording and later glass reports; studies plural avoids treating the different experimental stages as one undifferentiated sample.

original_record.label: Misinformation effect
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explore how misleading information after an event can alter later reports.

relations.note: These are different routes to memory distortion: external post-event suggestion versus confusion over a detail's source.

original_record.card: A small loudspeaker may reproduce a bass note's upper harmonics while barely producing its lowest frequency. Listeners can nevertheless hear the corresponding low pitch. For periodic tones, the spacing between surviving harmonics supplies information about the absent fundamental, so perceived pitch need not match the lowest audible component.

evidence.locator: Pitch, frequency, harmonics and missing fundamental
evidence.note: UNSW FAQ explains periodic-tone pitch from harmonic spacing and the bass-speaker example; it does not claim that arbitrary inharmonic sounds imply a unique missing fundamental.

original_record.label: Missing fundamental
original_record.learning_takeaway: Understand why a bass pitch remains audible when a speaker omits its fundamental.

relations.note: The source uses the missing fundamental to distinguish perceived pitch from the presence of a lowest-frequency component.

original_record.card: Miter lock gates close as a pair forming a wide V across a chamber. In Panama’s original design, hollow, watertight lower halves provide buoyancy that reduces hinge loading. This reduces effective gate weight while the structure must still resist water-pressure forces.

evidence.locator: Design Of The Locks; inspected passage indices 18, 19 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-19; paragraph-20
evidence.note: Paired V-closing gates use buoyant hollow construction to reduce hinge loads while retaining water.

original_record.label: Miter lock gate
original_record.learning_takeaway: Paired V-closing gates use buoyant hollow construction to reduce hinge loads while retaining water.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies these paired gates as moving components of the Panama lock chambers.

original_record.card: Mixed-member proportional representation combines constituency representatives with party-list seats intended to make overall representation proportional. In New Zealand's version, voters choose a local candidate and a party separately. The party vote largely determines each party's total seats, while electorate winners take individual constituency seats.

evidence.locator: Two votes; electorate MPs and list MPs
evidence.note: New Zealand Electoral Commission's MMP explanation supports separate votes and the overall party share; intended and largely accommodate allocation qualifications, and New Zealand's version prevents universalizing its exact rules.

original_record.label: Mixed-member proportional representation
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how constituency representation combines with a party-proportional seat total.

relations.note: The official MMP explanation identifies the threshold as the New Zealand eligibility rule operating within this electoral system, not as a universal property of MMP.

original_record.card: Möbius inversion recovers an arithmetic function from the sums of its values over divisors. A second divisor sum, weighted by the Möbius function, cancels the accumulated contributions. The formula turns information about totals over divisors back into information about the original individual values.

evidence.locator: Möbius Inversion Formula -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 3 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-4
evidence.note: Recover an arithmetic function from sums over its divisors using Möbius-weighted cancellation.

original_record.label: Möbius inversion formula
original_record.learning_takeaway: Recover an arithmetic function from sums over its divisors using Möbius-weighted cancellation.

relations.note: The operation is a concrete number-theoretic technique for undoing divisor sums.

original_record.card: A Möbius strip can be made by joining the ends of a band after giving one end a half-twist. The result has one continuous side and one boundary curve. Its nonorientability distinguishes it from an ordinary untwisted band, despite their similar local appearance.

evidence.locator: Möbius Strip -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 12 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-13
evidence.note: A half-twisted band creates a one-sided nonorientable surface with a single boundary.

original_record.label: Möbius strip
original_record.learning_takeaway: A half-twisted band creates a one-sided nonorientable surface with a single boundary.

relations.note: The source explicitly calls the Möbius strip nonorientable, providing a counterexample to orientable surfaces.

original_record.card: A bow alternately sticks to and slips against a string, sustaining a nearly periodic motion. That nonlinear drive can pull the string's slightly mismatched resonances into harmonic frequency ratios. The resulting steady note can therefore be more harmonically regular than the freely vibrating string's natural modes.

evidence.note: UNSW explicitly attributes harmonic locking to periodic stick-slip drive; can and steady note preserve its operating-condition qualification.

original_record.label: Mode locking in bowed strings
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how periodic bowing can enforce harmonic motion despite inharmonic string resonances.

relations.note: The source explains mode locking as the reason bowed motion can be harmonic despite slightly inharmonic natural resonances.

original_record.card: A modern roundabout channels entering vehicles through curved approaches and gives circulating traffic priority. Lower speeds and fewer crossing conflicts can reduce severe collisions. Its safety mechanism depends on the geometry and entry-yield rules, rather than merely placing a circular island in the middle of an intersection.

evidence.locator: Roundabouts | FHWA Lock U.S. Department of Transportation United States Department of Transportation; inspected passage indices 6, 8, 9 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-7; paragraph-9; paragraph-10
evidence.note: Curved approaches and entry-yield rules lower speeds and reduce vehicle conflict points.

original_record.label: Modern roundabout
original_record.learning_takeaway: Curved approaches and entry-yield rules lower speeds and reduce vehicle conflict points.

relations.note: The source connects junction geometry and right-of-way rules with traffic movement and collision severity, a specific transport-design problem.

original_record.card: Molecular solids consist of neutral molecules held near one another by intermolecular attractions. Their melting temperatures vary with those attractions: small nonpolar molecules can freeze only at very low temperatures, while larger or polar molecules may remain solid at much warmer temperatures.

evidence.locator: 10.5 The Solid State of Matter; inspected passage indices 16 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm41841264
evidence.note: Neutral molecules form solids whose melting behavior depends on intermolecular attractions.

original_record.label: Molecular solid
original_record.learning_takeaway: Neutral molecules form solids whose melting behavior depends on intermolecular attractions.

relations.note: The source distinguishes solids made from intact molecules from extended covalent networks; this is a comparison, not a parent edge.

original_record.card: Molly houses were meeting places associated with queer social life in Georgian London. They offered spaces for companionship and forms of gender expression while exposing participants to hostile policing and prosecution. Their history joins everyday sociability with the dangers created by criminalization.

evidence.locator: What was a molly house?; origins, lines 141–168
evidence.note: Gathering places, gender expression and legal vulnerability are described.

original_record.label: Molly houses
original_record.learning_takeaway: Georgian meeting places allowed queer social networks and gender expression under laws and policing that made participants vulnerable.

relations.note: Molly houses provide a specific historical case of sexual and gender diversity under criminalization.

original_record.card: Under the UK Parliament Acts, a Speaker-certified money bill can reach Royal Assent without Lords consent after a month without unamended passage. It must already have passed the Commons and reached the Lords at least a month before session-end; the Commons can direct otherwise.

evidence.locator: Bills subject to the Parliament Acts
evidence.note: The Parliamentary Counsel guidance, paragraphs 1.2, 1.5, 1.8 and 2.2, supplies certification and all timing/direction conditions; this supersedes the introductory page's misleading claim of automatic assent within a month and its absolute amendment claim.

evidence.locator: Paragraphs 1.2, 1.5, 1.8 and 2.2; 2.7 and 2.19 resolve misleading simplifications
evidence.note: Official guidance supports certification, Commons passage, session timing, a month without unamended Lords passage, Commons contrary direction and Royal Assent; not automatic enactment after a month.

original_record.label: Money bills under the Parliament Acts
original_record.learning_takeaway: Compare the Lords' restricted role over money bills with other public bills.

relations.note: The guidance expressly identifies section 1 of the 1911 Act as the money-bill procedure and reproduces its legal conditions.

original_record.card: A monotype transfers ink or paint from a flat plate to paper, usually producing one principal impression. The artist can alter the marks before printing rather than relying on a permanently carved image. This makes preparation on the plate a direct part of the image’s improvisation.

evidence.note: Flat plate, transfer and manipulable marks with usually one impression are described.

original_record.label: Monotype
original_record.learning_takeaway: Ink or paint worked on a flat plate transfers under pressure to damp paper, typically yielding a single impression whose marks can be changed before printing.

relations.note: Peyton’s account compares the process’s immediate working window with her more revised paintings.
MoMA explicitly calls monotype a printmaking process and explains its transferred impression.

original_record.card: Moore's paradox concerns the oddness of asserting a fact while denying that one believes it. The combination need not be logically contradictory: someone else could truthfully describe that situation. The puzzle is why the speaker's own present assertion appears to undermine the position it expresses.

evidence.note: SEP section 5.3 distinguishes first-person declarative oddity from third-person, conditional and past-tense counterparts; the card avoids calling the proposition itself a formal contradiction.

original_record.label: Moore's paradox
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explain why asserting a fact while denying belief in it sounds self-defeating.

relations.note: Both expose tensions involving belief, but Moore's case centers on an assertion's first-person stance, whereas the preface case concerns combining individually rational beliefs.

original_record.card: Moral hazard describes how protection from consequences can change behavior after an agreement. Insurance may reduce the incentive to prevent a loss when another party pays much of the cost. Insurers use monitoring and cost sharing to address this problem, although they cannot observe every risky action.

evidence.note: Checked incentive mechanism, limited observation and mitigation; avoided using the term as a judgment about a person's moral character.

original_record.label: Moral hazard
original_record.learning_takeaway: Trace how protection from losses can change behavior after insurance is in place.

relations.note: The insurance chapter explicitly presents deductibles and other cost-sharing arrangements as ways to reduce moral-hazard incentives.

original_record.card: Moral luck names a tension in judging people: responsibility seems to require control, yet praise and blame often depend on factors outside their control. Two equally reckless actions can have different outcomes. The puzzle asks whether, and how, those differences should affect moral assessment.

evidence.locator: The Problem: Control Principle and moral assessment
evidence.note: SEP's Control Principle and resultant-luck examples support the tension; the card asks rather than settles the normative question and does not create an additional resultant-luck identity.

original_record.label: Moral luck
original_record.learning_takeaway: Investigate how moral assessment can depend on circumstances outside an agent's control.

relations.note: The entry identifies circumstantial luck as one form of moral luck, involving which situations a person happens to face rather than only how an action ends.

original_record.card: The Morris worm spread across the early Internet in 1988 and disrupted computers and services without destroying their files. Its impact illustrates that availability can fail even when stored data remains intact. The incident also prompted organized response efforts, including an early computer emergency response team.

evidence.locator: Main history, propagation and operational impact paragraphs
evidence.note: Checked year, self-propagation, absence of file destruction, service disruption and response-team consequence; no detailed exploit instructions or precise uncertain damage totals.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The FBI's account of disruption without file destruction provides a concrete case for considering service availability within computer protection.

original_record.label: Morris worm
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how self-propagating code disrupted network services without destroying stored files in the 1988 incident.

relations.note: The FBI's account of disruption without file destruction provides a concrete case for considering service availability within computer protection.

original_record.card: A mortise-and-tenon joint fits a projecting end of one piece into a matching recess in another. Close-fitting faces provide contact for bonding, while the shoulders seat against the receiving piece. The arrangement connects shape and fit with joint performance, rather than relying on an end-to-end butt connection alone.

evidence.note: The original WOOD instruction defines projection/recess, glue surface and shoulder contact as components of the fitted joint.

original_record.label: Mortise-and-tenon joint
original_record.learning_takeaway: Connect a fitted projection, its matching recess and seated shoulders with a strong wooden joint.

relations.note: This is a specific geometric method of joining wooden components within woodworking.

original_record.card: A person can have genetically different groups of cells that all descend from the same fertilized egg. This is mosaicism: a change arising during development is inherited by that cell’s descendants. Its effects depend on the variant and which cells carry it.

evidence.note: NHGRI defines genetically distinct populations from one zygote and explains post-fertilization variants and variable consequences.

original_record.label: Mosaicism
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish genomic differences arising within descendants of one fertilized egg from chimerism.

relations.note: Mosaicism and chimerism can both involve different cell genomes, but their cell populations have different developmental origins.

original_record.card: Mulching covers the soil surface with a chosen material. The layer can slow evaporation, reduce light available to weeds and alter soil temperature. Those effects depend on the material, so a gardener’s choice of covering changes more than the appearance of the bed.

evidence.note: UMN explains surface cover, moisture conservation, weed-light restriction and material-dependent thermal effects.

original_record.label: Mulching
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explain how a surface covering changes evaporation, weed growth and soil temperature.

relations.note: A mulch layer is a specific gardening intervention affecting root-zone conditions.

original_record.card: A multi-column index orders records using several fields together. In SQLite's fruit example, indexing fruit and state lets the database locate California oranges directly instead of first finding all oranges and rejecting other states. Column order determines how that combined ordering can be used.

evidence.note: Checked combined conditions and ordered index columns; no blanket guarantee that any column order accelerates every query.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Composite ordering is a particular database access structure; the fruit-and-state example supports the concrete retrieval mechanism.

original_record.label: Multi-column index
original_record.learning_takeaway: Order index entries by several columns so combined constraints avoid filtering unrelated intermediate matches.

relations.note: Composite ordering is a particular database access structure; the fruit-and-state example supports the concrete retrieval mechanism.

original_record.card: Musical diminution shortens the rhythmic values of a motive or phrase, commonly by halving every duration. The pitch sequence can remain recognizable while the idea unfolds faster. Some uses of the term are less exact, referring more generally to a passage rewritten with shorter note values.

evidence.note: Section 11.2.3 supports both exact halving and the broader usage; commonly prevents treating halving as an exceptionless definition.

original_record.label: Musical diminution
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish proportional rhythmic shortening from changing only some durations.

relations.note: The textbook defines diminution in direct contrast with augmentation's usual doubling of durations.

original_record.card: Phase shifting changes the alignment of repeated musical patterns. One part can retain its timing while another gradually runs ahead, or a performer can jump directly to the next rotation. Reich's Piano Phase and Clapping Music demonstrate these different ways of reorganizing the same recurring material.

evidence.note: Section 35.2 explicitly contrasts gradual speeding in Piano Phase with discrete rotations in Clapping Music; no claim that both works require continuous tempo drift.

original_record.label: Musical phase shifting
original_record.learning_takeaway: Compare gradual desynchronization with discrete shifts of a repeated pattern.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly identifies Piano Phase as a live-performance application of Reich's phase-shifting process.

original_record.card: Mutualism is an interaction between species in which both participants benefit. Ants attending Karner blue butterfly larvae provide protection and receive carbohydrate-rich secretions in return. Examining what each partner gains turns a vague picture of cooperation into a testable account of a biological exchange.

evidence.note: OpenStax explicitly defines mutual benefit and supplies the ant–butterfly exchange used here.

original_record.label: Mutualism
original_record.learning_takeaway: Recognize interspecific exchanges in which both partners benefit, as in ant-tended butterfly larvae.

relations.note: Mutualism is a particular interspecific interaction studied at ecology’s community level.

original_record.card: An N-of-1 trial compares intervention and control periods repeatedly within the same person, often in randomized order. This can reveal an individual response that a group average obscures. It works best when effects can change or fade between periods, rather than permanently carrying into later comparisons.

evidence.note: UK guidance describes randomized multiple crossovers within individuals and limits for slow-onset or long-lasting interventions.

original_record.label: N-of-1 trial
original_record.learning_takeaway: Compare interventions repeatedly within one person rather than assuming a group average fits everyone.

relations.note: Washout periods can reduce carryover between the repeated intervention/control periods used in this design.

original_record.card: Narrative eventfulness concerns how a change becomes significant, surprising or unusual within a story’s context. Merely changing state is not enough for this stronger sense. Characters, narrators or readers interpret the change against expectations, so the same occurrence can acquire different importance in different settings.

evidence.note: Type-II events depend on relevance, unexpectedness and interpretation.

original_record.label: Narrative eventfulness
original_record.learning_takeaway: A change becomes especially eventful when interpreted as significant or unexpected against a story’s cultural and situational expectations.

relations.note: Significant interpreted changes can contribute to why a narrative is worth telling.

original_record.card: Narrative levels describe the relationship between an act of telling and the story world it presents. A character who begins another story can introduce a further level. The model tracks these thresholds, including relationships that exist even without an obvious frame tale.

evidence.note: Narrating acts, embedded stories and distinction from framing are explicit.

original_record.label: Narrative levels
original_record.learning_takeaway: A character’s act of telling can establish a further story level, creating nested relations between narration and narrated worlds.

relations.note: Frame stories use embedding, but the handbook explains why narrative levels cover a wider analytical relationship.

original_record.card: Narrative paralepsis supplies information that exceeds a particular text’s established focalization norm. The exception is defined against the work’s own pattern of disclosure. Identifying it therefore requires attention to narrative coherence rather than a universal rule about what a narrator could plausibly know.

evidence.note: Paralepsis and text-specific informational norms are explicitly defined.

original_record.label: Narrative paralepsis
original_record.learning_takeaway: A narrative can reveal information beyond its established focalization norm; identifying this excess depends on the particular text.

relations.note: Paralepsis is an alteration of the informational norm established by focalization.

original_record.card: Offering a narrator the chance to review an interview before public release can connect historical access with informed participation. The Oral History Association recommends building this opportunity into the process when possible, alongside clear expectations about preservation, access and the project’s timetable.

evidence.note: Preparation 3 recommends consent and possible pre-release approval.

original_record.label: Narrator review in oral history
original_record.learning_takeaway: Giving narrators an opportunity to review an interview before release connects historical access with consent and the terms of participation.

relations.note: Pre-release review is a recommended part of planning an oral-history project.

original_record.card: Natural-breaks classification groups similar values and places boundaries near larger gaps in the data. The resulting classes can reveal internal clusters, but their thresholds depend on the particular dataset. Maps classified separately this way may therefore be difficult to compare directly through their legends.

evidence.note: Dataset-specific groups and comparison limits are explicitly stated.

original_record.label: Natural-breaks map classification
original_record.learning_takeaway: Grouping similar values and separating large gaps creates dataset-specific classes that may hinder direct comparisons across maps.

relations.note: Both classify mapped values, but natural breaks follows data gaps rather than equalizing class counts.
Data-dependent class boundaries are a specific decision in representing attributes on maps.

original_record.card: The Neapolitan chord is a major chord built on the lowered second scale degree. In classical tonal analysis it commonly appears in first inversion and serves a predominant function. Its distinctive chromatic color therefore has a directional role, helping prepare the approach to dominant harmony.

evidence.note: Section 20.1 names flat II, most-common first inversion and predominant function; major quality follows the uppercase chord notation, not a claim that every flat-II sonority has this function.

original_record.label: Neapolitan chord
original_record.learning_takeaway: Recognize the flattened-supertonic major chord as a chromatic predominant.

relations.note: The Neapolitan's predominant role contrasts with the cadential six-four's dominant role, despite both often occurring near a cadence.

original_record.card: Negative space is the area around or between depicted forms that helps shape a composition. In Ruth Asawa’s 1965 lithograph Chair, unmarked gaps suggest chairs among patterned marks. These spaces show how an image can describe an object through areas left open.

evidence.locator: Object header, lines 61–68; gallery label, lines 78–79; medium, line 88; object number, line 98
evidence.note: Object header identifies the 1965 lithograph; the gallery label describes five patterned chairs and two additional negative-space chairs.

original_record.label: Negative space
original_record.learning_takeaway: Unmarked areas around or within depicted forms can describe an object, as blank chair shapes do in Ruth Asawa’s 1965 lithograph Chair (TAM.1558-II).

relations.note: The museum label identifies negative-space chairs in the work catalogued as the 1965 lithograph Chair (TAM.1558-II).

original_record.card: A networked team structure organizes work around flexible connections among task-focused teams. Teams may initially be assigned, then find additional collaborators and resources as the work develops. The distinctive feature is this evolving task arrangement, rather than treating every informal workplace friendship as an organizational design.

evidence.note: Checked the approved task-team distinction from informal organization and the wider organic orientation; no claim that reporting responsibilities vanish.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source explicitly lists networked team structure among organizational designs and describes teams forming useful links after initial assignment.

original_record.label: Networked team structure
original_record.learning_takeaway: Coordinate task-focused teams through flexible relationship networks rather than relying primarily on fixed reporting lines.

relations.note: The source explicitly lists networked team structure among organizational designs and describes teams forming useful links after initial assignment.

original_record.card: Under simple elastic beam bending, fibers on one side are stretched while those on the other are compressed. The neutral axis marks where the axial bending stress changes sign and becomes zero. Finding it helps locate the regions where tensile or compressive failure may begin.

evidence.locator: 4.2: Stresses in Beams; inspected passage indices 68, 70, 72 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: section_1; section_2
evidence.note: A bending beam has a zero-axial-stress line between tensile and compressive regions.

original_record.label: Neutral axis in beam bending
original_record.learning_takeaway: A bending beam has a zero-axial-stress line between tensile and compressive regions.

relations.note: The moment-of-area reference explicitly measures distance from the neutral axis to evaluate bending resistance.

original_record.card: The neutral theory of molecular evolution emphasizes mutation and genetic drift in explaining much genetic variation. When alternative gene versions do not differ in fitness, chance can change their frequencies. This does not mean all variation is neutral or that natural selection is unimportant.

evidence.note: Berkeley emphasizes mutation and drift and defines the illustrative neutral alternatives as having no difference in fitness. It explicitly rejects claims that all variation is neutral or selection is unimportant.

original_record.label: Neutral theory of molecular evolution
original_record.learning_takeaway: Separate neutral genetic variation and drift from the claim that all evolution is nonadaptive.

relations.note: Neutral theory assigns a major explanatory role to genetic drift for variants with no fitness difference, rather than introducing a different drift mechanism.

original_record.card: During the Panic of 1907, the New York Clearing House supported member banks with loans and later loan certificates. Trust companies outside its membership initially lacked that access. The case shows how an institution can provide collective liquidity while its eligibility boundary leaves other connected institutions exposed.

evidence.note: Checked member/nonmember distinction and timing; support is not represented as unlimited insurance for every institution or proof of solvency.

original_record.label: New York Clearing House
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how membership-based mutual liquidity support helped some banks while initially excluding distressed trust companies.

relations.note: The historical account explicitly describes clearing-house support, membership restrictions and loan certificates during the Panic of 1907.

original_record.card: New Zealand's MMP system gives parties two routes to parliamentary eligibility: at least five percent of the party vote or an electorate victory. The alternative route means a party below the percentage threshold can still qualify through local success. These are New Zealand's rules, not universal MMP requirements.

evidence.locator: Political parties try to win party votes and electorate votes
evidence.note: The Electoral Commission explicitly states the five-percent or electorate-seat alternatives; the card does not claim an exact seat entitlement or apply the threshold to other countries.

original_record.label: New Zealand MMP threshold
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explore two alternative routes to eligibility for proportional representation.

relations.note: The official page locates the threshold within New Zealand's MMP allocation and explains it alongside separate party and electorate votes.

original_record.card: The no-false-lemmas condition proposes repairing justified true belief by excluding beliefs inferred from false premises. It blocks some Gettier examples, but deceptive perceptual environments pose a further challenge. A belief can apparently be accidentally true without having been inferred from any false proposition.

evidence.note: SEP section 4 states the proposed fourth condition and noninferential counterexamples; the card does not claim the repair is accepted or sufficient.

original_record.label: No-false-lemmas condition
original_record.learning_takeaway: Evaluate the proposed repair that knowledge cannot be inferred from false premises.

relations.note: The entry expressly develops no false lemmas as an attempted additional condition for solving the Gettier problem, then presents objections.

original_record.card: No-till farming establishes crops while limiting soil disturbance and retaining previous plant residues at the surface. Planting directly into that cover differs from turning the whole field before sowing. The practice changes both how soil is worked and how residues remain part of the growing environment.

evidence.locator: Residue and Tillage Management, No Till
evidence.note: NRCS states limits on soil disturbance, year-round residue retention and direct planting into the residue.

original_record.label: No-till farming
original_record.learning_takeaway: Reduce soil disturbance by establishing crops without full-width tillage.

relations.note: Retaining residue through reduced disturbance differs from growing a seasonal cover crop, though both address soil cover.

original_record.card: Joining two normalized Unicode strings does not guarantee that the result stays normalized. A combining mark at the boundary may need reordering or composition with the preceding text. Software can therefore need to normalize the join even when both original pieces were already normalized.

evidence.note: Checked concatenation versus substring behavior; the claim is limited to joins and does not say every concatenation changes normalization.

original_record.label: Normalization across string concatenation
original_record.learning_takeaway: Recheck normalization at concatenation boundaries because joining normalized strings can require reordering or composition.

relations.note: UAX 15 section 1.4 explicitly explains normalization's failure to be closed under concatenation and shows boundary examples.

original_record.card: Normalizing a count divides it by a relevant denominator before mapping it. Cases per resident, for example, answer a different question from total cases. The choice helps distinguish prevalence from population size, although the denominator must fit the comparison the map is intended to make.

evidence.note: Dividing counts by appropriate totals supports rate-based comparison.

original_record.label: Normalization for choropleth maps
original_record.learning_takeaway: Dividing a count by a relevant denominator distinguishes prevalence or intensity from the size of a region’s population.

relations.note: Normalization is a specific preparation choice for meaningful choropleth comparisons.

original_record.card: Normative social influence draws people toward a group's position because acceptance matters. Someone may publicly give an answer they privately doubt to avoid ridicule or fit in. Agreement in this case need not mean believing the group has better information about the question.

evidence.locator: Why conform? normative versus informational influence
evidence.note: Section 12.4 distinguishes fitting in from information-based conformity and notes public agreement without private acceptance in Asch's setting; the card allows rather than requires private disagreement.

original_record.label: Normative social influence
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish joining a group to gain acceptance from believing its answer is correct.

relations.note: The text explicitly contrasts acceptance-seeking with trusting the group's information, identifying two different motivations for conformity.

original_record.card: Numerical identity means being one and the same thing; qualitative identity means being alike in qualities. The distinction matters for change: a persisting object can remain the same object while its features alter. Similarity of appearance alone does not settle whether two descriptions pick out one thing.

evidence.note: SEP Identity Over Time section 1 distinguishes one object from exact resemblance and connects persistence with qualitative change; the card does not assume the controversial converse identity-of-indiscernibles principle.

original_record.label: Numerical and qualitative identity
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish being one and the same object from being perfectly alike.

relations.note: The introduction moves directly from numerical/qualitative identity to Leibniz's Law, exposing the need to explain how qualitative change fits identity through time.

original_record.card: NuSTAR uses high-energy X-rays to study regions around black holes, exploding stars, and active galaxies. Its observations have helped estimate black-hole spin, illustrating how radiation from an object’s surroundings can carry information about the object itself.

evidence.locator: NuSTAR; inspected passage indices 5 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-6
evidence.note: High-energy X-ray observations reveal black-hole dynamics and enabled a precise spin measurement.

original_record.label: NuSTAR
original_record.learning_takeaway: High-energy X-ray observations reveal black-hole dynamics and enabled a precise spin measurement.

relations.note: The mission description explicitly identifies black-hole dynamics and spin measurements as results of NuSTAR observations.

original_record.card: Nutrient-film technique moves a shallow stream of nutrient solution through channels containing plant roots. The solution circulates back toward a reservoir while roots retain access to air.
