original_record.learning_takeaway: Explore Glass's additive process through repetitions that successively omit final notes.

relations.note: The textbook analyzes the opening of Glass's Two Pages as an example of additive process, with shortening repetitions inside the expanding unit.

original_record.card: Indian Buddhist discussions of two truths distinguish conventional understanding from an ultimate perspective. Ordinary language and practices operate conventionally, while ultimate analysis asks how things really are. Buddhist schools interpret both levels and their relationship differently, so the distinction does not express one uniform doctrine across traditions.

evidence.note: SEP opening differentiates conventional and ultimate perspectives and explicitly warns that the schools can be radically opposed; the card avoids attributing one settled metaphysics or historical origin to all Buddhism.

original_record.label: Two truths in Indian Buddhist philosophy
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish conventional and ultimate truth while recognizing that Buddhist schools interpret the distinction differently.

relations.note: The distinction concerns perspectives on truth and knowledge, inviting comparison with epistemology's study of cognitive success without assimilating all Buddhist schools to a single Western theory.

original_record.card: Tympanometry changes air pressure in the ear canal and records how the eardrum responds. The resulting graph helps assess the mechanics of the eardrum and middle ear. It differs from asking someone whether they can hear a tone: movement and hearing threshold are separate measurements.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus describes a pressure-varying probe and eardrum-movement graphs, separately from behavioral audiometry.

original_record.label: Tympanometry
original_record.learning_takeaway: Assess middle-ear mechanics by measuring eardrum movement as pressure changes.

relations.note: Comparing mechanical eardrum response with a person’s detection of tones distinguishes two hearing-assessment questions.

original_record.card: An uncodified constitution lacks one consolidated constitutional text, not necessarily written rules. The United Kingdom's constitutional arrangements include many statutes alongside other sources. Calling the constitution unwritten can therefore mislead: the important distinction is whether its basic rules are collected in a single authoritative document.

evidence.locator: Parliamentary sovereignty and the UK constitution
evidence.note: UK Parliament's sovereignty page expressly describes the constitution as partly written and wholly uncodified; the card does not equate uncodified with informal, unenforceable or absent.

original_record.label: Uncodified constitution
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish lacking a single constitutional document from lacking written constitutional rules.

relations.note: The page identifies uncodified as the form of the UK's constitution, while explaining that many constitutional rules are nevertheless written in statutes.

original_record.card: A pawn reaching its final rank need not become a queen. Underpromotion chooses a rook, bishop or knight instead. The new piece takes effect immediately, and the available choices do not depend on which pieces were captured earlier in the game.

evidence.note: FIDE 3.7.3.3–5 support all alternatives, immediate effect and independence from captured pieces; no unsupported tactical claim explains why a particular choice wins.

original_record.label: Underpromotion
original_record.learning_takeaway: Recognize that promotion may choose a rook, bishop or knight instead of queen.

relations.note: FIDE's pawn-promotion rule explicitly permits the three non-queen choices described here.

original_record.card: Understitching secures a seam allowance to the facing on the inside of a garment. This encourages the seam to roll inward and helps prevent the facing from showing on the outside. It controls an already assembled edge, rather than stabilizing a loose pattern piece before sewing.

evidence.locator: Seam-allowance understitching; Tips for Applying Facings
evidence.note: NMSU describes pressing the allowance toward the facing, understitching and preventing the facing from rolling outside.

original_record.label: Understitching
original_record.learning_takeaway: Keep a facing from rolling to the garment’s outside by securing its seam allowance to the facing.

relations.note: These stitching operations differ in timing and purpose: control of an assembled facing versus stabilization of an unjoined cut edge.

original_record.card: A Unicode code point is a numbered position in the character space, rather than the bytes stored in a file. UTF-8 encodes valid scalar values with different byte lengths. Keeping the number separate from its encoding helps explain why counting bytes need not count characters.

evidence.note: Checked character-number terminology and variable-length storage; wording does not claim all code points are assigned characters or valid scalar values.

original_record.label: Unicode code point
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish the integer assigned to a character from the bytes used by an encoding.

relations.note: RFC 3629 explicitly distinguishes character numbers from the octet sequences used to encode them.

original_record.card: Unicode normalization gives equivalent text sequences a common representation. It decomposes characters, orders combining marks, and sometimes recomposes them. The chosen normalization form matters: canonical forms preserve distinctions that compatibility forms may remove, so normalization is more specific than simply making text look alike.

evidence.note: Checked decomposition, ordering, recomposition, and canonical versus compatibility behavior; normalization is not a general visual-similarity matcher.

original_record.label: Unicode normalization
original_record.learning_takeaway: Transform equivalent character sequences into a common binary representation through decomposition, ordering, and optional recomposition.

relations.note: UAX 15 sections 1.1–1.3 explicitly use canonical equivalence to define normalization forms and their transformations.

original_record.card: A unit cell is a repeating box used to describe a crystal lattice. Boundary points are shared with neighboring cells, so counting them requires fractions. A primitive cell contains one lattice point in total; a larger, nonprimitive cell contains more.

evidence.locator: Unit cell; inspected passage indices 8, 9 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-9; paragraph-10
evidence.note: Defines unit cell, primitive cell, and lattice-point multiplicity.

evidence.locator: 10.6 Lattice Structures in Crystalline Solids; inspected passage indices 10, 13 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm2181616; fs-idm15054992
evidence.note: Explains repetition and fractional counting of corner atoms in the simple cubic example.

original_record.label: Unit cell
original_record.learning_takeaway: Account for shared boundary atoms when identifying the repeating building block of a crystal.

relations.note: The crystallography references describe crystal repetition through unit cells.

original_record.card: A narrator can report events accurately yet interpret them poorly or evaluate them misleadingly. Unreliable narration therefore involves more than factual lying. Separating reporting, interpretation and judgment lets readers identify where an account becomes questionable and where it may remain dependable.

evidence.note: The source distinguishes reporting, interpreting and evaluating, including mixed reliability.

original_record.label: Unreliable narration
original_record.learning_takeaway: A narrator may report events accurately while interpreting or evaluating them misleadingly, so unreliability need not mean simple lying.

relations.note: The handbook explains the historical connection between unreliability and inferred norms of the work.

original_record.card: UTF-8 represents Unicode scalar values using one to four bytes. ASCII characters retain their familiar single-byte values, while other values use recognizable multibyte patterns. A character's assigned number and its encoded bytes are different things, which matters when counting or processing text.

evidence.note: Checked ASCII preservation, byte range, and distinction between scalar value and encoding; surrogate code points are not valid UTF-8 scalar values.

original_record.label: UTF-8
original_record.learning_takeaway: Encode Unicode scalar values in one to four bytes while preserving ASCII byte values.

relations.note: RFC 3629 sections 2–3 directly relate character numbers to their one-to-four-byte UTF-8 encodings.

original_record.card: Smelser's value-added theory analyzes collective behavior through a proposed combination of conditions, including structural strain, a shared interpretation, and a precipitating event. It asks what makes an episode possible and mobilizes action. The name refers to an explanatory sociological framework, rather than economic value added or a numerical prediction formula.

evidence.note: Checked named theory and selected conditions; qualification preserves that these are proposed explanatory requirements rather than a validated universal checklist.

original_record.label: Value-added theory of collective behavior
original_record.learning_takeaway: Analyze several proposed conditions for collective episodes, including strain, shared beliefs, and precipitating events.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly presents Smelser's conditions as a theoretical account of collective-behavior episodes.

original_record.card: A variable-area exhaust nozzle changes geometry to suit different engine operating conditions. Afterburning jet engines use adjustable converging-diverging passages to maintain useful flow conditions over a wider range. The moving structure adds weight, revealing a tradeoff between adaptable performance and the simplicity of a fixed nozzle.

evidence.locator: Nozzles; inspected passage indices 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-3
evidence.note: Adjustable nozzle geometry trades extra weight for efficient operation across a wider airflow range.

original_record.label: Variable-area exhaust nozzle
original_record.learning_takeaway: Adjustable nozzle geometry trades extra weight for efficient operation across a wider airflow range.

relations.note: NASA’s afterburning-engine example uses a variable-geometry converging-diverging nozzle; this is a supported design connection, not a claim that every variable-area nozzle has that form.

original_record.card: People with the same genetic condition can have different signs, symptoms or severity. Variable expressivity describes that range of manifestations. It differs from reduced penetrance, which concerns whether the condition appears at all, and helps explain why affected relatives need not look clinically identical.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus distinguishes a range of manifestations from the proportion showing a disorder and describes differences among affected people.

original_record.label: Variable expressivity
original_record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish variation in a condition’s manifestations from whether it appears at all.

relations.note: The source treats presence of manifestations and range of manifestations as separate questions.

original_record.card: Variable-rate irrigation changes water delivery across a field using control zones and prescription maps. Those maps specify irrigation amounts, but soil and crop information must guide the prescription. The technology applies the planned pattern; it does not independently determine how much water a crop needs.

evidence.note: UMN describes control zones and prescription maps, then explicitly distinguishes spatial application from determining crop water need. Agronomic information and irrigation-scheduling tools are required to assign appropriate amounts.

original_record.label: Variable-rate irrigation
original_record.learning_takeaway: Match irrigation amounts to different areas of a field instead of assuming every area needs the same water.

relations.note: Spatially varied application is a specific control approach within irrigation rather than a second identity for irrigation as a whole.

original_record.card: Variationist sociolinguistics studies language as people use it, asking how social settings and linguistic environments influence variation. Instead of imagining one perfectly uniform speaker, it examines patterns across actual speech. A person may use the same variant at different rates when chatting casually and reading aloud.

evidence.note: Checked focus on usage, social/linguistic context, and casual-versus-reading example; no fixed speech stereotype is assigned to a social group.

evidence.locator: §10.7, Labov comparison of casual speech and reading
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The variationist introduction and social-status example explicitly study context-dependent variant frequencies, including systematic style shifting.

original_record.label: Variationist sociolinguistics
original_record.learning_takeaway: Analyze how linguistic and social conditions alter the probability of variants in language as actually used.

relations.note: The variationist introduction and social-status example explicitly study context-dependent variant frequencies, including systematic style shifting.

original_record.card: Venice developed as an urban system of islands and waterways within a lagoon. Buildings, canals and hydraulic interventions cannot be understood independently of that surrounding water. The site shows a city whose form emerged through a long, changing relationship between settlement and environmental management.

evidence.note: Island settlement, waterways and sustained hydraulic intervention are explicit.

original_record.label: Venice and its lagoon
original_record.learning_takeaway: Island settlements and canals form an urban system inseparable from the surrounding lagoon and centuries of hydraulic intervention.

relations.note: The connected city-lagoon system demonstrates a sustained relationship between settlement and environment.

original_record.card: Villa Savoye demonstrates how columns and floor slabs can separate a building’s structural support from the placement of walls. This permits a free plan and an independently arranged facade. The villa makes a design program visible through the relationships among support, enclosure and inhabited space.

evidence.locator: Pilotis, free plan and free facade, lines 13–14 and 43–52
evidence.note: Pilotis, free plan and independent facade are explained on the official site.

original_record.label: Villa Savoye
original_record.learning_takeaway: The villa demonstrates how columns and floor slabs can separate structure from wall placement, enabling a free plan and an independently organized facade.

relations.note: The named building provides a concrete architectural case connecting structure and spatial organization.

original_record.card: A villanelle uses five three-line stanzas and a final four-line stanza, with two alternating refrains that come together at the end. Repetition provides a stable structure, while the surrounding lines can change how each returning phrase is heard or understood.

evidence.note: Stanza pattern and alternating refrains are explicit.

original_record.label: Villanelle
original_record.learning_takeaway: Two refrains alternate through five tercets and join in a final quatrain, letting recurring words acquire different force.

relations.note: The glossary identifies Bishop’s poem as a villanelle with variations in its refrains.
The Academy defines a structured poem through its stanza and refrain pattern.

original_record.card: Virginia Apgar developed a standardized way to assess a newborn soon after birth. Observations of heart rate, breathing effort, muscle tone, reflex response and color were combined into one score. Her work turned several immediate clinical observations into a repeatable assessment of the transition outside the womb.

evidence.note: NLM identifies Apgar’s standardized newborn assessment and the five observations arising from obstetrical-anesthesia research.

original_record.label: Virginia Apgar
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how a rapid standardized assessment made newborn condition more consistently observable.

relations.note: Apgar’s standardized assessment and laboratory reference intervals invite comparison of two ways clinical observations are organized, without treating the score as a laboratory reference range.

original_record.card: A virtual organization uses communication technologies to connect dispersed expertise and activities beyond a single stable workplace. It can draw on remote teams or outsourced functions. The flexibility also creates coordination problems: limited interaction may weaken trust and leave participants feeling isolated from colleagues or the organization.

evidence.note: Checked dispersion, technology dependence and qualified trust/isolation risks; not every organization using remote work is asserted to be wholly virtual.

original_record.label: Virtual organization
original_record.learning_takeaway: Coordinate geographically dispersed expertise and outsourced activities through communication technologies, with trust and isolation challenges.

relations.note: OpenStax explicitly compares virtual structures with networked teams and distinguishes their geographical and technological organization.

original_record.card: A volcano’s surface can move as conditions change below it. Repeated GPS positions and tilt measurements help researchers infer changes in a magma reservoir’s depth or volume. Monitoring deformation turns small surface shifts into clues about an inaccessible system, while still requiring interpretation alongside other evidence.

evidence.note: USGS Mount St. Helens monitoring describes surface movement, GPS/tilt instruments and estimates of reservoir depth, volume and volume change.

original_record.label: Volcano ground-deformation monitoring
original_record.learning_takeaway: Infer subsurface magma changes from repeated measurements of surface movement.

relations.note: Kīlauea’s connected summit and rift activity offers a named case for thinking about subsurface magma movement, while the method’s cited demonstration is at Mount St. Helens.

original_record.card: Vulnerability changes bridge's rewards and risks: successful contracts can earn higher bonuses, while failed contracts can incur greater penalties. In duplicate bridge, the board determines which partnership is vulnerable. This differs from rubber bridge, where winning a game changes a partnership's vulnerability.

evidence.note: ACBL vulnerability definition supports premiums, undertrick penalties and the two different assignment methods; does not conflate vulnerable status with the strength of a hand.

original_record.label: Vulnerability in bridge
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how increased bonuses and penalties change a contract's stakes.

relations.note: ACBL describes vulnerability as a scoring status affecting bridge bonuses and penalties, then distinguishes its assignment in duplicate and rubber formats.

original_record.card: In SQLite, a WAL checkpoint transfers committed changes from the write-ahead log into the main database file. It is separate from reading, writing, or committing a transaction. SQLite can schedule checkpoints automatically or let applications control when they run to manage the accumulated log.

evidence.note: Section 2.1 defines SQLite's checkpoint transfer and automatic/application-controlled timing. No claim is made that all database checkpoints transfer pages from a log or run on each commit.

original_record.label: WAL checkpointing
original_record.learning_takeaway: In SQLite, move committed log content into the database as a separate operation from reading, writing, and committing.

relations.note: SQLite's WAL documentation names checkpointing as a distinct operation within its write-ahead-log mode; the facet link concerns that documented implementation.

original_record.card: Walden recounts Thoreau’s time living by Walden Pond and has inspired readers to reconsider conventional society. An editorial reading treats the account as an experiment in ways of living. That interpretation invites reflection without claiming to establish why the book’s influence has endured.

evidence.note: The NEA note identifies the cabin account and its influence on dissenting readers.

original_record.label: Walden
original_record.learning_takeaway: Thoreau’s account of life by Walden Pond invites an editorial reading of withdrawal from conventional society as an experiment in ways of living.

relations.note: The guide connects Walden with the philosophy of Bradbury’s book-preserving community.

original_record.card: William Morris’s Wandle has a pattern repeat measuring 98.4 by 44.5 centimeters, which the V&A calls his largest attempt. An editorial comparison asks how such a large repeating unit shapes a fabric’s composition beyond the scale of its individual motifs.

evidence.note: The V&A gives Wandle’s repeat as 98.4 by 44.5 cm and calls it Morris’s largest attempt; the composition question is editorial.

original_record.label: Wandle textile design
original_record.learning_takeaway: Wandle’s repeat measures 98.4 by 44.5 centimeters; the V&A identifies it as the largest Morris attempted.

relations.note: The named pattern illustrates why repeat scale matters when considering textile composition.

original_record.card: Warp threads need suitable, reasonably even tension while weaving. On a rigid-heddle loom, too little can let the raised reed fall, while too much can make changing positions difficult and strain the yarn. Good control means balancing the working tension, not simply making every thread as tight as possible.

evidence.locator: Even tension, PDF pp. 8–10; Helpful Hints—Tension, PDF p. 15
evidence.note: Ashford instructs checking equal tension and explains too-low/too-high tension effects on its rigid-heddle reed and yarn.

original_record.label: Warp tension
original_record.learning_takeaway: Balance a warp firmly enough to form the shed without unnecessarily straining the yarn and loom.

relations.note: Warp-tension control is a specific part of managing the thread set held by a loom during weaving.

original_record.card: A warranty promises specified repair or replacement if a product fails within agreed conditions. It reduces the need for buyers to verify every aspect of quality before purchase by assigning some consequences to the seller. Its protection depends on the actual terms, rather than the label alone.

evidence.note: Checked repair/replacement commitment and time qualification; no assertion that warranties eliminate hidden defects or cover every possible failure.

original_record.label: Warranties as quality assurance
original_record.learning_takeaway: Shift specified repair or replacement obligations to a seller so buyers need not verify every quality claim beforehand.

relations.note: The textbook presents warranties as an explicit response to quality uncertainty between buyers and sellers; the response is distinct from the information gap itself.

original_record.card: In a crossover study, the effects of one treatment period can persist into the next. A washout period leaves time without the intervention so those effects can diminish. Its usefulness depends on how long effects last; an arbitrary pause does not guarantee an uncontaminated comparison.

evidence.note: UK N-of-1 guidance describes a no-intervention interval intended to diminish previous effects and discusses long-lasting/carryover limitations.

original_record.label: Washout periods in crossover trials
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explain why effects from one treatment period can contaminate the next comparison.

relations.note: A washout interval is one design provision for the repeated within-person comparisons described in N-of-1 trials.

original_record.card: In We Real Cool, Gwendolyn Brooks repeatedly places the collective pronoun at line endings before the poem’s final reference to death. An editorial reading hears group bravado meeting a sudden limit. The formal pattern makes the relation between a shared voice and its ending available for interpretation.

evidence.note: Pronoun placement and final death reference are directly visible in the poem excerpt.

original_record.label: We Real Cool
original_record.learning_takeaway: Brooks places a collective pronoun at line endings; an editorial reading connects the recurring group voice with the poem’s final reference to death.

relations.note: The glossary uses the poem’s line endings to explore how syntax continues across verse boundaries.

original_record.card: Weak ties are less-close relationships, such as acquaintances, that may connect someone to information outside their usual circle. Close friends often know many of the same people. An acquaintance can therefore provide a different route, although a tie's usefulness depends on its network position rather than weakness alone.

evidence.note: Checked information access and the nonidentity of weak ties and local bridges; no claim that every acquaintance supplies novel information.

original_record.label: Weak ties
original_record.learning_takeaway: See why acquaintances can connect people to information outside densely connected close-friend circles.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly connects weak ties with local bridges while separating interpersonal tie strength from the mathematical edge property.

original_record.card: Western Christian monasticism organized disciplined religious life through withdrawal from ordinary worldly pursuits. It could take solitary or communal forms, while monasteries also provided hospitality, learning and artistic production. Withdrawal therefore did not necessarily mean a complete absence of relationships with surrounding society.

evidence.note: Solitary/communal forms and practical/cultural services are documented.

original_record.label: Western Christian monasticism
original_record.learning_takeaway: Withdrawal into disciplined religious life could take solitary or communal forms and also sustain learning, hospitality and artistic work.

relations.note: The Benedictine rule supplies a particularly influential program for communal monastic life.

original_record.card: William Labov's study of New York speech compared linguistic variation with occupation, education, and income. It also examined differences between casual speech and reading. The case shows how social categories become research variables and why contextual variation must be considered alongside differences between groups.

evidence.note: Checked the three social measures and two contexts; correlations are not described as proof that class causes a pronunciation.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The textbook explicitly presents Labov's study as an example of quantitative sociolinguistic analysis of social status and speaking style.

original_record.label: William Labov
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how occupation, education, and income were used to compare linguistic variant frequencies across social strata.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly presents Labov's study as an example of quantitative sociolinguistic analysis of social status and speaking style.

original_record.card: An open pipe behaves acoustically as though it extends slightly beyond its physical opening. The air's motion spreads outward before the pressure reflection develops, increasing the effective vibrating length. A resonance therefore occurs slightly lower than a simple model using only the measured tube length predicts.

evidence.note: UNSW End effects explains delayed reflection and effective length; slightly and simple model preserve the approximation rather than asserting one universal correction distance.

original_record.label: Wind-instrument end correction
original_record.learning_takeaway: Understand why an open pipe resonates as though it were slightly longer.

relations.note: End corrections qualify ideal pipe predictions, including the simplified boundary-condition model used to explain clarinet register spacing.

original_record.card: The winner's curse can occur when the highest bidder also has an unusually high estimate of a shared uncertain value. Winning provides information about how optimistic that estimate was relative to others. Accounting for this selection before bidding differs from simply paying what one's initial estimate suggested.

evidence.note: Checked conditional-selection explanation; winning is not claimed to inevitably cause a loss when bidders already account for the effect.

original_record.label: Winner's curse
original_record.learning_takeaway: Condition an estimate on winning because the highest bid may reveal an unusually optimistic initial estimate.

relations.note: The lecture develops the winner's curse specifically through common-value bidding and the information revealed by winning.

original_record.card: Wood’s equilibrium moisture content can depend on whether it reached a humidity level by drying or by absorbing water. At the same temperature and relative humidity, the drying path can retain more moisture. This sorption hysteresis makes moisture history relevant even after equilibrium is reached.

evidence.note: USDA describes sorption isotherms at constant temperature and history-dependent equilibrium moisture content, with higher EMC on desorption than absorption at the same relative humidity.

original_record.label: Wood sorption hysteresis
original_record.learning_takeaway: Understand why wood’s moisture history can matter even at the same temperature and relative humidity.

relations.note: The hysteresis passage describes path dependence of wood’s equilibrium-moisture relationship, a specific aspect of that property.

original_record.card: A worked example shows a solution path rather than asking a beginner to discover every step unaided. Studying examples alongside similar problems can focus attention on how the procedure works. The IES guide also notes that the appropriate amount of guidance changes as learners develop greater expertise.

evidence.note: Checked demonstrated solutions, alternating practice, and expertise qualification; no claim that worked examples should replace all problem solving.

original_record.label: Worked example
original_record.learning_takeaway: Study a demonstrated solution path before attempting comparable problems, especially while building initial expertise.

relations.note: The worked-example recommendation explicitly discusses gradually fading examples as expertise increases.

original_record.card: Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model treats temporary mental activity as more than a single storage box. A central executive coordinates specialized systems for verbal and visual-spatial material. The later addition of an episodic buffer illustrates that this is a developing explanatory model, not an immutable anatomical diagram.

evidence.note: OpenStax 8.1 names the executive, subsystems and Baddeley 2000 buffer addition; explicitly a model, without unsupported localization or claims that the buffer belonged to the 1974 formulation.

original_record.label: Working memory model
original_record.learning_takeaway: Explore a model that separates temporary verbal and visual-spatial processing under executive control.

relations.note: The chapter introduces this as an alternative explanatory model of memory's short-term organization.

original_record.card: In SQLite's write-ahead-log mode, changes are appended to a separate log instead of immediately overwriting the main database file. A commit record marks completion, and readers can continue using an earlier view. Later checkpointing moves committed changes back into the database.

evidence.note: Checked SQLite's implementation: append changed pages, commit marker, concurrent readers and later checkpoint transfer. The card does not define every other database's WAL file layout or checkpoint semantics.

original_record.label: Write-ahead logging
original_record.learning_takeaway: See how SQLite's WAL mode appends changes separately before checkpointing them into the main database, allowing concurrent readers.

relations.note: SQLite's WAL documentation explicitly identifies checkpointing as the operation that transfers committed log content into the database.

original_record.card: Wudu is ritual washing associated with preparation for Muslim prayer. It belongs to the sequence leading into salat rather than functioning only as ordinary cleaning. An editorial comparison can consider how this bodily preparation marks the transition into formal prayer.

evidence.note: Prayer preparation includes ritual washing.

original_record.label: Wudu
original_record.learning_takeaway: Ritual washing prepares worshippers for salat, linking bodily preparation with the formal transition into prayer.

relations.note: Wudu provides a concrete preparation practice within Muslim prayer.
The salat account identifies ritual washing as preparation for Muslim prayer.

original_record.card: XMM-Newton focuses X-rays with nested mirrors struck at shallow grazing angles. Each of its three mirror modules contains fifty-eight shells, increasing the collecting surface in a compact assembly. Additional instruments separate X-ray wavelengths and observe optical and ultraviolet light, giving complementary information about the same targets.

evidence.locator: ESA; inspected passage indices 36, 37, 46, 48 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-37; paragraph-38; paragraph-47; paragraph-49
evidence.note: Nested grazing-incidence mirrors focus X-rays while separate instruments collect complementary spectra and optical data.

original_record.label: XMM-Newton
original_record.learning_takeaway: Nested grazing-incidence mirrors focus X-rays while separate instruments collect complementary spectra and optical data.

relations.note: Chandra uses the same grazing-reflection principle with a different mirror assembly, providing an engineering comparison rather than a hierarchy.

original_record.card: The Yerkes–Dodson relationship links arousal and performance while emphasizing task difficulty. A demanding task may be disrupted at an arousal level that suits a simple one. The useful lesson is not that moderate arousal always wins, but that an apparent optimum depends on the task.

evidence.note: Section 10.1 explicitly qualifies the middle-is-best simplification through difficulty; the card states a relationship and qualified example rather than a universal biological law or prescriptive stress target.

original_record.label: Yerkes–Dodson relationship
original_record.learning_takeaway: Investigate why task difficulty matters when relating arousal to performance.

relations.note: Compare performance's dependence on arousal and task difficulty with motivation's dependence on perceived capability; these are different explanations discussed in the motivation chapter.

original_record.card: Young’s modulus measures how much axial stress is needed to produce a given strain within a material’s linear elastic range. A larger value means greater stiffness, not necessarily a higher failure stress. The distinction helps separate resistance to small deformation from the limits of safe loading.

evidence.locator: 12.3 Stress, Strain, and Elastic Modulus; inspected passage indices 13, 14, 20 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1163713051760; fs-id1163713172253; fs-id1163713258776
evidence.note: Compare axial stiffness through the stress-to-strain ratio within a material’s linear elastic range.

original_record.label: Young’s modulus
original_record.learning_takeaway: Compare axial stiffness through the stress-to-strain ratio within a material’s linear elastic range.

relations.note: The elasticity source distinguishes elastic modulus from elastic limit, supporting a comparison of stiffness and permanent-deformation threshold.

original_record.card: In an ideal truss, a member can carry zero axial force under a particular load. At an unloaded joint with three members, if exactly two are collinear, the third is unloaded. It may still brace other members or carry force when the loading changes.

evidence.locator: 5.6: Methods of Truss Analysis; inspected passage indices 99, 100, 101, 102 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-100; paragraph-101; paragraph-102; paragraph-103
evidence.note: Joint geometry and loading can identify members carrying no axial force for the specific load case.

original_record.label: Zero-force truss member
original_record.learning_takeaway: Joint geometry and loading can identify members carrying no axial force for the specific load case.

relations.note: The source explains that recognizing zero-force members simplifies truss joint analysis.

original_record.card: A zero-order reaction consumes reactant at a constant rate over the conditions where its rate law applies. Increasing that reactant’s concentration does not speed the reaction. This cannot continue after the reactant is exhausted, so the constant-rate behavior has a limited operating range.

evidence.locator: 12.4 Integrated Rate Laws; inspected passage indices 59, 60 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idp474768; fs-idm91448320
evidence.note: Under specified conditions a reaction rate can remain concentration-independent until those conditions cease.

original_record.label: Zero-order reaction kinetics
original_record.learning_takeaway: Under specified conditions a reaction rate can remain concentration-independent until those conditions cease.

relations.note: Zero-order kinetics provides a concrete case of a measured concentration exponent being zero.

original_record.card: Zeugma uses one governing word to serve several parts of a sentence. Shared grammar links the elements without repeating that word. Some examples exploit different senses for wit, but the broader device does not require every instance to turn on a semantic joke.

evidence.note: BYU defines a governing word shared by multiple sentence parts.

original_record.label: Zeugma
original_record.learning_takeaway: One governing word serves multiple parts of a sentence, linking them through shared grammar rather than repeating the word.

relations.note: Grammatical yoking is a rhetorical way to organize expression and its effect.

original_record.card: Zheng He’s Ming fleets traveled through established Indian Ocean networks carrying envoys and projecting imperial prestige. Their journeys connected diplomacy, trade and demonstrations of power. Understanding those purposes shifts attention from a simple story of discovering unknown places to the political relationships the voyages sought to organize.

evidence.locator: The Emperor and His Ambition; The Seven Voyages
evidence.note: Imperial ambition, envoys and routes support the diplomatic interpretation.

original_record.label: Zheng He’s maritime expeditions
original_record.learning_takeaway: Ming fleets projected imperial prestige and carried envoys through Indian Ocean networks rather than simply opening an unknown sea route.

relations.note: Ma Huan’s participation illustrates the linguistic expertise used on one of the expeditions.

original_record.card: Zhuangzi's butterfly dream reverses the security of waking identity: was Zhuangzi dreaming of a butterfly, or is a butterfly dreaming of Zhuangzi? In the cited interpretation, the story encourages modesty about one's present perspective. Feeling released from an earlier error need not establish a final standpoint.

evidence.note: SEP's discussion around Zhuangzi 2:14 links the story to perspectival shifts and mild skepticism; in the cited interpretation avoids claiming one uncontested reading or that the story proves reality illusory.

original_record.label: Zhuangzi’s butterfly dream
original_record.learning_takeaway: Examine whether feeling awake guarantees a final, privileged perspective on experience.

relations.note: The dream provides a literary route into questions about certainty and cognitive perspective; this is an editorial learning bridge, not a claim that Zhuangzi adopted a modern epistemological doctrine.

original_record.card: Zone refining purifies silicon by moving a narrow molten region along a solid rod. Impurities more soluble in the melt travel with that moving zone. Removing an impurity-rich end improves the material’s purity, supporting the preparation of silicon for semiconductor manufacture.

evidence.locator: 18.3 Structure and General Properties of the Metalloids; inspected passage indices 24, 25 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm43188096; fs-idm29187152
evidence.note: A moving molten zone carries impurities toward the end of a silicon rod for removal.

original_record.label: Zone refining
original_record.learning_takeaway: A moving molten zone carries impurities toward the end of a silicon rod for removal.

relations.note: The source states that highly purified silicon is needed for semiconductor devices; zone refining is a material-preparation bridge.

original_record.card: Zora Neale Hurston brought her commitment to Black folklore and everyday speech into fiction. In Their Eyes Were Watching God, she also transformed experiences from her life, including surviving a hurricane. The connection shows how lived experience can become literary material without making a novel an autobiography.

evidence.note: The guide explicitly identifies folklore, idiom, a survived hurricane and non-autobiographical transformation.

original_record.label: Zora Neale Hurston
original_record.learning_takeaway: Hurston transformed lived experience, including a hurricane, into fiction while insisting on the value of Black folklore and idiom.

relations.note: The guide connects Hurston’s experience and cultural commitments with this novel.

evidence.note: Attractive interactions hold particles together; ionic solids demonstrate how charged ions produce material properties.
Supplementary inspected passage establishes the alternate example, field identity, or alias used in the takeaway.

evidence.locator: What are bonds?; What are the benefits and risks?
evidence.note: Treat a bond as an issuer's debt promise to pay specified interest and principal, with default still possible.

distinctness.reason: The chemical sense is interatomic attraction. The financial sense is a debt security with issuer repayment terms. Neither meaning subsumes or paraphrases the other.
distinctness.review_scope: Independent passage/meaning review in cross-batch report; Constitution also directly re-inspected by coordinator at freeze.

evidence.note: The source distinguishes constitutional functions from whether they occupy one document.
The clay can survive squashing although the statue cannot.

distinctness.reason: The political sense concerns basic governmental rules, powers and limits. Material constitution is the philosophical puzzle about an object and its constituting matter, illustrated by a statue and clay. These are different meanings.
distinctness.review_scope: Independent passage/meaning review in cross-batch report; Constitution also directly re-inspected by coordinator at freeze.

evidence.note: Apple scions determine the fruit variety while rootstocks influence tree size and other characteristics.

evidence.locator: What is a skin graft?; Risks—graft take
evidence.note: A graft moves detached skin to a wound; new vessels support graft take, which can fail.

distinctness.reason: Horticultural grafting joins plant scion and rootstock. Skin grafting transfers detached skin that must establish a blood supply. These are separate procedures and learning identities.
distinctness.review_scope: Independent passage/meaning review in cross-batch report; Constitution also directly re-inspected by coordinator at freeze.

evidence.note: Algebraic groups distinguish cycles that bound regions from cycles detecting holes in a space.
Tetrapod forelimbs are homologous; bird and bat wings are analogous as wings.

distinctness.reason: Biological homology concerns inherited correspondence through common ancestry. Mathematical homology uses algebraic objects to describe cycles and boundaries. Shared wording does not establish equivalence.
distinctness.review_scope: Independent passage/meaning review in cross-batch report; Constitution also directly re-inspected by coordinator at freeze.

evidence.note: Pitch may shatter under a quick blow yet flow extremely slowly over years.
The passage describes pitches rising toward the piano keyboard's right.

distinctness.reason: The selected tar-derived material has short-time brittleness and slow flow. Musical pitch is a perceived sound attribute related to frequency. Preserve both senses and their own evidence.
distinctness.review_scope: Independent passage/meaning review in cross-batch report; Constitution also directly re-inspected by coordinator at freeze.

execution.usage_note: Platform metrics not exposed; no estimates asserted.

missing_defensible_link.reason: The attached NHLBI passage establishes the target comparison but not random allocation; the generic RCT definition does not establish SPRINT’s particular design. After the auditor exhausted three primary-report alternatives, the unsupported editorial edge is removed. This is an evidence-verification gap, not a finding that SPRINT was nonrandomized.

source_locators.locator: How was the SPRINT study conducted?, lines 163–170

record.card: Genetics investigates inheritance: how genes and DNA differences relate to characteristics passed between generations. It also examines interactions with the environment. Exploring these interactions helps explain why genetic information matters while remaining only one part of the influences on an organism’s health and traits.

evidence.note: Supports inheritance, DNA variation, gene–environment interaction, and health having influences beyond genetics.

imported_records.description: Studying inheritance and variation in living organisms.

record.label: Genetics
record.learning_takeaway: Treat inheritance and gene–environment interaction as related parts of genetics.
record.original_description: Studying inheritance and variation in living organisms.

relations.note: Editorial learning connection between these selected concepts.

supplemental_full_inventory_rows.description: Studying inheritance and variation in living organisms.

record.card: Ecology studies living things together with their surroundings. It asks where organisms occur, why populations change, and how species interact. Following energy or nutrients through organisms, soil, and water offers a concrete entry into the larger systems ecologists investigate.

evidence.locator: Opening definition; Population Ecology; Community Ecology; Ecosystem Ecology
evidence.note: Supports definition, distribution, population change, species interactions, energy and nutrient flows.

imported_records.description: Studying relationships between organisms and their environments.

record.label: Ecology
record.learning_takeaway: Connect organism interactions and population changes with flows through whole ecosystems.
record.original_description: Studying relationships between organisms and their environments.

record.card: Ecology studies relationships among living things and their surroundings, from microbes to whole landscapes. A pest and its predator are one practical example: understanding where they meet and when pests are vulnerable can help protect crops through biological control.

evidence.locator: What does ecology have to do with me?; Who are Ecologists?; Pest Management, lines 96–104 and 137
evidence.note: ESA defines organism–environment relationships across scales and gives pest natural enemies and their timing as an applied example.

imported_records.description: Studying relationships between organisms and their environments.

record.label: Ecology
record.learning_takeaway: Understand relationships among organisms and their environments at scales from microbes to whole habitats.
record.original_description: Studying relationships between organisms and their environments.

relations.note: Editorial practical bridge: ecological knowledge about pest predators and their timing can inform biological pest control in cultivated spaces.

supplemental_full_inventory_rows.description: Studying relationships between organisms and their environments.

record.card: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions within workable ranges through continuing adjustments. When body temperature rises, responses such as sweating help increase heat loss. Tracing the sensors, control signals, and responses reveals negative feedback: a system acts against the change that triggered it.

evidence.locator: Opening paragraphs; Negative Feedback and Figure 1.10
evidence.note: Supports regulated ranges, temperature/sweating example, sensor-control-effector components and opposing deviations.

imported_records.description: the state of steady internal conditions maintained by living things
imported_records.subsection: Biology and health sciences / Medical sciences / Biological processes and Physiology

record.label: Homeostasis
record.learning_takeaway: Understand internal stability as active feedback regulation rather than an unchanging state.
record.original_description: the state of steady internal conditions maintained by living things

supplemental_full_inventory_rows.description: the state of steady internal conditions maintained by living things
supplemental_full_inventory_rows.subsection: Biology and health sciences / Medical sciences / Biological processes and Physiology

record.card: Kidneys partly regulate filtration by sampling their own tubular fluid. Macula densa cells detect increased flow and salt delivery, then local signals narrow the incoming arteriole and reduce filtration. This tubuloglomerular feedback links downstream sensing to the blood supply feeding the same filtering unit.

evidence.note: The tubuloglomerular section links increased tubular flow/salt with macula densa signaling, afferent constriction and reduced filtration.

record.label: Tubuloglomerular feedback
record.learning_takeaway: Trace macula densa sensing to local afferent-arteriole adjustment that opposes changes in kidney filtration.

relations.note: Editorial feedback classification: downstream salt/flow sensing changes the incoming arteriole so filtration moves back toward its regulated level.

record.card: Antidiuretic hormone changes kidney water handling by moving aquaporins, or water-channel proteins, into collecting-tubule cell membranes. More water can then leave the forming urine and return to the bloodstream. When the signal declines, channel removal reduces this permeability again.

evidence.note: The ADH section and Figure 26.12 describe insertion/removal of water channels and resulting changes in collecting-tubule permeability and water recovery.

record.label: ADH-dependent aquaporin trafficking
record.learning_takeaway: Explain reversible insertion of water channels into collecting-tubule membranes as a way to conserve body water.

relations.note: Editorial feedback classification: regulated water-channel insertion alters renal water loss, helping oppose changes in blood-plasma concentration.

record.card: Pulmonary surfactant is a mixture of lipids and proteins secreted by type II alveolar cells. It lowers surface tension in the fluid lining the lung’s air sacs. By reducing that inward pull, it helps the alveoli stay open during exhalation.

evidence.note: Type II alveolar cells secrete pulmonary surfactant composed of phospholipids and proteins, reducing surface tension.
Surfactant reduces alveolar fluid surface tension and helps prevent air-sac collapse during expiration.

record.label: Pulmonary surfactant
record.learning_takeaway: Connect type II alveolar secretion with lower surface tension and resistance to air-sac collapse.

relations.note: Surfactant lowers the alveolar surface tension that otherwise resists expansion and promotes collapse, a mechanical component of breathing.

record.card: The inner ear emits faint sounds as its outer hair cells respond to stimulation. A sensitive ear-canal microphone can record these otoacoustic emissions. Normal emissions indicate functioning outer hair cells, yet can coexist with disrupted signaling toward the brain, so they do not establish normal hearing.

evidence.locator: How is auditory neuropathy diagnosed?, lines 37–40
evidence.note: The diagnosis section describes microphone-recorded outer-hair-cell sounds and normal OAE coexisting with an abnormal brainstem response.

record.label: Otoacoustic emissions
record.learning_takeaway: Understand how sounds generated by outer hair cells can test one part of hearing without proving the entire pathway is normal.

relations.note: Editorial diagnostic bridge: emissions measure outer-hair-cell function within hearing, while the brainstem-response comparison shows why one sensory stage cannot represent the whole pathway.

record.card: A pulse oximeter estimates blood oxygen saturation using light. Skin pigmentation can affect its accuracy, and the FDA highlights concerns about poorer performance in darker skin. Circulation, skin temperature, and nail polish can also alter readings, making the displayed number an estimate with limitations.

evidence.locator: Opening explanation; FDA Efforts; February 2021 Safety Communication, lines 83, 97–131
evidence.note: The page explains optical oxygen estimates, FDA concern about darker-skin accuracy, and circulation, temperature and nail-polish effects.

record.label: Skin pigmentation and pulse oximetry
record.learning_takeaway: Explain why an optical oxygen estimate can have skin-pigmentation-dependent error and cannot be treated as an infallible reading.

relations.note: Editorial clinical bridge: interpreting an optical oxygen measurement requires accounting for pigmentation and other sources of device error.

record.card: Public health works to prevent illness and injury across communities. Outbreak tracking, vaccination programs, and workplace safety standards are among its tools. Exploring these examples shows how a population’s health can be shaped through shared systems and organized prevention.

evidence.locator: What is public health?; Why is public health important?; difference from health care
evidence.note: Supports population focus, prevention, and all three examples.

imported_records.description: Studying and supporting health at the level of populations and communities.

record.label: Public health
record.learning_takeaway: Recognize population-wide prevention across surveillance, vaccination, and safety systems.
record.original_description: Studying and supporting health at the level of populations and communities.

supplemental_full_inventory_rows.description: Studying and supporting health at the level of populations and communities.

record.card: Virginia Apgar turned observations familiar from anesthesia into a rapid assessment of newborn condition. Her system considered heart rate, breathing, reflex response, muscle tone, and color. A fixed set of signs made the first moments after birth easier to assess systematically across babies.

evidence.note: The NLM history identifies Apgar’s adaptation of anesthesia signs and lists heart rate, respiration, reflex irritability, muscle tone and color.

record.label: Virginia Apgar
record.learning_takeaway: Understand how Apgar transferred five anesthesia observations into a rapid standardized newborn assessment.

relations.note: Editorial historical bridge: Apgar transferred monitored physiological signs into a repeatable newborn assessment, linking anesthesiology to early neonatal care.

record.card: A lahar is a fast-moving mixture of water, mud, and volcanic rock flowing down a volcano’s drainage channels. Eruptions can create one by melting snow, but heavy rain or sudden water releases can also trigger flows while a volcano is not erupting.

evidence.note: The USGS summary defines the water/mud/volcanic-rock flow and lists snowmelt, rain and water releases as triggers, including inactive periods.

record.label: Lahar
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish water-rich volcanic debris flows from lava and recognize that an eruption is not required.

relations.note: Lahars transport volcanic debris and water through a volcano’s drainage network and may be triggered without an eruption.

record.card: Mountains can divide wet landscapes from dry ones. Rising air cools and loses moisture as precipitation on windward slopes; descending air warms and dries on the leeward side. Hawaii’s contrasting green and brown slopes make this rain-shadow mechanism visible in vegetation.

evidence.note: The Hawaii account explains windward cooling/precipitation, leeward warming/drying and the corresponding green/brown vegetation pattern.

record.label: Rain shadow
record.learning_takeaway: Trace orographic rain loss and leeward warming to contrasting vegetation on opposite mountain slopes.

relations.note: Editorial climatic bridge: mountain-forced ascent and descent repeatedly redistribute moisture, shaping wet and dry sides of a regional landscape.

record.card: El Niño–Southern Oscillation links changes in tropical Pacific waters with atmospheric circulation. El Niño weakens the usual trade winds, while La Niña strengthens them. Exploring the resulting shifts in warm water and upwelling shows how one ocean region can influence weather far away.

evidence.locator: Opening explanation; El Niño; La Niña
evidence.note: Supports ENSO name, opposed wind changes, warm-water movement, upwelling and global weather influence.

imported_records.description: climatic phenomenon occurring in the Pacific Ocean
imported_records.subsection: Physical sciences / Earth science / Air / Climatology

record.label: El Niño–Southern Oscillation
record.learning_takeaway: Explain distant weather connections through coupled Pacific winds and ocean conditions.
record.original_description: climatic phenomenon occurring in the Pacific Ocean

relations.note: Editorial connection between the selected learning takeaways, not a source-asserted hierarchy.

supplemental_full_inventory_rows.description: climatic phenomenon occurring in the Pacific Ocean
supplemental_full_inventory_rows.subsection: Physical sciences / Earth science / Air / Climatology

record.card: In an artesian aquifer, groundwater is confined under pressure beneath relatively impermeable layers. A well lets the water rise above the aquifer’s top. It flows onto the land only when the pressure-supported water level stands above the wellhead; great depth alone is insufficient.

evidence.locator: Artesian Water; Example of an aquifer system, lines 47–61
evidence.note: The confined-aquifer discussion distinguishes rising water from flowing wells and explains the wellhead-level condition; depth alone does not define artesian water.

record.label: Artesian aquifer
record.learning_takeaway: Explain why confined groundwater rises in a well but only sometimes flows out at ground level.

relations.note: Editorial hydrology placement: the aquifer’s confinement and hydraulic pressure determine how high water rises in a connected well.

record.card: Thermokarst develops when thawing ground ice lets the land surface subside. Water may collect in the resulting depressions. Continued thaw does not always enlarge these lakes: if a bank is breached, a lake can drain abruptly, leaving a very different landscape.

evidence.note: The thermokarst section describes ground-ice thaw, subsidence, water-filled depressions and possible abrupt drainage after a breach.

record.label: Thermokarst
record.learning_takeaway: Explain why ground-ice thaw can both create lake basins and cause existing lakes to drain.

relations.note: Editorial Earth-science placement: melting subsurface ice changes ground elevation and drainage, connecting frozen-ground physics with landform evolution.

record.card: Urban heat islands are developed areas warmer than their surroundings. Buildings and pavement absorb and slowly release heat, while reduced vegetation provides less shade and cooling through water loss. Exploring temperature differences between city blocks reveals how materials and land cover shape local conditions.

evidence.note: Supports warmer urban areas, built-surface heat storage, reduced shade/moisture, and within-city variation.

imported_records.description: Studying why built-up areas retain heat and how design can reduce it.

record.label: Urban heat islands
record.learning_takeaway: Relate neighborhood temperature differences to built surfaces and vegetation.
record.original_description: Studying why built-up areas retain heat and how design can reduce it.

relations.note: Editorial connection between the selected learning takeaways, not a source-asserted hierarchy.

record.card: Urban heat islands involve built-up areas that are warmer than their surroundings. Reduced vegetation limits shade and evaporative cooling, while buildings and pavement store heat. Surface temperatures and air temperatures are different measurements, so a hot roof does not directly describe the air above it.

evidence.note: EPA supports vegetation-related shade/moisture cooling, built-surface heat storage, and distinct surface versus atmospheric heat-island measurements.

imported_records.description: Studying why built-up areas retain heat and how design can reduce it.

record.label: Urban heat islands
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish hot urban surfaces from warmer urban air while linking both with built form and vegetation.
record.original_description: Studying why built-up areas retain heat and how design can reduce it.

relations.note: Editorial radiative bridge: the EPA describes reduced solar reflection by common urban materials; albedo formalizes that reflectivity, alongside other heat-island mechanisms.

supplemental_full_inventory_rows.description: Studying why built-up areas retain heat and how design can reduce it.

record.card: Gardening means growing plants for food, flowers, or decoration in a chosen space. That space can be a plot, balcony, or container. Comparing these settings reveals how the same activity takes different forms, from vegetable beds to indoor collections.

evidence.note: Supports plant-growing purposes and the plot, balcony, container, and indoor examples.

imported_records.description: Growing and caring for plants in gardens and small outdoor spaces.

record.label: Gardening
record.learning_takeaway: Recognize gardening as a range of plant-growing settings rather than only an outdoor vegetable plot.
record.original_description: Growing and caring for plants in gardens and small outdoor spaces.

supplemental_full_inventory_rows.description: Growing and caring for plants in gardens and small outdoor spaces.

record.card: Food fermentation uses desired microbial activity to transform ingredients. Different products reveal different effects: carbon dioxide helps bread rise, while organic acids contribute flavor and preservation in foods such as sauerkraut. The same broad practice can change taste, texture, or keeping qualities.

evidence.note: Supports intentional microbial activity, bread leavening, acids and sauerkraut, flavor, texture, and preservation.

imported_records.description: Using microorganisms to transform and preserve foods.

record.label: Fermentation (food processing)
record.learning_takeaway: Compare the distinct food transformations created by microbial products.
record.original_description: Using microorganisms to transform and preserve foods.

relations.note: Editorial connection between a food-processing practice and an overlapping cellular mechanism; this is not an identity equivalence.

record.card: Food fermentation directs microbial activity toward useful changes in an ingredient. In yogurt, bacteria produce acid that helps milk proteins form a curd and makes conditions less hospitable to many spoilage organisms. Preservation, texture, and flavor can therefore arise from the same microbial products.

evidence.note: FAO describes desired microbial transformations and yogurt’s lactic-acid curd formation and reduced spoilage susceptibility, linking flavor, texture and preservation.

imported_records.description: Using microorganisms to transform and preserve foods.

record.label: Fermentation (food processing)
record.learning_takeaway: Connect microbial acids with changes in food texture, flavor and resistance to spoilage.
record.original_description: Using microorganisms to transform and preserve foods.

relations.note: Desired microbial acid production makes conditions less favorable for many spoilage organisms, providing a documented route to food preservation.

supplemental_full_inventory_rows.description: Using microorganisms to transform and preserve foods.

record.card: Bread baking turns dough into a solid loaf through heat. In yeast-raised wheat bread, fermentation supplies gas and gluten helps trap it. Following the dough into the oven reveals how expanding gas and a setting structure produce the loaf’s familiar texture.

evidence.locator: Paragraphs on yeast, gluten, starch, and cooking
evidence.note: Supports yeast carbon dioxide, gluten gas retention, heating expansion, and solidification.

imported_records.description: Making bread through mixing, fermentation, shaping and baking.

record.label: Bread baking
record.learning_takeaway: Trace the interaction between leavening gas and dough structure during baking.
record.original_description: Making bread through mixing, fermentation, shaping and baking.

relations.note: Editorial learning connection between these selected concepts.

supplemental_full_inventory_rows.description: Making bread through mixing, fermentation, shaping and baking.

record.card: At Rothamsted, the Broadbalk Wheat Experiment has compared organic manures and mineral fertilizers since 1843. An untreated strip provides a long-running contrast. Repeated harvests let researchers examine crop and soil responses across many seasons, while documented changes in management matter when interpreting that history.

evidence.locator: Objectives and Description, lines 89–98; Experiment Design
evidence.note: The archive records 1843 establishment, mineral/manure treatments, an untreated strip, repeated harvests and soil measurements across changing design periods; interpretive caution is editorial.

record.label: Broadbalk Wheat Experiment
record.learning_takeaway: See how repeated fertilizer and manure treatments plus an untreated strip enable long-term agricultural comparisons.

relations.note: Editorial experimental application: contrasting nutrient treatments on winter wheat turns agricultural cultivation into a continuing test of crop and soil responses.

record.card: Woodworking makes useful or decorative objects from wood through crafts such as carving, turning, and joinery. Material choice influences the process. Exploring grain and workability reveals why different woods respond differently to cutting, gluing, and finishing.

evidence.note: Supports craft examples, grain, workability, tools, adhesives and finishes.

imported_records.description: Shaping and joining wood to create practical or decorative objects.

record.label: Woodworking
record.learning_takeaway: Connect woodworking techniques with the properties that shape material choice.
record.original_description: Shaping and joining wood to create practical or decorative objects.

relations.note: Editorial learning connection between these selected concepts.

record.card: Woodworking includes carving, turning, and joining wood into useful or decorative objects. Choosing a shape also means working with a changing material: wood gains and loses moisture. Drying and design can reduce the dimensional changes that otherwise affect a finished piece.

evidence.locator: Lead, line 172; Factors in choosing materials, lines 305–307
evidence.note: The lead identifies woodworking practices, including carving, turning and joinery.

evidence.locator: Drying Stresses, pp. 13–7 to 13–8; introductory moisture-control discussion p. 13–1
evidence.note: Introductory discussion explains moisture changes and how drying and design limit subsequent dimensional problems.

imported_records.description: Shaping and joining wood to create practical or decorative objects.

record.label: Woodworking
record.learning_takeaway: Connect shaping and joining wood with the need to accommodate wood’s moisture-driven movement.
record.original_description: Shaping and joining wood to create practical or decorative objects.

relations.note: Editorial making bridge: grain-dependent movement and moisture changes help explain why material choice and joinery must accommodate dimensional change.

supplemental_full_inventory_rows.description: Shaping and joining wood to create practical or decorative objects.

record.card: A dovetail joint connects boards with interlocking, tapered pins and tails that resist being pulled apart. Drawer corners are a familiar use. Comparing through dovetails with half-blind versions reveals how the same joining principle can either display or conceal the ends of the joint.

evidence.note: Supports pins/tails, pull-apart resistance, drawers and the two visibility variants.
Verifies the exact added joinery identity.

record.label: Dovetail joint
record.learning_takeaway: Compare dovetail interlocking geometry with choices about visible and concealed joinery.

relations.note: The source explicitly places dovetail joints within woodworking joinery.

record.card: Weaving builds cloth by interlacing lengthwise warp threads with crosswise weft threads. A loom holds the warp while the weft passes through. Comparing plain, twill, and satin weaves shows how changing the crossing pattern changes the structure of the resulting fabric.

evidence.note: Supports warp/weft orientation, loom function and three named weave structures.

imported_records.description: Interlacing threads or fibers to create textiles.

record.label: Weaving
record.learning_takeaway: Recognize warp and weft and connect their crossing pattern with fabric structure.
record.original_description: Interlacing threads or fibers to create textiles.

relations.note: Editorial learning connection between these selected concepts.

supplemental_full_inventory_rows.description: Interlacing threads or fibers to create textiles.

concepts.card: Genetics studies inheritance and variation, including how genes interact with the environment. A DNA difference can influence a trait without determining it alone. Studying genes alongside behavior and surroundings helps explain why genetic information is only part of the story of health.

evidence.note: NHGRI defines inheritance, DNA variation and environmental interaction; its narration explicitly treats behavior and surroundings as additional health influences.

imported_records.description: Studying inheritance and variation in living organisms.

concepts.label: Genetics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect inherited DNA variation with environmental influences rather than treating genes as destiny.
concepts.original_description: Studying inheritance and variation in living organisms.

relations.note: Mosaicism extends the inheritance discussion to DNA differences arising after fertilization, showing why genetic variation need not be shared by every cell.

concepts.card: DNA methylation adds small chemical tags to particular places on DNA. These marks can change how proteins interact with the molecule and whether nearby genes are used. The underlying DNA sequence stays the same, while its activity can change.

evidence.note: The epigenomics explanation describes methyl groups attached to DNA bases, changed DNA–protein interactions and altered gene use without sequence rewriting.

concepts.label: DNA methylation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how methyl tags influence DNA–protein interactions without rewriting the DNA sequence.

relations.note: Both are epigenomic marks, but methylation tags DNA directly while histone modification tags its packaging proteins.

concepts.card: DNA wraps around histone proteins inside the nucleus. Chemical tags placed on these proteins can be recognized by other cellular machinery, helping determine whether a region of DNA is used. This regulates access through DNA packaging rather than changing the genetic letters.

evidence.note: The histone paragraphs describe DNA wrapped around histones and reader proteins responding to attached chemical tags; epigenomic regulation does not rewrite sequence.

concepts.label: Histone modification
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish marks on DNA-packaging proteins from chemical marks directly on DNA.

relations.note: Comparing tags on histones with tags directly on DNA distinguishes two documented routes of epigenomic regulation.

concepts.card: For some genes, the copy inherited from one parent is active while the other copy is largely switched off. Genomic imprinting establishes this parent-of-origin pattern through epigenetic regulation. It shows why inheriting a gene copy and using that copy are different questions.

evidence.note: The imprinting section identifies maternal-only and paternal-only expression for a small subset of genes and says the epigenome distinguishes their copies.

concepts.label: Genomic imprinting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain parent-of-origin gene expression without a difference in the inherited DNA sequence.

relations.note: Parent-of-origin expression is a specific inheritance-related phenomenon within the study of genetics.

concepts.card: A person can have genetically different groups of cells that all descend from the same fertilized egg. This is mosaicism: a change arising during development is inherited by that cell’s descendants. Its effects depend on the variant and which cells carry it.

evidence.note: NHGRI defines genetically distinct populations from one zygote and explains post-fertilization variants and variable consequences.

concepts.label: Mosaicism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish genomic differences arising within descendants of one fertilized egg from chimerism.

relations.note: Mosaicism and chimerism can both involve different cell genomes, but their cell populations have different developmental origins.

concepts.card: Chimerism means that genetically distinct cell populations within one individual originated from different fertilized eggs. Mosaicism instead arises among descendants of a single fertilized egg. The distinction concerns the populations’ origins, even when both situations produce a body containing more than one cellular genome.

evidence.note: The NHGRI mosaicism narration explicitly contrasts chimerism from distinct zygotes with mosaicism from one zygote.

concepts.label: Chimerism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish cell populations derived from different zygotes from mosaicism within one zygote.

relations.note: The shared glossary directly contrasts different-zygote cell origins with variation within one zygote’s descendants.

concepts.card: A gene’s RNA can be assembled in different ways by joining different combinations of exons. Alternative splicing therefore produces related RNA transcripts from one gene, and these can encode proteins with different structures or functions. One gene need not yield just one protein product.

evidence.note: NHGRI’s definition states different exon combinations, related mRNA transcripts and possible proteins with distinct structure/function.

concepts.label: Alternative splicing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how different exon combinations produce multiple related transcripts from one gene.

relations.note: Alternative splicing is a specific way gene information produces varied outputs, an editorial route from the broad genetics field into gene processing.

concepts.card: Nearby positions on a chromosome tend to travel together from parent to offspring. Recombination during the formation of eggs or sperm can separate them, but closer markers are less likely to be split. Genetic linkage turns patterns of joint inheritance into clues about chromosome organization.

evidence.note: NHGRI linkage describes neighboring loci and recombination-dependent joint inheritance; the map definition links proximity to co-inheritance.

concepts.label: Genetic linkage
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect physical proximity on a chromosome with the likelihood of joint inheritance.

relations.note: Linkage mapping uses the co-inheritance pattern described by genetic linkage to infer marker order.

concepts.card: A centimorgan measures genetic recombination, not a fixed physical length of DNA. Two nearby markers separated by one centimorgan have about a one-percent chance of being separated by recombination in meiosis. Equal genetic distances therefore need not correspond to equal numbers of DNA bases.

evidence.note: The NHGRI definition gives the one-percent recombination interpretation and explicitly describes base-pair equivalence as an average.

imported_records.description: unit for measuring genetic linkage
imported_records.hook: Why can genetic distance differ from physical distance along a chromosome?

concepts.label: Centimorgan
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish recombination frequency from a fixed number of DNA base pairs.
concepts.original_description: unit for measuring genetic linkage

relations.note: Recombination-based units help interpret linkage maps, which infer marker positions from inheritance rather than directly counting bases.

concepts.card: Genetic linkage mapping follows how markers are inherited together across generations. Markers that are rarely separated by recombination are generally closer together on a chromosome. Comparing inheritance patterns lets researchers infer relative order and position, rather than directly reading a physical sequence of DNA bases.

evidence.note: The inspected NHGRI Genetic Map definition specifically identifies linkage maps, co-inheritance, relative marker order and location.

concepts.label: Genetic linkage mapping
concepts.learning_takeaway: Infer marker order from joint inheritance rather than directly measuring physical DNA length.

relations.note: This mapping method applies the proximity-dependent co-inheritance relationship described by genetic linkage.

concepts.card: Carrying a disease-associated genetic variant does not always mean developing the condition. Reduced penetrance describes this incomplete appearance among people with the variant. Genetic background, environment and lifestyle may contribute, making a family’s inheritance pattern harder to interpret than a simple all-or-nothing prediction.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus defines penetrance as the proportion with signs and identifies incomplete expression and probable multifactorial causes.

concepts.label: Reduced penetrance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why not everyone carrying a disease-associated variant develops that condition.

relations.note: Penetrance asks whether a condition appears, while expressivity asks how its manifestations differ among affected people.
