concepts.card: People with the same genetic condition can have different signs, symptoms or severity. Variable expressivity describes that range of manifestations. It differs from reduced penetrance, which concerns whether the condition appears at all, and helps explain why affected relatives need not look clinically identical.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus distinguishes a range of manifestations from the proportion showing a disorder and describes differences among affected people.

concepts.label: Variable expressivity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish variation in a condition’s manifestations from whether it appears at all.

relations.note: The source treats presence of manifestations and range of manifestations as separate questions.

concepts.card: The International HapMap Project charted common patterns of human DNA variation, especially groups of variants often inherited together. These genomic neighborhoods helped researchers connect variation with disease. Its contribution was a map of shared variation patterns, rather than merely another sequence from a single individual.

evidence.note: NHGRI identifies the project, co-inherited haplotypes, common human variation and the use of linkage-disequilibrium patterns in disease studies.

concepts.label: International HapMap Project
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how patterns of co-inherited DNA variants helped connect genomic variation with disease.

relations.note: HapMap’s co-inherited variant neighborhoods give a named research example of genomic linkage patterns; the project is not the general linkage mechanism.

concepts.card: ENCODE, the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements, investigates the working parts of the genome. Its research includes epigenomic maps from different cell types, helping distinguish the DNA sequence a cell carries from the regions it uses. A shared genome can support different cellular patterns of activity.

evidence.locator: How are researchers exploring the epigenome?
evidence.note: NHGRI states that ENCODE catalogs working genomic parts and includes cell-type epigenomic maps; the same fact sheet explains differentiated cells and altered marks.

concepts.label: ENCODE
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish identifying functional genomic elements from merely obtaining a DNA sequence.

relations.note: Histone marks are one kind of epigenomic information that makes ENCODE’s cell-type maps useful for studying differential genome use.

concepts.card: Some inherited disorders appear earlier or become more severe in successive generations. Genetic anticipation can arise when unstable repeated DNA sequences expand during transmission. Differences between relatives alone do not establish it: researchers consider the disorder’s genetic cause and patterns across several generations.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus connects anticipation with earlier/more severe manifestations and repeat expansion, while warning that ordinary variation among relatives has other causes.

concepts.label: Genetic anticipation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect expanding repeat sequences with earlier or more severe inherited disease in some families.

relations.note: Contrasting anticipation with variable expressivity prevents ordinary differences among affected relatives from being mistaken for a generational expansion pattern.

concepts.card: Ecology investigates how organisms interact with one another and with their surroundings. A butterfly’s food plant, predators and climate can all shape where it survives. Moving between individuals, populations and communities helps researchers connect small interactions with larger patterns of abundance and distribution.

evidence.note: OpenStax defines ecology and its levels, then uses the Karner blue butterfly to connect organismal requirements with community interactions.

imported_records.description: Studying relationships between organisms and their environments.

concepts.label: Ecology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect organisms’ distribution and abundance with living and nonliving surroundings.
concepts.original_description: Studying relationships between organisms and their environments.

relations.note: The Karner blue example connects the field’s organism and community scales through habitat requirements and ant–larva interactions.

concepts.card: Karner blue butterfly larvae can exchange a sugary secretion for protection from ants. The ants gain food, while their attendance can reduce threats to the caterpillars. This butterfly offers a concrete example of mutualism, with the particular ant partners varying between locations.

evidence.note: The community-ecology passage describes carbohydrate-rich larval secretions, ant protection and variation in attending ant species.

concepts.label: Karner blue butterfly
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how ant attendance can protect butterfly larvae while the ants receive carbohydrate-rich secretions.

relations.note: The documented food-for-protection exchange illustrates mutualism in this named butterfly.

concepts.card: Mutualism is an interaction between species in which both participants benefit. Ants attending Karner blue butterfly larvae provide protection and receive carbohydrate-rich secretions in return. Examining what each partner gains turns a vague picture of cooperation into a testable account of a biological exchange.

evidence.note: OpenStax explicitly defines mutual benefit and supplies the ant–butterfly exchange used here.

concepts.label: Mutualism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize interspecific exchanges in which both partners benefit, as in ant-tended butterfly larvae.

relations.note: Mutualism is a particular interspecific interaction studied at ecology’s community level.

concepts.card: Two species competing for exactly the same limiting resources cannot indefinitely occupy the same niche under the competitive exclusion principle. Laboratory comparisons with Paramecium illustrate one competitor displacing another. Coexistence becomes more plausible when species differ in resource use, habitat or feeding time.

evidence.note: The OpenStax exclusion section presents same-niche competition and the Paramecium example, then explains resource partitioning as an avoidance route.

concepts.label: Competitive exclusion principle
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why competing for all the same limiting resources can prevent stable coexistence.

relations.note: Partitioning reduces the overlap in resource use on which competitive exclusion depends.

concepts.card: Species can reduce direct competition by using different foods, different parts of a habitat or different feeding times. Resource partitioning separates their ecological niches even when they live nearby. The key distinction is how resources are used, rather than simply how many species are present.

evidence.note: The resource-partitioning paragraph names different resources, habitat areas and feeding times as ways to minimize direct competition.

concepts.label: Resource partitioning
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how different food, places or feeding times can reduce direct competition.

relations.note: The exclusion discussion introduces resource partitioning as a way species avoid complete niche overlap.

concepts.card: Foundation species help build the physical setting of a community. Kelp forms underwater forests, while reef-building corals create habitats used by many other organisms. Their importance comes from shaping the environment that supports the community, rather than simply being another species within it.

evidence.note: OpenStax’s Foundation Species passage identifies kelp forests and coral habitat construction as community-shaping examples.

concepts.label: Foundation species
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect habitat structure supplied by organisms with the communities that depend on it.

relations.note: Habitat construction by foundation species can be compared with ecosystem engineering, while avoiding an assertion that the two categories are identical.

concepts.card: A keystone species plays an especially important role in its community. On rocky shores, sea stars eat mussels that might otherwise dominate available space. Removing that predator can therefore change which other organisms are able to persist alongside the mussels.

evidence.note: The NPS sea-star account identifies keystone predation and mussel competition for intertidal space, with diversity effects.

concepts.label: Keystone species
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how a predator can maintain community diversity by limiting a space-dominating competitor.

relations.note: Pisaster ochraceus is the named sea-star example behind the predator–mussel community mechanism.

concepts.card: The ochre sea star, Pisaster ochraceus, feeds on mussels along rocky shores. By limiting mussels that would otherwise occupy much of the available surface, it helps other organisms retain space. This makes its feeding behavior a useful case of a predator shaping community diversity.

evidence.note: NPS names the sea star and California mussels and explains how predation prevents mussels from crowding out other intertidal species.

concepts.label: Pisaster ochraceus
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore why ochre sea-star predation on mussels helps preserve rocky-shore diversity.

relations.note: The named sea star provides the documented ecological example for the keystone-species concept.

concepts.card: Ecological succession describes changes in a community through time, often after disturbance. Research at Mount St. Helens showed that surviving organisms and other biological legacies strongly affected recovery. Different places followed different trajectories, challenging the idea that every recovering landscape passes through one fixed sequence.

evidence.note: The USFS account defines succession and highlights biological legacies, varied recovery rates and differing post-eruption trajectories.

imported_records.description: process of change in the species structure of an ecological community over time
imported_records.hook: How does a community change as organisms transform their habitat?

concepts.label: Ecological succession
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace community change after disturbance while allowing surviving organisms to shape recovery.
concepts.original_description: process of change in the species structure of an ecological community over time

relations.note: Succession is community change through time, a specific problem within ecology’s study of interacting populations and environments.

concepts.card: On Isle Royale in Lake Superior, a long-running study follows wolves, moose and their environment. Predator numbers matter, but disease, climate and available food also influence population changes. The island illustrates why a predator–prey relationship cannot be understood from two population counts alone.

evidence.locator: Why is Isle Royale a Unique Research Location?; Predator-Prey Relationships
evidence.note: NPS locates the island in Lake Superior and documents the long-running study, disease effects and changing roles of climate and forage.

concepts.label: Isle Royale
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use an isolated island study to distinguish predator effects from climate, disease and food availability.

relations.note: The island study demonstrates ecology’s need to consider interacting predators, prey and environmental conditions.

concepts.card: Organisms can alter the physical environment that other species use. Beavers, for example, build dams that create aquatic habitats and change local living conditions. Ecosystem engineering draws attention to these habitat modifications, extending the study of species interactions beyond who eats whom.

evidence.note: The NPS Wolves and Beaver passage explicitly calls beavers ecosystem engineers and describes dams creating aquatic habitat.

concepts.label: Ecosystem engineering
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how organisms change physical habitat for other species, using beaver dams.

relations.note: Physical habitat modification by organisms is an ecological interaction connecting species with the environment they create.

concepts.card: Stressed corals can lose the symbiotic algae living in their tissues, leaving them pale or white. This bleaching also removes an important food source. A bleached coral is not necessarily dead, but prolonged stress makes recovery harder and can ultimately lead to death.

evidence.note: NOAA explains stress-driven expulsion of symbiotic algae, loss of color and food, possible recovery and death if stress persists.

concepts.label: Coral bleaching
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish stress-driven loss of symbiotic algae from immediate coral death.

relations.note: Bleaching shows what can happen when a coral’s beneficial partnership with algae is disrupted.

concepts.card: Organisms leave genetic traces in water, sediment and other surroundings through shed cells and biological material. Environmental DNA sampling uses those traces to investigate which organisms may be present. It can reveal a species without requiring researchers to catch or directly observe that organism.

evidence.note: The USGS EDNA definition lists environmental samples and genetic material shed by organisms; this supports indirect detection.

concepts.label: Environmental DNA
concepts.learning_takeaway: Detect organisms through genetic traces in environmental samples without having to capture them.

relations.note: Metabarcoding is one way to analyze mixed environmental DNA for multiple species.

concepts.card: DNA metabarcoding examines a mixed sample for traces of multiple species. Broadly targeted primers amplify DNA fragments, and high-throughput sequencing reads the resulting mixture. The approach turns one pooled sample into a multispecies assessment rather than a test focused on only one organism.

evidence.note: USGS defines metabarcoding through nonspecific primers, PCR, high-throughput sequencing and identifying multiple species in a pooled sample.

concepts.label: DNA metabarcoding
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify multiple species from a pooled DNA sample using broad primers and sequencing.

relations.note: The glossary presents metabarcoding as a multispecies analysis of a pooled DNA sample, making it an editorial application link to environmental-DNA investigation.

concepts.card: A negative eDNA test may mean the assay was inhibited, not that the species was absent. Substances such as humic acids can interfere with PCR. An internal positive control helps reveal this problem by checking whether DNA amplification succeeds inside the tested sample.

evidence.note: USGS defines inhibited samples, names humic acids and describes internal positive controls detecting inhibition or false negatives.

concepts.label: PCR inhibition in eDNA samples
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why a negative molecular detection can reflect assay inhibition rather than species absence.

relations.note: Inhibition is a specific limitation of interpreting environmental-DNA tests; it concerns assay performance rather than the biological absence of a species.

concepts.card: Genetic drift changes how common gene variants are through chance differences in which individuals reproduce. A variant can become common or disappear without providing an advantage. This distinguishes random sampling across generations from natural selection, which links reproductive differences to traits affecting success.

evidence.note: Berkeley distinguishes chance changes in variant frequency from adaptive natural selection and describes variants spreading or disappearing.

imported_records.description: variation in the relative frequency of different genotypes in a small population
imported_records.subsection: Biology and health sciences / Biological sciences in general / Genetics

imported_records.description: variation in the relative frequency of different genotypes in a small population
imported_records.hook: Explore how chance changes the frequency of gene variants in a population.

concepts.label: Genetic drift
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish chance differences in reproduction from selection favoring a useful trait.
concepts.original_description: variation in the relative frequency of different genotypes in a small population

relations.note: A population bottleneck supplies a demographic setting in which random loss of variants can become especially strong.

concepts.card: A population bottleneck sharply reduces the number of individuals contributing genes to later generations. Chance can eliminate variants during that small-population period. Even if numbers subsequently rebound, the lost diversity need not return, as the history of heavily hunted northern elephant seals illustrates.

evidence.locator: Population bottlenecks; An example of a bottleneck
evidence.note: Berkeley defines bottlenecks and uses northern elephant seals to show numerical recovery with persistently reduced genetic variation.

concepts.label: Population bottleneck
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why rapid numerical recovery need not restore lost genetic diversity.

relations.note: A bottleneck is a demographic circumstance that magnifies genetic drift through a small surviving sample.

concepts.card: When a new population begins with only a few colonists, its genetic frequencies can differ markedly from the source population. The founder effect arises because those founders are a small sample. Their descendants may inherit unusual frequencies without the variants offering any local advantage.

evidence.note: The Berkeley founder-effect section describes colonization by a few individuals and altered genetic variation/frequencies through sampling.

concepts.label: Founder effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how a few colonists can establish unrepresentative genetic frequencies.

relations.note: Founding a population from a small sample is a specific demographic route to drift, distinct from survival after a population crash.

concepts.card: A trait can improve success in obtaining mates while making survival harder. Sexual selection explains why conspicuous ornaments or risky mating behavior can spread despite such costs. The relevant outcome is contribution to the next generation, not simply how long an individual stays alive.

evidence.note: Berkeley contrasts mating success with survival costs and describes conspicuous ornaments and risky redback mating behavior.

concepts.label: Sexual selection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish mating success from survival when explaining conspicuous or risky traits.

relations.note: Redback sexual cannibalism offers a documented case for examining reproductive success despite a survival cost.

concepts.card: Coevolution occurs when interacting species influence one another’s evolution. A change in one partner can alter the selection pressures faced by the other, prompting a reciprocal response. Merely finding two species together, or observing both change, does not by itself demonstrate this evolutionary feedback.

evidence.note: Berkeley defines coevolution as reciprocal evolutionary influence and qualifies inference from the acacia–ant example.

imported_records.description: two or more species evolving together

concepts.label: Coevolution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize reciprocal evolutionary effects rather than merely two species changing at the same time.
concepts.original_description: two or more species evolving together

relations.note: Mutualistic partners can provide a setting for reciprocal selection, but mutual benefit alone does not establish coevolution.

concepts.card: In biology, homologous features resemble one another because they descend from a shared ancestral feature. Bird and bat forelimbs are homologous, even though their wings evolved separately as flight structures. The comparison shows why common ancestry and similarity of present-day function must be distinguished.

evidence.note: Berkeley explicitly treats bird/bat forelimbs as homologous and their wings as independently evolved analogous flight structures.

concepts.label: Homology (biology)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify similarity inherited from common ancestry, even when present-day functions differ.

relations.note: The same bird–bat comparison separates common-ancestry resemblance from independently evolved similarity in flight.

concepts.card: Convergent evolution produces similar features in separate evolutionary lineages. Bird and bat wings both serve flight, but their wing structures arose independently. Their underlying forelimbs still share ancestry, showing that the answer depends on which feature and evolutionary level a comparison is examining.

evidence.note: Berkeley connects analogous wings with convergent evolution while distinguishing homologous forelimbs.

concepts.label: Convergent evolution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain similar functions that evolved separately rather than being inherited from a shared ancestor.

relations.note: Contrasting wing function with forelimb ancestry makes convergence and biological homology distinguishable without making them mutually exclusive at every level.

concepts.card: The neutral theory of molecular evolution emphasizes mutation and genetic drift in explaining much genetic variation. When alternative gene versions do not differ in fitness, chance can change their frequencies. This does not mean all variation is neutral or that natural selection is unimportant.

evidence.note: Berkeley emphasizes mutation and drift and defines the illustrative neutral alternatives as having no difference in fitness. It explicitly rejects claims that all variation is neutral or selection is unimportant.

concepts.label: Neutral theory of molecular evolution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate neutral genetic variation and drift from the claim that all evolution is nonadaptive.

relations.note: Neutral theory assigns a major explanatory role to genetic drift for variants with no fitness difference, rather than introducing a different drift mechanism.

concepts.card: Gene duplication produces an extra copy of a gene or DNA segment. Such changes have contributed to genome evolution, but they can also cause disease. Duplication of the human PMP22 gene, for example, is a common cause of one form of Charcot–Marie–Tooth neuropathy.

evidence.note: NHGRI defines duplicated DNA segments, evolutionary importance and the PMP22 example of Charcot–Marie–Tooth type 1A.

imported_records.description: duplication of a gene sequence within a genome

concepts.label: Gene duplication
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how extra gene copies can alter dosage and contribute to genomic evolution.
concepts.original_description: duplication of a gene sequence within a genome

relations.note: Duplication changes the inherited genomic material studied by genetics and offers both evolutionary and disease examples.

concepts.card: Maydianne Andrade investigated why male redback spiders sometimes risk being eaten during mating. Her observations and experiments compared nutritional, remating and paternity explanations. The case shows how an apparently self-defeating behavior can be studied by separating competing hypotheses and measuring reproductive consequences.

evidence.note: Berkeley’s teaching case names Andrade, lays out the three hypotheses and describes observations and laboratory experiments.

concepts.label: Maydianne Andrade
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how competing explanations for redback mating behavior can be tested with observations and experiments.

relations.note: Andrade’s named research program supplies the experiments used to study the redback sexual-cannibalism case.

concepts.card: In laboratory redback-spider observations, second males that were cannibalized mated longer, and longer mating was associated with more paternity. This offers a possible reproductive explanation for a behavior that risks death. The evidence concerns a small experimental sample, not a guaranteed outcome for every male.

evidence.note: The case specifies second males, longer mating among cannibalized males, a positive mating-duration/paternity association and ten matings.

concepts.label: Sexual cannibalism in redback spiders
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore why a mating behavior that risks death can still correlate with increased paternity.

relations.note: The case illustrates the sexual-selection question of reproductive benefit despite a survival cost, without making every death adaptive.

concepts.card: A feature’s current job need not be the reason it originally evolved. Exaptation describes a trait co-opted for a use that did not originally shape it by natural selection. Feathers possibly selected for insulation before flight illustrate the distinction between origin and later function.

evidence.note: Berkeley defines co-option and presents insulation-first feathers as a possible historical example.

concepts.label: Exaptation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a trait’s present use from the selective context in which it arose.

relations.note: Comparing exaptation with convergence separates a change of function in an inherited feature from the independent evolution of similar functions.

concepts.card: Mitochondria retain their own genetic material, divide in a bacteria-like way and have surrounding membranes consistent with an engulfed ancestor. These clues support endosymbiotic origins from once-independent cells. The broad ancestry is well supported even while details of the earliest host–partner sequence remain debated.

evidence.note: OpenStax discusses mitochondrial genomes, fission-like division, membranes and unresolved ordering relative to the host nucleus.

concepts.label: Endosymbiotic theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use organelle genomes, division and membranes as evidence of ancestry from once-independent cells.

relations.note: Organelle similarities and shared ancestry offer a molecular/cellular setting for the ancestry reasoning introduced by biological homology.

concepts.card: Genetic information can move between cells outside ordinary parent-to-offspring inheritance. In prokaryotes, transformation takes up environmental DNA, transduction uses viruses, and conjugation transfers DNA through cell contact. Horizontal gene transfer therefore offers several routes for acquiring genetic material without reproducing a whole new organism.

evidence.note: OpenStax defines horizontal transfer and separately describes transformation, transduction and conjugation.

concepts.label: Horizontal gene transfer
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish DNA exchange outside parent-to-offspring inheritance from ordinary reproduction.

relations.note: Horizontal transfer broadens the genetics discussion from vertical inheritance to acquisition of DNA from other cells.

concepts.card: In the E. coli Long-Term Evolution Experiment, researchers replayed evolution using bacteria from different points in one population’s history. Later samples were more likely to evolve aerobic citrate use. The result showed how earlier genetic changes could enable a later innovation, making evolutionary history experimentally testable.

evidence.note: The 2008 primary abstract reports replay experiments from different generations and a higher probability of aerobic citrate use in later clones, supporting historical contingency under the experiment’s oxic conditions.

concepts.label: E. coli Long-Term Evolution Experiment
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how revived archived populations let researchers test whether prior mutations enabled a later innovation.

relations.note: Replaying different inherited genetic backgrounds links this experiment to genetics through the effect of prior changes on a later trait.

concepts.card: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions within workable ranges through continuous adjustment. Sensors detect changes, and responses can oppose those deviations through negative feedback. Stability therefore does not mean that temperature, pressure or other values never move; it means regulation limits their departures from suitable conditions.

evidence.note: OpenStax defines stable internal conditions with dynamic fluctuations and explains negative feedback through sensing and corrective responses.

imported_records.description: the state of steady internal conditions maintained by living things
imported_records.subsection: Biology and health sciences / Medical sciences / Biological processes and Physiology

concepts.label: Homeostasis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand stable internal conditions as ongoing sensing and correction rather than complete constancy.
concepts.original_description: the state of steady internal conditions maintained by living things

relations.note: The baroreflex supplies a concrete pressure-control example of negative-feedback regulation.

concepts.card: When arterial pressure rises, stretch-sensitive baroreceptors increase their signaling to the brainstem. Reflex changes reduce cardiac output and relax peripheral vessels, helping oppose the rise. Falling pressure produces responses in the other direction. The baroreflex links mechanical stretch to rapid cardiovascular adjustment.

evidence.note: The baroreceptor passage gives increased stretch/firing, brainstem integration, reduced cardiac output and vasodilation, with opposite responses to falling pressure.

concepts.label: Baroreflex
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace a blood-pressure change from arterial stretch receptors to rapid cardiac and vascular responses.

relations.note: A sensed pressure deviation evokes opposing cardiac and vascular responses, making this a specific homeostatic feedback mechanism.

concepts.card: Reduced pressure at the kidney can trigger renin release and a cascade producing angiotensin II. This constricts vessels and stimulates aldosterone, which promotes sodium retention; water retention then supports blood volume. The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system connects circulation with the kidney’s handling of salt and water.

evidence.note: OpenStax describes renal renin release, angiotensin II vasoconstriction and aldosterone-mediated sodium/water retention.

concepts.label: Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect reduced renal pressure with vasoconstriction and sodium retention through a hormonal cascade.

relations.note: Comparing this volume-retaining cascade with atrial natriuretic peptide shows hormonal responses acting in opposing directions.

concepts.card: Stretch of the heart’s atria can stimulate release of atrial natriuretic peptide. The signal promotes sodium and water loss through the kidneys and suppresses hormones that retain them. It connects increased cardiac filling with a response that helps reduce excess circulating volume.

evidence.note: The atrial-natriuretic paragraph describes stretch-triggered secretion, sodium/water loss and opposition to renin, aldosterone and ADH.

concepts.label: Atrial natriuretic peptide
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how cardiac stretch signals the kidneys to lose sodium and water.

relations.note: ANP’s excretory response opposes the sodium/water-retaining hormonal cascade, a physiological comparison rather than identity equivalence.

concepts.card: The kidney’s incoming arteriole responds directly to pressure changes. Rising pressure stretches its smooth muscle, which contracts and increases resistance; falling pressure permits relaxation. This local myogenic response helps stabilize renal blood flow without requiring a fresh instruction from nerves or circulating hormones.

evidence.note: OpenStax’s renal myogenic mechanism identifies the afferent arteriole, stretch-induced contraction, lower-pressure relaxation and intrinsic autoregulation.

concepts.label: Renal myogenic autoregulation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how pressure-induced contraction of an afferent arteriole stabilizes renal flow.

relations.note: Both contribute to renal autoregulation, but the myogenic response senses vessel stretch while tubuloglomerular feedback senses tubular conditions.

concepts.card: Cells along a kidney tubule sense changes in the fluid and salt reaching them. Their local signals adjust resistance in the arteriole feeding the filter. Tubuloglomerular feedback therefore uses information downstream of filtration to help regulate how much new fluid is filtered.

evidence.note: The renal-flow passage identifies macula densa sensing of tubular conditions and local afferent-arteriole responses that change glomerular filtration.

concepts.label: Tubuloglomerular feedback
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace tubular salt delivery to local changes in afferent-arteriole resistance.

relations.note: Tubular sensing and direct vessel-wall stretch are two different inputs to renal autoregulation.

concepts.card: Antidiuretic hormone increases the number of aquaporin water channels in the kidney’s collecting-duct cell membranes. Water can then leave the forming urine along an osmotic gradient. With less hormone, fewer channels are inserted, less water is recovered and the urine can remain more dilute.

evidence.locator: Collecting Ducts and Recovery of Water
evidence.note: The collecting-duct passage states ADH-dependent apical insertion, osmotic water movement and fewer channels/more dilute urine with less ADH.

concepts.label: ADH-dependent aquaporin trafficking
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how reversible water-channel insertion changes collecting-duct water recovery.

relations.note: Aquaporin-dependent water recovery uses the medullary osmotic gradient generated in part by countercurrent multiplication.

concepts.card: Fluid travels in opposite directions through neighboring limbs of the kidney’s loop of Henle. The descending limb allows water to leave, while the thick ascending limb moves salt outward without water following. These differences help build the medullary concentration gradient used to recover water.

evidence.locator: Descending Loop; Ascending Loop; Countercurrent Multiplier System
evidence.note: The descending/thick-ascending passages support unequal water permeability, active salt reabsorption and the opposing-flow arrangement.

concepts.label: Renal countercurrent multiplication
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how opposite flows and unequal permeability build a medullary concentration gradient.

relations.note: The gradient-building arrangement supports the water recovery that ADH-regulated collecting-duct channels permit.

concepts.card: When metabolism makes the blood too acidic, increased ventilation can remove more carbon dioxide. This shifts the carbonic-acid balance and helps raise pH toward its usual range. Respiratory compensation can limit the disturbance, but it does not itself remove the underlying metabolic cause.

evidence.locator: Respiratory Regulation of Acid-Base Balance, paragraphs on CO2 removal
evidence.note: The respiratory-regulation section connects increased rate/depth of breathing, CO2 loss, lower carbonic acid and upward pH adjustment.

concepts.label: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect increased ventilation with lower carbon dioxide and partial correction of low blood pH.

relations.note: An arterial blood gas sample measures both carbon dioxide and pH, the quantities needed to examine this compensation mechanism.

concepts.card: Hemoglobin releases oxygen more readily when its surroundings become more acidic. This pH-dependent change in oxygen affinity is the Bohr effect. It helps connect local chemical conditions with oxygen unloading, rather than treating hemoglobin as a container that releases oxygen at one fixed rate.

evidence.locator: Oxygen Dissociation from Hemoglobin, pH paragraph
evidence.note: OpenStax explicitly states that lower pH promotes oxygen dissociation and higher pH inhibits it.

concepts.label: Bohr effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why lower pH promotes oxygen unloading from hemoglobin.

relations.note: The Bohr effect concerns acidity changing oxygen affinity; the Haldane effect concerns oxygenation changing carbon-dioxide carriage.

concepts.card: Hemoglobin binds carbon dioxide more readily when less oxygen is attached to it. Oxygenation therefore changes its capacity to carry carbon dioxide, a relationship called the Haldane effect. This differs from the Bohr effect, where acidity changes how readily hemoglobin releases oxygen.

evidence.note: The Haldane paragraph compares CO2 binding by oxygenated and less-oxygenated hemoglobin; the Bohr paragraph provides the contrasting pH relationship.

concepts.label: Haldane effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish oxygenation-dependent carbon-dioxide carriage from pH-dependent oxygen affinity.

relations.note: These paired effects concern different directions of influence between hemoglobin’s gases and the chemical environment.

concepts.card: Low thyroid-hormone levels stimulate a signaling chain from hypothalamic TRH to pituitary TSH and then the thyroid gland. As thyroid hormones rise, they reduce further stimulation through negative feedback. The system regulates output through returning information, rather than a one-way sequence of commands.

evidence.note: The thyroid regulation section describes low T3/T4, TRH, anterior-pituitary TSH, thyroid secretion and inhibition of further TSH production.

concepts.label: Hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid feedback
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace TRH and TSH stimulation together with thyroid-hormone feedback.

relations.note: The returning thyroid-hormone signal provides a specific endocrine example of negative-feedback homeostasis.

concepts.card: Insulin and glucagon help keep blood glucose within a usable range. Insulin favors glucose uptake and storage after levels rise; glucagon helps mobilize glucose, including from liver glycogen, when levels fall. Their opposing actions connect changing food availability with the body’s ongoing fuel needs.

evidence.note: The pancreas chapter describes insulin-associated uptake/storage and glucagon-associated liver glycogen breakdown during low glucose.

concepts.label: Insulin–glucagon regulation of blood glucose
concepts.learning_takeaway: Contrast glucose storage and uptake after a meal with glucose mobilization during fasting.

relations.note: Opposing responses to rising and falling glucose provide a concrete regulated-variable example within homeostasis.

concepts.card: Sweat cools the body when it evaporates from the skin and carries heat into the surrounding air. Producing liquid alone is not the whole cooling mechanism. The response works alongside changes in skin blood flow as part of the body’s feedback control of temperature.

evidence.note: The homeostasis passage links increased sweating, skin blood flow and heat removed as sweat evaporates.

concepts.label: Evaporative cooling by sweating
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why sweat cools the body when it evaporates from the skin.

relations.note: Sweating is an effector response in the cited temperature-regulation feedback example.

concepts.card: Pulmonary surfactant helps the lungs remain expanded so air sacs can participate in breathing. Premature newborns may have too little, allowing lung collapse and making breathing much harder. The example connects a substance within the lung with the mechanical ability to keep air spaces open.

evidence.note: NHLBI identifies inadequate surfactant as a cause of neonatal respiratory distress, lung collapse and increased work of breathing.

concepts.label: Pulmonary surfactant
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect surfactant deficiency with air-sac collapse and difficult breathing in premature newborns.

relations.note: Surfactant concerns lung mechanics, while spirometry measures aspects of breathing performance; the link is a learning comparison, not a claim that neonatal surfactant deficiency is diagnosed by spirometry.

concepts.card: Spirometry records how much air a person can blow out and how quickly it leaves the lungs. A forceful breath into a measuring device produces information about airflow and volume. It is one part of lung-function assessment, rather than a single test that identifies every breathing disorder.

evidence.locator: Common lung function tests; Spirometry procedure
evidence.note: MedlinePlus describes forceful expiration into a spirometer and measurement of exhaled amount and speed.

concepts.label: Spirometry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Measure both the amount and speed of exhaled air to investigate lung function.

relations.note: Spirometry’s exhaled airflow/volume measurements contrast with the total and residual lung-volume information from body plethysmography.

concepts.card: Body plethysmography measures lung volumes, including air that remains after a person breathes out as fully as possible. Testing takes place in an enclosed booth. This adds information beyond the air a person can blow through a spirometer, helping distinguish different aspects of lung function.

evidence.locator: Lung volume test; Body plethysmography procedure
evidence.note: MedlinePlus’s lung-volume test description includes the enclosed booth, total capacity and remaining air after full expiration.

concepts.label: Body plethysmography
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish measuring residual lung volume from measuring only air that can be exhaled.

relations.note: The two procedures assess different aspects of lung function: exhaled flow/volume versus volumes including retained air.

concepts.card: A pulse oximeter shines light through tissue to estimate blood oxygen saturation. A small sensor can provide this information without drawing arterial blood. The reading is an estimate, however, and factors including poor circulation, cold skin or skin pigmentation can affect its accuracy.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus describes the optical sensor and estimated oxygen saturation; its listed limitations include poor circulation, cold skin and darker skin pigmentation.

concepts.label: Pulse oximetry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Estimate blood oxygen saturation from light passing through tissue.

relations.note: Skin pigmentation is one specifically documented limitation of the broader optical measurement method.

concepts.card: An arterial blood gas test analyzes a blood sample for oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH. These measurements address oxygenation, removal of carbon dioxide and acid–base balance together. Unlike a light-based pulse-oximeter reading, the test requires blood from an artery and supplies information beyond oxygen saturation.

evidence.locator: What is an arterial blood gas test?
evidence.note: Supports arterial blood sampling and the oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH measurements.
Supports the light-based, noninvasive oxygen-saturation comparison.

concepts.label: Arterial blood gas testing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish blood oxygenation, carbon-dioxide removal and acid-base measurements in one arterial sample.

relations.note: An arterial sample can assess CO2 and pH alongside oxygen, whereas the optical method estimates saturation; the methods are not interchangeable.

concepts.card: Tympanometry changes air pressure in the ear canal and records how the eardrum responds. The resulting graph helps assess the mechanics of the eardrum and middle ear. It differs from asking someone whether they can hear a tone: movement and hearing threshold are separate measurements.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus describes a pressure-varying probe and eardrum-movement graphs, separately from behavioral audiometry.

concepts.label: Tympanometry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Assess middle-ear mechanics by measuring eardrum movement as pressure changes.

relations.note: Comparing mechanical eardrum response with a person’s detection of tones distinguishes two hearing-assessment questions.

concepts.card: The cochlea can produce very quiet sounds when its sensory hair cells respond to stimulation. An otoacoustic-emission test records these responses through a probe in the ear canal. Weak or absent emissions need careful interpretation because outer- or middle-ear problems can also obstruct the returning sound.

evidence.note: The hearing-test source describes cochlear hair-cell responses and warns that blockage or middle-ear problems can prevent emissions from being recorded.

concepts.label: Otoacoustic emissions
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use tiny cochlear sounds as evidence about inner-ear function while considering transmission blockages.

relations.note: Middle-ear assessment can help interpret an emission result because sound must pass through that pathway to be recorded.

concepts.card: Pure-tone audiometry measures the quietest tones a person can detect at different pitches. Through headphones, sounds are presented while the listener signals when they hear them. The resulting pattern separates sensitivity across frequencies, rather than reducing hearing to a single yes-or-no ability.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus describes pure-tone presentation at varied pitches/volumes and the listener’s response to the softest audible sound.

concepts.label: Pure-tone audiometry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Map the quietest tones a person detects at different frequencies.

relations.note: Pure-tone detection and eardrum movement are complementary but distinct types of hearing-test evidence.

concepts.card: Hemoglobin A1c testing measures glucose attached to hemoglobin, providing a picture of blood-glucose exposure over roughly two to three months. It differs from a glucose reading at one moment. Conditions affecting red blood cells can distort the result, so the measurement needs appropriate clinical context.

evidence.locator: What is the test?; Is there anything else?
evidence.note: MedlinePlus supports glycated hemoglobin, the approximate two-to-three-month window, the momentary-glucose contrast and red-cell-related limitations.

concepts.label: Hemoglobin A1c testing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect glycated hemoglobin with longer-term glucose exposure and recognize red-cell-related limitations.

relations.note: Glucose-regulating hormones act over changing daily conditions, while A1c offers a longer-term measure of exposure to that regulated substance.

concepts.card: A laboratory reference interval describes results found in a selected comparison population. Being outside it does not automatically establish disease, and being inside it does not guarantee health. Different laboratories, methods and patient groups can use different ranges, so the reported context matters.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus bases ranges on healthy comparison groups and explicitly warns about out-of-range healthy results, in-range illness and method/group differences.

concepts.label: Laboratory reference intervals
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why being outside a population reference range does not by itself establish disease.

relations.note: A1c illustrates why a laboratory number must be interpreted with the test’s purpose and biological limitations, alongside any reported range.

concepts.card: Diagnostic sensitivity asks: among people who have the target condition, how often is the test positive? A highly sensitive test misses fewer affected people. This is different from asking whether a particular positive result means disease, which requires a probability conditioned on the test result.

evidence.note: NCI defines sensitivity as positive-test probability given cancer and separately defines predictive value in the reverse conditional direction.

concepts.label: Diagnostic sensitivity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read sensitivity as the chance of a positive test among people who have the target condition.

relations.note: Sensitivity conditions on disease status, while positive predictive value conditions on a positive test.

concepts.card: Diagnostic specificity asks: among people without the target condition, how often is the test negative? Higher specificity means fewer false positives in that group. It complements sensitivity, but neither quantity alone tells a patient the probability of disease after receiving a positive result.

evidence.note: NCI defines specificity as negative-test probability without cancer and distinguishes it from sensitivity and positive predictive value.

concepts.label: Diagnostic specificity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read specificity as the chance of a negative test among people without the target condition.

relations.note: Sensitivity and specificity describe test behavior in different disease-status groups; they are complementary rates, not interchangeable names.

concepts.card: Positive predictive value is the probability of having a condition after a positive test. Even with unchanged sensitivity and specificity, it falls when the condition is rarer in the tested population. A positive result therefore gains meaning from both test performance and the starting prevalence.

evidence.note: NCI defines PPV and explicitly states that lower prevalence reduces PPV for given sensitivity and specificity.

concepts.label: Positive predictive value
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why a positive test is less convincing when the target condition is rare.

relations.note: The distinction shows why knowing sensitivity does not directly answer the question posed by a positive result.

concepts.card: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring collects repeated readings while a person goes about ordinary life, usually over twenty-four hours. A worn monitor is returned after the recording period. This provides a pattern across time and circumstances, rather than relying only on one measurement taken in a clinic.

evidence.note: NHS describes a monitor worn at home for 24 hours and returned the next day for repeated blood-pressure assessment.

concepts.label: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish repeated measurements during ordinary activity from one clinic reading.

relations.note: The baroreflex regulates a changing pressure, while ambulatory monitoring samples that variable over everyday conditions; this is an editorial physiology-to-measurement bridge.

concepts.card: Pulse oximeters estimate oxygen saturation using light, and skin pigmentation is one factor that can affect the result. A displayed number should therefore not be treated as equally exact in every person or circumstance. Understanding this limitation separates a convenient estimate from an infallible measurement.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus lists darker pigmentation among factors affecting pulse-oximetry accuracy and describes its light-based method.

concepts.label: Skin pigmentation and pulse oximetry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize skin pigmentation as one factor that can make an optical oxygen estimate inaccurate.

relations.note: Pigmentation-related error is a documented measurement limitation within pulse oximetry, not a second method for measuring oxygen.

concepts.card: Public health works to prevent illness and protect health across communities. Vaccination, safer environments and reducing exposure to hazards can change risks before an individual needs treatment. Its population focus connects personal health with shared conditions, policies and collective actions that affect many people at once.

evidence.locator: What is public health?; Prevention examples
evidence.note: APHA describes community-wide prevention, protective environments and examples including vaccination and health-hazard reduction.

imported_records.description: Studying and supporting health at the level of populations and communities.

concepts.label: Public health
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect community-wide prevention with safer water, vaccination and protection from health hazards.
concepts.original_description: Studying and supporting health at the level of populations and communities.

relations.note: Framingham’s population follow-up illustrates how evidence about shared risk factors can inform preventive public-health work.

concepts.card: A randomized controlled trial uses chance to assign participants to an intervention or comparison group. Comparing outcomes helps separate the intervention’s effects from differences that might influence who receives it. Randomization is a design tool; clear follow-up and careful analysis are still needed for a trustworthy result.

evidence.note: Supports chance assignment and comparing experimental and control outcomes.
Supports the qualification that randomization alone does not remove analysis or missing-outcome concerns.

concepts.label: Randomized controlled trial
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use chance-based assignment and a comparison group to assess an intervention’s effects.

relations.note: Concealing forthcoming assignments protects the random allocation process against selective enrollment.

concepts.card: Allocation concealment keeps the next trial assignment unknown until enrollment is settled. If recruiters can predict the group a person will enter, they may selectively include participants and undermine randomization. This protection operates at recruitment, whereas blinding addresses knowledge of treatment after assignment.

evidence.note: Cochrane §8.3 defines unknown forthcoming assignments; §8.3.2 explains selective enrollment and explicitly distinguishes concealment from later blinding.

concepts.label: Allocation concealment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why recruiters must not know the next treatment assignment before enrollment.

relations.note: Concealment is a specific protection of assignment within a randomized controlled trial, rather than a synonym for random sequence generation.

concepts.card: Intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in their originally assigned trial groups, even when they do not follow treatment as planned. This preserves the comparison created by randomization for estimating assignment effects. Missing outcome data still require attention; the label alone does not solve that separate problem.

evidence.note: Cochrane §8.2.2 states original-group analysis regardless of received intervention and separately treats bias from missing outcomes.

concepts.label: Intention-to-treat analysis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Preserve original randomized groups when estimating the effect of treatment assignment.

relations.note: This analysis principle preserves the original randomized grouping when assessing assignment to an intervention.

concepts.card: An N-of-1 trial compares intervention and control periods repeatedly within the same person, often in randomized order. This can reveal an individual response that a group average obscures. It works best when effects can change or fade between periods, rather than permanently carrying into later comparisons.

evidence.note: UK guidance describes randomized multiple crossovers within individuals and limits for slow-onset or long-lasting interventions.

concepts.label: N-of-1 trial
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare interventions repeatedly within one person rather than assuming a group average fits everyone.

relations.note: Washout periods can reduce carryover between the repeated intervention/control periods used in this design.

concepts.card: In a crossover study, the effects of one treatment period can persist into the next. A washout period leaves time without the intervention so those effects can diminish. Its usefulness depends on how long effects last; an arbitrary pause does not guarantee an uncontaminated comparison.

evidence.note: UK N-of-1 guidance describes a no-intervention interval intended to diminish previous effects and discusses long-lasting/carryover limitations.

concepts.label: Washout periods in crossover trials
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why effects from one treatment period can contaminate the next comparison.

relations.note: A washout interval is one design provision for the repeated within-person comparisons described in N-of-1 trials.

concepts.card: A surrogate endpoint is a measured indicator used in place of an outcome that matters directly to patients. Tumor shrinkage, for example, can be observed sooner than longer survival. The substitution is useful only to the extent that the indicator reliably reflects the benefit being sought.

evidence.note: NCI gives tumor shrinkage and biomarkers as faster substitutes for survival/quality-of-life endpoints and warns they are not always true indicators.

concepts.label: Surrogate endpoint
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a quickly measured biological indicator from a direct patient benefit.

relations.note: Endpoint choice is a specific trial-design decision: the measured comparison may concern a surrogate rather than a direct patient outcome.

concepts.card: Screening can move a diagnosis earlier without changing when a person dies. Survival measured from diagnosis then looks longer simply because the clock started sooner. Lead-time bias explains why improved survival after detection does not, by itself, prove that a screening program saves lives.

evidence.note: NCI explains earlier diagnosis adding lead time to measured survival without necessarily delaying death.

concepts.label: Lead-time bias
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how earlier diagnosis can lengthen measured survival without delaying death.

relations.note: Lead-time bias shifts the survival clock, whereas overdiagnosis adds cases that would not have become clinically harmful; both can distort apparent screening success.

concepts.card: People who choose to participate in screening may differ from those who do not, including in health behaviors and other risks. Better outcomes in volunteers can therefore reflect those starting differences. Healthy-volunteer bias makes a simple screened-versus-unscreened comparison an unreliable measure of the screening’s effect.

evidence.note: NCI’s study-design discussion identifies self-selected participants’ different health behavior and lower unrelated mortality as a screening-evaluation concern.

concepts.label: Healthy-volunteer bias in screening studies
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why screened and unscreened groups can differ in outcomes for reasons unrelated to the screening.

relations.note: A randomized comparison can address initial selection differences that a simple volunteer/nonvolunteer contrast cannot, though later participation and follow-up still matter.

concepts.card: Overdiagnosis occurs when testing finds a real condition that would never have caused symptoms or harm during a person’s life. The finding is not necessarily a false-positive result. Detecting it can still expose someone to unnecessary investigations or treatment, so more diagnoses need not mean better health.

evidence.note: NCI describes screen-detected cancers that would never become clinically apparent and ensuing harms from diagnosis/treatment.

concepts.label: Overdiagnosis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish detecting a real condition from finding one that would ever have harmed the patient.

relations.note: Overdiagnosis changes which cases are counted, while lead time changes when the survival clock begins; they are separate screening biases/harms.

concepts.card: The Framingham Heart Study follows community participants over time, with repeated examinations and later generations joining the research. It connected factors such as blood pressure and cholesterol with future cardiovascular disease. Its long view shows how risk can be studied before illness becomes apparent.

evidence.note: NHLBI describes repeated cohort examinations, multigenerational participation and identification of cardiovascular risk factors including pressure and cholesterol.

concepts.label: Framingham Heart Study
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how repeated examinations across generations established patterns of cardiovascular risk.

relations.note: Population follow-up can identify prevention targets, linking this specific study with public health’s community-level focus.

concepts.card: SPRINT compared systolic-pressure targets below 120 and 140 mmHg in higher-risk adults aged fifty or older with initial systolic pressure at least 130 mmHg, excluding diabetes and prior stroke. Intensive treatment reduced cardiovascular events and deaths but increased some adverse effects; eligibility limits matter.

evidence.locator: Why was SPRINT important?; Key findings
evidence.note: NHLBI states the two targets, age fifty or older, initial systolic pressure at least 130 mmHg, additional cardiovascular risk, diabetes/prior-stroke exclusions, cardiovascular/death benefit and increased hypotension-related, electrolyte and kidney adverse effects.

concepts.label: Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial
concepts.learning_takeaway: Interpret a blood-pressure target comparison together with its enrollment limits and adverse effects.

concepts.card: In 1747, James Lind compared different remedies among sailors with scurvy; those given citrus improved. Yet he did not understand vitamin deficiency and retained other theories about the disease. His work separates the value of a treatment comparison from a correct explanation of its mechanism.

evidence.note: RCPE recounts the remedy groups, lemons/oranges outcome and Lind’s digestive/excretory theory without vitamin-deficiency understanding.

concepts.label: James Lind
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate a useful controlled comparison from a correct explanation of why the treatment worked.

relations.note: Lind’s historical comparison offers a contrast with modern randomized trials; the relationship does not claim that his allocation was randomized.

concepts.card: Virginia Apgar developed a standardized way to assess a newborn soon after birth. Observations of heart rate, breathing effort, muscle tone, reflex response and color were combined into one score. Her work turned several immediate clinical observations into a repeatable assessment of the transition outside the womb.

evidence.note: NLM identifies Apgar’s standardized newborn assessment and the five observations arising from obstetrical-anesthesia research.

concepts.label: Virginia Apgar
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how a rapid standardized assessment made newborn condition more consistently observable.

relations.note: Apgar’s standardized assessment and laboratory reference intervals invite comparison of two ways clinical observations are organized, without treating the score as a laboratory reference range.

concepts.card: Florence Nightingale used mortality data to argue for changes in military health care after the Crimean War. Her campaign involved checking inconsistent records and communicating results through writing and the Rose Diagram. The example joins data reconstruction with making statistical evidence understandable to a broader audience.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Rose Diagram; mortality dataset reconstruction
evidence.note: The historical research article describes seven months of dataset checking, the sanitary-reform campaign and collaboration with Martineau using prose and the Rose Diagram.

concepts.label: Florence Nightingale
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how checking mortality records and explaining them visually supported sanitary reform.

relations.note: Using population mortality evidence to campaign for sanitary reform is a specific historical example of public-health reasoning.

concepts.card: A skin graft moves a piece of detached skin onto a wound that needs coverage. For the graft to survive, it must gain a blood supply from the receiving area. Successful placement therefore depends on biological attachment and nourishment, not merely covering the wound’s surface.

evidence.locator: What is a skin graft?; Risks—graft take
evidence.note: The NHS explanation defines transferred skin and describes new blood-vessel supply as part of graft take, with possible failure.

concepts.label: Skin grafting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why transferred skin must acquire blood supply from its new wound bed.

relations.note: Both practices transfer living tissue, but medical skin grafting depends on revascularization while horticultural grafting joins plant parts with different roles. This is an explicitly editorial cross-domain comparison, not equivalence.

concepts.card: Geology investigates Earth’s materials, physical processes and history. Rocks preserve evidence of earlier conditions, while tectonics, weathering and erosion continue to change landscapes. Reading a place geologically means connecting what is visible today with the processes and timescales that produced it.

evidence.note: NPS defines geology through Earth’s physical features/processes/history and names rocks, tectonics, weathering and erosion as fundamentals.

imported_records.description: Investigating Earth's materials, structures and history.

concepts.label: Geology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read Earth’s materials and landscapes as evidence of processes and planetary history.
concepts.original_description: Investigating Earth's materials, structures and history.

relations.note: Subduction offers one concrete tectonic process through which geology connects material movement and landscape formation.

concepts.card: At a subduction zone, one tectonic plate descends beneath another. Material can be scraped from the descending plate, while fluids released at depth help generate magma above it. The same plate boundary can therefore produce coastal mountain building and a separate inland belt of volcanoes.

evidence.note: NPS’s convergent-boundary account describes plate descent, accreted material and fluid-related magma generation using Cascadia.

imported_records.description: geological process at tectonic plate boundaries
imported_records.hook: Follow what happens when one tectonic plate sinks beneath another.

concepts.label: Subduction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect the descent of an oceanic plate with earthquakes, accretion and volcanic arcs.
concepts.original_description: geological process at tectonic plate boundaries

relations.note: Cascadia is the named plate-boundary example that links coastal ranges and inland volcanism in the inspected account.

concepts.card: Rocks beside a locked fault can deform as plate movement continues. When the fault slips, stored elastic strain is released and the rocks rebound toward a less-deformed shape. Elastic rebound theory connects gradual stress buildup with the sudden energy release of many earthquakes.

evidence.note: USGS’s Reid account describes progressive deformation, locked-fault strain and sudden release/rebound inferred from the 1906 earthquake.

concepts.label: Elastic rebound theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain earthquakes as sudden release of strain accumulated while rocks deform elastically.

relations.note: Slow-slip events provide a contrast to the abrupt strain-release picture, showing that fault displacement can unfold over different timescales.

concepts.card: Strong shaking can make loose, water-saturated sediment lose much of its supporting strength. During soil liquefaction, ground that previously carried buildings or other loads can deform and fail. The hazard depends on the material and water conditions, not just the earthquake’s size.

evidence.note: USGS defines loss of strength in saturated sediment during shaking and illustrates damage to supported structures.

concepts.label: Soil liquefaction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how shaking can make loose water-saturated sediment lose supporting strength.

relations.note: Earthquake energy release and liquefaction concern different steps: the shaking source and a susceptible ground material’s response.

concepts.card: Not all fault slip occurs as a sudden earthquake rupture. In Cascadia, slow-slip events produce deformation over longer periods and are observed through precise position measurements together with unusual seismic signals. They reveal movement on the plate boundary that the ordinary locked-then-breaking picture leaves incomplete.

evidence.note: The USGS review describes geodetic transient deformation, associated seismic signals and slower, prolonged slip in Cascadia.

concepts.label: Slow-slip events
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish prolonged transient fault slip from the rapid rupture of ordinary earthquakes.

relations.note: The Cascadia review supplies a named setting where slow-slip behavior has been observed and studied.

concepts.card: Seismic tomography infers structures inside Earth from seismic information. Its models can address targets ranging from fault zones to the whole planet, but their usefulness depends on data quality, geographic coverage and uncertainty. A tomographic image is therefore an interpreted model, not a direct photograph underground.

evidence.note: The USGS-hosted 2024 review abstract identifies interior-structure applications and explicitly discusses inversion, coverage, data quality and uncertainty quantification.

concepts.label: Seismic tomography
concepts.learning_takeaway: Treat inferred Earth-interior structure as a model constrained by coverage, data quality and uncertainty.

relations.note: Inferring hidden Earth structure from measurements is a geologic investigation method, with the cited model/uncertainty qualifications retained.

concepts.card: A volcano’s surface can move as conditions change below it. Repeated GPS positions and tilt measurements help researchers infer changes in a magma reservoir’s depth or volume. Monitoring deformation turns small surface shifts into clues about an inaccessible system, while still requiring interpretation alongside other evidence.

evidence.note: USGS Mount St. Helens monitoring describes surface movement, GPS/tilt instruments and estimates of reservoir depth, volume and volume change.

concepts.label: Volcano ground-deformation monitoring
concepts.learning_takeaway: Infer subsurface magma changes from repeated measurements of surface movement.

relations.note: Kīlauea’s connected summit and rift activity offers a named case for thinking about subsurface magma movement, while the method’s cited demonstration is at Mount St. Helens.

concepts.card: A lahar is a moving mixture of water and volcanic debris, not a stream of molten lava. It can rush through valleys during an eruption, afterward or even while a volcano is quiet. Recognizing the mixture and its possible timing changes how volcanic hazards are understood.

evidence.note: The USGS lahar explanation distinguishes debris-and-water flows from lava and states that lahars can occur during eruptions or inactivity.

concepts.label: Lahar
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish fast volcanic debris-and-water flows from molten lava.

relations.note: Lahars and lava tubes contrast water–debris transport with molten-rock transport, avoiding a common conflation of volcanic flow types.

concepts.card: Cooling lava can contract and fracture into columns separated by polygonal joints. Seen from above, the cracks may resemble a honeycomb. Columnar jointing records a material response to cooling, distinguishing these fractures from a structure that necessarily formed through later faulting or folding.

evidence.note: USGS Shenandoah’s igneous-structures passage identifies cooling basalt, contraction and polygonal/honeycomb cracks.

concepts.label: Columnar jointing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect contraction during cooling with polygonal fractures in volcanic rock.

relations.note: Both structures preserve cooling history, but columns reflect contraction fractures while pillows reflect lava cooling in water.

concepts.card: When lava flows into water, its exposed surface cools rapidly, producing rounded forms known as pillow lava. These shapes can survive within ancient rock. Recognizing them helps geologists infer that molten rock once met water, rather than assuming every lava flow formed in open air.

evidence.note: USGS describes pillow basalts forming when lava enters water and is rapidly cooled from exposed sides, including preserved examples at Shenandoah.

concepts.label: Pillow lava
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize rounded lava forms as evidence of rapid cooling in water.

relations.note: Pillow forms illustrate how geologists use a rock’s preserved structure to infer its formation environment.

concepts.card: A caldera is a volcanic depression associated with collapse above a magma reservoir. At Kīlauea in 2018, magma draining toward lower-elevation vents removed support beneath the summit, which repeatedly subsided. The example connects a surface hollow with changes in the volcano’s internal plumbing.

evidence.note: USGS documents summit-reservoir drainage, unsupported caldera-floor collapse and the lower-elevation eruptive pathway in 2018.

imported_records.description: cauldron-like volcanic feature usually formed by the collapse of land following a volcanic eruption
imported_records.subsection: Physical sciences / Earth science / Earth / Geomorphology

concepts.label: Caldera
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain a volcanic depression through loss of support above a draining magma reservoir.
concepts.original_description: cauldron-like volcanic feature usually formed by the collapse of land following a volcanic eruption

relations.note: Kīlauea’s 2018 collapse provides the documented case used to explain caldera subsidence.

concepts.card: A lava tube begins when the surface of a flowing lava stream cools into a crust while molten material continues beneath it. If the lava later drains away, an empty passage remains. The cave records a former flow route rather than a space carved by underground water.

evidence.note: NPS’s formation account describes a roof forming over flowing lava and subsequent drainage leaving a tube.

concepts.label: Lava tube
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace a volcanic cave from a crusted-over lava stream to an emptied conduit.

relations.note: Lava tubes and karst passages can both be caves, but their formation mechanisms differ: cooling/drainage versus dissolution by water.

concepts.card: Kīlauea’s 2018 eruption linked activity far apart on the same volcano. Magma moved from summit storage toward the lower East Rift Zone, while the summit floor repeatedly collapsed. Increased pressure after collapse could boost the distant eruption rate, revealing a connected underground magma system.

evidence.note: USGS describes summit drainage and collapse, the hydraulic connection and post-collapse surges at the lower-rift vent.

concepts.label: Kīlauea
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how a flank eruption and summit collapse can be connected through a magma system.

relations.note: The named volcano’s 2018 summit subsidence illustrates collapse within a caldera and links it to distant magma discharge.

concepts.card: In the Cascadia Subduction Zone, the Juan de Fuca Plate descends beneath North America. Scraped-off material helps build coastal ranges, while deeper processes support the Cascade volcanic arc inland. The region shows how one convergent boundary can produce distinct landscape features at different distances.

evidence.note: NPS’s Cascadia section links the descending Juan de Fuca Plate, coastal accreted material and inland volcanic chain.

concepts.label: Cascadia Subduction Zone
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain the paired coastal and volcanic ranges produced by the descending Juan de Fuca Plate.

relations.note: Cascadia is a particular geographic example of the broader subduction process.

concepts.card: In karst terrain, water enlarges soluble-rock fractures and can travel through underground openings before emerging at springs. Surface streams alone may therefore miss important drainage routes. Rapid movement through these openings can also carry contamination with little filtration, linking rock structure to water quality.

evidence.note: NPS describes dissolution-created underground drainage and rapid water transport with limited filtration in karst aquifers.

concepts.label: Karst drainage
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace water through fractures enlarged by dissolution rather than assuming it remains in surface streams.

relations.note: Comparing solution-driven drainage with an emptied lava conduit distinguishes two very different origins of underground passages.

concepts.card: Oceanography studies the ocean through its water movement, chemistry, living communities and seafloor history. These perspectives overlap: circulation can move nutrients that influence marine life. Field observations, experiments and models connect the ocean’s physical setting with the organisms and chemical processes operating within it.

evidence.note: Supports the field’s physical, chemical, biological and geological scope and research methods.
Supports the example connecting circulation, nutrients and marine productivity.

imported_records.description: Investigating the physical, chemical and biological properties of oceans.

concepts.label: Oceanography
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect ocean chemistry, life, seafloor history and water movement as interacting research areas.
concepts.original_description: Investigating the physical, chemical and biological properties of oceans.

relations.note: Coastal upwelling illustrates how circulation delivers nutrients and connects physical with biological oceanography.

concepts.card: Moist air rising over a mountain cools and can release precipitation on the windward side. After crossing the summit, descending air warms and becomes drier. This rain-shadow effect helps explain why nearby places on opposite sides of a mountain can have sharply different rainfall.

evidence.locator: Windward precipitation and leeward drying mechanism
evidence.note: NOAA’s Hawaii explanation connects windward ascent/cooling/precipitation with leeward descent/warming/drying.

concepts.label: Rain shadow
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace contrasting mountain rainfall through rising moist air and descending dry air.

relations.note: Comparing a mountain’s lifting effect with atmospheric-river moisture transport separates where vapor arrives from how terrain can release it as precipitation.

concepts.card: Wind sets surface water in motion, and friction passes some movement into deeper layers. Earth’s rotation deflects those layers as their speeds decrease, producing the turning pattern called an Ekman spiral. It describes changing current direction with depth, rather than a single uniform flow beneath the wind.

evidence.note: NOAA explains downward momentum transfer through friction, decreasing speed and successive Coriolis deflection.

concepts.label: Ekman spiral
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why a wind-driven current changes direction and weakens with depth.

relations.note: The Ekman spiral is a specific physical-oceanography pattern linking wind, friction and rotation.

concepts.card: When winds move coastal surface water away, colder water can rise from below to replace it. This upwelling often brings nutrients into sunlit waters and supports high biological productivity. The process connects a change in water movement with conditions that can benefit marine food webs.

evidence.note: NOAA describes displaced surface water, rising cold nutrient-rich replacement and frequently high productivity/fishing grounds.

concepts.label: Coastal upwelling
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect offshore displacement of surface water with rising cold nutrient-rich water.

relations.note: Coastal upwelling is a circulation process linking the physical and biological parts of oceanography.
