concepts.card: Temperature and salinity affect seawater density. In places where water becomes sufficiently cold and salty, it can sink and contribute to deep-ocean circulation, with other water moving to replace it. Thermohaline circulation highlights these density differences alongside the wind-driven motions visible at the surface.

evidence.note: NOAA describes cold, salty dense water sinking and helping drive deep circulation.

concepts.label: Thermohaline circulation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect temperature and salinity differences with density-driven deep-ocean flow.

relations.note: Comparing density-driven sinking with wind/friction-driven Ekman motion distinguishes two contributions to ocean circulation.

concepts.card: El Niño–Southern Oscillation couples tropical Pacific ocean conditions with the atmosphere. El Niño weakens the usual trade winds and changes warm-water distribution and upwelling; La Niña strengthens the winds. These shifts can alter weather far from the Pacific, linking a regional ocean pattern with wider climate effects.

evidence.locator: Normal Pacific conditions; El Niño; La Niña
evidence.note: NOAA describes the coupled Pacific pattern, opposite trade-wind behavior, warm-water/upwelling changes and distant weather effects.

imported_records.description: climatic phenomenon occurring in the Pacific Ocean
imported_records.subsection: Physical sciences / Earth science / Air / Climatology

concepts.label: El Niño–Southern Oscillation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect changes in equatorial Pacific winds and ocean temperatures with distant weather patterns.
concepts.original_description: climatic phenomenon occurring in the Pacific Ocean

relations.note: Changes in Pacific winds alter upwelling, giving a concrete link between the climate pattern and a circulation process.

concepts.card: A marine heatwave is unusually warm ocean water measured against the normal conditions for that place and season. A common definition requires temperatures above the seasonal ninetieth percentile for at least five consecutive days. The comparison is local and time-specific, not one temperature threshold for every sea.

evidence.note: NOAA NCEI gives a local seasonal 90th-percentile threshold and persistence of at least five consecutive days.

concepts.label: Marine heatwave
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify unusual ocean warmth relative to local seasonal history rather than one worldwide temperature threshold.

relations.note: Unusual ocean warmth can be a coral stressor, but a heatwave definition and the biological bleaching response are different subjects.

concepts.card: When seawater absorbs carbon dioxide, chemical reactions increase hydrogen ions and reduce the availability of carbonate ions. Ocean acidification can therefore make building some shells and skeletons more difficult. The change concerns a shift in ocean chemistry, not a claim that seawater has become acidic in everyday terms.

evidence.note: NOAA explains CO2 uptake, increased hydrogen ions, reduced carbonate availability and effects on calcifying organisms.

concepts.label: Ocean acidification
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect absorbed atmospheric CO2 with more hydrogen ions and less available carbonate.

relations.note: Acidification and bleaching are distinct pressures on marine organisms: carbonate chemistry versus loss of coral symbiotic algae.

concepts.card: A thermocline is a layer where water temperature changes rapidly with depth, separating warmer surface water from colder water below. Its depth and strength vary with place and season. Recognizing the layer helps describe an ocean’s vertical structure instead of assuming its temperature is uniform.

evidence.note: NOAA defines the rapid-temperature-change zone beneath a warm mixed layer and describes seasonal/regional variation.

concepts.label: Thermocline
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize a depth interval where temperature drops rapidly below a warm mixed surface layer.

relations.note: Argo’s repeated temperature-versus-depth profiles provide a measurement approach for studying vertical structures such as thermoclines.

concepts.card: An atmospheric river is a concentrated corridor of water vapor moving through the atmosphere. When it reaches land, that moisture can fall as rain or snow. Such events supply useful water, but stronger or persistent landfalls can also produce flooding, so their effects depend on the event.

evidence.note: NOAA defines water-vapor transport and explains landfall precipitation, water-supply importance and potential flooding.

concepts.label: Atmospheric river
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a concentrated corridor of water-vapor transport with both useful precipitation and flood risk.

relations.note: Mountain lifting can turn transported vapor into uneven precipitation, connecting atmospheric-river supply with rain-shadow geography.

concepts.card: A temperature inversion occurs where air becomes warmer with height. Near the ground, warm air above cooler air can suppress mixing and trap pollution. Such inversions may form through nighttime surface cooling or warm-air advection above an existing cool layer.

evidence.note: NWS defines an inversion as air temperature increasing with height. Its near-ground examples describe nighttime surface cooling or warm-air advection, with a stable lid that can trap pollution.

concepts.label: Temperature inversion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how warmer air above cooler air can suppress mixing and trap near-surface pollution.

relations.note: The marine-cloud source places coastal stratus within stable atmospheric structure; comparison with inversions helps explain persistence and mixing limits without equating cloud and inversion.

concepts.card: Cold air moving across a warmer, unfrozen lake gains heat and moisture. As that air rises, narrow cloud bands can form and deliver lake-effect snow downwind. Wind direction strongly affects where the snow falls, so heavy snowfall can occur close to places receiving very little.

evidence.note: NWS describes heat/moisture transfer over unfrozen Great Lakes, rising air, narrow snow bands and strong wind-direction dependence.

concepts.label: Lake-effect snow
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace narrow snow bands to cold air gaining heat and moisture over unfrozen lake water.

relations.note: These are different routes to precipitation: local moisture uptake over a lake versus concentrated long-distance vapor transport.

concepts.card: Argo floats repeatedly move through the ocean to measure conditions such as temperature and salinity. Pumping oil into an external bladder changes volume without changing mass, allowing a float to rise or sink. On a typical profiling cycle, it surfaces to transmit data, then descends again.

evidence.locator: What does an Argo float do?; External bladder
evidence.note: The Argo program describes its standard profiling mission, CTD measurements, buoyancy changes through an oil bladder and satellite communication at the surface. The card marks this as a typical cycle.

concepts.label: Argo
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how buoyancy-changing floats repeatedly profile the ocean and return data by satellite.

relations.note: Argo is a named observational system that supplies oceanographic measurements through repeated profiles.

concepts.card: Mauna Loa Observatory’s carbon-dioxide record depends on more than taking repeated readings. Air samples are assessed for background conditions, and the analyzer is frequently checked against reference gases. Reporting carbon dioxide in dry air helps prevent changing water vapor from masquerading as a change in carbon dioxide.

evidence.note: NOAA explains background selection, frequent calibration and why dry-air mole fraction removes dilution effects of variable water vapor.

concepts.label: Mauna Loa Observatory
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how representative air sampling and repeated calibration support an atmospheric CO2 record.

relations.note: Mauna Loa and Landsat offer different long-term environmental records whose comparability depends on calibration, an editorial measurement-practice bridge.

concepts.card: Marine stratus forms a low cloud layer associated with coastal ocean air. Winds can carry it inland, while daytime warming and mixing with drier air can make it evaporate. Its changing extent reflects both movement of the cloudy air and changes in temperature and humidity.

evidence.locator: What are Marine Layer Clouds?; Advection; Dissipation
evidence.note: NWS’s marine-layer account describes formation over ocean, advection inland and dissipation through heating or drier-air mixing.

concepts.label: Marine stratus
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain coastal low-cloud sheets through ocean formation, inland advection and daytime evaporation.

relations.note: Comparing stable marine-layer structure with temperature inversions connects the cloud’s persistence to vertical mixing conditions without asserting identity.

concepts.card: Aquatic organisms use oxygen dissolved in water, which is different from the oxygen chemically bound inside water molecules. Microorganisms decomposing organic matter can consume this available oxygen. If consumption outpaces replenishment, oxygen levels fall and conditions can become difficult for other aquatic life.

evidence.note: USGS’s BOD account distinguishes dissolved available oxygen and describes microbial decomposition consuming it with ecological consequences.

concepts.label: Dissolved oxygen in water
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish biologically available dissolved oxygen from the oxygen bound inside water molecules.

relations.note: Biochemical oxygen demand measures an oxygen-consuming process that can lower the dissolved-oxygen concentration.

concepts.card: Biochemical oxygen demand measures the oxygen microorganisms consume while breaking down organic material under specified conditions. A high demand can help explain why a water body loses oxygen even when it initially contains plenty. The measure concerns consumption, rather than simply the oxygen concentration at one moment.

evidence.note: USGS defines microbial oxygen use during aerobic decomposition and its relationship to organic loading and depleted dissolved oxygen.

concepts.label: Biochemical oxygen demand
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use microbial oxygen consumption as an indicator of biodegradable organic loading.

relations.note: The distinction separates the amount of dissolved oxygen present from biological demand that consumes it.

concepts.card: Turbidity describes water cloudiness associated with suspended particles and other material that interferes with light. Sediment or algae can reduce visibility and the light reaching underwater plants. Cloudy water is not automatically polluted, since some waters are naturally turbid, but the change can still matter ecologically.

evidence.note: EPA’s clarity account links suspended matter/algae, lower visibility and light available to aquatic plants, including naturally turbid waters.

concepts.label: Turbidity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect suspended matter with light scattering, absorption and reduced underwater visibility.

relations.note: A Secchi disk provides a visual clarity assessment, while turbidity describes the clouding property influencing underwater light.

concepts.card: A Secchi disk uses a contrasting black-and-white target to assess water clarity. It offers a simple visual way to compare how readily something can be seen through water. Clarity matters because it influences how much light can reach submerged plants and other photosynthetic organisms.

evidence.note: EPA identifies the black-and-white Secchi target for visual clarity measurement and explains ecological importance through underwater light.

concepts.label: Secchi disk
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use a simple black-and-white visual target to assess water clarity.

relations.note: The visual clarity measure responds to water’s light-obscuring properties, but is not asserted to be numerically identical to turbidity.

concepts.card: Bottom-dwelling aquatic invertebrates differ in their tolerance of pollution and other stress. Because many move little, the community found at a site can reflect conditions over time. Bioassessment uses this living evidence to complement a water sample that captures only the moment it was collected.

evidence.locator: Why evaluate them?; What do they tell us?
evidence.note: EPA describes benthic macroinvertebrates’ varying tolerances, limited mobility and integration of environmental stress over time.

concepts.label: Benthic macroinvertebrate bioassessment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read aquatic-community composition as an integrated record of environmental stress.

relations.note: Community composition can complement a direct dissolved-oxygen measurement by reflecting longer exposure to conditions, rather than measuring the same instantaneous quantity.

concepts.card: A riparian forest buffer places trees, shrubs or other perennial vegetation beside water. The strip can filter runoff, stabilize banks and shade aquatic habitat. Its effectiveness depends on site conditions and continuity, so the presence of a few trees alone does not guarantee the same conservation benefit everywhere.

evidence.note: USFS defines streamside perennial buffers, identifies runoff filtering/bank stability/shade and lists site, landscape and continuity factors affecting effectiveness.

concepts.label: Riparian forest buffer
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect streamside vegetation with filtering runoff, stabilizing banks and shading aquatic habitat.

relations.note: A buffer changes habitat and runoff conditions, while benthic bioassessment can provide evidence of biological conditions in receiving waters.

concepts.card: A constructed treatment wetland uses wetland plants, soils and associated microorganisms as part of an engineered water-treatment system. Water-quality improvement depends on these natural processes working within a designed setting. The vegetation is therefore part of the treatment approach, not merely decoration around a pond.

evidence.note: EPA’s opening definition identifies treatment systems using vegetation, soils and microbial communities to improve water quality.

concepts.label: Constructed treatment wetland
concepts.learning_takeaway: Treat wastewater with deliberately arranged vegetation, soils and microbial processes.

relations.note: Both approaches use vegetation and surrounding ecological processes for water-quality goals, but a treatment wetland and a streamside buffer have different layouts and roles.

concepts.card: Living shorelines use plants and other natural materials, sometimes with low structural elements, to stabilize estuarine coasts. They can buffer waves while preserving habitat and allowing marsh processes to continue. The approach connects erosion protection with ecological functions rather than treating the shoreline only as a rigid boundary.

evidence.note: NOAA describes vegetation/natural materials with optional low sills, estuarine settings, wave buffering, habitat and marsh processes.

concepts.label: Living shoreline
concepts.learning_takeaway: Stabilize sheltered coasts using vegetation and natural materials while retaining habitat functions.

relations.note: A living shoreline and a riparian buffer both connect protective vegetation with aquatic habitat, while addressing different boundary conditions.

concepts.card: Landsat’s repeated satellite observations provide a long record of changes on Earth’s surface. Careful calibration helps researchers compare images across years and distinguish real changes in forests, cities or coastlines from changes in measurement. The archive’s value grows through continuity as well as through individual pictures.

evidence.locator: About Landsat, calibration and long-term comparisons
evidence.note: NASA describes the long continuous record, science-grade calibration and applications to cities, coasts, crops and forests.

concepts.label: Landsat
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use consistently calibrated imagery to distinguish real long-term land changes from sensor differences.

relations.note: The NPS thermokarst account uses Landsat images to monitor lake-area change, providing a concrete application of the long surface record.

concepts.card: Removing dams from the Elwha River restored connections between upstream habitat and the sea. The project reopened routes used by migrating fish and allowed sediment to move again. It demonstrates that river restoration can involve reconnecting processes across a whole watershed, not only repairing one riverbank.

evidence.note: NPS describes the dams’ barriers to fish and sediment and the restoration through dam removal.

concepts.label: Elwha River restoration
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how removing dams reconnects fish migration and sediment movement.

relations.note: Reconnecting fish movement and sediment transport makes the Elwha project an ecological case linking organisms with physical processes.

concepts.card: Utah’s Sand Hollow Reservoir stores water at the surface while also allowing it to infiltrate the underlying Navajo Sandstone aquifer. Monitoring showed recharge rates changing over time, with clogging and hydraulic conditions among the likely influences. The site illustrates why recharge performance must be measured after construction.

evidence.locator: Sand Hollow case, infiltration rates and monitoring
evidence.note: USGS describes the reservoir’s dual purpose, infiltration to Navajo Sandstone and changing recharge rates with likely clogging/gradient influences.

concepts.label: Sand Hollow Reservoir
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why engineered recharge performance can change as gradients and clogging evolve.

relations.note: Sand Hollow is the inspected field example of deliberately recharging an aquifer through surface-basin infiltration.

concepts.card: Managed aquifer recharge deliberately adds water to underground storage. At Sand Hollow, water spread in a reservoir seeps into the underlying sandstone aquifer. Monitoring water levels, infiltration rates and chemistry helps determine where that water goes and how effectively the recharge system is working.

evidence.note: The USGS case documents intentional reservoir infiltration and monitoring of levels, recharge rates and chemical signals tracking recharge movement.

concepts.label: Managed aquifer recharge
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish deliberate underground replenishment from simply storing surface water.

relations.note: The general recharge practice is illustrated by the specifically monitored Sand Hollow Reservoir.

concepts.card: An artesian aquifer holds groundwater under pressure beneath relatively impermeable layers. Water in a well tapping it can rise above the aquifer’s top, but water flows out at the surface only if the pressure level is high enough. Depth alone does not make a well artesian.

evidence.locator: Artesian Water; Example of an aquifer system
evidence.note: USGS distinguishes confined pressure, rise above the aquifer, flowing versus nonflowing wells and the insufficiency of depth alone.

concepts.label: Artesian aquifer
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why confined water rises in a well but may not flow out at the surface.

relations.note: Pressure in confined groundwater and deliberate recharge address different aspects of underground water storage; the comparison does not imply Sand Hollow is an artesian system.

concepts.card: When ice within the ground thaws, the land can subside and form thermokarst depressions. Some fill with lakes or ponds; elsewhere, thaw can breach a basin’s edge and drain a lake. Warming can therefore produce both expanding water bodies and abrupt losses of surface water.

evidence.note: NPS defines thermokarst through ground-ice thaw/subsidence and explicitly describes lake formation/enlargement and drainage through breached banks.

concepts.label: Thermokarst
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use thaw-related ground subsidence to understand both lake formation and drainage.

relations.note: Landsat imagery is used in the inspected NPS study to monitor changing thermokarst-lake area.

concepts.card: Buildings and paved surfaces absorb and later release heat, while reduced vegetation limits shade and evaporative cooling. These differences can make urban areas warmer than their surroundings. Surface temperatures and air temperatures describe related but distinct heat-island patterns, so the measurement being compared matters.

evidence.note: EPA identifies stored/released heat, reduced shade/moisture and the distinction between surface and atmospheric heat islands.

imported_records.description: Studying why built-up areas retain heat and how design can reduce it.

concepts.label: Urban heat islands
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish hot built surfaces from warmer urban air and identify their different measurements.
concepts.original_description: Studying why built-up areas retain heat and how design can reduce it.

relations.note: Urban heat measurements and Mauna Loa’s gas record illustrate why an environmental variable and its sampling method must be specified; neither is a parent of the other.

concepts.card: Gardening involves shaping the conditions in which plants grow. A mulch layer, for example, can conserve soil moisture, suppress weeds and alter temperature around roots. Such choices show that caring for plants includes managing their immediate environment, as well as sowing, planting or tending the plants themselves.

evidence.note: UMN’s mulch guide provides the specific moisture, weed and temperature example within garden care.

imported_records.description: Growing and caring for plants in gardens and small outdoor spaces.

concepts.label: Gardening
concepts.learning_takeaway: See soil cover as one of the ways gardeners manage the growing conditions around plants.
concepts.original_description: Growing and caring for plants in gardens and small outdoor spaces.

relations.note: Mulching supplies a concrete soil-environment management practice within gardening.

concepts.card: Crop rotation changes the crops grown in a field through a planned sequence over time. This can interrupt recurring pest associations and diversify how the field is used. It is a preventive management practice, rather than simply moving an existing pest after it has become a problem.

evidence.note: Identifies crop rotation as a way to prevent pest problems within IPM.
Defines planned crop sequence over time on the same field and reduced pest pressure as a possible benefit.

concepts.label: Crop rotation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Disrupt recurring crop-pest associations by changing the crop grown in a field over time.

relations.note: EPA explicitly includes rotation among preventive practices within integrated pest management.

concepts.card: Cover crops are grown primarily to keep living vegetation on the soil and provide conservation benefits, rather than as the main harvested crop. Their roots and residues can reduce erosion and add organic matter. Timing and management determine how those functions fit around the farm’s other crops.

evidence.note: NRCS defines seasonal vegetative cover rather than cash crops and identifies erosion reduction, organic matter and soil-structure benefits.

concepts.label: Cover crops
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a crop grown for soil cover and ecosystem functions from one grown primarily for harvest.

relations.note: Cover crops supply living cover, while no-till changes soil disturbance and residue handling; they can serve complementary but distinct soil-management functions.

concepts.card: No-till farming establishes crops while limiting soil disturbance and retaining previous plant residues at the surface. Planting directly into that cover differs from turning the whole field before sowing. The practice changes both how soil is worked and how residues remain part of the growing environment.

evidence.locator: Residue and Tillage Management, No Till
evidence.note: NRCS states limits on soil disturbance, year-round residue retention and direct planting into the residue.

concepts.label: No-till farming
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reduce soil disturbance by establishing crops without full-width tillage.

relations.note: Retaining residue through reduced disturbance differs from growing a seasonal cover crop, though both address soil cover.

concepts.card: Mulching covers the soil surface with a chosen material. The layer can slow evaporation, reduce light available to weeds and alter soil temperature. Those effects depend on the material, so a gardener’s choice of covering changes more than the appearance of the bed.

evidence.note: UMN explains surface cover, moisture conservation, weed-light restriction and material-dependent thermal effects.

concepts.label: Mulching
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how a surface covering changes evaporation, weed growth and soil temperature.

relations.note: A mulch layer is a specific gardening intervention affecting root-zone conditions.

concepts.card: Integrated pest management combines identification, monitoring, prevention and selective control. Finding an organism does not automatically justify spraying: its identity and the likelihood of damage matter. The approach uses evidence to decide whether action is needed and which available method fits the particular problem.

evidence.locator: Monitor and Identify Pests; Prevention; Control
evidence.note: EPA describes identification/monitoring, prevention, thresholds and control choices in the IPM sequence.

imported_records.description: approach for economic control of pests
imported_records.hook: How can monitoring and multiple control methods guide pest-management decisions?

concepts.label: Integrated pest management
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine identification, prevention and selective interventions rather than treating every organism as a pest.
concepts.original_description: approach for economic control of pests

relations.note: Action thresholds provide the explicit decision trigger within the broader IPM process.

concepts.card: An IPM action threshold marks conditions under which pest management becomes warranted. It may reflect a pest population level or environmental circumstances indicating unacceptable harm. The threshold separates seeing a pest from deciding to intervene, making control a decision based on context rather than mere presence.

evidence.note: EPA defines action thresholds by pest populations or environmental conditions indicating that control action is needed.

concepts.label: IPM action thresholds
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish the presence of a pest from a level that warrants an intervention.

relations.note: Threshold-setting is a named decision step within EPA’s integrated pest-management framework.

concepts.card: Trap cropping uses a more attractive planting to draw pests away from the crop being protected. The result depends on the pest, the plants and their arrangement. Extension examples include useful flea-beetle diversion and unsuccessful combinations, showing why companion-planting claims need evidence for the particular situation.

evidence.note: UMN describes trap cropping, a brassica flea-beetle example and a failed eggplant–potato combination.

concepts.label: Trap cropping
concepts.learning_takeaway: Redirect a pest toward a more attractive planting, while checking that the arrangement works for that pest and crop.

relations.note: Pest diversion is one specific management technique that can be considered within an evidence-led IPM strategy.

concepts.card: Grafting joins a selected shoot, or scion, to a rootstock so the parts contribute different traits. In apple trees, the scion determines the fruit variety, while the rootstock strongly influences tree size and time to bearing. The resulting tree combines roles from two genetically different individuals.

evidence.note: UMN’s rootstock section explicitly describes genetically distinct scion/rootstock parts and their fruit, size and bearing-time roles.

concepts.label: Horticultural grafting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Join a selected shoot variety to a different root system so each contributes different traits.

relations.note: Dwarfing is one consequence of rootstock choice within the broader scion–rootstock propagation method.

concepts.card: A dwarfing rootstock can limit an apple tree’s size while its scion determines the fruit variety. If a buried scion forms its own roots, the rootstock’s dwarfing influence can be lost. Tree size therefore depends partly on which root system supports the grafted shoot.

evidence.note: UMN explains rootstock control of size and warns that scion rooting above a buried graft union can defeat dwarfing.

concepts.label: Rootstock dwarfing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why the same apple variety can grow to different sizes on different rootstocks.

relations.note: This is a specific growth consequence of choosing the root system in a grafted tree.

concepts.card: A growing shoot tip can suppress the development of lateral buds. Apical dominance involves hormonal signals, including auxin from the tip, while cytokinins can favor bud growth. Removing the tip changes that balance, helping explain why pruning can encourage a plant to branch.

evidence.note: OpenStax’s auxin and cytokinin passages describe tip-related lateral inhibition, bud promotion and release after tip removal.

concepts.label: Apical dominance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect growth at a shoot tip with suppression of lateral buds and the effects of pruning.

relations.note: Pruning applies knowledge of shoot-tip control to a practical gardening decision about branching.

concepts.card: Plants can use the duration of light and darkness as a seasonal signal. Photoperiodism helps regulate events such as flowering or winter-bud formation, with different species responding differently. A plant’s calendar can therefore depend on day–night timing, rather than only on whether the weather is warm.

evidence.note: OpenStax describes photoperiod-dependent flowering/bud formation and different plant responses.

concepts.label: Photoperiodism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain seasonal plant responses through the duration of light and darkness rather than temperature alone.

relations.note: Seasonal light signals can influence flowering, while bolting is the crop-quality consequence of an early shift into reproductive growth.

concepts.card: Bolting is a crop’s shift into flowering earlier than the grower wants. In cool-season vegetables, heat or long days can help trigger it, depending on the crop and its history. Once reproductive growth begins, the quality of leaves or roots harvested for food can decline.

evidence.note: UMN explains premature flowering in cool-season crops, heat/daylength influences and losses of edible quality.

concepts.label: Bolting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize premature flowering as a shift that can reduce the edible quality of a leafy or root crop.

relations.note: Daylength response provides one possible timing influence on flowering, but bolting is a crop-development outcome rather than photoperiodism itself.

concepts.card: Some greenhouse cucumber varieties can form seedless fruit without pollination, an example of parthenocarpy. Pollinating those varieties may instead introduce seeds. The case separates fruit development from seed production, while reminding growers that a pollination rule useful for one cucumber type may not fit another.

evidence.note: UMN’s cucumber passage specifically identifies parthenocarpic greenhouse varieties, fruit without pollination and possible seed production if pollinated.

concepts.label: Parthenocarpy
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish fruit formation without pollination in selected cucumber varieties from ordinary pollination-dependent fruit set.

relations.note: The cucumber case contrasts fruit formation without pollination with fruit crops that need pollen from a compatible partner.

concepts.card: Some fruit varieties cannot reliably set fruit using their own pollen and need a different compatible variety nearby. Hybrid plums provide an example, whereas some European plums are self-compatible. Planning pollination therefore requires matching varieties, not merely counting the number of trees in the garden.

evidence.note: UMN explicitly contrasts self-incompatible hybrid plums with self-compatible European plums and identifies specific compatible pollenizer varieties.

concepts.label: Self-incompatibility in fruit crops
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why some fruit trees need pollen from a different compatible variety to crop well.

relations.note: Variety compatibility is a practical planning issue in fruit gardening, rather than a rule that all gardens need two trees of every kind.

concepts.card: Food fermentation uses microorganisms to transform a food’s ingredients. Products such as acids can change flavor and texture and, under suitable conditions, help inhibit spoilage. The culinary practice depends on the organisms and process conditions, rather than treating every uncontrolled microbial change as desirable fermentation.

evidence.note: FAO describes microbial food transformations, fermentation products and preservation effects; the bounded wording avoids equating fermentation with guaranteed safety.

imported_records.description: Using microorganisms to transform and preserve foods.

concepts.label: Fermentation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize food fermentation through microbial products that change flavor, texture and keeping qualities.
concepts.original_description: Using microorganisms to transform and preserve foods.

relations.note: Yeast activity in bread dough is one culinary use of microbial transformation within a larger baking process.

concepts.card: Bread dough needs both expanding gas and a structure that can retain it. In wheat bread, yeast produces gas while hydrated flour proteins form a stretchy gluten network. Baking expands the pockets and sets the dough, connecting fermentation, material structure and heat in one everyday craft.

evidence.note: Exploratorium describes yeast gas production, gluten development, gas pockets expanding during cooking and dough solidification.

imported_records.description: Making bread through mixing, fermentation, shaping and baking.

concepts.label: Bread baking
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect dough structure and microbial gas production with the rise of bread.
concepts.original_description: Making bread through mixing, fermentation, shaping and baking.

relations.note: Gluten formation is a specific material mechanism within the broader bread-baking process.

concepts.card: When starch is heated with water, its granules absorb water and swell, thickening the mixture. This gelatinization helps give sauces and puddings their texture. It is a change in the hydrated starch structure, distinct from simply dissolving a sweetener or cooling a gelatin dessert.

evidence.note: The pastry text defines heat-and-water-driven swelling and thickening and names sauces/puddings as examples.

concepts.label: Starch gelatinization
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain thickening when starch granules absorb water and swell during heating.

relations.note: Gelatinization during heating and starch reassociation during storage are distinct stages in starch-based food structure.

concepts.card: After starch has been cooked, its molecules can associate again and develop more ordered structures during storage. This retrogradation changes the starch matrix and can affect texture and digestibility. It is a later rearrangement, distinct from the initial water uptake and swelling of heated starch granules.

evidence.note: Supports chain reassociation and ordering during storage and effects on structure and digestibility.
Supports initial water uptake/swelling during heating, used as the explicit comparison.

concepts.label: Starch retrogradation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish molecular re-ordering during storage from the initial swelling of starch during cooking.

relations.note: The comparison separates initial heat-driven granule swelling from later chain reassociation.

concepts.card: Wheat flour contains glutenin and gliadin, proteins that form gluten when mixed with water. Working the dough develops a stretchy network that can hold gas bubbles. This connects mixing and kneading with a dough’s ability to expand, rather than treating rising as the yeast’s job alone.

evidence.note: Exploratorium identifies the two wheat proteins, hydration, kneading and gas-retaining gluten structure.

concepts.label: Gluten formation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect flour hydration and mechanical working with a network that can hold expanding gas.

relations.note: Developing the gas-retaining wheat-protein network is one physical step within bread baking.

concepts.card: Heating egg white unfolds proteins and allows them to connect with one another. The resulting network traps water, changing a flowing liquid into a firmer structure. Too much heating can make that network rubbery, showing how the same molecular process can produce very different cooking textures.

evidence.note: Exploratorium describes heat unfolding egg-white proteins, intermolecular bonds, trapped water and rubberiness after excessive heating.

concepts.label: Egg protein coagulation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why a liquid egg becomes a network that traps water as it is heated.

relations.note: Eggs can stabilize food in different ways: heat-linked protein networks versus yolk emulsifiers separating fat droplets.

concepts.card: Cutting an apple exposes its tissues to oxygen, allowing enzymes to drive browning reactions. Changing conditions such as acidity can slow the process. The color change therefore connects damage to plant cells with chemical activity, rather than being explained solely by the fruit drying out.

evidence.note: ACS’s explanatory section connects exposed apple tissue, oxygen, enzymes and the slowing effect of acidity.

concepts.label: Enzymatic browning
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a cut fruit surface, oxygen and enzyme activity with a change in color.

relations.note: Both topics concern food-quality changes mediated by enzymes, while acidifying an exposed surface and heat-blanching before freezing are different interventions.

concepts.card: Pectin molecules can form a network that gives fruit spreads their gel structure. Setting conditions depend on the pectin formulation: conventional types rely on appropriate sugar and acid, while other types can work with little or no sugar. Substituting one formulation blindly can therefore change the result.

evidence.note: UMN defines the pectin mesh and distinguishes formulation-specific sugar/acid needs and low/no-sugar products.

concepts.label: Pectin gelation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain fruit-spread setting as a network whose requirements depend on the kind of pectin used.

relations.note: Pectin gel formation can be compared with syneresis, where a gel later releases liquid; no claim is made that every pectin gel will weep.

concepts.card: A watery layer on a gel-like food can result from syneresis: the structure contracts and releases some of the liquid it held. Yogurt and sour cream offer familiar examples. The liquid separation reflects a change within the gel, rather than proving that water was added afterward.

evidence.note: K-State defines gel contraction and water release during storage, using yogurt and sour cream examples.

concepts.label: Syneresis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish water expelled by a contracting gel from water merely added to a food.

relations.note: Comparing gel formation with subsequent liquid expulsion gives two separate questions about food-gel structure.

concepts.card: Tempering chocolate encourages cocoa butter to form a suitable stable crystal structure. That preparation helps the finished chocolate set with gloss, a clean snap and useful contraction. Simply letting melted chocolate become cold does not necessarily produce the same arrangement of crystals or the same finish.

evidence.note: Callebaut explains precrystallizing cocoa butter into a stable structure and resulting shine, snap and contraction.

concepts.label: Chocolate tempering
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect controlled cocoa-butter crystallization with gloss, snap and contraction as chocolate sets.

relations.note: Tempering concerns the desired crystal structure, while fat bloom is a visible defect involving fat migration and surface crystallization.

concepts.card: One form of chocolate bloom occurs when fat moves toward the surface and later crystallizes into a pale coating. Warm storage can encourage this migration. Understanding fat bloom links a visible change in appearance with the movement of cocoa butter, without assuming every pale chocolate coating has that cause.

evidence.note: Callebaut’s warm-storage account describes fat migration and visible bloom; the card explicitly limits the mechanism to fat bloom.

imported_records.description: coating that can appear on chocolate

concepts.label: Chocolate bloom
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize fat bloom as one kind of pale chocolate coating caused by fat reaching the surface.
concepts.original_description: coating that can appear on chocolate

relations.note: The comparison links two chocolate-fat phenomena while distinguishing controlled crystallization from a surface-migration defect.

concepts.card: In hollandaise, whisking disperses melted butter into tiny droplets within a water-based mixture. Egg-yolk emulsifiers help keep those droplets from merging again. The sauce’s stability therefore depends on both forming small droplets and maintaining their separation, rather than merely stirring fat and water together once.

evidence.note: Exploratorium describes whisking butter into droplets and yolk proteins/lecithin stabilizing the oil–water interface against coalescence.

concepts.label: Hollandaise emulsification
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how egg yolk helps tiny fat droplets remain dispersed in the water phase of a sauce.

relations.note: Hollandaise is a documented culinary oil-in-water emulsion; yolk supplies the stabilizers that keep its dispersed fat droplets separate.

concepts.card: Water activity compares the equilibrium water-vapor pressure above a food with that above pure water at the same temperature. It differs from total moisture content because some water is tightly associated with food components. This distinction helps explain why foods containing water can support microbes differently.

evidence.note: FDA’s physical definition gives the vapor-pressure ratio and distinguishes strongly bound water from available moisture relevant to microbial growth.

imported_records.description: one of the main factor limiting microbial activity

concepts.label: Water activity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish available water from total moisture when reasoning about food stability.
concepts.original_description: one of the main factor limiting microbial activity

relations.note: Fermentation changes a food biologically, while water activity describes one environmental constraint on microbial growth; they are complementary food-stability concepts.

concepts.card: Briefly heating vegetables before freezing can slow or stop enzymes that would otherwise degrade flavor, color and texture during storage. This blanching step protects quality, but its duration depends on the vegetable and its size. Too little or too much heating can undermine the intended result.

evidence.note: NCHFP explains enzyme inactivation/quality preservation and the vegetable/size-dependent harms of under- and overblanching.

concepts.label: Blanching vegetables before freezing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain a brief heat treatment as a way to slow enzyme-driven quality loss during frozen storage.

relations.note: Both explain enzyme-mediated changes in food, but blanching uses heat before frozen storage while enzymatic browning describes a particular reaction after tissue exposure.

concepts.card: Drip irrigation delivers water through small outlets placed near individual plants. In the inspected hydroponic example, a hose system supplies nutrient solution at plant bases instead of sending a continuous stream down a channel. The delivery arrangement targets the root area rather than wetting an entire surface uniformly.

evidence.note: UMN’s drip-system passage describes hoses and small holes/outlets located at each plant base, contrasted with nutrient-film channels.

concepts.label: Drip irrigation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Deliver water or nutrient solution near individual plants through controlled small outlets.

relations.note: Localized delivery through outlets is a particular irrigation method within the broader application of water to plants.

concepts.card: A soil tensiometer uses a water-filled tube, a porous ceramic tip and a gauge to assess soil-water tension. It measures how tightly the soil holds water, not simply the fraction of soil volume occupied by water. That distinction matters when judging how hard roots must work to extract moisture.

evidence.note: UMN explains tension as extraction energy and describes the tensiometer’s water-filled tube, ceramic tip and gauge.

concepts.label: Soil tensiometer
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish how tightly soil holds water from the amount of water it contains.

relations.note: Water-availability measurements can inform irrigation decisions, while variable-rate irrigation concerns varying delivery across zones; no automatic control connection is assumed.

concepts.card: Hydroponics grows plants without relying on soil as the nutrient medium. A water-based solution supplies mineral nutrients, while the system must also accommodate the roots’ need for oxygen. Different arrangements support or bathe the roots differently, so soilless growing is more than placing a plant in plain water.

evidence.note: UMN defines soilless growing with nutrient solution and discusses root aeration and several system arrangements.

concepts.label: Hydroponics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Grow plants using a nutrient solution without making soil the source of their nutrients.

relations.note: Nutrient-film technique is one particular arrangement for supplying roots within hydroponics.

concepts.card: Nutrient-film technique moves a shallow stream of nutrient solution through channels containing plant roots. The solution circulates back toward a reservoir while roots retain access to air. The arrangement differs from deeply immersing the whole root system, and depends on keeping that moving supply available.

evidence.note: UMN describes shallow continuous flow through channels, return circulation and the root-zone arrangement.

concepts.label: Nutrient-film technique
concepts.learning_takeaway: Circulate a shallow nutrient stream past roots while retaining access to oxygen.

relations.note: The channel-and-shallow-flow arrangement is a specific hydroponic system described in the source.

concepts.card: Variable-rate irrigation changes water delivery across a field using control zones and prescription maps. Those maps specify irrigation amounts, but soil and crop information must guide the prescription. The technology applies the planned pattern; it does not independently determine how much water a crop needs.

evidence.note: UMN describes control zones and prescription maps, then explicitly distinguishes spatial application from determining crop water need. Agronomic information and irrigation-scheduling tools are required to assign appropriate amounts.

concepts.label: Variable-rate irrigation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Match irrigation amounts to different areas of a field instead of assuming every area needs the same water.

relations.note: Spatially varied application is a specific control approach within irrigation rather than a second identity for irrigation as a whole.

concepts.card: Marker-assisted selection chooses breeding material using DNA markers associated with traits of interest. A breeder reads the marker pattern rather than relying only on the trait’s visible expression. The method depends on an established marker–trait relationship, so detecting a genetic difference alone is not enough.

evidence.locator: Plant breeding and marker-assisted selection introduction
evidence.note: UNL defines genotype-based selection and explicitly requires marker patterns known to be associated with the target traits.

concepts.label: Marker-assisted selection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Select breeding candidates using genetic markers associated with a useful trait.

relations.note: Linked markers can track a trait during breeding, applying the co-inheritance relationship introduced by genetic linkage.

concepts.card: An F1 hybrid is the first generation produced by crossing distinct parental lines. In crop varieties, that cross can combine useful traits, but saved seed from the hybrid need not reproduce the same combination. Later offspring can vary, even when the original hybrid plants seemed very consistent.

evidence.note: Verifies F1 as first filial generation from a cross of parental strains.
Supports combining traits of different parental varieties in crop hybrids.
Explicitly supports the variability of offspring grown from seed saved from F1 hybrids.

imported_records.description: first-generation hybrid (or crossbreed) animal or plant

concepts.label: F1 hybrid
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a deliberate parental cross from the variable offspring produced by saving seed from that hybrid.
concepts.original_description: first-generation hybrid (or crossbreed) animal or plant

relations.note: A deliberate parental cross and variation in later generations provide a practical crop-breeding application of inheritance and variation.

concepts.card: IR8 emerged from crossing the tall rice variety Peta with the dwarf Dee-geo-woo-gen, followed by selection of useful offspring. Released by IRRI in 1966, it became an influential semidwarf variety. Its history makes crop improvement visible as a sequence of crosses, observations and selection.

evidence.note: IRRI’s breeding history identifies Peta and Dee-geo-woo-gen, the crossing/selection sequence, 1966 release and semidwarf significance.

concepts.label: IR8
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace a historically influential semi-dwarf rice variety to a specific cross and selection program.

relations.note: IR8’s crossing-and-selection history can be compared with later marker-assisted selection, without falsely claiming IR8 was originally created using that later method.

concepts.card: Swarna-Sub1 adds temporary flood tolerance to a widely grown rice variety through the SUB1 breeding trait. It can survive periods of submergence that threaten ordinary crops, but longer floods still pose serious limits. The case shows why a tolerant variety is not an invulnerable one.

evidence.note: IRRI names Swarna-Sub1 and describes SUB1-enabled temporary submergence survival with sharply reduced performance in longer floods.

concepts.label: Swarna-Sub1
concepts.learning_takeaway: See flood tolerance as a bounded crop trait rather than an ability to survive indefinitely underwater.

relations.note: The two named rice varieties illustrate different breeding objectives: semidwarf crop architecture and temporary flood tolerance.

concepts.card: Broadbalk compares wheat grown under different nutrient treatments across many years. An unfertilized strip maintained since 1843 provides a persistent reference against which fertilized plots can be read. The experiment shows how a long-lived control helps separate treatment effects from the changing background of agricultural seasons.

evidence.note: Rothamsted states the nutrient-treatment purpose and unfertilized control strip maintained since 1843.

concepts.label: Broadbalk Wheat Experiment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use a persistent untreated comparison to interpret crop responses to fertilizer over many years.

relations.note: Broadbalk and Park Grass are separate long-term Rothamsted experiments, useful for comparing arable nutrient studies with permanent-grassland treatment histories.

concepts.card: Park Grass has studied grassland responses to fertilizer and liming since the nineteenth century. Its long record is not a single unchanging protocol: later liming subplots and changes in harvesting affect comparisons. Reading the experiment requires the treatment and measurement history alongside the hay-yield numbers.

evidence.locator: Study description; Liming design; Harvest methods
evidence.note: The e-RA dataset describes the experiment’s 1856 origin, 1965 liming subplots, hay yields and historical harvesting changes affecting comparability.

concepts.label: Park Grass Experiment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Interpret a long-term grassland experiment in light of treatment design and changes in measurement methods.

relations.note: Both experiments offer long records, but the inspected Park Grass design is a distinct grassland/liming study rather than another name for Broadbalk wheat plots.

concepts.card: Woodworking shapes and joins wood into useful or decorative objects. Adhesive bonds, for example, let separate pieces share loads and form structures that a single piece could not easily provide. Understanding the material and the joint together helps explain why successful making involves more than choosing a shape.

evidence.note: The USDA adhesive chapter describes load transfer, bonded panels/structures and furniture uses; the registered field description supplies shaping/joining scope.

imported_records.description: Shaping and joining wood to create practical or decorative objects.

concepts.label: Woodworking
concepts.learning_takeaway: See joining wood as a way to build objects whose size and behavior differ from a single solid piece.
concepts.original_description: Shaping and joining wood to create practical or decorative objects.

relations.note: End-grain gluing provides a specific example of how wood’s cellular structure influences a woodworking joint.

concepts.card: Wood exchanges moisture with the air around it. Its equilibrium moisture content is the point at which it is neither gaining nor losing moisture under those conditions. Because temperature and relative humidity matter, wood does not have one universally correct moisture level for every room or season.

evidence.note: USDA Chapter 4 defines EMC by no net gain/loss and relates it to surrounding temperature and relative humidity.

concepts.label: Equilibrium moisture content of wood
concepts.learning_takeaway: Relate a wood component’s stable moisture level to its surrounding air rather than one universally dry state.

relations.note: Sorption hysteresis adds moisture-history dependence to the environmental conditions that determine a wood specimen’s EMC.

concepts.card: Wood’s equilibrium moisture content can depend on whether it reached a humidity level by drying or by absorbing water. At the same temperature and relative humidity, the drying path can retain more moisture. This sorption hysteresis makes moisture history relevant even after equilibrium is reached.

evidence.note: USDA describes sorption isotherms at constant temperature and history-dependent equilibrium moisture content, with higher EMC on desorption than absorption at the same relative humidity.

concepts.label: Wood sorption hysteresis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why wood’s moisture history can matter even at the same temperature and relative humidity.

relations.note: The hysteresis passage describes path dependence of wood’s equilibrium-moisture relationship, a specific aspect of that property.

concepts.card: The open cells exposed at wood’s end grain can draw adhesive away from a joint’s interface. Excessive penetration leaves voids and helps explain why a simple end-to-end butt bond can be weak. Joint geometry matters because increasing useful bonded area can change how loads pass between pieces.

evidence.locator: Density and Porosity, p. 10–6; End-Grain Joints, pp. 10–16 to 10–17
evidence.note: USDA describes end-grain porosity, overpenetration/bond-line voids and the increased area achieved by scarf/finger arrangements.

concepts.label: End-grain gluing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect end-grain porosity with adhesive overpenetration and weak butt-joint behavior.

relations.note: Adhesive penetration at end grain is a specific material-and-joint problem within woodworking.

concepts.card: Steam bending uses heat and moisture to make suitable wood more flexible. The piece is shaped and then restrained while it cools and dries, helping it retain the curve. Moisture changes later can still alter that shape, so bending success involves both forming and conditioning the material.

evidence.locator: Principles of Plasticizing and Bending; Fixing the Bend
evidence.note: USDA Chapter 19 describes heat/moisture plasticization, restraint during cooling/drying and later moisture-dependent curvature changes.

concepts.label: Steam bending
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use heat and moisture to soften wood, then retain a curved shape while it cools and dries.

relations.note: Steam bending is a wood-shaping process whose success depends on the material’s moisture and heat response.

concepts.card: Machine-made paper often has fibers preferentially aligned in one direction, called its grain. Folding across that direction can produce uneven creases, and moisture from adhesive causes greater expansion across the grain. These directional differences matter when arranging folds and glued parts in bookbinding.

evidence.note: Cornell’s preservation tutorial describes machine-aligned fibers, cross-grain fold puckering and larger moisture expansion across grain.

concepts.label: Paper grain direction in bookbinding
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect aligned paper fibers with easier folding along the grain and unequal expansion when adhesive wets the sheet.

relations.note: Grain direction is a specific material consideration when folds and glued paper elements are assembled in bookbinding.

concepts.card: Wet clay shrinks as water between its particles leaves and the particles pack closer together. If different parts dry unevenly, they can shrink by different amounts and develop cracks as the piece stiffens. This drying change occurs before the separate transformations produced by firing in a kiln.

evidence.locator: Opening definition; differential drying and cracking
evidence.note: Digitalfire describes inter-particle water loss, packing, uneven drying and stress-driven cracks as clay becomes less plastic.

concepts.label: Clay drying shrinkage
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain shrinkage before firing through particle packing as inter-particle water leaves the clay.

relations.note: Drying shrinkage is a material behavior encountered between shaping clay and firing a pottery object.

concepts.card: Leather temper describes how readily a hide bends, drapes or holds its shape. It is different from thickness: equally thick pieces can feel quite different. A soft garment panel and a firm structured bag may require different tempers, so flexing a sample reveals information a thickness measurement cannot.

evidence.locator: Definition; Matching temper to the job; Describing temper
evidence.note: United Leather distinguishes temper from thickness and relates soft/firm behavior to garment and structured-bag uses; Tandy independently defines pliability.
The independent supplier glossary defines temper as finished-leather pliability from stiff to supple.

concepts.label: Leather temper
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a hide’s pliability from its thickness when choosing between draping and shape-holding uses.

relations.note: Temper is a particular mechanical property of finished leather, not a different material identity or simply its thickness.

concepts.card: A mortise-and-tenon joint fits a projecting end of one piece into a matching recess in another. Close-fitting faces provide contact for bonding, while the shoulders seat against the receiving piece. The arrangement connects shape and fit with joint performance, rather than relying on an end-to-end butt connection alone.

evidence.note: The original WOOD instruction defines projection/recess, glue surface and shoulder contact as components of the fitted joint.

concepts.label: Mortise-and-tenon joint
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a fitted projection, its matching recess and seated shoulders with a strong wooden joint.

relations.note: This is a specific geometric method of joining wooden components within woodworking.

concepts.card: Dovetail joints connect boards through interlocking pins and tails. Through dovetails show the joint on both faces, while half-blind versions hide it from the front, as in a drawer. The same joining principle can therefore support different choices about how much of the construction remains visible.

evidence.locator: Transcript opening, through and half-blind variants
evidence.note: WOOD’s original demonstration describes interlocking holding power and the visible through/hidden-front half-blind distinction.

concepts.label: Dovetail joint
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect interlocking pins and tails with a choice about whether the joint is visible at the front.

relations.note: Dovetails are a documented woodworking joinery method whose geometry and visibility can be compared with other joints.

concepts.card: Drawboring deliberately offsets peg holes in a mortise-and-tenon joint. Driving a wooden peg through them pulls the pieces tightly together. A tapered metal drawbore pin can first test the fit, but the temporary pin and the wooden peg securing the finished joint have different roles.

evidence.note: Lee Valley explains offset holes drawing the joint tight and distinguishes temporary tapered test pins from final wooden pegs.

concepts.label: Drawboring
concepts.learning_takeaway: Pull a mortise-and-tenon joint tight by driving a peg through intentionally offset holes.

relations.note: Drawboring is a specific way to tighten and secure a mortise-and-tenon assembly.

concepts.card: Kerf bending cuts a series of slots into one side of wood while leaving a thin outer layer intact. The remaining web can flex around a curve. Slot spacing and depth affect the result, and the weakened piece usually needs a supporting form or backing to hold its shape.

evidence.note: WOOD’s demonstrated method describes cross-grain slots, retained outer material, spacing/depth tradeoffs and supporting attachment.

concepts.label: Kerf bending
concepts.learning_takeaway: Create a bend by cutting relief slots while retaining an outer web of material.

relations.note: Kerf bending removes material to permit flexure, while steam bending softens intact wood through heat and moisture.

concepts.card: A French cleat hangs a fixture using two matching beveled strips: one attached to the wall and one to the object. Their opposing slopes engage to carry the load while allowing a flexible storage layout. Secure anchoring and suitable load distribution remain part of the system.

evidence.note: Lee Valley’s workshop account describes wall strips, opposing fixture bevels, movable storage and added cleats for heavier objects.

concepts.label: French cleat
concepts.learning_takeaway: Support a removable wall fixture with two mating beveled strips.

relations.note: The paired wooden strips apply shaped joinery to mounting movable fixtures rather than permanently joining board ends.

concepts.card: A story stick carries a project’s important dimensions as full-size marks on one physical strip. The marks preserve their relationship to one another and provide a reusable layout reference. Transferring those positions can reduce the need to repeatedly reinterpret a list of separate numerical measurements.

evidence.note: WOOD’s explanation defines a strip bearing critical full-scale dimensions and a visual representation of the project.

concepts.label: Story stick
concepts.learning_takeaway: Preserve project dimensions together on a physical reference rather than repeatedly translating separate numbers.

relations.note: A story stick preserves designed positions, while scribing transfers an existing irregular contour; both are layout aids with different inputs.

concepts.card: Scribing to fit transfers the contour of an existing surface onto a new workpiece. A cabinet panel beside an uneven wall, for example, can be marked to match that wall’s profile. The method handles irregularity directly instead of assuming that every surrounding surface is straight.

evidence.locator: Transferring wall contours onto a panel
evidence.note: Lee Valley describes transferring contours and specifically copying an old irregular wall profile onto a cabinet panel.

concepts.label: Scribing to fit
concepts.learning_takeaway: Fit a new component to an irregular existing surface by transferring its contour onto the workpiece.

relations.note: The contrast separates copying an encountered contour from reusing dimensions already stored on a story stick.

concepts.card: Sharpening a blade can leave a thin wire edge, or burr, along the cutting edge. An unwanted burr may feel sharp initially but break away during use, leaving a rougher edge. Honing removes this fragile remnant, so forming an edge and finishing it are distinct parts of sharpening.

evidence.note: Tormek’s official answer describes wire-edge formation, breakoff during use and removal through honing.

concepts.label: Sharpening burr
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize the fragile wire edge left by sharpening and why it must be removed from a finished cutting edge.

relations.note: An unwanted sharpening burr is a particular edge condition addressed during the broader edge-refinement process.

concepts.card: Weaving interlaces two sets of threads to build cloth. The warp is held on the loom under tension, while the weft passes over and under it. Separating those roles helps explain how a loom organizes many individual strands into a stable, patterned textile structure.

evidence.note: Ashford defines warp held under tension and weft passing over/under it to form woven fabric.

imported_records.description: Interlacing threads or fibers to create textiles.

concepts.label: Weaving
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish the held warp from the interlacing weft that creates woven cloth.
concepts.original_description: Interlacing threads or fibers to create textiles.

relations.note: Managing the held warp’s tension is a specific operational concern within the interlacing process.

concepts.card: Warp threads need suitable, reasonably even tension while weaving. On a rigid-heddle loom, too little can let the raised reed fall, while too much can make changing positions difficult and strain the yarn. Good control means balancing the working tension, not simply making every thread as tight as possible.

evidence.locator: Even tension, PDF pp. 8–10; Helpful Hints—Tension, PDF p. 15
evidence.note: Ashford instructs checking equal tension and explains too-low/too-high tension effects on its rigid-heddle reed and yarn.

concepts.label: Warp tension
concepts.learning_takeaway: Balance a warp firmly enough to form the shed without unnecessarily straining the yarn and loom.

relations.note: Warp-tension control is a specific part of managing the thread set held by a loom during weaving.

concepts.card: A bias facing uses a narrow strip of fabric cut on the bias to finish a curved edge. The strip can be shaped to follow the curve without the bulk of a wider facing. Its usefulness comes from how the fabric direction allows the finish to conform.

evidence.note: NMSU describes narrow bias strips shaped to curves and their use to reduce visible or heavy facings.

concepts.label: Bias facings
concepts.learning_takeaway: Finish a curved fabric edge using a narrow strip whose bias orientation allows it to conform to the curve.

relations.note: A bias facing is a specific sewn curved-edge finish within garment construction.

concepts.card: Staystitching adds a permanent row of stitches to an individual fabric piece before assembly. Placed within the seam allowance, it helps keep vulnerable curves or bias edges from stretching during handling. It stabilizes the cut shape, rather than serving as the seam that joins two pieces together.

evidence.locator: What is it?; When to staystitch
evidence.note: ASG defines single-layer pre-assembly stabilization within the allowance, especially at curved/bias areas, and states the stitches remain in the garment.

concepts.label: Staystitching
concepts.learning_takeaway: Stabilize an individual cut fabric edge before handling and assembly stretch it out of shape.

relations.note: Staystitching stabilizes a cut edge before assembly; understitching controls a facing after its seam has been sewn.

concepts.card: Understitching secures a seam allowance to the facing on the inside of a garment. This encourages the seam to roll inward and helps prevent the facing from showing on the outside. It controls an already assembled edge, rather than stabilizing a loose pattern piece before sewing.

evidence.locator: Seam-allowance understitching; Tips for Applying Facings
evidence.note: NMSU describes pressing the allowance toward the facing, understitching and preventing the facing from rolling outside.

concepts.label: Understitching
concepts.learning_takeaway: Keep a facing from rolling to the garment’s outside by securing its seam allowance to the facing.

relations.note: These stitching operations differ in timing and purpose: control of an assembled facing versus stabilization of an unjoined cut edge.

concepts.card: A French seam encloses raw fabric edges inside a second seam. The first pass joins the fabric with wrong sides together; after turning, another pass hides that initial allowance. This creates a tidy enclosed finish, useful when exposed edges would show through a sheer fabric.

evidence.note: BERNINA’s original tutorial defines two-part edge enclosure, wrong-sides-first sequencing and usefulness for sheer fabrics.

concepts.label: French seam
concepts.learning_takeaway: Enclose raw fabric edges inside a second seam rather than leaving them exposed to fray.

relations.note: Both enclose raw edges, but a French seam contains the first seam within a second while a flat-felled seam is secured down flat.

concepts.card: A flat-felled seam wraps one fabric edge within a folded edge and secures the assembly flat with stitching. The enclosed raw edges and additional stitching produce a durable finish familiar from jeans and other hard-wearing garments. Its flattened construction distinguishes it from a French seam’s enclosed ridge.

evidence.note: Supports folded enclosure, stitching flat, durability and jeans use.
Supports the contrast with enclosing one seam inside another.

concepts.label: Flat-felled seam
concepts.learning_takeaway: Create an enclosed-edge seam that is folded down and secured flat with visible stitching.

relations.note: The connection compares two genuinely different enclosed-edge constructions rather than counting synonymous finishes.

concepts.card: Knitting gauge counts stitches and rows within a given length of fabric. A swatch tests the yarn, needles and stitch pattern together before a larger project is made. If the gauge differs from the pattern, the same stitch count can produce a different finished size.

evidence.note: Craft Yarn Council defines stitch/row density, the gauge swatch and changing needle size when the swatch dimensions differ.

concepts.label: Knitting gauge
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect stitches and rows per unit length with the dimensions a knitting pattern will produce.

relations.note: Blocking can change fabric dimensions, so the source’s recommendation to test blocking on a swatch links finishing behavior with measured gauge.

concepts.card: Blocking shapes a knitted piece and evens its fabric using moisture, sometimes with steam. The method should suit the yarn and its care instructions. Testing a swatch first helps reveal how the material responds before trying to bring a finished garment to its intended dimensions.

evidence.note: Knit Picks explains shaping/evening, wet/spray/steam methods, yarn-care dependence and a test on the gauge swatch.

concepts.label: Blocking knitted fabric
concepts.learning_takeaway: Set a knitted piece’s dimensions and even its fabric using a method suited to the yarn.

relations.note: Blocking is a post-knitting shaping and finishing practice applied to the loop-based fabric, rather than a stitch-forming technique.

issues.label: Blinding in clinical trials
issues.reason: Omitted to avoid a cross-batch duplicate. Coordinator confirmed batch 007 owns double-blind studies; allocation concealment and intention-to-treat remain separately supported mechanisms.
Skin grafting is a sourced reconstructive method. It does not fit diagnostic methods, so its new subfield is explicit; all three assigned health starting subfields still have at least 14 proposals.
issues.resolution: Selected with explicit scope/ownership in the approved manifest; original proposal issue is retained in the hashed Stage A artifact.

issues.reason: OpenStax physiological mechanism passages were inspected selectively. Do not reuse its paper-bag or diabetic-coma treatment remarks, broad insulin-receptor claims, active urea-pump wording, or clinical threshold advice. These are unnecessary to the selected learning takeaways and contain concerning simplifications or errors.

issues.label: Chesapeake Bay hypoxia case
issues.reason: The promising public discovery page returned failures on two attempts. Its search excerpt is retained in 045-environment-discovery.json but was not admitted as passage evidence. The inspected Sand Hollow field case fills the environmental case-study slot instead.

The Shenandoah source is used only for its inspected igneous-structure passages. Its broad ancient-supercontinent wording is not used. The oceanography resources landing pages were not treated as explanatory support; dedicated NOAA articles were inspected instead.

issues.detail: Coordinator confirmed batch 004 does not reserve the proposed food mechanisms or generic Emulsion control. Food owns these proposals subject to baseline review. Batch 006 owns Subak; no Subak identity is proposed here.

Horticultural grafting and skin grafting are separately sourced practices. Shared Graft wording is supported by the apple propagation and NHS tissue-transfer passages. Existing cambial alignment remains a narrower plant-grafting facet, not a synonym of either full practice.
issues.resolution: Selected with explicit scope/ownership in the approved manifest; original proposal issue is retained in the hashed Stage A artifact.

issues.detail: Variable-rate manure application was dropped after two 429 responses; variable-rate irrigation was independently discovered and inspected. Park Grass landing page and a 2014 Swarna page each failed twice; an actual e-RA dataset and a different IRRI research account supplied support. Marker-assisted selection used UNL after a failed extension page and an inaccessible IRRI PDF. Failed sources are not explanatory evidence.

Water-activity source is historical and used for the physical definition, not current regulatory guidance. Chocolate-bloom evidence supports the fat-bloom form only. Pectin gelation retains formulation differences. No universal companion-planting benefit, indefinite flood survival or assumption that all saved seed breeds true is asserted.

Wood checking was not proposed because its mechanism risked repeating existing drying-stress reversal. Wood sorption hysteresis is independently supported equilibrium-history behavior. Steam bending is proposed as a moisture/heat forming process, not a merely renamed sheet-metal springback facet. Bias facings has the scope of the actually inspected curved-edge method, not the whole bias-cut garment practice.

CYC knitting handbook exceeded web fetch size; Knit Picks supplied an actual inspected blocking account. A Lee Valley PDF had unsupported content type; the official Tormek answer supplied burr evidence. Dovetail Wikipedia was inspected as background, but the proposed source is the original WOOD workshop transcript. PDF-based claims use extracted text; no numerical diagram reading is claimed.

issues.reason: The attached NHLBI passage establishes the target comparison but not random allocation; the generic RCT definition does not establish SPRINT’s particular design. After the auditor exhausted three primary-report alternatives, the unsupported editorial edge is removed. This is an evidence-verification gap, not a finding that SPRINT was nonrandomized.

historical_stage_a_issues.note: Discrete Laplace operator is the registered broader/operator meaning. A graph Laplacian is a standard discrete Laplace operator on a graph, so label difference is insufficient evidence of novelty. This proposal is quarantined pending central equivalence/facet adjudication and does not count toward the recommended 200.

The registered Precession entry covers axis-direction change generally. The proposal is explicitly the torque-induced gyroscope case: a torque perpendicular to angular momentum turns its direction, with the fast-spin assumption stated in the inspected section. This is proposed as a narrower supported facet, not as a second general precession identity.

The registered Cauchy stress tensor is the tensor representation of the complete stress state at a point. The proposed introductory topic distinguishes force-per-area loading modes; retaining this broader physical quantity separately from its full tensor representation requires central review of the breadth distinction.

Failed and redirected sources are recorded in access-log.json. No candidate is supported only by a search snippet, failed URL, or redirect page. Brayton-cycle exploration was stopped after three unsuccessful candidate references; it is not selected.

Some accessible educational pages contain stale or overbroad statements outside the selected claim set. Examples not carried forward: current Forth Bridge painting practice, ASCE Eiffel Tower cast-iron wording, OpenStax room-temperature ammonia equilibrium-constant value, claims that Otto models all internal-combustion engines, and unqualified memorylessness claims. These sources do not certify excluded statements.

The recommended 200 have 50 per assigned domain. Ten evidence-backed reserves permit substitutions; unresolved Graph Laplacian is additional and not counted. Counts remain provisional until central reconciliation.

Sources serving several independently meaningful proposals, especially crystal structures, must receive claim-specific source review and careful source-reuse management in Stage B. No discovery-card prose has been authored.

concepts.card: For a slender, uniform beam simply supported and loaded at its midpoint, an ideal three-point bending test links force and deflection. evidence.note: The small-angle Euler–Bernoulli derivation uses constant flexural rigidity EI; a simply supported beam with a midpoint load has maximum deflection PL³/(48EI).
