It illustrates how independent member enterprises can coordinate through a federation without becoming a single ordinary business under one owner.

evidence.note: Checked founding aims and cooperative membership; no claim about current membership counts or authority over every cooperative.

evidence.locator: Principle 4, Autonomy and Independence; Principle 6, Cooperation among Cooperatives
evidence.note: Principle 4 states member control and cooperative autonomy when entering agreements; Principle 6 describes cooperation through local, national, regional and international structures. Together they support the independence/coordination premise. The 1895 founding aims are separately supported by the history source.

concepts.label: International Cooperative Alliance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how an international federation coordinated information, common principles, and trade among otherwise separate cooperatives.

relations.note: The Alliance's history expressly describes delegates from cooperatives establishing an international body to support their shared principles and trade.

concepts.card: Grameen Bank developed from a village-based research project in Bangladesh into a bank in 1983. Its account emphasizes lending without collateral and bringing services close to borrowers through village centers. The design changes how people reach credit; that alone does not establish every claimed effect on poverty.

evidence.locator: About Grameen Bank, pilot and collateral paragraphs
evidence.note: Checked pilot-to-bank history, collateral and village access; omitted promotional success rates and causal poverty-reduction claims.

concepts.label: Grameen Bank
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine collateral-free village-based lending as an institutional design for reaching borrowers conventional banking may exclude.

relations.note: Grameen's official history explicitly describes its transformation into a bank and its collateral-free, locally delivered banking model.

concepts.card: Toyota's official production-system account combines just-in-time flow with jidoka, the practice of responding to abnormalities. One coordinates when work and parts are needed; the other helps prevent defects from continuing unnoticed. The case presents production as linked processes, rather than equating productivity only with machines running faster.

evidence.note: Checked the two-component account and distinct functions; the company's explanation is not treated as independent proof of superiority in every setting.

concepts.label: Toyota Motor Corporation
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how the company's production system joins abnormality detection with demand-coordinated flow rather than optimizing only machine speed.

relations.note: Toyota explicitly identifies jidoka as a central component of its own production system and explains its abnormality-stopping mechanism.

concepts.card: Sakichi Toyoda's loom work connects a named invention history with jidoka. Toyota describes looms that stopped automatically when yarn broke or ran out, reducing the need for constant watching. The lesson is a design response to abnormal conditions, rather than automation understood only as continuous unattended operation.

evidence.locator: Roots of Ideas, How did the idea of Jidoka come about?
evidence.note: Checked yarn-related stopping and historical lineage; no claim that the loom independently diagnosed or repaired the cause.

concepts.label: Sakichi Toyoda
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect his self-stopping loom experiments with the later manufacturing principle of detecting abnormalities at their source.

relations.note: Toyota directly traces jidoka's origin to Sakichi Toyoda's self-stopping loom developments.

concepts.card: Kiichiro Toyoda advocated coordinating automobile parts just when they were needed while working with limited resources. Toyota's history connects that concern with just-in-time production and later downstream pull arrangements. The case shows how production timing emerged from a concrete coordination problem, rather than from simply demanding faster work.

evidence.locator: Roots of Ideas, How did the idea of Just-in-Time come about?
evidence.note: Checked the founder's timing concern and later development; did not credit one person with every subsequent Toyota-system technique.

concepts.label: Kiichiro Toyoda
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how limited resources shaped his effort to coordinate automobile parts just when production needed them.

relations.note: Toyota expressly connects Kiichiro Toyoda's resource-constrained manufacturing plans with the origins of just-in-time production.

concepts.card: Sociology studies patterns in how people interact, form groups, and organize societies. It connects small encounters with larger institutions and historical conditions. A conflict between work and family responsibilities, for example, can be examined as more than one person's private failure to manage time well.

evidence.locator: §1.1, What Are Society and Culture?; Studying Patterns
evidence.note: Checked micro/macro scope and role-conflict example; not claimed that personal decisions are entirely determined by social structure.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The introductory field definition and the role-conflict example connect individual experiences to patterned expectations across social roles.

imported_records.description: social science that studies human society and its development
imported_records.subsection: Society and social sciences / Society / Sociology

concepts.label: Sociology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect everyday interactions with patterned relationships and institutions at larger social scales.
concepts.original_description: social science that studies human society and its development

relations.note: The introductory field definition and the role-conflict example connect individual experiences to patterned expectations across social roles.

concepts.card: A social network represents people or other social actors through the relationships connecting them. Looking at those links reveals patterns that a list of individuals misses. Some positions connect otherwise separate circles, while others sit inside densely linked groups, creating different opportunities for information and cooperation.

evidence.note: Checked actors/links representation and contrasting network positions; network diagrams are models of selected relationships, not complete descriptions of people.

imported_records.description: theoretical concept in sociology
imported_records.subsection: Society and social sciences / Society / Social structure, society as a social system / Groups

concepts.label: Social network
concepts.learning_takeaway: Represent people and relationships to inspect how local connections shape access to wider social worlds.
concepts.original_description: theoretical concept in sociology

relations.note: The network text explicitly uses strong and weak ties to explain how relationship structure connects local groups with wider information.

concepts.card: Weak ties are less-close relationships, such as acquaintances, that may connect someone to information outside their usual circle. Close friends often know many of the same people. An acquaintance can therefore provide a different route, although a tie's usefulness depends on its network position rather than weakness alone.

evidence.note: Checked information access and the nonidentity of weak ties and local bridges; no claim that every acquaintance supplies novel information.

concepts.label: Weak ties
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why acquaintances can connect people to information outside densely connected close-friend circles.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly connects weak ties with local bridges while separating interpersonal tie strength from the mathematical edge property.

concepts.card: Triadic closure is the tendency for two people with a shared friend to become connected themselves. Meeting opportunities and social context can help such ties form. It is a pattern of network development, not a guarantee that every pair of friends-of-friends will eventually know each other.

evidence.note: Checked shared-neighbor tendency and distinction from a universal rule; no inevitability or fixed time scale is asserted.

concepts.label: Triadic closure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why two people sharing a friend are more likely to form a connection, without treating this as inevitable.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly develops the stronger formal closure property from the qualitative tendency and warns that the formal version is an extreme assumption.

concepts.card: A local bridge connects two nodes that have no common neighbor. Removing it leaves no two-step alternative route between its endpoints; reaching the other side takes a longer path, if one exists. This precise edge property helps distinguish network-spanning connections from ties embedded among mutual friends.

evidence.note: Checked no-common-neighbor definition and possible disconnection; a local bridge need not disconnect the entire graph when removed.

concepts.label: Local bridge in a network
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify a tie whose endpoints have no mutual neighbor and whose removal makes their shortest connecting path longer.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly states that local bridges have zero edge embeddedness because their endpoints share no neighbors.

concepts.card: Structural holes are gaps between groups that do not otherwise interact closely. Someone whose connections span such a gap may obtain information from different circles or broker their contact. The position can offer opportunities, but it can also create conflicting expectations and incentives to preserve the gap.

evidence.note: Checked informational/brokerage opportunities and competing incentives; correlations with success are not recast as guaranteed causal rewards.

concepts.label: Structural holes
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize opportunities for brokerage where otherwise weakly connected groups hold different information.

relations.note: The chapter connects brokerage across structural holes with boundary-spanning ties, while distinguishing a network position from how emotionally close a relationship is.

concepts.card: Betweenness centrality measures a node's or edge's share of shortest paths between other points in a network. When several shortest paths exist, their contribution is divided. This highlights potential intermediary positions that simple neighbor counts miss, while remaining a model of routes rather than a measurement of actual message traffic.

evidence.note: Checked shortest-path splitting and node/edge definitions; hypothetical flow is not claimed to be the route all real information follows.

concepts.label: Betweenness centrality
concepts.learning_takeaway: Measure how much shortest-path traffic passes through a node or edge rather than simply counting its immediate contacts.

relations.note: Shortest-path mediation is a specific way to analyze positions in social-network representations, distinct from describing the network or counting direct ties.

concepts.card: The strong triadic closure property is an idealized rule: if someone has strong ties to two others, those two must have at least some tie between them. It permits deductions about network structure. The source explicitly warns that real social networks need not satisfy this rule everywhere.

evidence.note: Checked strong-to-two condition, either-strength closing edge, and explicit nonuniversality; the conditional model is not described as an observed social law.

concepts.label: Strong triadic closure property
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use an explicitly idealized rule that two strong neighbors must also have some tie to derive network consequences.

relations.note: The source introduces the named property as a formal, deliberately stronger version of the qualitative triadic-closure tendency.

concepts.card: Edge embeddedness counts how many common neighbors the two ends of a tie share. Mutual contacts create a social setting around the relationship and may make misconduct more visible. A local bridge has zero embeddedness, connecting people without that immediate shared-neighbor context.

evidence.note: Checked shared-neighbor count and zero case; mutual friends are not claimed to ensure trust or prevent all misconduct.

concepts.label: Edge embeddedness
concepts.learning_takeaway: Count the mutual neighbors of a connected pair to describe the social context surrounding their tie.

relations.note: The chapter directly equates zero embeddedness with the local-bridge condition and discusses mutual neighbors' reputational role.

concepts.card: Structural balance studies patterns of friendly and antagonistic ties. In its basic signed-triangle model, triangles with one or three positive edges count as balanced. Other combinations represent proposed tensions, such as being friends with two people who dislike each other; the model simplifies real relationships deliberately.

evidence.note: Checked the one-or-three-positive rule for the basic model; not confused with weaker balance variants or asserted as universal human behavior.

concepts.label: Structural balance in social networks
concepts.learning_takeaway: Model consistency of positive and negative ties by distinguishing balanced triangles from potentially conflicting configurations.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly develops structural balance by assigning positive and negative signs to network edges and examining triangle configurations.

concepts.card: A signed social network records whether a relationship is positive or negative, rather than only whether a tie exists. This allows friendship and antagonism to appear in the same representation. Researchers can then examine configurations such as shared enemies or incompatible alliances, while recognizing that two signs simplify richer relationships.

evidence.note: Checked positive/negative interpretation and modeling simplification; no claim that all real relations fit a complete friend-or-enemy classification.

concepts.label: Signed social network
concepts.learning_takeaway: Represent both friendly and antagonistic relations with edge signs instead of recording only whether a relationship exists.

relations.note: The source introduces signed relationship graphs specifically as the representation used to investigate structural balance.

concepts.card: A dyad is a two-person social group. Its existence depends directly on both participants: when one leaves, no two-person group remains. This gives the relationship a different structure from a larger group, where some members can continue interacting after another person withdraws.

evidence.note: Checked two-member dependence; not claimed that all social consequences or obligations disappear when a dyad ends.

concepts.label: Dyad (social group)
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why a two-person group depends on both members' continued participation and cannot outlast either member's departure.

relations.note: OpenStax explicitly contrasts Simmel's two-member and three-member groups by withdrawal and the continuing relationships available.

concepts.card: A triad is a three-person social group. Adding the third member creates possibilities unavailable in a dyad, including two-against-one coalitions and a majority view. If someone withdraws, the remaining pair can still interact, so the group's relationships are not all dependent on one uninterrupted two-person bond.

evidence.note: Checked coalition and withdrawal distinctions; a remaining pair is not inaccurately called a three-person triad.

concepts.label: Triad (social group)
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how adding a third member permits coalitions and lets the group persist after one member leaves.

relations.note: The group-size chapter explicitly contrasts triads with dyads through coalition possibilities and survival of a remaining pair.

concepts.card: A reference group supplies a standard people use to compare themselves with others. It need not be a group they actually belong to: admired athletes or an older sibling's friends may serve that role. Several reference groups can matter at once and convey competing expectations.

evidence.note: Checked comparison versus membership and multiple competing groups; no assumption that a reference group is necessarily beneficial or deliberately chosen.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source explicitly links reference groups with comparisons that guide behavior and establish social norms.

concepts.label: Reference groups
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish groups used as comparison standards from groups someone actually joins.

relations.note: The source explicitly links reference groups with comparisons that guide behavior and establish social norms.

concepts.card: Social norms are shared expectations about conduct. Some are written and formally enforced, while others are learned through observation and everyday reactions. A person's behavior can follow a norm even without an official watching, because approval, disapproval, and anticipated consequences also help sustain expectations.

evidence.note: Checked formal/informal expectations and social reactions; norms are distinguished from ideals and from a claim that everyone always complies.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The social-reality chapter explicitly defines institutionalization through establishing conventions or norms within society.

concepts.label: Social norms
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize shared expectations for conduct, including unwritten rules learned by observing others and their consequences.

relations.note: The social-reality chapter explicitly defines institutionalization through establishing conventions or norms within society.

concepts.card: Institutionalization establishes a convention or norm as a durable part of social life. A school functions as more than a building because people recognize roles and shared expectations around it. Those arrangements can predate current participants, showing how socially created institutions can still have real consequences.

evidence.note: Checked school example and persistence through shared recognition; not equated with any building, any formal organization, or putting a person into residential care.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source directly describes institutionalization as establishing conventions or norms and illustrates it with a school.

concepts.label: Institutionalization
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how shared conventions become established social institutions that outlast the original participants.

relations.note: The source directly describes institutionalization as establishing conventions or norms and illustrates it with a school.

concepts.card: An ascribed status is a social position assigned without the person's choosing it, such as being someone's child. The status comes with expectations and relationships. It describes how the position is acquired, which is different from the behavior people perform while occupying that position.

evidence.note: Checked acquisition without choice and child example; no inference about an individual's worth, ability or immutable destiny.

concepts.label: Ascribed status
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify social positions assigned without personal choice and the expectations attached to them.

relations.note: The roles-and-status passage explicitly contrasts ascribed positions with achieved ones and separates status from expected role behavior.

concepts.card: An achieved status is a social position acquired through activity or choice, such as becoming a nurse. The term distinguishes its route of acquisition from an ascribed position. Status names the position; role describes the patterns of behavior expected of someone who holds it.

evidence.note: Checked nurse example and position-versus-behavior distinction; not claimed that achieved outcomes reflect effort alone or equal opportunity.

concepts.label: Achieved status
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify social positions acquired through activity or choice, while separating the position from its expected behaviors.

relations.note: The source directly presents achieved and ascribed statuses as contrasting acquisition categories, alongside the status/role distinction.

concepts.card: A role-set is the array of role relationships attached to a particular social status. Being a student, for example, involves more than one expectation or relationship. The concept differs from simply listing all the separate statuses a person holds, such as student, worker, and family member.

evidence.note: Checked Merton's single-status role-set definition; did not imply that having several attached roles necessarily creates conflict.

concepts.label: Role-set
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize that one social status can carry several distinct role relationships and expectations.

relations.note: A role-set organizes expectations attached to one status, while role conflict concerns incompatible demands; the concepts address different structural and experiential questions.

concepts.card: Role conflict occurs when obligations associated with different roles pull in incompatible directions. A parent may need to collect a sick child while an employer expects work on a deadline. The problem concerns competing roles, rather than only having too many demands inside one role.

evidence.note: Checked cross-role incompatibility and parent/work example; preserved the existing identity and distinction from role strain.

concepts.label: Role conflict
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish incompatible obligations between different roles from excessive demands within one role.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly contrasts parent-worker role conflict with strain arising from demands within a single role.

concepts.card: Role strain arises when the demands inside a single role become difficult to satisfy together. Parenting, for example, includes care, organization, transport, and guidance. A person can experience that pressure without also holding a conflicting job role, which distinguishes strain from conflict between separate roles.

evidence.note: Checked single-role pressure and multiple parenting duties; preserved the prior card's sense rather than merging it with role conflict.

concepts.label: Role strain
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize competing or excessive demands within a single role even without a clash between separate roles.

relations.note: The source explicitly defines within-role strain and contrasts it with incompatible obligations across multiple roles.

concepts.card: Collective behavior involves group activity that is not governed through an established institution's rules. Crowds, dispersed publics, and shared fashions can take different forms. Studying these episodes does not require assuming that participants lose reason; sociological theories also examine coordination, interpretation, and newly developing norms.

evidence.note: Checked noninstitutionalized activity and variety of forms; no claim that all gatherings lack organization or have identical motives.

concepts.label: Collective behavior
concepts.learning_takeaway: Study noninstitutionalized group activity while distinguishing a shared gathering from a formally regulated organization.

relations.note: The collective-behavior chapter directly introduces emergent-norm theory as one framework for understanding these activities without assuming irrational crowds.

concepts.card: Emergent norm theory explains crowd behavior through guidelines that participants develop in unfamiliar situations. People bring prior expectations, interact, and may accept new ways of acting as circumstances change. The theory treats crowds as more than irrational masses, while leaving questions about how norms spread and gain acceptance.

evidence.note: Checked explanatory status and the source's unresolved acceptance/spread questions; the theory is not presented as a universally established causal law.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source explicitly makes changing and newly established norms central to the emergent-norm account of crowds.

concepts.label: Emergent norm theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain crowd conduct through locally developing guidelines in unfamiliar situations rather than assuming all crowds act irrationally.

relations.note: The source explicitly makes changing and newly established norms central to the emergent-norm account of crowds.

concepts.card: Smelser's value-added theory analyzes collective behavior through a proposed combination of conditions, including structural strain, a shared interpretation, and a precipitating event. It asks what makes an episode possible and mobilizes action. The name refers to an explanatory sociological framework, rather than economic value added or a numerical prediction formula.

evidence.note: Checked named theory and selected conditions; qualification preserves that these are proposed explanatory requirements rather than a validated universal checklist.

concepts.label: Value-added theory of collective behavior
concepts.learning_takeaway: Analyze several proposed conditions for collective episodes, including strain, shared beliefs, and precipitating events.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly presents Smelser's conditions as a theoretical account of collective-behavior episodes.

concepts.card: The assembling perspective examines what people in crowds actually do: gather, orient together, move, speak, or manipulate objects. It shifts attention toward component actions and the lifecycle of gatherings. This makes coordination observable, though critics argue that focusing so closely on actions can miss wider cultural context.

evidence.note: Checked component examples, gathering lifecycle and criticism; not portrayed as evidence that every crowd has one mind or one shared purpose.

concepts.label: Assembling perspective
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine how gatherings form and act through observable component processes instead of treating a crowd as one mind.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly presents McPhail's assembling perspective as a process-focused approach to collective behavior and notes its contextual limitation.

concepts.card: Resource mobilization theory explains social movements partly through their ability to obtain time, money, and participants. Grievances alone do not describe the practical work of organizing transport, meetings, or sustained action. The perspective directs attention to the resources and connections that make collective efforts possible.

evidence.note: Checked resource definitions and organizing examples; no claim that more money automatically guarantees movement success or that interpretation is irrelevant.

concepts.label: Resource mobilization theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain collective organizing partly through acquiring time, money, and people rather than grievances alone.

relations.note: Resource mobilization concerns practical capacity, whereas frame alignment concerns shared interpretations and goals; the source presents both as distinct movement perspectives.

concepts.card: Frame alignment connects a movement's interpretations and goals with potential participants or allied groups. Shared concerns may be bridged, emphasized, extended, or transformed to support cooperation. The concept focuses on how people understand an issue and their relationship to it, rather than only counting the movement's resources.

evidence.note: Checked the four named alignment processes and audience/goal connection; not reduced to organizational merger alone or asserted as a guarantee of recruitment.

concepts.label: Frame alignment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a movement's interpretations and goals with prospective participants or allied groups to support coordinated action.

relations.note: Comparing interpretive alignment with resource acquisition distinguishes two ways the source analyzes collective organizing.

concepts.card: Conversational turn-taking coordinates who speaks and when. Experiments with conversation fragments show that listeners can anticipate turn endings, supporting accounts that involve preparation before silence arrives. Such laboratory tasks isolate useful cues, but do not establish how every transition is managed in natural conversation.

evidence.note: The abstract and experiments report button-press anticipation with conversation fragments; the introduction distinguishes anticipation ability from proof of use in every natural exchange. The card now states the observed ability and the limited inference, while retaining the turn-completion framework.

concepts.label: Conversational turn-taking
concepts.learning_takeaway: Coordinate alternating speakers partly by anticipating possible turn endings rather than waiting only to react after silence.

relations.note: The research paper explicitly relates turn anticipation to possible completion points called transition-relevance places.

concepts.card: A transition-relevance place is a point where a conversational turn could be complete and speaker change becomes possible. The current speaker may select someone, another participant may begin, or the speaker may continue. It is an opportunity for transition, rather than an automatic instruction that the turn must end.

evidence.locator: Introduction, turn-constructional units and allocation rules
evidence.note: Checked possible completion and optional transition; a pause is not automatically classified as a completed conversational turn.

concepts.label: Transition-relevance place
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize a possible completion point where another speaker may take over, although the current speaker can continue.

relations.note: The paper explicitly defines transition-relevance places and summarizes the three turn-allocation possibilities in the turn-taking model.

concepts.card: An adjacency pair links two conversational actions, such as a question and its answer or an invitation and its response. Once the first action occurs, a particular kind of second action becomes relevant. An appropriate response can also show whether the listener understood what the first speaker meant.

evidence.note: Checked conditional relevance and understanding evidence; no claim that paired actions must be physically consecutive without inserted clarification.

concepts.label: Adjacency pair
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how an initial conversational action makes a specific kind of response relevant, such as an answer after a question.

relations.note: Clark and Brennan explicitly discuss relevant second actions as positive evidence of understanding within grounding.

concepts.card: Other-initiated repair occurs when a listener signals trouble with someone else's message and the original speaker helps resolve it. The response may repeat words, clarify a missing detail, or confirm an interpretation. This creates a collaborative detour aimed at restoring understanding so the conversation can proceed.

evidence.locator: Introduction; Materials and Methods, repair-sequence definition
evidence.note: The paper defines trouble source, repair initiator and repair solution. Repair may require more than one attempt; reported brief durations are averages in the sampled corpus. The card describes the collaborative aim without guaranteeing a brief or immediately successful outcome.

evidence.locator: Opening; Grounding in Conversation; contribution model
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Repair makes a breakdown explicit, while grounding also includes routine evidence of understanding; the two sources support their connection without making them equivalent.

concepts.label: Other-initiated conversational repair
concepts.learning_takeaway: Signal trouble with another speaker's message so the original speaker can repeat, clarify, or confirm it.

relations.note: Repair makes a breakdown explicit, while grounding also includes routine evidence of understanding; the two sources support their connection without making them equivalent.

concepts.card: An open repair request signals that something in the previous message was unclear without identifying the troublesome part. A brief Huh? is one example. Because the speaker receives little information about the problem, resolving it may require repeating or reformulating more of the earlier utterance.

evidence.locator: Results, Three basic types recur in all languages, pp. 4–5
evidence.note: Checked unspecified trouble and qualified longer/repeated response tendency; not treated as interchangeable with a targeted question.

concepts.label: Open repair request
concepts.learning_takeaway: Request help with an unclear message without specifying which part caused difficulty.

relations.note: The repair study explicitly defines open requests as one of three functionally distinct other-initiated repair types and describes their response patterns.

concepts.card: A restricted repair request identifies a particular part of a message that needs clarification. Asking Who? narrows the trouble to a person reference instead of rejecting the whole utterance. This gives the original speaker a more focused task, such as specifying the missing identity or repeating that component.

evidence.locator: Results, Three basic types recur in all languages, pp. 4–5
evidence.note: Checked targeted slot and request format; unlike a restricted offer, it does not already supply a proposed interpretation for confirmation.

concepts.label: Restricted repair request
concepts.learning_takeaway: Target a specific missing or unclear component so the original speaker can give a focused clarification.

relations.note: The study explicitly defines restricted requests through targeted specification or clarification of a component of the prior turn.

concepts.card: Candidate-understanding repair offers a possible interpretation and asks the original speaker to confirm or correct it. Repeating a guessed phrase with questioning intonation can make the proposed solution explicit. The task differs from simply asking for clarification: the speaker can often resolve the trouble with a short confirmation.

evidence.locator: Results, restricted offer definition and response patterns, pp. 4–5
evidence.note: Checked proposed interpretation and short-confirmation tendency; no assumption that the candidate is correct or confirmation is always sufficient.

concepts.label: Candidate-understanding repair
concepts.learning_takeaway: Offer a possible interpretation of the prior message and ask the original speaker to confirm or correct it.

relations.note: The study's restricted-offer category explicitly proposes a candidate understanding and invites confirmation, distinguishing it from both request types.

concepts.card: Grounding in communication is collaborative work toward mutual belief that a message has been understood well enough for the current purpose. Responses and acknowledgments provide evidence for that belief. What counts as sufficient understanding can change with the task and communication medium.

evidence.locator: Opening; Grounding in Conversation; contribution model
evidence.note: The chapter defines the grounding criterion as participants mutually believing understanding is sufficient for current purposes. Responses supply evidence for this belief; neither perfect comprehension nor truth agreement is guaranteed. Grounding remains the process, distinct from common ground as the shared state.

concepts.label: Grounding in communication
concepts.learning_takeaway: Establish mutual evidence that a message is understood well enough for the participants' current purpose.

relations.note: Clark and Brennan explicitly describe grounding as the process by which contributions become part of common ground.

concepts.card: Common ground consists of knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions participants take to be mutually shared. It gives them a starting point for coordination, but is updated as they communicate. Two people separately knowing the same fact is not automatically the same as recognizing it as shared between them.

evidence.note: Checked mutual-recognition requirement and updating; common ground is distinct from private knowledge and from the process that establishes it.

concepts.label: Common ground in communication
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use mutually taken-for-granted knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions as the shared basis for coordinated communication.

relations.note: The source explicitly defines common ground and explains how grounding updates it during interaction.

concepts.card: A conversational acknowledgment gives brief evidence that a listener is following or understanding, often without taking the speaking turn. Responses such as yeah or a head nod can serve this function. Their role is feedback within coordination, rather than necessarily endorsing the truth of everything the speaker says.

evidence.note: Checked brief verbal/gestural evidence and turn status; understanding is not equated with agreement or complete comprehension of every detail.

concepts.label: Conversational acknowledgment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Provide brief verbal or gestural evidence of understanding, often without taking over the speaking turn.

relations.note: The grounding chapter explicitly lists acknowledgments and head nods as positive evidence of understanding, generally without taking a turn.

concepts.card: The principle of least collaborative effort proposes that conversational partners minimize their combined work through mutual acceptance of a contribution. A perfectly prepared utterance is not always cheapest overall. A shorter presentation followed by a quick clarification may require less total effort than preventing every possible misunderstanding in advance.

evidence.note: Checked combined rather than speaker-only effort and completion through acceptance; this is an explanatory principle, not a measured law of every conversation.

concepts.label: Least collaborative effort
concepts.learning_takeaway: Model conversational choices by the combined work of both participants through mutual acceptance, rather than minimizing only speaking effort.

relations.note: Clark and Brennan explicitly introduce the joint-effort principle to explain grounding choices, repairs and differences across media.

concepts.card: Reviewability is a communication medium's ability to leave messages available for the recipient to inspect again. Written or recorded messages can support checking details that ordinary unrecorded speech leaves behind only briefly. This changes the effort needed for grounding, and differs from the sender's ability to revise before sending.

evidence.locator: Grounding Changes with the Medium, constraint 7
evidence.note: Checked recipient reinspection versus sender revisability; ordinary speech is qualified as unrecorded, and no medium is assumed perfectly persistent.

concepts.label: Reviewability of communication
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use persistent messages that an addressee can revisit, changing the need and cost of repetition during coordination.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly identifies reviewability as a medium constraint that changes available grounding techniques and their costs.

concepts.card: Impression management concerns how people present themselves through behavior, surroundings, and visible cues. Goffman's theatrical analogy highlights how different settings invite different performances; a judge's robe and courtroom props help shape expectations. The process need not imply deliberate deception or a completely invented identity.

evidence.locator: §4.3, Goffman's role performance and courtroom props
evidence.note: Checked dramaturgical presentation and courtroom example; not equated with research-demand bias or assumed to be conscious manipulation in every case.

evidence.locator: §1.1, What Are Society and Culture?; Studying Patterns
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Goffman's interactional account offers a specific sociological lens on how settings and shared expectations shape everyday encounters.

concepts.label: Impression management
concepts.learning_takeaway: Shape how others interpret a social performance through behavior, setting, and visible cues.

relations.note: Goffman's interactional account offers a specific sociological lens on how settings and shared expectations shape everyday encounters.

previous_record.card: Archaeology investigates human lives through physical remains, from stone tools to recent buildings. An object’s location and its relationship to other finds help explain past activities. Explore how recording that context helps reconstruct activities that written records may overlook.

batch.source_reuse_note: Cards and interpretive notes are original paraphrases. No poems, artwork images or large source passages are reproduced in the candidate. Public availability and evidentiary support are not statements of reuse rights for the underlying source material; raw tool captures remain separate research evidence.
batch.usage_note: Platform token/cost measurements are unavailable; no estimates presented as measured usage.

concepts.card: Archaeology reconstructs human lives from material remains, including objects, traces of structures and environmental evidence. A find gains meaning through its location and associations. Recording those circumstances lets researchers connect a surviving object with the activities that produced or used it.

evidence.note: Material-remains definition and artifact categories; contextual inference requires h02.
Location, associations and cultural setting support the contextual claims.

imported_records.description: Understanding past societies through material remains and landscapes.

concepts.label: Archaeology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Study material traces alongside their find circumstances to reconstruct human activity rather than treating an object as an isolated collectible.
concepts.original_description: Understanding past societies through material remains and landscapes.

relations.note: Context explains how the material evidence studied by archaeology becomes interpretable.

concepts.card: Oral history turns recorded recollections into historical sources through preparation, interviewing, preservation and arrangements for access. The narrator’s perspective remains part of the evidence. Researchers therefore contextualize the account and, when possible, check factual statements against other information.

evidence.note: Four stages and contextualization of subjective recollection are explicit.

imported_records.description: Recording and interpreting people's firsthand accounts of past experiences.

concepts.label: Oral history
concepts.learning_takeaway: An interview becomes a usable historical source through preparation, recording, preservation and access arrangements, with attention to the narrator’s perspective.
concepts.original_description: Recording and interpreting people's firsthand accounts of past experiences.

relations.note: Narrator review makes the access and participation arrangements concrete.

concepts.card: Mean ceramic dating estimates occupation timing from an assemblage of pottery whose production periods are known. Combining the ceramics gives a date estimate for the group. It does not turn every sherd into an exact timestamp for the deposit containing it.

evidence.note: Assemblage production dates supply occupation estimates.

concepts.label: Mean ceramic dating
concepts.learning_takeaway: An assemblage’s production periods can estimate occupation timing; the method uses multiple ceramics rather than a single object.

relations.note: Compare an assemblage estimate with a lower chronological bound from associated finds.
The NPS describes mean ceramic dating as a method archaeologists use to estimate occupation.

concepts.card: A terminus post quem is an earliest possible date for a deposit or event. In archaeology, the most recently introduced securely associated artifact can supply that bound. An old coin may circulate for years, so its minting need not date burial exactly.

evidence.note: TPQ row defines the lower bound from the latest-occurring artifact.

concepts.label: Terminus post quem
concepts.learning_takeaway: A deposit cannot predate its youngest securely associated object’s earliest possible date; this supplies a lower bound, not an exact deposition date.

relations.note: A lower bound and an assemblage estimate answer different dating questions.

concepts.card: Archaeological context includes where a find lay, what accompanied it and its chronological, social and cultural setting. These relationships constrain interpretation. The same object can support different historical explanations when found in different associations, which is why documenting its surroundings matters.

evidence.note: Spatial, chronological, cultural and social contexts and associations are explicit.

concepts.label: Archaeological context
concepts.learning_takeaway: An object’s location, associations and chronological, social and cultural setting determine what historical inferences it can support.

relations.note: Context is one of the evidential concerns within archaeological investigation.

concepts.card: An ecofact is a natural remain that provides archaeological evidence, such as an animal bone or plant seed associated with human activity. Its importance comes from what it can reveal about past lives, even though people did not manufacture it as an artifact.

evidence.locator: What is an Archeologist?, ecofacts definition
evidence.note: Natural remains and seed/bone examples distinguish ecofacts from manufactured artifacts.

concepts.label: Ecofact
concepts.learning_takeaway: Unmanufactured remains such as seeds and animal bones can be archaeological evidence of human resource use.

relations.note: Associations establish why an unmanufactured remain is evidence of human activity.
The NPS explicitly includes ecofacts among the evidence archaeologists study.

concepts.card: An archaeological feature is a nonportable trace of human activity, such as a hearth or posthole. Excavators record it where it occurs rather than lifting it out like a complete object. Its shape and position help preserve evidence of an earlier activity.

evidence.locator: What is an Archeologist?, features definition
evidence.note: Nonportable features and examples support recording in place.

imported_records.description: archaeological term to describe a collection of one or more contexts representing some human non-portable activity

concepts.label: Feature (archaeology)
concepts.learning_takeaway: A hearth, soil stain or posthole is evidence that must be recorded in place rather than collected as a portable artifact.
concepts.original_description: archaeological term to describe a collection of one or more contexts representing some human non-portable activity

relations.note: A feature’s position and associations are part of the context needed for interpretation.
The archaeological teaching source identifies nonportable features as a category of site evidence.

concepts.card: Seriation arranges archaeological evidence into a relative sequence by tracking changes in artifact styles. Styles rise and fall in popularity, producing overlapping periods of use. Comparing those patterns can order assemblages, even when the method alone supplies no precise calendar date.

evidence.note: Style popularity and battleship-curve discussion support relative ordering.

concepts.label: Archaeological seriation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Changes in the relative popularity of artifact styles allow assemblages to be arranged into a relative chronological sequence.

relations.note: Both compare evidence to establish chronology, but seriation emphasizes ordered style change.
The NPS explains seriation among methods used to date archaeological sites.

concepts.card: Archaeological stratigraphy uses the sequence of deposited layers to investigate earlier human activity. In an undisturbed sequence, lower layers generally precede those above. The qualification matters: rearranged deposits cannot automatically be read as a simple oldest-to-newest stack.

evidence.note: Superposition is explicitly conditional on undisturbed deposits.

concepts.label: Archaeological stratigraphy
concepts.learning_takeaway: In undisturbed deposits, the ordering of layers supplies relative evidence for the sequence of human activities.

relations.note: Apply the stratigraphic ordering of layers to archaeological deposits and activities.

concepts.card: Archaeological cross-dating compares evidence from different contexts to establish their relative ages. A recognizable pattern at one site can be compared with another, or across layers within a site. The comparison links sequences without necessarily giving either context an exact calendar date.

evidence.note: Cross-dating row explicitly covers comparisons within and between sites.

concepts.label: Archaeological cross-dating
concepts.learning_takeaway: Matching evidence across archaeological contexts can place otherwise undated finds in a relative sequence.

relations.note: Seriation offers one neighboring way to compare patterns of chronological evidence.
The dating-methods table includes cross-dating for archaeological evidence.

concepts.card: Offering a narrator the chance to review an interview before public release can connect historical access with informed participation. The Oral History Association recommends building this opportunity into the process when possible, alongside clear expectations about preservation, access and the project’s timetable.

evidence.note: Preparation 3 recommends consent and possible pre-release approval.

concepts.label: Narrator review in oral history
concepts.learning_takeaway: Giving narrators an opportunity to review an interview before release connects historical access with consent and the terms of participation.

relations.note: Pre-release review is a recommended part of planning an oral-history project.

concepts.card: An oral-history lead-in records basic context at the start of a session: who is speaking, when and where it happens, and the intended subject. Appropriate names or pseudonyms preserve identification while avoiding unnecessary exposure, such as stating a private home address.

evidence.note: Interviewing 2 specifies contextual identifiers and cautions about residential addresses.

concepts.label: Oral-history interview lead-in
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recording participant names or pseudonyms, date, setting and proposed subject preserves the interview’s context for future users.

relations.note: A recorded lead-in is a specific interviewing practice within oral history.

concepts.card: Original order preserves the arrangement a record creator used, when that order can be established and remains meaningful. Keeping the sequence may reveal how an office or person worked. Rearranging everything by a modern subject scheme can erase those functional connections.

evidence.note: Creator arrangement and evidential relationships support the principle.

concepts.label: Original order in archives
concepts.learning_takeaway: Preserving a creator’s record sequence can retain evidence of how the records functioned, rather than replacing it with a modern subject arrangement.

relations.note: Creator-based grouping and internal arrangement preserve different relationships among records.

concepts.card: Archival provenance keeps records connected to the person or organization that created them. Records from different origins are not simply mixed because they discuss the same subject. Preserving that grouping helps researchers reconstruct the activities and relationships that generated the documents.

evidence.note: Creator-origin grouping and nonintermingling are explicit archival principles.

concepts.label: Archival provenance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Keeping records grouped by their creating person or organization preserves relationships that would disappear if unrelated origins were mixed.

relations.note: Provenance preserves origin groups; original order addresses arrangement within them.

concepts.card: Historical sourcing asks who made a document, for what purpose and in what setting. Those questions affect how its claims become evidence. Two apparently conflicting accounts may make sense together once their authors’ positions and the circumstances of production are considered.

evidence.locator: Opposition to the Philippine-American War example, lines 20–22
evidence.note: Philippine-American War teaching example demonstrates author and context analysis.

concepts.label: Historical sourcing
concepts.learning_takeaway: A document’s author, purpose and production setting affect what it can count as evidence, even when its account differs from other documents.

relations.note: Sourcing is a method for interpreting historical documents as evidence.

concepts.card: The Silk Road was an interconnected set of routes linking Eurasian societies through trade and travel. Merchants carried ideas and practices as well as goods. Sogdian communities show how commercial intermediaries could also transmit religions, languages and artistic traditions between regions.

evidence.note: Networked exchange and Sogdian intermediary roles support the example.

imported_records.description: trade routes through Asia connecting China to the Mediterranean Sea
imported_records.subsection: History / Prehistory and Ancient history / Asia

concepts.label: Silk Road
concepts.learning_takeaway: Overlapping routes and merchant intermediaries carried luxury goods together with religious, artistic and musical traditions across Eurasia.
concepts.original_description: trade routes through Asia connecting China to the Mediterranean Sea

relations.note: Sogdian communities provide a documented intermediary case within Silk Road exchange.

concepts.card: Indian painted and printed cottons attracted overseas buyers because their colors endured washing and their designs could be adapted to different tastes. European demand encouraged imitation and restrictive import policies. A textile’s commercial history therefore reveals both shared fashions and competition between producers.

evidence.locator: Indian Painted and Printed Cottons, lines 145–148
evidence.note: Colorfast cottons, adapted designs, imitation and restrictions are discussed.

concepts.label: Chintz in global trade
concepts.learning_takeaway: Washable, colorfast Indian cottons were adapted to foreign tastes and prompted European restrictions and domestic imitation.

relations.note: Palampores give a particular form through which Indian painted cotton entered overseas markets.

concepts.card: A palampore is a large Indian painted cotton textile often used as a bedcover or hanging. Many export examples arrange abundant flowers around a central tree. Their designs show how makers shaped local techniques and motifs for the tastes of distant buyers.

evidence.locator: Indian Painted and Printed Cottons, line 147
evidence.note: Large painted cottons, central-tree patterns and European-market adaptation are explicit.

concepts.label: Palampore
concepts.learning_takeaway: Indian hand-painted cotton bedcovers commonly organized luxuriant flowers around a central tree and were tailored to European markets.

relations.note: The museum presents palampores within the overseas trade in Indian painted cottons.

concepts.card: Sarasa textiles made for Japanese buyers show that restrictions on overseas travel did not end foreign exchange. Indian cotton designs were adapted for this market and circulated through trade. Their surviving patterns make selective connections visible within a period often associated with isolation.

evidence.locator: Chinese Silk Exports and Trade Textiles in Japan, lines 132–136
evidence.note: Trade textiles for Japanese buyers continued despite travel restrictions.

concepts.label: Japanese sarasa trade textiles
concepts.learning_takeaway: Indian cottons designed for Japanese buyers circulated despite restrictions on Japanese overseas travel, showing selective trade rather than total isolation.

relations.note: Compare Japanese-market adaptation with Indian cottons made for other overseas buyers.

concepts.card: The Manila galleon trade connected Asian commerce with Spanish America across the Pacific. Silver traveled west, while Asian goods passed through Manila toward Mexico. Imported textiles and other objects also influenced local artistic production, making the route a channel of cultural as well as commercial exchange.

evidence.note: Silver, Asian goods and artistic influence are stated in the essay.

concepts.label: Manila galleon trade
concepts.learning_takeaway: American silver moved west across the Pacific while Asian goods traveled through Manila to Mexico, where imports influenced local artistic production.

relations.note: Imported objects provide a material record of commercial and artistic exchange.

concepts.card: Sogdian merchants established communities along Eurasian trade networks rather than merely passing through them. These dispersed settlements helped goods, languages, religions and artistic practices circulate. Their history shows how sustained social connections could make merchants influential cultural intermediaries.

evidence.note: Dispersed communities and transmission of cultural practices are explicit.

concepts.label: Sogdian merchant diasporas
concepts.learning_takeaway: Sogdian commercial communities also transmitted religious traditions, artistic practices and languages through their dispersed trading networks.

relations.note: Sogdian trading communities operated within the Silk Road networks described by the museum.

concepts.card: The Columbian Exchange names the movements of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and other regions after 1492. New crops changed diets, while disease and coercive colonial relationships brought devastating consequences. Exchange here describes connected transformations, not an equal bargain.

evidence.note: Post-1492 biological transfers, disease and unequal consequences support the account.

concepts.label: Columbian Exchange
concepts.learning_takeaway: Post-1492 transfers of plants, animals, people and disease reshaped societies across the Atlantic in unequal and often destructive ways.

relations.note: The movement of crops is one route from this exchange into the history of diets.

concepts.card: Food history traces how familiar meals emerge from changing production, exchange and habits of eating. Crops such as maize, potatoes and cacao traveled far beyond their American origins. Following those movements reveals that everyday diets preserve histories of migration and contact.

evidence.note: American crops and their movement support the dietary example.

imported_records.description: Exploring how food production, trade and eating practices change over time.

concepts.label: Food history
concepts.learning_takeaway: Following the movement of crops such as maize, potatoes and cacao reveals how familiar diets are products of historical migration and exchange.
concepts.original_description: Exploring how food production, trade and eating practices change over time.

relations.note: Transatlantic crop movement gives a documented case for studying changing diets.

concepts.card: Mamluks were enslaved recruits trained for military service who could later be freed into powerful households. In the Mamluk Sultanate, ties to commanders and fellow soldiers shaped political loyalties. Rival households could therefore influence succession as well as the conduct of warfare.

evidence.note: Military enslavement, training, manumission, household loyalty and rivalry are described.

imported_records.description: slave soldiers, mercenaries, or warriors of the Islamic world (9th-19th centuries)

concepts.label: Mamluk
concepts.learning_takeaway: Enslaved boys were trained and later freed into military households whose loyalty and rivalry could determine political succession.
concepts.original_description: slave soldiers, mercenaries, or warriors of the Islamic world (9th-19th centuries)

relations.note: Compare two historically distinct military institutions whose recruitment could detach service from hereditary local elites.

concepts.card: The Ottoman devshirme forcibly recruited Christian boys for conversion, education and state service. Some entered military units, while others pursued administrative roles. The system linked coercive removal from families with the state’s attempt to train personnel whose careers depended on the ruler.

evidence.note: Recruitment, conversion, schooling and military/administrative destinations are explicit.

concepts.label: Devshirme
concepts.learning_takeaway: The Ottoman state forcibly gathered Christian boys, converted and educated them, and assigned them to military or administrative service.

relations.note: Devshirme supplied some recruits to the Janissaries while also serving other state roles.

concepts.card: The Janissaries were an elite Ottoman infantry corps and household guard. Recruits trained for service to the ruler, including boys taken through devshirme. The sultans intended this force to reduce dependence on hereditary nobles, expecting recruits’ status and privileges to bind them to the ruler.

evidence.note: Elite corps, recruitment and reduced noble dependence are explicit.

concepts.label: Janissary corps
concepts.learning_takeaway: The Ottoman elite infantry and household guard drew recruits from state training and was intended to reduce dependence on hereditary nobles.

relations.note: The text connects the recruitment system with the formation of the corps.

concepts.card: An Ottoman timar granted the right to collect revenue from a specified area in return for service. It supported its holder without a regular state salary. Because the grant could be revoked and did not automatically pass to heirs, it also limited independent hereditary power.

evidence.note: Revenue rights, service, revocation and noninheritance are described.

concepts.label: Timar
concepts.learning_takeaway: A revocable right to collect revenue supported Ottoman service personnel without making their assignments automatically hereditary.

relations.note: Compare two distinct imperial systems that linked service with reassigned revenue.

concepts.card: Under Akbar, mansabdars held ranks that connected administrative service with responsibility for supplying cavalry. Revenue from assigned land supported them, and allocations could be shifted as their rank or position changed. This tied officeholders’ resources to imperial appointment rather than secure hereditary possession.

evidence.note: Rank, cavalry recruitment and reassigned revenue support the mechanism.

concepts.label: Mansabdari system
concepts.learning_takeaway: Under Akbar, administrators’ ranks combined civil service and cavalry responsibilities with revenue allocations that could be reassigned.

relations.note: Both cases connect service and revenue, but belong to different imperial arrangements.

concepts.card: Khipus used knotted cords to record information in the Inka world. Differences in knots, colors and cord arrangements supported numerical administration, including accounts of labor and goods. They demonstrate a system of record keeping whose organization cannot be understood by looking for written alphabetic words.

evidence.note: Knot/color structure and administrative recording are described.

concepts.label: Khipu
concepts.learning_takeaway: Knotted cords with differing colors and structures recorded numerical information used to administer labor, goods and taxation.

relations.note: Record keeping and state storage offer complementary views of Inka administration.

concepts.card: Colcas were Inka state storehouses for food, textiles and other goods collected from different regions. Their placement and construction could use natural airflow to help preserve supplies. Clusters of storehouses supported redistribution, including when harvests were poor or officials needed stored resources.

evidence.note: State collection, airflow preservation and redistribution are explicit.

concepts.label: Colca
concepts.learning_takeaway: Inka state storehouses combined regional collection and redistribution with storage designed to exploit natural airflow.

relations.note: Storage and accounting illuminate different material operations of the Inka state.

concepts.card: Great Zimbabwe’s dry-stone walls enclose the remains of a major Shona-built center. Archaeological finds, including imported objects, connect it with long-distance trade. The site brings monumental construction and commercial relationships together as evidence for the region’s own complex historical development.

evidence.note: Shona construction, dry-stone architecture and imported trade objects are documented.

concepts.label: Great Zimbabwe
concepts.learning_takeaway: Dry-stone enclosures and imported objects reveal a Shona-built urban center connected to long-distance trade.

relations.note: Architecture and associated imported finds show why relationships among remains matter.

concepts.card: The Haitian Revolution arose in a colony built on plantation slavery and led to independence. U.S. responses varied as leaders weighed slavery concerns, trade and relations with France. Official U.S. recognition came only in 1862, illustrating the distinction between achieving independence and receiving foreign recognition.

evidence.note: The account documents the slave revolt, independence, changing U.S. policies and delayed U.S. recognition in 1862.

concepts.label: Haitian Revolution
concepts.learning_takeaway: An uprising against plantation slavery led to independence, while U.S. policy and delayed recognition reflected shifting concerns about slavery, trade and diplomacy.

relations.note: The French Revolution changed factions and claims to civil rights in Saint-Domingue before and during the uprising.

concepts.card: Material culture examines social life through objects and their uses. A coffee-house trade token, for example, advertised goods while presenting a particular image of the business. Its wording and pictures let a small commercial object become evidence about consumption, exchange and public identity.

evidence.note: Token description supports the concrete example and its advertised goods.

imported_records.description: Understanding social life through objects and their uses.

concepts.label: Material culture
concepts.learning_takeaway: A trade token’s imagery and product list provide evidence of commercial life and how a coffee house represented itself.
concepts.original_description: Understanding social life through objects and their uses.

relations.note: The named token supplies a specific object through which to investigate commercial representation.

concepts.card: This penny token advertised a coffee house in London’s Exchange Alley through a list of goods and the image of a Turkish ruler. Coffee, chocolate and tea appeared together, showing how a small circulating object could advertise an establishment’s offerings and associations.

evidence.note: Penny token, place, listed drinks and ruler image are specified in the collection record.

concepts.label: The New Coffee House trade token
concepts.learning_takeaway: A penny token from Exchange Alley advertised coffee, chocolate, tea and other goods while associating the shop with a Turkish ruler.

relations.note: The token’s imagery and product list support an object-based inquiry into social and commercial life.

concepts.card: Molly houses were meeting places associated with queer social life in Georgian London. They offered spaces for companionship and forms of gender expression while exposing participants to hostile policing and prosecution. Their history joins everyday sociability with the dangers created by criminalization.

evidence.locator: What was a molly house?; origins, lines 141–168
evidence.note: Gathering places, gender expression and legal vulnerability are described.

concepts.label: Molly houses
concepts.learning_takeaway: Georgian meeting places allowed queer social networks and gender expression under laws and policing that made participants vulnerable.

relations.note: Molly houses provide a specific historical case of sexual and gender diversity under criminalization.

concepts.card: Tea’s early expense in Britain made its storage and consumption a marker of status. Valuable supplies could be kept under lock. As imports expanded, tea became more widely available, showing how a once-exclusive luxury could become part of ordinary shopping and domestic routine.

evidence.note: High cost, guarded tea and expanding availability are discussed.

concepts.label: Tea as a British status good
concepts.learning_takeaway: Early expensive tea was guarded and consumed by elites; expanding imports helped transform it into a more widely accessible grocery.

relations.note: Changing tea consumption offers a specific case of food and drink acquiring new social meanings.

concepts.card: Tudor Londoners could buy prepared hot food from cookshops, especially when cramped homes lacked cooking facilities. Commercial ovens supplied ready-to-eat meals outside the household. The museum notes that evidence about the exact meals and their customers is limited, preserving uncertainty alongside the practical explanation.

evidence.note: The museum describes commercial ovens serving households without cooking facilities and explicitly notes limited evidence for exact menus and clientele.

concepts.label: Tudor London cookshops
concepts.learning_takeaway: Commercial ovens supplied hot ready-made food to city residents whose cramped homes lacked cooking facilities.

relations.note: Cookshops connect the history of meals with urban housing and commercial provision.

concepts.card: History investigates the past by interpreting surviving evidence. A document’s statements become more useful when its author, audience and circumstances are considered. Comparing sources can reveal why people described events differently, rather than reducing historical inquiry to choosing the account that sounds most convincing.

evidence.locator: Opposition to the Philippine-American War example, lines 20–22
evidence.note: The teaching example shows sourcing and contextual comparison of apparently conflicting documents.

imported_records.description: past events and their documentation, studied through historiography, archaeology, and related disciplines

concepts.label: History
concepts.learning_takeaway: Accounts of the past depend on interpreting evidence in its setting; apparently conflicting documents can illuminate the same historical concern.
concepts.original_description: past events and their documentation, studied through historiography, archaeology, and related disciplines

relations.note: Sourcing provides a concrete practice for interpreting historical evidence.

concepts.card: Magna Carta began as a 1215 settlement between King John and rebellious barons, and its first version failed to secure lasting peace. Later reissues gave it a different career. Its constitutional reputation grew from that subsequent history, rather than arriving fully formed in 1215.

evidence.note: Failed initial settlement, later reissues and subsequent influence are described.

concepts.label: Magna Carta
concepts.learning_takeaway: The failed settlement of 1215 was reissued in later versions; its later constitutional influence should be distinguished from its baronial setting.

relations.note: Distinguishing the original political setting from later interpretations is a contextual reading exercise.

concepts.card: A Hanseatic kontor was an overseas trading establishment where merchants organized commercial activity and maintained privileges. At Bryggen, warehouses and living quarters preserve evidence of this arrangement. The built setting offers a case for studying how trading institutions organized commerce and merchant life.

evidence.note: Bryggen’s trading offices, privileges, warehouses and residences support the account.

concepts.label: Hanseatic kontor
concepts.learning_takeaway: Overseas trading offices combined commercial privileges, merchant residences and warehouses, as surviving Bryggen illustrates.

relations.note: The surviving merchant buildings make an institutional form legible through material evidence.

aliases: Civil service examinations in imperial China
concepts.card: Chinese imperial examinations linked literary and Confucian learning with entry into government. In the Song period, growing candidate numbers competed for limited posts, and most never became officials. This example exposes both a route to advancement and strong constraints on success.

evidence.note: The Song-specific discussion connects literary/Confucian examinations with fixed available posts, growing candidate numbers and widespread failure to obtain office.

concepts.label: Chinese imperial examinations
concepts.learning_takeaway: In the Song case, literary and Confucian examinations offered a route into government, but most candidates never became officials.

relations.note: The examination system helps explain the educational basis of scholar-official status.

concepts.card: Song examination procedures could replace candidates’ names with numbers and have clerks recopy their answers. These steps reduced clues supplied by identity and handwriting. The practice shows a historical attempt to make assessment depend more on the submitted work than on recognizing its author.

evidence.note: Numbering and recopying are explicit anti-recognition measures.

concepts.label: Anonymization in Song examinations
concepts.learning_takeaway: Numbers replaced candidates’ names and clerks recopied answers to reduce recognition through identity or handwriting.

relations.note: Name removal and recopying are specific examination procedures described within this system.

concepts.card: Song scholar-officials joined literary cultivation with government service. Their education helped define elite status, while their duties could include criticizing a ruler’s conduct. The role therefore linked political participation with a learned ideal of responsibility that could place officials in tension with authority.

evidence.note: Literary education, service and criticism of rulers are described.

concepts.label: Song scholar-officials
concepts.learning_takeaway: Literary education and service linked elite prestige with duties that could include criticizing rulers’ policies.

relations.note: Examinations connect the scholar-official role with the cultivation and testing of learning.

concepts.card: Zheng He’s Ming fleets traveled through established Indian Ocean networks carrying envoys and projecting imperial prestige. Their journeys connected diplomacy, trade and demonstrations of power. Understanding those purposes shifts attention from a simple story of discovering unknown places to the political relationships the voyages sought to organize.

evidence.locator: The Emperor and His Ambition; The Seven Voyages
evidence.note: Imperial ambition, envoys and routes support the diplomatic interpretation.

concepts.label: Zheng He’s maritime expeditions
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ming fleets projected imperial prestige and carried envoys through Indian Ocean networks rather than simply opening an unknown sea route.

relations.note: Ma Huan’s participation illustrates the linguistic expertise used on one of the expeditions.

concepts.card: Ma Huan was a Muslim translator and chronicler who joined Zheng He’s fourth voyage. His role puts written observation alongside travel through foreign ports. As a learning case, it invites attention to the people who recorded and interpreted encounters during imperial expeditions.

evidence.locator: The Seven Voyages, fourth voyage paragraph, line 96
evidence.note: The fourth-voyage paragraph identifies Ma Huan as a Muslim translator and the voyages’ main chronicler.

concepts.label: Ma Huan
concepts.learning_takeaway: A Muslim translator accompanied Zheng He’s fourth voyage, illustrating the role of linguistic and cultural expertise in imperial travel records.

relations.note: The source explicitly places Ma Huan on the fourth voyage.

concepts.card: Cartography turns spatial information into maps through choices about selection, symbols and presentation. A map made to compare population rates may look very different from one designed for navigation. Thinking about its purpose helps explain both what a map emphasizes and what it leaves out.

evidence.note: Map design and use define the field; contrasting purposes are editorial illustrations.

imported_records.description: Designing maps to represent spatial information.

concepts.label: Cartography
concepts.learning_takeaway: Making a map requires selecting features and symbols to communicate spatial relationships for a particular use.
concepts.original_description: Designing maps to represent spatial information.

relations.note: Choropleth design supplies a specific example of choosing how spatial information is represented.

concepts.card: A map projection converts locations on Earth’s curved surface to a flat map. That transformation changes some combination of area, shape, distance and direction. Choosing a projection means deciding which distortions are acceptable for the geographic extent and purpose of the map.

evidence.note: Curved-to-planar transformation and competing properties are explained.

imported_records.description: representation of the surface of a sphere or ellipsoid onto a plane map

concepts.label: Map projection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Flattening Earth trades off shape, area, distance and direction, so projection choice should follow a map’s purpose.
concepts.original_description: representation of the surface of a sphere or ellipsoid onto a plane map

relations.note: Projection choice is one design decision that changes the representation a map presents.

concepts.card: A geodetic datum supplies a reference framework for measuring positions. Coordinates become meaningful when their reference is known, and horizontal position and height may use different datums. This is why matching numbers alone does not ensure that two geographic measurements identify the same location.

evidence.note: Horizontal and vertical reference frameworks are distinguished.

imported_records.description: reference frame used in geodesy, surveying, cartography and navigation
imported_records.hook: Examine the reference systems that make precise geographic coordinates meaningful.

concepts.label: Geodetic datum
concepts.learning_takeaway: Coordinate measurements require a shared reference framework; horizontal position and height can rely on different datums.
concepts.original_description: reference frame used in geodesy, surveying, cartography and navigation

relations.note: A datum establishes the coordinate reference; a projection transforms that referenced surface for mapping.

concepts.card: A choropleth map shades geographic areas according to an attribute such as a rate or ratio.
