Closed-book questions ask learners to retrieve an answer instead of rereading it. Corrective feedback helps when recall fails, making quizzes useful as learning activities as well as assessments.

evidence.note: Checked recall-versus-rereading distinction and feedback; retained baseline Testing effect identity instead of creating a duplicate retrieval-practice card.

imported_records.description: memory effect in educational psychology

concepts.label: Testing effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use effortful recall with corrective feedback as a learning activity rather than treating quizzes only as measurement.
concepts.original_description: memory effect in educational psychology

relations.note: The IES guide discusses retrieval and delayed re-exposure as complementary learning approaches; their mechanisms remain distinct from one another.

concepts.card: A political constitution sets out basic principles governing public power, including institutional structure, governmental duties and people's rights. Those principles need not appear in a single document. Constitutional arrangements can combine written provisions with other sources, so a state's constitution is more than a document's title.

evidence.note: OpenStax section 1.1 identifies constitutional structure, duties and rights and gives multi-source examples; no claim that every constitutional guarantee is effectively enforced.

imported_records.description: set of fundamental principles or established precedents according to which a state or other organization is governed
imported_records.subsection: Society and social sciences / Law / Constitutional law

concepts.label: Constitution (politics)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how basic rules assign governmental powers, duties and limits.
concepts.original_description: set of fundamental principles or established precedents according to which a state or other organization is governed

relations.note: The passage explicitly distinguishes constitutional functions from having a single constitutional document, with the UK among its examples.

concepts.card: Water activity compares the equilibrium water-vapor pressure above a food with that above pure water at the same temperature. It differs from total moisture content because some water is tightly associated with food components. This distinction helps explain why foods containing water can support microbes differently.

evidence.note: FDA’s physical definition gives the vapor-pressure ratio and distinguishes strongly bound water from available moisture relevant to microbial growth.

imported_records.description: one of the main factor limiting microbial activity

concepts.label: Water activity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish available water from total moisture when reasoning about food stability.
concepts.original_description: one of the main factor limiting microbial activity

relations.note: Fermentation changes a food biologically, while water activity describes one environmental constraint on microbial growth; they are complementary food-stability concepts.

concepts.card: El Niño–Southern Oscillation couples tropical Pacific ocean conditions with the atmosphere. El Niño weakens the usual trade winds and changes warm-water distribution and upwelling; La Niña strengthens the winds. These shifts can alter weather far from the Pacific, linking a regional ocean pattern with wider climate effects.

evidence.locator: Normal Pacific conditions; El Niño; La Niña
evidence.note: NOAA describes the coupled Pacific pattern, opposite trade-wind behavior, warm-water/upwelling changes and distant weather effects.

imported_records.description: climatic phenomenon occurring in the Pacific Ocean
imported_records.subsection: Physical sciences / Earth science / Air / Climatology

concepts.label: El Niño–Southern Oscillation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect changes in equatorial Pacific winds and ocean temperatures with distant weather patterns.
concepts.original_description: climatic phenomenon occurring in the Pacific Ocean

relations.note: Changes in Pacific winds alter upwelling, giving a concrete link between the climate pattern and a circulation process.

concepts.card: Economics studies how people and societies make choices when resources are limited. Specialization can increase what people produce, but it also makes them depend on exchange and coordination. Studying those choices includes asking how information, incentives, and institutions affect whether the potential gains are actually realized.

evidence.note: Checked scarcity and specialization from the introduction and information-related trade obstacles from section 16.1; no claim that monetary value measures every human goal.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The introductory scarcity-and-exchange framework leads to the specific question of how unequal information can obstruct mutually beneficial transactions.

imported_records.description: social science that studies the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services
imported_records.subsection: Society and social sciences / Business and economics

concepts.label: Economics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect choices under scarce resources with the gains and coordination problems of specialization and exchange.
concepts.original_description: social science that studies the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services

relations.note: The introductory scarcity-and-exchange framework leads to the specific question of how unequal information can obstruct mutually beneficial transactions.

concepts.card: An archaeological feature is a nonportable trace of human activity, such as a hearth or posthole. Excavators record it where it occurs rather than lifting it out like a complete object. Its shape and position help preserve evidence of an earlier activity.

evidence.locator: What is an Archeologist?, features definition
evidence.note: Nonportable features and examples support recording in place.

imported_records.description: archaeological term to describe a collection of one or more contexts representing some human non-portable activity

concepts.label: Feature (archaeology)
concepts.learning_takeaway: A hearth, soil stain or posthole is evidence that must be recorded in place rather than collected as a portable artifact.
concepts.original_description: archaeological term to describe a collection of one or more contexts representing some human non-portable activity

relations.note: A feature’s position and associations are part of the context needed for interpretation.
The archaeological teaching source identifies nonportable features as a category of site evidence.

concepts.card: A catalyst accelerates a reaction by providing an alternative mechanism with a lower activation barrier. It participates in intermediate steps but is regenerated overall. Changing the route can make a transformation faster without changing the identities of its initial reactants and final products.

evidence.locator: 12.7 Catalysis; inspected passage indices 5, 6 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm241568976; fs-idm627108512
evidence.note: A regenerated catalyst changes the reaction pathway and can reduce the activation barrier.

imported_records.description: process of increasing the rate of a chemical reaction

concepts.label: Catalysis
concepts.learning_takeaway: A regenerated catalyst changes the reaction pathway and can reduce the activation barrier.
concepts.original_description: process of increasing the rate of a chemical reaction

relations.note: The catalysis passage explains faster reaction through a lower activation-energy pathway.

concepts.card: In ordinary single-photon photoemission, light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons from a metal. The stopping voltage measures their maximum kinetic energy. At fixed frequency, brighter illumination can increase photocurrent without increasing that maximum energy, separating electron number from energy per electron.

evidence.locator: 6.2 Photoelectric Effect; inspected passage indices 6, 14, 15, 20, 21, 22, 23, 25 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1163709773708; fs-id1163713174554; fs-id1163713274860; fs-id1163713428401; fs-id1163709678905; fs-id1163713527138; fs-id1163713118837; fs-id1163713536791
evidence.note: The monochromatic, individual-photon model links threshold and maximum electron energy to photon frequency; varying intensity at fixed frequency changes current rather than stopping voltage.

imported_records.description: emission of electrons when light hits a material

concepts.label: Photoelectric effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons whose maximum energy is measured with a stopping potential.
concepts.original_description: emission of electrons when light hits a material

relations.note: Photoelectric observations reveal particle-like energy transfer by light, while de Broglie waves extend wave descriptions to matter.

concepts.card: The second moment of area measures how cross-sectional material is distributed about a chosen axis. Contributions grow with the square of distance from that axis. Together with elastic modulus, this geometric quantity influences bending stiffness; it is not the same as the mass moment of inertia.

evidence.locator: 17.5: Area Moments of Inertia via Integration; inspected passage indices 67, 71, 72 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-68; section_1
evidence.note: Defines the second area moment and squared-distance weighting about the bending axis.

evidence.locator: Chapter 8: Beam Bending, Buckling, and Torsion; inspected passage indices 217 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-218
evidence.note: The ideal three-point deflection relation scales inversely with elastic modulus times second moment of area.

imported_records.description: mathematical construct in engineering

concepts.label: Second moment of area
concepts.learning_takeaway: Material farther from the neutral axis contributes disproportionately to a cross-section’s bending resistance.
concepts.original_description: mathematical construct in engineering

relations.note: The ideal three-point bending relation explicitly contains the product of elastic modulus and second moment of area.

concepts.card: A database organizes stored information so programs can retrieve and change it systematically. Tables can hold related records, while indexes help find selected entries. SQLite illustrates another useful feature: transactions group changes so applications can treat several updates as a coherent operation.

evidence.note: Checked tables, indexes, and transactions in SQLite as an example; not all databases are asserted to use the relational model.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: SQLite's official description explicitly identifies the software as a transactional SQL database engine containing tables and indexes.

imported_records.description: organized collection of data in computing

concepts.label: Database
concepts.learning_takeaway: Organize related tables and indexes so stored information can be queried and updated consistently.
concepts.original_description: organized collection of data in computing

relations.note: SQLite's official description explicitly identifies the software as a transactional SQL database engine containing tables and indexes.

concepts.card: The Euler characteristic packages a space’s structure into a number. For a finite triangulation of a closed surface, vertices minus edges plus faces gives this invariant. A sphere and a torus have different values, revealing a distinction that persists when either surface is smoothly reshaped.

evidence.locator: Euler Characteristic -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 4, 6, 7 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-5; paragraph-7; paragraph-8
evidence.note: A topological invariant connects combinatorial counts with the number and type of surface holes.

imported_records.description: topological invariant in mathematics

concepts.label: Euler characteristic
concepts.learning_takeaway: A topological invariant connects combinatorial counts with the number and type of surface holes.
concepts.original_description: topological invariant in mathematics

relations.note: The source explicitly relates a closed surface’s Euler characteristic to its genus.

concepts.card: A periodic crystal structure is a repeating pattern of atoms. Its ordered arrangement extends through space rather than ending at the edge of a drawn box. Describing the repeating cell and atomic positions separates the geometry of repetition from the substance occupying it.

evidence.locator: Crystal pattern; inspected passage indices 8, 9, 10, 11 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-9; paragraph-10; paragraph-11; paragraph-12
evidence.note: A crystal structure is an atomic pattern satisfying periodicity and discreteness.

evidence.locator: 10.6 Lattice Structures in Crystalline Solids; inspected passage indices 10 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm2181616
evidence.note: A complete crystal structure is described through repeating unit cells.

imported_records.description: unique arrangement of atoms or molecules in a crystalline liquid or solid

concepts.label: Crystal structure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Describe a solid through a repeating unit cell and its spatial arrangement.
concepts.original_description: unique arrangement of atoms or molecules in a crystalline liquid or solid

relations.note: The unit-cell passage describes the complete crystal as repetitions of a unit cell.

concepts.card: The burden of proof concerns who must establish a proposition and what standard their evidence must meet. In US criminal cases, the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; most civil claims use preponderance of evidence. Different proceedings therefore demand different levels of evidentiary persuasion.

evidence.note: Cornell's criminal/civil examples, production/persuasion distinction and jurisdictional qualifications support the card; most civil claims preserves exceptions and the criminal claim is confined to proving guilt.

imported_records.description: in law, the obligation on a party in a trial to produce evidence
imported_records.hook: Who must establish a claim, and what does that requirement mean?

concepts.label: Burden of proof
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare who must prove a proposition with how much proof the proceeding requires.
concepts.original_description: in law, the obligation on a party in a trial to produce evidence

relations.note: Compare the standard governing proof with a procedure asking whether a material factual dispute requires trial. Summary judgment does not simply replace evidentiary burdens with a judge's preference.

concepts.card: Hindu traditions encompass diverse deities, texts and forms of practice that change across regions and communities. Puja offers one entry point: worship can involve images, offerings and visual encounters with a deity. Exploring a particular practice makes that diversity more concrete than assuming one universal religious routine.

evidence.note: Diversity is supported by the introduction; ritual details are checked in r01.
Images, offerings and deity encounter support the ritual example.

imported_records.description: religion widely practiced in the Indian subcontinent
imported_records.subsection: Religion and theology / Religious systems and faiths / Indian religions

concepts.label: Hinduism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Diverse deities, texts and practices are woven through Hindu traditions, whose forms change across regions and diaspora communities.
concepts.original_description: religion widely practiced in the Indian subcontinent

relations.note: Puja supplies a documented practice through which to explore the broader traditions.

concepts.card: Topspin helps a tennis ball dip into the court after clearing the net, allowing a faster shot to remain in play. Producing it depends on the racket's upward motion relative to the incoming ball, its tilt, and the ball's existing motion and spin.

evidence.note: Cross's Ball Spin discussion supports dipping trajectory and multiple determinants; this is a tennis example of the registered generic topspin identity, not a novel application ID.

imported_records.description: property of a rotating ball
imported_records.hook: Explore how a spinning ball's motion changes a shot's trajectory and bounce.

concepts.label: Topspin
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how topspin permits a faster shot to dip back into court.
concepts.original_description: property of a rotating ball

relations.note: Cross explicitly explains topspin production and its effect on shot trajectories in tennis.

concepts.card: Psychology studies mind and behavior through empirical methods. Mental processes are not directly visible, so researchers draw inferences from behavior, biological indicators and people's reports. A claim about thought becomes scientifically testable by connecting it to observations that could support or challenge an explanation.

evidence.note: Section 1.1 explicitly links indirect mental inference to observable behavior, biological indicators and self-report; the card does not imply that introspection alone proves a mental mechanism.

imported_records.description: study of mental functions and behaviours
imported_records.subsection: Anthropology, psychology and everyday life / Psychology

concepts.label: Psychology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how observable behavior and reports support inferences about mental processes.
concepts.original_description: study of mental functions and behaviours

relations.note: Inferring an unobservable psychological process from a measure creates the construct-validity question: does that measure capture the intended concept? The two inspected sections supply these premises.

concepts.card: Mamluks were enslaved recruits trained for military service who could later be freed into powerful households. In the Mamluk Sultanate, ties to commanders and fellow soldiers shaped political loyalties. Rival households could therefore influence succession as well as the conduct of warfare.

evidence.note: Military enslavement, training, manumission, household loyalty and rivalry are described.

imported_records.description: slave soldiers, mercenaries, or warriors of the Islamic world (9th-19th centuries)

concepts.label: Mamluk
concepts.learning_takeaway: Enslaved boys were trained and later freed into military households whose loyalty and rivalry could determine political succession.
concepts.original_description: slave soldiers, mercenaries, or warriors of the Islamic world (9th-19th centuries)

relations.note: Compare two historically distinct military institutions whose recruitment could detach service from hereditary local elites.

concepts.card: Gardening involves shaping the conditions in which plants grow. A mulch layer, for example, can conserve soil moisture, suppress weeds and alter temperature around roots. Such choices show that caring for plants includes managing their immediate environment, as well as sowing, planting or tending the plants themselves.

evidence.note: UMN’s mulch guide provides the specific moisture, weed and temperature example within garden care.

imported_records.description: Growing and caring for plants in gardens and small outdoor spaces.

concepts.label: Gardening
concepts.learning_takeaway: See soil cover as one of the ways gardeners manage the growing conditions around plants.
concepts.original_description: Growing and caring for plants in gardens and small outdoor spaces.

relations.note: Mulching supplies a concrete soil-environment management practice within gardening.

concepts.card: Food fermentation uses microorganisms to transform a food’s ingredients. Products such as acids can change flavor and texture and, under suitable conditions, help inhibit spoilage. The culinary practice depends on the organisms and process conditions, rather than treating every uncontrolled microbial change as desirable fermentation.

evidence.note: FAO describes microbial food transformations, fermentation products and preservation effects; the bounded wording avoids equating fermentation with guaranteed safety.

imported_records.description: Using microorganisms to transform and preserve foods.

concepts.label: Fermentation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize food fermentation through microbial products that change flavor, texture and keeping qualities.
concepts.original_description: Using microorganisms to transform and preserve foods.

relations.note: Yeast activity in bread dough is one culinary use of microbial transformation within a larger baking process.

concepts.card: Buildings and paved surfaces absorb and later release heat, while reduced vegetation limits shade and evaporative cooling. These differences can make urban areas warmer than their surroundings. Surface temperatures and air temperatures describe related but distinct heat-island patterns, so the measurement being compared matters.

evidence.note: EPA identifies stored/released heat, reduced shade/moisture and the distinction between surface and atmospheric heat islands.

imported_records.description: Studying why built-up areas retain heat and how design can reduce it.

concepts.label: Urban heat islands
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish hot built surfaces from warmer urban air and identify their different measurements.
concepts.original_description: Studying why built-up areas retain heat and how design can reduce it.

relations.note: Urban heat measurements and Mauna Loa’s gas record illustrate why an environmental variable and its sampling method must be specified; neither is a parent of the other.

concepts.card: Confirmation bias makes evidence supporting an existing belief easier to notice than evidence challenging it. Someone convinced a teacher is unfriendly may remember curt exchanges while overlooking pleasant ones. The resulting impression can feel well supported because counterexamples received less attention.

evidence.note: Section 7.3's professor example supports selective attention to confirming episodes; retain authored control local:authored:000049 and its prior version, with Q431498 left as a historical equivalence proposal rather than a second meaning.

imported_records.description: Examining the tendency to favor information that supports existing beliefs.

concepts.label: Confirmation bias
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize selective attention to information supporting an existing belief.
concepts.original_description: Examining the tendency to favor information that supports existing beliefs.

relations.note: Confirmation bias favors evidence fitting a prior belief; the availability heuristic favors accessible examples. This comparison separates two reasons an evidence sample may be selective.

concepts.card: Oral history turns recorded recollections into historical sources through preparation, interviewing, preservation and arrangements for access. The narrator’s perspective remains part of the evidence. Researchers therefore contextualize the account and, when possible, check factual statements against other information.

evidence.note: Four stages and contextualization of subjective recollection are explicit.

imported_records.description: Recording and interpreting people's firsthand accounts of past experiences.

concepts.label: Oral history
concepts.learning_takeaway: An interview becomes a usable historical source through preparation, recording, preservation and access arrangements, with attention to the narrator’s perspective.
concepts.original_description: Recording and interpreting people's firsthand accounts of past experiences.

relations.note: Narrator review makes the access and participation arrangements concrete.

concepts.card: Archaeology reconstructs human lives from material remains, including objects, traces of structures and environmental evidence. A find gains meaning through its location and associations. Recording those circumstances lets researchers connect a surviving object with the activities that produced or used it.

evidence.note: Material-remains definition and artifact categories; contextual inference requires h02.
Location, associations and cultural setting support the contextual claims.

imported_records.description: Understanding past societies through material remains and landscapes.

concepts.label: Archaeology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Study material traces alongside their find circumstances to reconstruct human activity rather than treating an object as an isolated collectible.
concepts.original_description: Understanding past societies through material remains and landscapes.

relations.note: Context explains how the material evidence studied by archaeology becomes interpretable.

concepts.card: Food history traces how familiar meals emerge from changing production, exchange and habits of eating. Crops such as maize, potatoes and cacao traveled far beyond their American origins. Following those movements reveals that everyday diets preserve histories of migration and contact.

evidence.note: American crops and their movement support the dietary example.

imported_records.description: Exploring how food production, trade and eating practices change over time.

concepts.label: Food history
concepts.learning_takeaway: Following the movement of crops such as maize, potatoes and cacao reveals how familiar diets are products of historical migration and exchange.
concepts.original_description: Exploring how food production, trade and eating practices change over time.

relations.note: Transatlantic crop movement gives a documented case for studying changing diets.

concepts.card: Citizens' assemblies bring selected members of the public together to learn, hear contrasting evidence and deliberate on a policy question. In Ireland's process, participants discuss in small groups and make recommendations. Those recommendations are advisory: elected institutions retain responsibility for deciding legislation and government policy.

evidence.locator: How does the Citizens' Assembly work?; recommendations
evidence.note: Ireland's official FAQ supports evidence, facilitated discussion and advisory recommendations; the card explicitly bounds decision authority to the Irish process rather than every citizens' assembly internationally.

imported_records.description: Bringing selected members of the public together to examine policy questions.

concepts.label: Citizens' assemblies
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore informed public deliberation whose recommendations remain advisory in Ireland.
concepts.original_description: Bringing selected members of the public together to examine policy questions.

relations.note: The FAQ directly explains stratified random recruitment as the method for forming an Irish assembly intended to broadly reflect the wider population.

concepts.card: Worker cooperatives place ownership with the people working in the enterprise. Worker-owners can choose those who manage everyday operations, so democratic oversight need not eliminate a workplace hierarchy. The important distinction is to whom managers are accountable, not whether every operational decision is made by everyone together.

evidence.note: Checked ownership, manager selection and continuing hierarchy; preserved the prior worker-cooperative identity and did not generalize every example's profit-sharing formula.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: CORE's worker-ownership and selected-manager arrangement provides a concrete case for separating governance authority from everyday organizational coordination.

imported_records.description: Operating enterprises owned and democratically governed by their workers.

concepts.label: Worker cooperatives
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate worker ownership and selection of managers from the day-to-day hierarchy that may still coordinate production.
concepts.original_description: Operating enterprises owned and democratically governed by their workers.

relations.note: CORE's worker-ownership and selected-manager arrangement provides a concrete case for separating governance authority from everyday organizational coordination.

concepts.card: Public health works to prevent illness and protect health across communities. Vaccination, safer environments and reducing exposure to hazards can change risks before an individual needs treatment. Its population focus connects personal health with shared conditions, policies and collective actions that affect many people at once.

evidence.locator: What is public health?; Prevention examples
evidence.note: APHA describes community-wide prevention, protective environments and examples including vaccination and health-hazard reduction.

imported_records.description: Studying and supporting health at the level of populations and communities.

concepts.label: Public health
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect community-wide prevention with safer water, vaccination and protection from health hazards.
concepts.original_description: Studying and supporting health at the level of populations and communities.

relations.note: Framingham’s population follow-up illustrates how evidence about shared risk factors can inform preventive public-health work.

concepts.card: Linguistics investigates how people actually use language, rather than simply declaring which usages they ought to prefer. Researchers compare patterns and test possible explanations against observations. A word that sounds impossible in a language can be informative evidence about its structure, even when no rule was explicitly taught.

evidence.note: Checked empirical versus prescriptive distinction and possible-word judgments; not every intuition is treated as unbiased or sufficient evidence alone.

imported_records.description: Studying the structures, meanings and uses of human language.

concepts.label: Linguistics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Investigate language through systematic observations rather than treating preferred usage as an empirical rule.
concepts.original_description: Studying the structures, meanings and uses of human language.

relations.note: The descriptive scientific approach becomes concrete in phonology's investigation of permitted sound combinations and recurring pronunciation patterns.

concepts.card: Peer learning develops understanding through exchanges between learners. Explaining why an answer seems right and listening to another person's reasoning can expose gaps that solitary work misses. Peer Instruction provides one structured classroom example, but the broader activity is not limited to that particular voting-and-discussion sequence.

evidence.note: Checked reasoning exchange and specific protocol example; no guarantee that every peer discussion corrects errors or improves learning.

imported_records.description: Developing understanding through collaboration and exchange among learners.

concepts.label: Peer learning
concepts.learning_takeaway: Develop understanding by explaining reasoning to other learners and considering their explanations.
concepts.original_description: Developing understanding through collaboration and exchange among learners.

relations.note: The Peer Instruction paper explicitly describes learners explaining reasoning to each other within a collaborative classroom protocol.

concepts.card: Bread dough needs both expanding gas and a structure that can retain it. In wheat bread, yeast produces gas while hydrated flour proteins form a stretchy gluten network. Baking expands the pockets and sets the dough, connecting fermentation, material structure and heat in one everyday craft.

evidence.note: Exploratorium describes yeast gas production, gluten development, gas pockets expanding during cooking and dough solidification.

imported_records.description: Making bread through mixing, fermentation, shaping and baking.

concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect dough structure and microbial gas production with the rise of bread.
concepts.original_description: Making bread through mixing, fermentation, shaping and baking.

relations.note: Gluten formation is a specific material mechanism within the broader bread-baking process.

concepts.card: Chess ends in checkmate when the opposing king is attacked and no legal move can remove the threat. The king is never actually captured. A different ending, stalemate, occurs when a player has no legal move but their king is not attacked.

evidence.note: Articles 1.4 and 5.2.1 support the objective, prohibition of king capture and contrasting stalemate condition; no claim that every immobile king is stalemated.

imported_records.description: Exploring strategic play, tactics and positional thinking in chess.

concepts.label: Chess
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why checkmate ends play without capturing the king.
concepts.original_description: Exploring strategic play, tactics and positional thinking in chess.

relations.note: The laws distinguish checkmate from stalemate through whether the immobile side's king is attacked.

concepts.card: Shogi is Japanese chess with a distinctive form of piece reuse. Captured pieces become reserves for their captor. Instead of moving a piece already on the board, a player can spend a turn returning a captured piece to play on their own side.

concepts.card: Backgammon combines a race with obstacles. Each player moves fifteen checkers according to dice rolls, aiming to gather them in the home board and remove them. Landing on a lone opposing checker sends it to the bar, where it must re-enter before other checkers move.

concepts.original_description: Exploring strategic play involving movement, probability and dice.

concepts.card: Woodworking shapes and joins wood into useful or decorative objects. Adhesive bonds, for example, let separate pieces share loads and form structures that a single piece could not easily provide. Understanding the material and the joint together helps explain why successful making involves more than choosing a shape.

concepts.original_description: Shaping and joining wood to create practical or decorative objects.

concepts.card: Weaving interlaces two sets of threads to build cloth. The warp is held on the loom under tension, while the weft passes over and under it. Separating those roles helps explain how a loom organizes many individual strands into a stable, patterned textile structure.

concepts.card: Color theory examines relationships among colors and the effects those relationships can produce. A color’s appearance depends partly on its surroundings and on what was seen before it. Comparing these situations reveals why choosing a color is also choosing a context in which viewers will encounter it.

evidence.note: Simultaneous and successive contrast support context-dependent appearance.

imported_records.description: Exploring how colors interact perceptually and compositionally.

concepts.label: Color theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Color relationships include changes caused by neighboring colors and by colors seen immediately beforehand.
concepts.original_description: Exploring how colors interact perceptually and compositionally.

relations.note: Neighboring-color effects supply a specific case of perceptual color interaction.

concepts.card: Epistemology investigates knowledge, justification, understanding and other kinds of cognitive success. It asks how evidence should constrain belief and what separates knowing from merely being right. Different approaches examine individual reasoning, sensory experience or the social interests that influence which evidence receives attention.

evidence.locator: Opening historical overview and cognitive-success definition
evidence.note: SEP's opening survey explicitly discusses knowledge versus true opinion, sensory justification, formal evidence constraints and feminist attention to interests; the card avoids reducing the field to one proposed knowledge analysis.

imported_records.description: Investigating knowledge, justification and the limits of understanding.

concepts.label: Epistemology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Investigate what distinguishes knowledge, justified belief and other forms of cognitive success.
concepts.original_description: Investigating knowledge, justification and the limits of understanding.

relations.note: The tripartite analysis is one particular attempt to explain knowledge within a broader field that also studies justification, understanding and evidence; it is not the definition of epistemology itself.

concepts.card: Religious studies examines religion through historical, social and interpretive methods. What researchers count as religion affects which practices and institutions enter their questions. Comparing definitions and methods therefore matters alongside learning about any one tradition’s beliefs, texts or ceremonies.

evidence.note: Academic methods and definitional consequences are discussed.

imported_records.description: Investigating religions through historical, cultural and social approaches.

concepts.label: Religious studies
concepts.learning_takeaway: The academic study of religion uses multiple methods, and different definitions change which practices or institutions enter its questions.
concepts.original_description: Investigating religions through historical, cultural and social approaches.

relations.note: Comparing traditions is one approach within a wider academic study of religious phenomena.

concepts.card: Islamic religious life is shaped by commitments to God, Muhammad and the Qur’an, while communities differ in interpretation and practice. Prayer offers a concrete entry point: preparation and orientation connect shared commitments with repeated bodily actions performed in many different settings.

evidence.note: Introduction supports foundations and diversity; r02 supports the prayer example.
Prayer preparation and orientation supply the embodied example.

imported_records.description: Exploring Islamic beliefs, practices, institutions and histories.

concepts.label: Islam
concepts.learning_takeaway: Commitments to God, Muhammad and the Qur’an coexist with differing interpretations of leadership, scripture and religious practice.
concepts.original_description: Exploring Islamic beliefs, practices, institutions and histories.

relations.note: Prayer direction makes one shared orientation within Muslim practice concrete.

concepts.card: Jewish life connects sacred texts and religious practice with collective history, culture and changing communities. Scriptural interpretation offers one way to explore these connections. The Talmud’s preserved arguments, for example, show how teaching can develop through discussion rather than only through a single final statement.

evidence.note: Introduction supports communal/textual context; r11 supports preserved argument.
Rabbinic disputation supports the argumentative-text example.

imported_records.description: Exploring Jewish religious traditions, practices and intellectual histories.

concepts.label: Judaism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Jewish religious life connects sacred texts and monotheistic traditions with collective history, culture and changing communal practices.
concepts.original_description: Exploring Jewish religious traditions, practices and intellectual histories.

relations.note: The Talmud provides a documented example of rabbinic learning through discussion.

concepts.card: Buddhist traditions look to Buddha, Dharma and Sangha: the awakened teacher, the teaching and the community. Those shared points of reference coexist with varied practices and interpretations. Beginning with the community’s relationship to teaching helps make that diversity visible without reducing Buddhism to one uniform routine.

evidence.note: Three Treasures and traditions’ diversity are described.

imported_records.description: Exploring Buddhist traditions, communities, teachings and practices.

concepts.label: Buddhism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Buddhist traditions share reference to Buddha, Dharma and Sangha while interpreting and practicing these commitments in diverse ways.
concepts.original_description: Exploring Buddhist traditions, communities, teachings and practices.

relations.note: Sangha is one of the Three Treasures identified in the introduction.

concepts.card: Shinto shrine traditions center on the veneration of kami in places called jinja. Visits, festivals and sacred objects connect these places with ordinary life. An ofuda taken home, for example, can extend a shrine relationship into the household through an object treated with religious reverence.

evidence.locator: Opening, lines 6–9; Taking it Home, line 46
evidence.note: Shrine/kami description and home tablet practice are documented.
Household altar placement supports the domestic example.

imported_records.description: Exploring Japanese religious traditions associated with kami and ritual life.

concepts.label: Shinto
concepts.learning_takeaway: Kami are enshrined and venerated in diverse jinja; visits, festivals and protective objects connect sacred places with everyday life.
concepts.original_description: Exploring Japanese religious traditions associated with kami and ritual life.

relations.note: Jinja Honcho presents ofuda as one way a shrine relationship enters domestic practice.

concepts.card: Distributed systems spread computation across machines that communicate over a network. Keeping their work coordinated becomes difficult when messages are delayed or machines fail. Replicated state machines offer one approach: replicas agree on commands and execute them deterministically in the same order to maintain matching results.

evidence.note: The paper, Section 2, requires deterministic state machines as well as an agreed command order for matching states and outputs. This is one distributed-systems pattern, not a condition met by all distributed programs.

imported_records.description: Coordinating computation across multiple networked machines.

concepts.label: Distributed systems
concepts.learning_takeaway: Coordinate machines through messages while preserving shared results despite some machine failures.
concepts.original_description: Coordinating computation across multiple networked machines.

relations.note: The Raft paper's replicated-state-machine discussion gives one concrete coordination approach within the broad distributed-systems field.

concepts.card: Cryptography uses keyed mathematical techniques to protect information and verify messages or participants. Encryption can hide content, while authentication and integrity mechanisms help detect impersonation or alteration. TLS illustrates how several cryptographic tools are combined into a communication protocol rather than relying on secrecy of the design.

evidence.note: Checked TLS security goals and key/design distinction; encryption alone is not claimed to provide every cryptographic property.

evidence.locator: Section I.A, design principle d (open design)
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: TLS provides a concrete protocol combining encryption, authentication and integrity goals; Saltzer's open-design principle clarifies the distinction between public mechanisms and secret keys.

imported_records.description: Protecting information through mathematical encoding and verification techniques.

concepts.label: Cryptography
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine keyed encryption and authentication to protect message confidentiality, integrity, and peer identity.
concepts.original_description: Protecting information through mathematical encoding and verification techniques.

relations.note: TLS provides a concrete protocol combining encryption, authentication and integrity goals; Saltzer's open-design principle clarifies the distinction between public mechanisms and secret keys.

concepts.card: Probability studies uncertain outcomes by assigning them numerical likelihoods and organizing those likelihoods into distributions. A distribution can describe individual possible values or a continuous range. Cumulative probability combines the possibilities up to a threshold, connecting uncertainty about outcomes with quantities that can be compared.

evidence.locator: Probability -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 3, 5 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-4; paragraph-6
evidence.note: Represent uncertainty through outcomes, numerical likelihoods, and distributions whose total probability is one.

imported_records.description: Modeling uncertainty and random events mathematically.

concepts.label: Probability
concepts.learning_takeaway: Represent uncertainty through outcomes, numerical likelihoods, and distributions whose total probability is one.
concepts.original_description: Modeling uncertainty and random events mathematically.

concepts.card: Graph theory studies structures made of vertices and connecting edges. A graph’s drawing or numbering can change without altering its connections. An adjacency matrix provides one numerical representation, making it possible to analyze the same underlying network through different arrangements of symbols.

evidence.locator: Graph Theory -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2
evidence.note: Defines graph theory as the study of mathematical graphs.

evidence.locator: Adjacency Matrix -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 3 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-4
evidence.note: Defines adjacency representation and explains why relabeling gives different matrices for the same graph.

imported_records.description: Studying networks of vertices and connecting edges.

concepts.label: Graph theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate a network’s underlying connections from the way its vertices and edges are drawn or labeled.
concepts.original_description: Studying networks of vertices and connecting edges.

relations.note: The adjacency-matrix reference explicitly represents graph connections while allowing different vertex labelings.

concepts.card: Topology studies properties of spaces preserved by continuous, reversible changes of shape. Stretching a circle into an ellipse changes lengths but preserves its connected loop. Focusing on such structure lets mathematicians compare objects without treating every geometric distortion as a fundamentally new space.

evidence.locator: Topology -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 4, 6, 7 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-5; paragraph-7; paragraph-8
evidence.note: Study connectivity and properties preserved by continuous changes rather than exact lengths or angles.

imported_records.description: Studying properties of spaces preserved under continuous deformation.

concepts.label: Topology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Study connectivity and properties preserved by continuous changes rather than exact lengths or angles.
concepts.original_description: Studying properties of spaces preserved under continuous deformation.

concepts.card: Information theory measures the choices involved in sending messages and the limits of communication systems. In Shannon's formulation, a message is selected from possible alternatives; its personal meaning is a separate question. Using base-two logarithms measures those choices in bits.

evidence.note: Checked the message-selection problem, explicit separation from semantics, and logarithm-base choice in the introduction; no claim that human meaning is unimportant generally.

imported_records.description: Quantifying information, uncertainty and communication limits.

concepts.label: Information theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Measure communication choices without treating message meaning as the engineering quantity.
concepts.original_description: Quantifying information, uncertainty and communication limits.

relations.note: Shannon's paper provides a concrete historical entry into the field by formulating message selection and its bit-based measure.

concepts.card: Physics seeks common explanations for matter, energy, motion, and interactions across scales. The gravity governing a galaxy’s stars is connected with the gravity involved in water flowing through a dam. Such links let a few tested principles explain phenomena that initially seem unrelated.

evidence.locator: 1.1 The Scope and Scale of Physics; inspected passage indices 7, 9, 12, 13 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1168329107844; fs-id1168329113035; fs-id1168329192865; fs-id1168326800853
evidence.note: Use common laws of matter, energy, space, and time to connect laboratory and cosmic phenomena.

imported_records.description: Studying matter, energy and their fundamental interactions.

concepts.label: Physics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use common laws of matter, energy, space, and time to connect laboratory and cosmic phenomena.
concepts.original_description: Studying matter, energy and their fundamental interactions.

concepts.card: Optics studies light’s behavior and its interactions with materials. Refraction offers a concrete example: a ray can change direction when it enters a medium where light travels at a different speed. The same principle helps explain lenses, distorted underwater views, and optical-fiber systems.

evidence.locator: 1.3 Refraction; inspected passage indices 5, 6, 7 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1172098567922; fs-id1172098389853; fs-id1172098560537
evidence.note: Explain image formation and light guidance through refraction and related behavior at material boundaries.

imported_records.description: Studying light and its interactions with matter.

concepts.label: Optics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain image formation and light guidance through refraction and related behavior at material boundaries.
concepts.original_description: Studying light and its interactions with matter.

concepts.card: Chemistry connects observable substances with the particles and interactions that explain their behavior. A visible change can be described through a molecular model and represented by a formula or equation. Moving among these descriptions helps make sense of experiments.

evidence.locator: 1.1 Chemistry in Context; inspected passage indices 14, 19, 23 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm183676832; fs-idm148555376; fs-idm166065136
evidence.note: Connect observable changes in matter with particle-level explanations and chemical representations.

imported_records.description: Studying substances, their properties and their transformations.

concepts.label: Chemistry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect observable changes in matter with particle-level explanations and chemical representations.
concepts.original_description: Studying substances, their properties and their transformations.

concepts.card: Geology investigates Earth’s materials, physical processes and history. Rocks preserve evidence of earlier conditions, while tectonics, weathering and erosion continue to change landscapes. Reading a place geologically means connecting what is visible today with the processes and timescales that produced it.

evidence.note: NPS defines geology through Earth’s physical features/processes/history and names rocks, tectonics, weathering and erosion as fundamentals.

imported_records.description: Investigating Earth's materials, structures and history.

concepts.label: Geology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read Earth’s materials and landscapes as evidence of processes and planetary history.
concepts.original_description: Investigating Earth's materials, structures and history.

relations.note: Subduction offers one concrete tectonic process through which geology connects material movement and landscape formation.

concepts.card: Oceanography studies the ocean through its water movement, chemistry, living communities and seafloor history. These perspectives overlap: circulation can move nutrients that influence marine life. Field observations, experiments and models connect the ocean’s physical setting with the organisms and chemical processes operating within it.

evidence.note: Supports the field’s physical, chemical, biological and geological scope and research methods.
Supports the example connecting circulation, nutrients and marine productivity.

imported_records.description: Investigating the physical, chemical and biological properties of oceans.

concepts.label: Oceanography
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect ocean chemistry, life, seafloor history and water movement as interacting research areas.
concepts.original_description: Investigating the physical, chemical and biological properties of oceans.

relations.note: Coastal upwelling illustrates how circulation delivers nutrients and connects physical with biological oceanography.

concepts.card: Genetics studies inheritance and variation, including how genes interact with the environment. A DNA difference can influence a trait without determining it alone. Studying genes alongside behavior and surroundings helps explain why genetic information is only part of the story of health.

evidence.note: NHGRI defines inheritance, DNA variation and environmental interaction; its narration explicitly treats behavior and surroundings as additional health influences.

imported_records.description: Studying inheritance and variation in living organisms.

concepts.label: Genetics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect inherited DNA variation with environmental influences rather than treating genes as destiny.
concepts.original_description: Studying inheritance and variation in living organisms.

relations.note: Mosaicism extends the inheritance discussion to DNA differences arising after fertilization, showing why genetic variation need not be shared by every cell.

concepts.card: Ecology investigates how organisms interact with one another and with their surroundings. A butterfly’s food plant, predators and climate can all shape where it survives. Moving between individuals, populations and communities helps researchers connect small interactions with larger patterns of abundance and distribution.

evidence.note: OpenStax defines ecology and its levels, then uses the Karner blue butterfly to connect organismal requirements with community interactions.

imported_records.description: Studying relationships between organisms and their environments.

concepts.label: Ecology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect organisms’ distribution and abundance with living and nonliving surroundings.
concepts.original_description: Studying relationships between organisms and their environments.

relations.note: The Karner blue example connects the field’s organism and community scales through habitat requirements and ant–larva interactions.

concepts.card: Material culture examines social life through objects and their uses. A coffee-house trade token, for example, advertised goods while presenting a particular image of the business. Its wording and pictures let a small commercial object become evidence about consumption, exchange and public identity.

evidence.note: Token description supports the concrete example and its advertised goods.

imported_records.description: Understanding social life through objects and their uses.

concepts.label: Material culture
concepts.learning_takeaway: A trade token’s imagery and product list provide evidence of commercial life and how a coffee house represented itself.
concepts.original_description: Understanding social life through objects and their uses.

relations.note: The named token supplies a specific object through which to investigate commercial representation.

concepts.card: Human geography studies how communities, cultures and economies relate to places and environments. Questions about settlement, movement or work become spatial questions: where activities occur, how places connect and how people shape their surroundings. Different methods reveal different parts of those relationships.

evidence.locator: Lead, lines 207–208; Fields and urban geography, lines 237–308
evidence.note: The inspected lead defines spatial human-environment relationships and multiple methods.

imported_records.description: Studying relationships among people, places and spatial organization.

concepts.label: Human geography
concepts.learning_takeaway: Social life, economies and settlement patterns can be studied through their relationships to locations and environments.
concepts.original_description: Studying relationships among people, places and spatial organization.

relations.note: Cultural landscapes provide material examples of relationships between communities and environments.

concepts.card: Cartography turns spatial information into maps through choices about selection, symbols and presentation. A map made to compare population rates may look very different from one designed for navigation. Thinking about its purpose helps explain both what a map emphasizes and what it leaves out.

evidence.note: Map design and use define the field; contrasting purposes are editorial illustrations.

imported_records.description: Designing maps to represent spatial information.

concepts.label: Cartography
concepts.learning_takeaway: Making a map requires selecting features and symbols to communicate spatial relationships for a particular use.
concepts.original_description: Designing maps to represent spatial information.

relations.note: Choropleth design supplies a specific example of choosing how spatial information is represented.

concepts.card: Cultural landscapes record relationships between people and their environments. Cultivation, settlement, engineering and sacred practices can give a place its visible form and meaning. Reading terraces or water channels as cultural evidence connects practical land use with the institutions and values that sustained it.

evidence.note: Human-environment interaction and examples are described in the UNESCO introduction.

imported_records.description: Examining landscapes shaped by relationships between people and environments.

concepts.label: Cultural landscapes
concepts.learning_takeaway: Terraces, gardens and sacred sites show how communities shape environments and give them practical or symbolic meaning.
concepts.original_description: Examining landscapes shaped by relationships between people and environments.

relations.note: The linked irrigation and temple landscape supplies a documented example of cultural landscape formation.

concepts.card: John Cage's 4′33″ directs attention toward sounds already present around a performance. The John Cage Trust's official app makes this idea concrete by recording ambient sound in three movements. The example shifts attention from supplying a new melody to noticing the listening environment itself.

evidence.note: The Trust's description supports ambient listening and its three-movement app realization; wording does not infer every original score instruction from the app or claim literal absence of sound.

concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore a three-movement performance that directs attention toward ambient sound.

relations.note: The Trust identifies this as Cage's composition; its ambient-sound focus offers a boundary-testing example of musical listening.

concepts.card: Shannon's 1948 paper, A Mathematical Theory of Communication, framed communication as selecting and reproducing messages from possible alternatives. It separated that engineering problem from what messages mean to people. Its logarithmic measure also explained why base-two units could conveniently be called bits.

evidence.note: Checked title, date, engineering-versus-semantics distinction, and bits passage; no unsupported sole-inventor claim.

concepts.label: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how Shannon's 1948 paper separated message selection from semantics to formulate an engineering theory.

relations.note: The paper's formulation supplies a historically specific route into the broader field of information theory, without treating work and field as equivalent identities.

aliases: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte
concepts.card: Seurat’s A Sunday on La Grande Jatte arranges separate colored strokes within a large composition. The Met describes it as a major demonstration of Neo-Impressionist technique. It offers a case for comparing visible brushwork with the optical effects the movement’s artists hoped to achieve.

evidence.locator: Grande Jatte and separated brushwork, lines 80–84
evidence.note: Separated strokes, the named painting and optical-mixture ambitions are described.

concepts.label: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
concepts.learning_takeaway: Seurat organized separate, contrasting strokes into a large composition that became a central demonstration of Neo-Impressionist optical-mixture aims.

relations.note: The Met essay explicitly connects the painting with Neo-Impressionist optical-mixture theory.

concepts.card: An absolute sensory threshold is usually defined as the stimulus intensity detected on half of repeated presentations under specified conditions. It is therefore a probabilistic measurement, not a magical boundary below which detection never happens. The testing conditions matter when comparing how sensitive different observers appear.

evidence.note: OpenStax 5.1 supplies the fifty-percent criterion and controlled conditions; probabilistic interpretation follows that definition without importing unsupported exact sensitivity estimates.
Provides the decision-theoretic premise for the editorial comparison.

concepts.label: Absolute sensory threshold
concepts.learning_takeaway: Interpret detection threshold as a probability under controlled conditions.

relations.note: A detection percentage alone does not separate available sensory information from a decision criterion; signal detection theory analyzes that distinction.

concepts.card: An access control list associates a protected object with the principals permitted to use it. When access is requested, that object-centered list helps determine authority. This differs from a capability system, where a principal presents an unforgeable ticket naming the object and conveying access authority.

evidence.locator: Glossary, Access control list and List-oriented
evidence.note: Checked object-to-principal list meaning and contrast with capabilities; no assumption that every list has identical permission syntax.

concepts.label: Access control list
concepts.learning_takeaway: Associate an object with a list of principals authorized to access it.

relations.note: The glossary's list-oriented and ticket-oriented descriptions provide the factual basis for contrasting two arrangements of authority.

concepts.card: An achieved status is a social position acquired through activity or choice, such as becoming a nurse. The term distinguishes its route of acquisition from an ascribed position. Status names the position; role describes the patterns of behavior expected of someone who holds it.

evidence.note: Checked nurse example and position-versus-behavior distinction; not claimed that achieved outcomes reflect effort alone or equal opportunity.

concepts.label: Achieved status
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify social positions acquired through activity or choice, while separating the position from its expected behaviors.

relations.note: The source directly presents achieved and ascribed statuses as contrasting acquisition categories, alongside the status/role distinction.

concepts.card: An acid–base indicator has differently colored acid and base forms. Changing pH shifts their relative amounts, producing a visible transition rather than an infinitely sharp switch. An indicator therefore reports a range of acidity, and its useful color interval depends on its own acid–base equilibrium.

evidence.locator: 14.7 Acid-Base Titrations; inspected passage indices 48, 50, 52 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm39085312; fs-idm68547888; fs-idm188576256
evidence.note: Different colors of a weak acid and its conjugate base report the solution’s pH range.

concepts.label: Acid-base indicator
concepts.learning_takeaway: Different colors of a weak acid and its conjugate base report the solution’s pH range.

relations.note: The titration section uses indicator color-change intervals to choose suitable endpoint signals.

concepts.card: An acid–base titration uses a reagent of known concentration to measure an unknown acid or base. Tracking pH reveals progress toward stoichiometric equivalence. The equivalence point is not always neutral: titrating a weak acid with a strong base typically leaves a basic solution.

evidence.locator: 14.7 Acid-Base Titrations; inspected passage indices 6, 8, 35 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm43847120; fs-idp135875056; fs-idm40620912
evidence.note: Use controlled neutralization and a pH curve to determine acid or base concentration.

concepts.label: Acid-base titration
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use controlled neutralization and a pH curve to determine acid or base concentration.

relations.note: The source explicitly presents acid–base titrimetry as a quantitative analytical technique.

concepts.card: In a collision model, activation energy marks the barrier reactants must overcome to reach a transition state. Collisions can fail even when molecules meet: insufficient energy prevents productive rearrangement. A higher barrier leaves fewer collisions energetic enough to react at a given temperature.

evidence.locator: 12.5 Collision Theory; inspected passage indices 18, 21, 23 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm58992896; fs-idm102149680; fs-idm92123120
evidence.note: Relate the energy barrier between reactants and the transition state to successful molecular collisions.

concepts.label: Activation energy
concepts.learning_takeaway: Relate the energy barrier between reactants and the transition state to successful molecular collisions.

relations.note: The Arrhenius equation in the same section relates activation energy to the temperature dependence of the rate constant.

concepts.card: Actuarially fair insurance charges a premium equal to the expected claim payment for the relevant risk group. It is a benchmark, not necessarily the price an insurer can sustainably offer. Administration, other business costs, and profit require additional funding beyond that expected-claims amount.

evidence.note: Checked expected payment definition and excluded expense/profit loading; fairness here is a technical pricing term rather than an ethical verdict.

concepts.label: Actuarially fair insurance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate a premium equal to expected claims from one that also funds operating expenses and profit.

relations.note: The source explicitly derives insurance premiums from group losses before distinguishing expected claims from operating costs and profit.

concepts.card: Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings provides a textbook example of a 4–3 suspension. A prepared note becomes dissonant against the bass before resolving downward by step. The numbers describe the suspension and resolution as interval classes, so compound intervals can receive the same analytical label.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 10.9 labels the Barber example 4–3 and explains reduction of compound intervals in suspension labels. The revised card does not require the sounding interval to occupy a literal simple-fourth register.

concepts.label: Adagio for Strings
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear how a 4–3 suspension delays resolution in Barber's work.

relations.note: The named score example is explicitly introduced as a 4–3 suspension.

concepts.card: Adaptive optics counters atmospheric blurring by measuring distortion and rapidly changing the shape of a flexible mirror. The corrections help incoming light reach a sharper focus. A ground-based telescope can therefore recover detail that its aperture permits but turbulent air would otherwise obscure.

evidence.locator: 6.2 Telescopes Today; inspected passage indices 37, 41 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1167471084189; fs-id1167470614614
evidence.note: Rapidly reshape a flexible mirror to compensate for atmospheric distortion of incoming starlight.

concepts.label: Adaptive optics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Rapidly reshape a flexible mirror to compensate for atmospheric distortion of incoming starlight.

relations.note: The source explicitly presents adaptive optics as a correction for atmospheric image distortion.

concepts.card: Additive minimalism develops music by expanding repeated material in small steps. In Glass's examples, repetitions may be added or chords given extra subdivisions. The listener can follow a process of gradual growth rather than waiting for an entirely new theme to replace the existing pattern.

evidence.locator: 35.1 Two Pages and Einstein on the Beach examples
evidence.note: Section 35.1 supplies Two Pages, Music in Fifths and lengthened chords in Einstein on the Beach; this describes the demonstrated processes rather than all minimalist composition.

concepts.label: Additive minimalism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Track growth by gradually extending repeated musical patterns.

relations.note: The textbook uses Glass's Two Pages as an explicit example of additive process combined with subtraction within repetitions.

concepts.card: Antidiuretic hormone increases the number of aquaporin water channels in the kidney’s collecting-duct cell membranes. Water can then leave the forming urine along an osmotic gradient. With less hormone, fewer channels are inserted, less water is recovered and the urine can remain more dilute.

evidence.locator: Collecting Ducts and Recovery of Water
evidence.note: The collecting-duct passage states ADH-dependent apical insertion, osmotic water movement and fewer channels/more dilute urine with less ADH.

concepts.label: ADH-dependent aquaporin trafficking
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how reversible water-channel insertion changes collecting-duct water recovery.

relations.note: Aquaporin-dependent water recovery uses the medullary osmotic gradient generated in part by countercurrent multiplication.

concepts.card: An adjacency pair links two conversational actions, such as a question and its answer or an invitation and its response. Once the first action occurs, a particular kind of second action becomes relevant. An appropriate response can also show whether the listener understood what the first speaker meant.

evidence.note: Checked conditional relevance and understanding evidence; no claim that paired actions must be physically consecutive without inserted clarification.

concepts.label: Adjacency pair
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how an initial conversational action makes a specific kind of response relevant, such as an answer after a question.

relations.note: Clark and Brennan explicitly discuss relevant second actions as positive evidence of understanding within grounding.

concepts.card: Adverse selection can arise when insurance buyers know more about their own risk than the insurer. A pooled premium may attract high-risk buyers while discouraging lower-risk ones. The changing mix can then raise average claims, making coverage harder to price even before anyone changes their behavior.

evidence.note: Checked buyer composition, pooled pricing and before-versus-after agreement distinction; not every insurance pool is claimed to unravel.

concepts.label: Adverse selection
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how privately known risk changes which people seek insurance and can push low-risk buyers out.

relations.note: The insurance source contrasts hidden-risk selection with behavior changes after coverage; the comparison separates two different information problems.

concepts.card: Five protected Omani aflaj systems connect water sources, channels, cultivated land and settlement. Their structures also reveal arrangements for sharing and protecting scarce water. Looking across the systems shows how technical infrastructure and collective management together shaped inhabited landscapes in an arid region.

evidence.note: Five systems, linked built features and shared management are described.

concepts.label: Aflaj irrigation landscapes of Oman
concepts.learning_takeaway: Five protected systems display how water sources, channels, agriculture, defensive buildings and shared management shaped arid settlements.

relations.note: These named systems are documented cases of the wider water-sharing settlement pattern.

concepts.card: Aflaj water systems use gravity-fed channels to distribute water through arid settlements and agricultural land. Sharing access requires arrangements for timing, upkeep and allocation. Their geography is therefore institutional as well as hydraulic: reliable flow depends on people maintaining both channels and rules.

evidence.note: Gravity-fed distribution, timed shares and communal management are described.

concepts.label: Aflaj water-sharing settlements
concepts.learning_takeaway: Gravity-fed water channels and timed access support permanent settlement and require communities to coordinate maintenance and distribution.

relations.note: The protected Omani systems give named examples of channels, agriculture and cooperative water management.

concepts.card: Agha Shahid Ali helped bring the classical ghazal into English-language poetry and edited Ravishing DisUnities. The Academy’s account emphasizes his understanding of autonomous couplets and the anthology’s varied formal fidelity. His work offers a case for studying poetic adaptation across languages.

evidence.note: The glossary identifies Ali’s classical-ghazal advocacy, autonomous-couplet comparison and editorship of Ravishing DisUnities; it notes varied formal fidelity in the anthology.

concepts.label: Agha Shahid Ali
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ali promoted the traditional ghazal in English through poetry and anthology editorship, emphasizing the autonomy of its couplets.

relations.note: The source connects Ali’s work with transmitting the ghazal’s formal constraints into English.

concepts.card: Ait-Ben-Haddou groups earthen houses and communal facilities inside defensive walls along a former pre-Saharan trade route. Its compact arrangement shows collective settlement in built form. Examining the whole ksar connects domestic life with shared spaces, defense and the movement of goods through the region.

evidence.note: Earthen collective settlement, walls, communal facilities and trade-route setting are documented.

concepts.label: Ait-Ben-Haddou
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compact earthen dwellings and communal facilities inside walls show how a pre-Saharan trading post organized defense and shared life.

relations.note: UNESCO identifies Ait-Ben-Haddou as an example of the fortified collective settlement form.

concepts.card: An akhand path is an uninterrupted reading of the Guru Granth Sahib. Readers take successive turns so the recitation continues through the entire scripture. The practice combines sustained attention to the text with shared responsibility, making continuity possible through the coordinated participation of several people.

evidence.note: Readers rotate through an uninterrupted complete reading.

concepts.label: Akhand path
concepts.learning_takeaway: Readers work in successive shifts so the entire Guru Granth Sahib can be read without interruption.

relations.note: The scripture is the text read in full during akhand path.

concepts.card: Al Ain’s oasis landscape brings tombs, settlement remains and irrigation works into a long record of life at a desert crossroads. These different kinds of evidence connect burial, habitation and water management. Together they reveal how communities sustained settled activity within an arid environment.

evidence.note: Tombs, settlements and irrigation establish the archaeological sequence.

concepts.label: Al Ain oasis landscape
concepts.learning_takeaway: Tombs, settlement remains and irrigation works record long-term sedentary life at a desert crossroads.

relations.note: The named landscape is an archaeological case of settlement supported by managed water.

concepts.card: Allocation concealment keeps the next trial assignment unknown until enrollment is settled. If recruiters can predict the group a person will enter, they may selectively include participants and undermine randomization. This protection operates at recruitment, whereas blinding addresses knowledge of treatment after assignment.

evidence.note: Cochrane §8.3 defines unknown forthcoming assignments; §8.3.2 explains selective enrollment and explicitly distinguishes concealment from later blinding.

concepts.label: Allocation concealment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why recruiters must not know the next treatment assignment before enrollment.

relations.note: Concealment is a specific protection of assignment within a randomized controlled trial, rather than a synonym for random sequence generation.

concepts.card: Allomorphs are different forms expressing one morpheme. English a and an vary with the following sound, while plural forms show both predictable sound changes and word-specific patterns. Recognizing the shared grammatical function helps distinguish this variation from entirely different morphemes that merely resemble each other.

evidence.note: Checked a/an, plural variants and phonological versus lexical conditioning; variation is not limited to written spelling changes.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The morphology chapter explicitly presents allomorphy as variation in a morpheme's form while its function remains consistent.

concepts.label: Allomorph
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize different forms of one morpheme, with variants conditioned by sounds or specific lexical roots.

relations.note: The morphology chapter explicitly presents allomorphy as variation in a morpheme's form while its function remains consistent.

concepts.card: Allophones are physically different realizations of one phoneme. In many North American English varieties, the consonant in atom differs from the aspirated consonant in atomic, yet both are analyzed as versions of /t/. Their distribution depends partly on the surrounding sounds and stress pattern.

evidence.locator: §4.1, The phonological units of spoken language
evidence.note: Checked atom/atomic and stress environment; retained variety qualification and avoided claiming the analysis is the only possible theoretical treatment.

concepts.label: Allophone
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize physically different pronunciations treated as realizations of a single abstract phoneme.

relations.note: Section 4.1 explicitly identifies determining phonemes, allophones, and their environments as a central task of phonology.

concepts.card: A gene’s RNA can be assembled in different ways by joining different combinations of exons. Alternative splicing therefore produces related RNA transcripts from one gene, and these can encode proteins with different structures or functions. One gene need not yield just one protein product.
