evidence.note: NHGRI’s definition states different exon combinations, related mRNA transcripts and possible proteins with distinct structure/function.

concepts.label: Alternative splicing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how different exon combinations produce multiple related transcripts from one gene.

relations.note: Alternative splicing is a specific way gene information produces varied outputs, an editorial route from the broad genetics field into gene processing.

concepts.card: A curveball's behavior depends partly on the air around it. In NASA's simplified model, lower air density weakens the aerodynamic deflection of a spinning pitch, all else equal. High-altitude conditions can therefore make a curveball travel along a straighter path.

evidence.note: NASA's equation discussion directly links lower density with larger curvature radius; all-else-equal and simplified-model language avoid unsupported prediction of every pitch or game statistic.

concepts.label: Altitude effects on baseball pitches
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore why thinner air weakens a spinning baseball's curvature, other factors equal.

relations.note: The source derives the altitude effect as a particular prediction of its curveball trajectory model.

concepts.card: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring collects repeated readings while a person goes about ordinary life, usually over twenty-four hours. A worn monitor is returned after the recording period. This provides a pattern across time and circumstances, rather than relying only on one measurement taken in a clinic.

evidence.note: NHS describes a monitor worn at home for 24 hours and returned the next day for repeated blood-pressure assessment.

concepts.label: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish repeated measurements during ordinary activity from one clinic reading.

relations.note: The baroreflex regulates a changing pressure, while ambulatory monitoring samples that variable over everyday conditions; this is an editorial physiology-to-measurement bridge.

concepts.card: In US court practice, an amicus curiae is a nonparty offering arguments or information through a brief. An interest in the case does not make the contributor a litigant. Each court's applicable rules govern when and how such outside submissions may be made.

evidence.note: Cornell defines the nonparty role and cites US Supreme Court Rule 37 and Federal Appellate Rule 29. US scope is explicit, while court-specific requirements avoid a universal permission or party-status claim.

concepts.label: Amicus curiae
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how a nonparty can contribute a brief to a court's consideration.

relations.note: Compare a nonparty's rule-governed contribution with the injury-based requirements for a plaintiff's federal standing. An amicus brief does not itself give its author party status.

concepts.card: Anadiplosis repeats the end of one clause or line at the beginning of the next. The shared wording acts as a hinge between units, allowing the second statement to grow from the first. Its chained position differs from repeating all beginnings or all endings.

evidence.note: Boundary-to-boundary repetition is defined and exemplified.

concepts.label: Anadiplosis
concepts.learning_takeaway: The closing word of one unit becomes the opening word of the next, linking statements into a chain.

relations.note: Compare a chain across adjacent units with repetition at each unit’s opening.

concepts.card: Anamorphosis deliberately distorts an image so that it becomes recognizable from a particular viewing position or arrangement. Holbein’s stretched skull in The Ambassadors resolves from an oblique angle. The viewer’s position therefore becomes part of how the image is constructed and encountered.

evidence.note: The skull’s distortion and resolving viewpoint are explicitly described.

concepts.label: Anamorphosis
concepts.learning_takeaway: A deliberately distorted image becomes recognizable from a particular viewing position, as the stretched skull in Holbein’s Ambassadors does from the lower right.

relations.note: The gallery identifies the painting’s skull as an anamorphic image.

concepts.card: Rhetorical anaphora repeats a word or phrase at the beginnings of successive units. The shared opening creates a recognizable pattern while later words accumulate differences. It can shape momentum or emphasis, whether the units are poetic lines, clauses or statements in a longer passage.

evidence.note: Initial repetition and accumulative rhetorical effects are described.

concepts.label: Anaphora (rhetoric)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Repeating initial words across phrases or lines can build rhythmic and emotional accumulation.

relations.note: The glossary contrasts repeated beginnings with repeated endings.

concepts.card: For a classical particle, angular momentum combines linear momentum with position relative to a chosen origin. Even straight-line motion can have angular momentum about a point away from that path. A different origin changes the lever arm, so this quantity is not defined by speed alone.

evidence.locator: 11.2 Angular Momentum; inspected passage indices 9, 11, 13, 17 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1165038184327; fs-id1165038218862; fs-id1165038332421; fs-id1165038202948
evidence.note: Rotational momentum depends on linear momentum and position relative to a chosen origin.

concepts.label: Angular momentum
concepts.learning_takeaway: Rotational momentum depends on linear momentum and position relative to a chosen origin.

relations.note: The gyroscope passage explains torque-induced precession as a change in angular-momentum direction.

concepts.card: Song examination procedures could replace candidates’ names with numbers and have clerks recopy their answers. These steps reduced clues supplied by identity and handwriting. The practice shows a historical attempt to make assessment depend more on the submitted work than on recognizing its author.

evidence.note: Numbering and recopying are explicit anti-recognition measures.

concepts.label: Anonymization in Song examinations
concepts.learning_takeaway: Numbers replaced candidates’ names and clerks recopied answers to reduce recognition through identity or handwriting.

relations.note: Name removal and recopying are specific examination procedures described within this system.

concepts.card: A growing shoot tip can suppress the development of lateral buds. Apical dominance involves hormonal signals, including auxin from the tip, while cytokinins can favor bud growth. Removing the tip changes that balance, helping explain why pruning can encourage a plant to branch.

evidence.note: OpenStax’s auxin and cytokinin passages describe tip-related lateral inhibition, bud promotion and release after tip removal.

concepts.label: Apical dominance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect growth at a shoot tip with suppression of lateral buds and the effects of pruning.

relations.note: Pruning applies knowledge of shoot-tip control to a practical gardening decision about branching.

concepts.card: Rhetorical apostrophe directly addresses an absent person, an abstraction or something nonhuman as if it could listen. The address creates a speaker’s imagined relationship with its recipient. It is a figure of speech, distinct from the punctuation mark that shares its name.

evidence.note: The glossary defines direct address to absent or nonhuman recipients.

concepts.label: Apostrophe (rhetoric)
concepts.learning_takeaway: A speaker directly addresses an absent person, an abstraction or a nonhuman thing, creating an imagined listener.

relations.note: Distinguish the recipient invoked by a speaker from the recipient-image inferred from a whole work.

concepts.card: Apple's historical iPhone supply-chain example in The Economy separates product ownership, component manufacturing, and final assembly across different firms and countries. The case shows why calling a product American or Chinese can conceal several distinct production roles, rather than identifying one place where all its value was created.

evidence.note: Checked historical framing and distinct production roles; no current supplier arrangement, percentage or national value-added estimate is asserted.

concepts.label: Apple Inc.
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine a historically documented separation of product ownership, component sourcing, and final assembly across firms and countries.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly identifies Foxconn as the assembler in its historical Apple supply-chain example.

concepts.card: An appoggiatura is a non-chord tone approached by a leap and left by a step. It is usually accented, placing the dissonance on a strong moment before resolution. The resolving step can go upward or downward; the expressive effect does not require one fixed direction.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 10.4 supports leap approach, step departure, usual accent and either resolution direction; maintain its analytical sense rather than every historical ornamental use of the term.
The prepared same-note approach of a suspension supports the editorial contrast.

concepts.label: Appoggiatura
concepts.learning_takeaway: Follow an expressive non-chord note approached by leap and resolved by step.

relations.note: Both can create accented non-chord tension, but an appoggiatura arrives by leap whereas a suspension is prepared by the same note.

concepts.card: Archaeological context includes where a find lay, what accompanied it and its chronological, social and cultural setting. These relationships constrain interpretation. The same object can support different historical explanations when found in different associations, which is why documenting its surroundings matters.

evidence.note: Spatial, chronological, cultural and social contexts and associations are explicit.

concepts.label: Archaeological context
concepts.learning_takeaway: An object’s location, associations and chronological, social and cultural setting determine what historical inferences it can support.

relations.note: Context is one of the evidential concerns within archaeological investigation.

concepts.card: Archaeological cross-dating compares evidence from different contexts to establish their relative ages. A recognizable pattern at one site can be compared with another, or across layers within a site. The comparison links sequences without necessarily giving either context an exact calendar date.

evidence.note: Cross-dating row explicitly covers comparisons within and between sites.

concepts.label: Archaeological cross-dating
concepts.learning_takeaway: Matching evidence across archaeological contexts can place otherwise undated finds in a relative sequence.

relations.note: Seriation offers one neighboring way to compare patterns of chronological evidence.
The dating-methods table includes cross-dating for archaeological evidence.

concepts.card: Seriation arranges archaeological evidence into a relative sequence by tracking changes in artifact styles. Styles rise and fall in popularity, producing overlapping periods of use. Comparing those patterns can order assemblages, even when the method alone supplies no precise calendar date.

evidence.note: Style popularity and battleship-curve discussion support relative ordering.

concepts.label: Archaeological seriation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Changes in the relative popularity of artifact styles allow assemblages to be arranged into a relative chronological sequence.

relations.note: Both compare evidence to establish chronology, but seriation emphasizes ordered style change.
The NPS explains seriation among methods used to date archaeological sites.

concepts.card: Archaeological stratigraphy uses the sequence of deposited layers to investigate earlier human activity. In an undisturbed sequence, lower layers generally precede those above. The qualification matters: rearranged deposits cannot automatically be read as a simple oldest-to-newest stack.

evidence.note: Superposition is explicitly conditional on undisturbed deposits.

concepts.label: Archaeological stratigraphy
concepts.learning_takeaway: In undisturbed deposits, the ordering of layers supplies relative evidence for the sequence of human activities.

relations.note: Apply the stratigraphic ordering of layers to archaeological deposits and activities.

concepts.card: Archival provenance keeps records connected to the person or organization that created them. Records from different origins are not simply mixed because they discuss the same subject. Preserving that grouping helps researchers reconstruct the activities and relationships that generated the documents.

evidence.note: Creator-origin grouping and nonintermingling are explicit archival principles.

concepts.label: Archival provenance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Keeping records grouped by their creating person or organization preserves relationships that would disappear if unrelated origins were mixed.

relations.note: Provenance preserves origin groups; original order addresses arrangement within them.

concepts.card: Territory scoring counts enclosed empty points and captured stones; area scoring counts enclosed points and stones still occupying the board. That difference changes whether filling your own territory costs a point. AGA rules use pass stones to permit territory-style counting within an area-scoring framework.

evidence.note: BGA comparison explicitly supports both definitions, defensive-fill consequence and pass-stone accommodation; the card avoids claiming universal exact equality of final counts.

concepts.label: Area and territory scoring in Go
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare counting occupied points with counting territory plus prisoners.

relations.note: The comparison identifies these as alternative Go scoring systems and explains their practical counting differences.

concepts.card: An area cartogram resizes places according to a chosen quantity, such as population. Geographic area becomes a visual measure of that variable instead of land size. The transformation can make comparisons striking, while distorting familiar shapes or spatial relationships that help readers recognize places.

evidence.note: Variable-proportional area and distortion tradeoffs are explained.

concepts.label: Area cartogram
concepts.learning_takeaway: Resizing geographic units according to a quantity displays that variable directly, at a cost to familiar shape or adjacency.

relations.note: Cartograms alter area to encode quantity; choropleths typically retain areas and change their shading.
Resizing areas to encode a variable is a particular representational choice in mapmaking.

concepts.card: Argo floats repeatedly move through the ocean to measure conditions such as temperature and salinity. Pumping oil into an external bladder changes volume without changing mass, allowing a float to rise or sink. On a typical profiling cycle, it surfaces to transmit data, then descends again.

evidence.locator: What does an Argo float do?; External bladder
evidence.note: The Argo program describes its standard profiling mission, CTD measurements, buoyancy changes through an oil bladder and satellite communication at the surface. The card marks this as a typical cycle.

concepts.label: Argo
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how buoyancy-changing floats repeatedly profile the ocean and return data by satellite.

relations.note: Argo is a named observational system that supplies oceanographic measurements through repeated profiles.

concepts.card: The Arrhenius equation connects a reaction’s rate constant with temperature and activation energy. Measuring rates at several temperatures can reveal the barrier through a graph of logarithmic rate constant against inverse temperature. This inference assumes the reaction follows the Arrhenius model over that range.

evidence.locator: 12.5 Collision Theory; inspected passage indices 24, 25, 26, 29, 30 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm93458160; fs-idp69522176; fs-idm378964576; fs-idm217118448; fs-idm161357136
evidence.note: Use temperature-dependent rate measurements to infer activation energy under the Arrhenius model.

concepts.label: Arrhenius equation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use temperature-dependent rate measurements to infer activation energy under the Arrhenius model.

relations.note: The source presents an Arrhenius plot as a method of determining activation energy.

concepts.card: An arterial blood gas test analyzes a blood sample for oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH. These measurements address oxygenation, removal of carbon dioxide and acid–base balance together. Unlike a light-based pulse-oximeter reading, the test requires blood from an artery and supplies information beyond oxygen saturation.

evidence.locator: What is an arterial blood gas test?
evidence.note: Supports arterial blood sampling and the oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH measurements.
Supports the light-based, noninvasive oxygen-saturation comparison.

concepts.label: Arterial blood gas testing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish blood oxygenation, carbon-dioxide removal and acid-base measurements in one arterial sample.

relations.note: An arterial sample can assess CO2 and pH alongside oxygen, whereas the optical method estimates saturation; the methods are not interchangeable.

concepts.card: An artesian aquifer holds groundwater under pressure beneath relatively impermeable layers. Water in a well tapping it can rise above the aquifer’s top, but water flows out at the surface only if the pressure level is high enough. Depth alone does not make a well artesian.

evidence.locator: Artesian Water; Example of an aquifer system
evidence.note: USGS distinguishes confined pressure, rise above the aquifer, flowing versus nonflowing wells and the insufficiency of depth alone.

concepts.label: Artesian aquifer
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why confined water rises in a well but may not flow out at the surface.

relations.note: Pressure in confined groundwater and deliberate recharge address different aspects of underground water storage; the comparison does not imply Sand Hollow is an artesian system.

concepts.card: An ascending open auction raises the price while bidders remain active or drop out. When only one bidder remains willing to continue, that bidder wins. Unlike sealed bids, the process makes others' continued participation visible, so the sequence itself can convey information during the auction.

evidence.note: Checked rising-price/dropout mechanism and observable participation; no claim that every online auction implements this exact format.

concepts.label: Ascending open auction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reveal progressively higher offers until only one bidder remains willing to pay the rising price.

relations.note: The lecture contrasts open ascending participation with privately submitted sealed bids, explaining each format's sequence.

concepts.card: In Asch's line-judgment experiments, participants heard a group give an obviously wrong answer before responding aloud. Many agreed with the group at least once. Dissenting allies and private responding changed conformity, showing that agreement depended partly on the social arrangement of the task.

evidence.note: Section 12.4 supports confederates' wrong answers, public responses and effects of dissent/privacy; many avoids generalizing one percentage to all studies or people.

concepts.label: Asch's conformity experiments
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine public agreement with a clearly mistaken majority in a particular experimental setting.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly interprets conformity in the unambiguous Asch task as fitting in and avoiding ridicule, an instance of normative influence.

concepts.card: An ascribed status is a social position assigned without the person's choosing it, such as being someone's child. The status comes with expectations and relationships. It describes how the position is acquired, which is different from the behavior people perform while occupying that position.

evidence.note: Checked acquisition without choice and child example; no inference about an individual's worth, ability or immutable destiny.

concepts.label: Ascribed status
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify social positions assigned without personal choice and the expectations attached to them.

relations.note: The roles-and-status passage explicitly contrasts ascribed positions with achieved ones and separates status from expected role behavior.

concepts.card: The assembling perspective examines what people in crowds actually do: gather, orient together, move, speak, or manipulate objects. It shifts attention toward component actions and the lifecycle of gatherings. This makes coordination observable, though critics argue that focusing so closely on actions can miss wider cultural context.

evidence.note: Checked component examples, gathering lifecycle and criticism; not portrayed as evidence that every crowd has one mind or one shared purpose.

concepts.label: Assembling perspective
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine how gatherings form and act through observable component processes instead of treating a crowd as one mind.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly presents McPhail's assembling perspective as a process-focused approach to collective behavior and notes its contextual limitation.

concepts.card: Astronomical interferometry combines signals from separated antennas so they operate together as an observing instrument. In ALMA, changing antenna configurations changes the maximum separation and the angular detail the array resolves. The arrangement turns carefully coordinated measurements into a larger effective observing baseline.

evidence.locator: ALMA; inspected passage indices 14 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-15
evidence.note: Combine separated antennas as one telescope and vary their spacing to change angular resolution.

concepts.label: Astronomical interferometry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine separated antennas as one telescope and vary their spacing to change angular resolution.

relations.note: ESO explicitly identifies ALMA’s cooperating antennas as an interferometer.

concepts.card: Astronomical seeing describes the blurring produced when starlight crosses turbulent air. Patches with different temperatures bend rays differently, and moving air continually changes those paths. The resulting image shifts and blurs; related fluctuations can also make stars appear to twinkle when seen from the ground.

evidence.locator: 6.2 Telescopes Today; inspected passage indices 37, 38, 39 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1167471084189; fs-id1167470709434; fs-id1167470679458
evidence.note: Turbulent air continually redirects starlight, blurring ground-based images and making stars twinkle.

concepts.label: Astronomical seeing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Turbulent air continually redirects starlight, blurring ground-based images and making stars twinkle.

relations.note: The telescope section explains adaptive optics immediately as a response to this atmospheric blurring.

concepts.card: The Atlas linguistique de la France turned regional speech observations into maps. Around the turn of the twentieth century, fieldwork gathered detailed transcriptions from hundreds of French locations. The atlas shows how systematically placing comparable forms on maps can make geographical variation visible rather than merely listing local words.

evidence.note: Checked survey scale, transcription and mapping; omitted the source's apparent fieldworker-name typo rather than reproducing it.

concepts.label: Atlas linguistique de la France
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how mapped transcriptions from many places make regional language variation inspectable.

relations.note: The atlas is a named collection of geographically organized language observations, providing a historical comparison with modern sociolinguistic corpora.

concepts.card: Atmospheric perspective suggests distance by changing the color and tone of receding forms. A landscape can gradually shift from foreground to background as though intervening air alters its appearance. The painter creates depth through these transitions rather than relying only on the geometry of drawn edges.

evidence.note: Distance-related color and tonal changes are explicitly described.

concepts.label: Atmospheric perspective
concepts.learning_takeaway: Changing color and tone as a landscape recedes can represent the effect of atmosphere and create pictorial depth.

relations.note: Compare distance-dependent tonal changes with soft contour transitions; the pictorial purposes differ.

concepts.card: An atmospheric river is a concentrated corridor of water vapor moving through the atmosphere. When it reaches land, that moisture can fall as rain or snow. Such events supply useful water, but stronger or persistent landfalls can also produce flooding, so their effects depend on the event.

evidence.note: NOAA defines water-vapor transport and explains landfall precipitation, water-supply importance and potential flooding.

concepts.label: Atmospheric river
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a concentrated corridor of water-vapor transport with both useful precipitation and flood risk.

relations.note: Mountain lifting can turn transported vapor into uneven precipitation, connecting atmospheric-river supply with rain-shadow geography.

concepts.card: Atomic commit makes a transaction's changes appear all-or-nothing, even though storage writes occur sequentially. SQLite uses recovery mechanisms to preserve that appearance across crashes or power failures under documented storage assumptions. The guarantee concerns which changes take effect, rather than requiring hardware to write everything simultaneously.

evidence.locator: Section 1 Introduction; Section 2 Hardware Assumptions; Section 3.5 Creating A Rollback Journal File
evidence.note: The all-or-nothing appearance is described in Section 1; Section 2 explicitly states storage/OS assumptions behind crash recovery, including correct flush behavior and uncorrupted stored content. Section 3.5 supplies rollback-journal preservation as the related mechanism.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: SQLite's atomic-commit documentation explains rollback journals as the recovery mechanism used for atomic commit in rollback mode.

concepts.label: Atomic commit
concepts.learning_takeaway: Make a transaction appear all-or-nothing even though storage writes happen sequentially and can be interrupted.

relations.note: SQLite's atomic-commit documentation explains rollback journals as the recovery mechanism used for atomic commit in rollback mode.

concepts.card: Stretch of the heart’s atria can stimulate release of atrial natriuretic peptide. The signal promotes sodium and water loss through the kidneys and suppresses hormones that retain them. It connects increased cardiac filling with a response that helps reduce excess circulating volume.

evidence.note: The atrial-natriuretic paragraph describes stretch-triggered secretion, sodium/water loss and opposition to renin, aldosterone and ADH.

concepts.label: Atrial natriuretic peptide
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how cardiac stretch signals the kidneys to lose sodium and water.

relations.note: ANP’s excretory response opposes the sodium/water-retaining hormonal cascade, a physiological comparison rather than identity equivalence.

concepts.card: An augmented sixth chord contains notes a semitone below and above the dominant scale degree. The raised fourth moves upward while the lowered sixth moves downward toward dominant pitches. This characteristic voice-leading explains the chord family's predominant role in the cited tonal framework.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 21.1 states simultaneous semitone approaches to scale degree five and predominant function. Revised wording avoids describing the voices as converging in register; it only states the supported pitch-class movements.

concepts.label: Augmented sixth chord
concepts.learning_takeaway: Follow two chromatic voices approaching the dominant from opposite semitone directions.

relations.note: Both are chromatic predominant devices, but their construction differs: semitone approaches to dominant pitches versus a lowered-supertonic major triad.

concepts.card: Authentication rate limiting restricts repeated failed login attempts. A verifier might impose waiting periods or disable an authenticator after too many failures. These controls make online guessing harder, but designers must also consider attackers who deliberately trigger the limit to lock out legitimate users.

evidence.note: Checked throttling, increasing waits, disabling, and lockout tradeoff; no fixed attempt count is presented as a universal recommendation.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Limiting online authentication guesses protects access decisions; NIST explicitly discusses both guessing resistance and malicious lockout risks.

concepts.label: Authentication rate limiting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Constrain failed online guesses while balancing attack resistance against legitimate users being locked out.

relations.note: Limiting online authentication guesses protects access decisions; NIST explicitly discusses both guessing resistance and malicious lockout risks.

concepts.card: Autochrome makes a color transparency on glass using a screen of tiny colored starch grains. Light passes through this filtering layer as part of the photographic process. The resulting color image depends on the arrangement of the grains, not simply on coloring a monochrome print afterward.

evidence.note: Colored starch filter and glass transparency are described.

concepts.label: Autochrome
concepts.learning_takeaway: A layer of colored starch grains acts as a filter in a glass photographic plate, producing a color transparency rather than an ordinary monochrome print.

relations.note: Autochrome is a particular material solution for making color photographic images.

concepts.card: Bach's C-minor fugue from the first Well-Tempered Clavier offers a compact lesson in contrapuntal development. Its opening exposition introduces the subject in every voice. Episodes then work with smaller fragments of subjects and countersubjects, allowing recognizable material to generate passages without a complete subject statement.

evidence.note: The detailed analysis identifies first exposition, all-voice entries and fragmented material in episodes; no unsupported numerical count of voices or episodes is added.

concepts.label: Bach's Fugue in C minor, BWV 847
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace full subject entries alternating with development through fragmented motives.

relations.note: The source explicitly analyzes BWV 847 as a fugue with expositions and episodes.

concepts.card: Bach's C-major Invention shows how a short idea can sustain development. The opening notes return with their melodic direction inverted, and fragments also appear in rhythmic augmentation. These transformations preserve recognizable material while changing its contour or the amount of time it occupies.

evidence.note: Section 11.2 identifies the first seven notes inverted later and an augmented fragment; the wording does not claim every occurrence transforms the whole theme.

concepts.label: Bach's Invention in C major, BWV 772
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize inversion and rhythmic augmentation within one tightly developed keyboard work.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly labels the invention's returning opening notes as melodic inversion.

concepts.card: Back-calculation anti-windup feeds information about an actuator’s saturation back into a controller’s integrator. The feedback unwinds internal demand that the actuator cannot realize. This helps the controller return to its usable range more quickly after saturation, rather than waiting for accumulated error to disappear unaided.

evidence.locator: Anti-Windup Control Using PID Controller Block; inspected passage indices 16, 17, 18 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-17; paragraph-18; paragraph-19
evidence.note: Feed saturation information back into a controller’s integrator so it unwinds toward an achievable output.

concepts.label: Back-calculation anti-windup
concepts.learning_takeaway: Feed saturation information back into a controller’s integrator so it unwinds toward an achievable output.

relations.note: The reference explicitly describes back-calculation as a response to integrator windup under saturation.

concepts.card: Bali’s protected subak landscape links forests, water temples, canals and rice terraces across volcanic watersheds. These components show how farming and ritual organization work through the same environment. The place makes an irrigation institution visible through the connected spaces and structures that sustain it.

evidence.note: Linked landscape components and water-temple organization are described.

concepts.label: Bali’s subak cultural landscape
concepts.learning_takeaway: Linked forests, water temples, canals and terraces demonstrate how a volcanic island’s watersheds are organized through farming and ritual.

relations.note: UNESCO connects the physical landscape with the institutions that coordinate its irrigation.

concepts.card: The Bank of England began in 1694 as a privately owned bank helping finance the government. It also accepted public deposits, and much later was nationalized. Its history shows that a public financial role and private ownership can coexist, rather than central banking always beginning with government ownership.

evidence.note: Checked foundation, financing role, deposits and 1946 nationalization; no assertion about current governors, policies or unused legal powers.

concepts.label: Bank of England
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace the transition from a privately owned government banker to a nationalized central bank.

relations.note: The Bank's history explicitly connects its government-banking position with competition from the South Sea Company and the 1720 crisis.

concepts.card: A lone backgammon checker hit by an opponent goes to the bar. Its owner must bring barred checkers back into the opponent's home board before moving other pieces. If the dice offer no open entry point, the player's turn is lost.

evidence.note: USBGF Hitting and Entering supports hit, priority and failed entry; the chosen example concerns no available entry, not partial entry with several checkers.

concepts.label: Bar entry in backgammon
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why a hit checker must return before other pieces can move.

relations.note: The rules make bar entry a compulsory recovery step after a checker is hit.

concepts.card: When arterial pressure rises, stretch-sensitive baroreceptors increase their signaling to the brainstem. Reflex changes reduce cardiac output and relax peripheral vessels, helping oppose the rise. Falling pressure produces responses in the other direction. The baroreflex links mechanical stretch to rapid cardiovascular adjustment.

evidence.note: The baroreceptor passage gives increased stretch/firing, brainstem integration, reduced cardiac output and vasodilation, with opposite responses to falling pressure.

concepts.label: Baroreflex
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace a blood-pressure change from arterial stretch receptors to rapid cardiac and vascular responses.

relations.note: A sensed pressure deviation evokes opposing cardiac and vascular responses, making this a specific homeostatic feedback mechanism.

concepts.card: The Bauhaus sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau connect teaching and social ambitions with built experiments in modern design. Structural frames, glass surfaces and simplified forms helped express new approaches to use and construction. The ensemble lets an educational movement be studied through particular buildings and spaces.

evidence.note: UNESCO connects the ensemble’s materials, forms, pedagogy and social aims.

concepts.label: Bauhaus sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau
concepts.learning_takeaway: This ensemble links Bauhaus teaching and social ambitions to buildings whose structural frames, glass surfaces and basic forms reworked the relation between use and architectural expression.

relations.note: UNESCO explicitly connects these buildings with the Bauhaus school and its teaching.

concepts.card: Despite its familiar name, the Bayeux Tapestry is embroidery rather than a woven pictorial tapestry. Wool stitches form the narrative on joined linen panels. Examining the stitched surface offers a concrete way to distinguish applied needlework from an image created by weaving.

evidence.note: Wool embroidery, joined linen and narrative construction are explicit.

concepts.label: Bayeux Tapestry
concepts.learning_takeaway: The Bayeux Tapestry’s narrative is embroidered in wool on joined linen panels rather than woven as a pictorial tapestry.

relations.note: Construction and narrative imagery make the object evidence about both making and historical representation.

concepts.card: Bearing off removes checkers from a backgammon board, but only after all your active checkers reach your home board. A roll normally removes a checker from its matching point. An oversized roll can remove the highest remaining checker when no checker occupies a higher point.

evidence.note: USBGF Bearing Off supplies prerequisites and oversized-roll rule; wording avoids requiring removal when another legal move is possible.

concepts.label: Bearing off in backgammon
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore the conditions for removing checkers and using an oversized die roll.

relations.note: Bearing off is explicitly the final removal process that completes backgammon's race.

concepts.card: Beemster’s reclaimed lakebed was organized through a geometric network of fields, roads, canals and settlement. Its regular pattern expresses both a design ambition and the practical need to manage water. The landscape shows how engineering and planned land division can structure everyday agricultural space together.

evidence.note: Reclamation, geometric planning and coordinated land/water divisions are documented.

concepts.label: Beemster Polder
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reclaimed lake land was laid out with a geometric grid that coordinated fields, roads, canals and settlement.

relations.note: Beemster is a specific reclaimed and managed polder landscape.

concepts.card: Bottom-dwelling aquatic invertebrates differ in their tolerance of pollution and other stress. Because many move little, the community found at a site can reflect conditions over time. Bioassessment uses this living evidence to complement a water sample that captures only the moment it was collected.

evidence.locator: Why evaluate them?; What do they tell us?
evidence.note: EPA describes benthic macroinvertebrates’ varying tolerances, limited mobility and integration of environmental stress over time.

concepts.label: Benthic macroinvertebrate bioassessment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read aquatic-community composition as an integrated record of environmental stress.

relations.note: Community composition can complement a direct dissolved-oxygen measurement by reflecting longer exposure to conditions, rather than measuring the same instantaneous quantity.

concepts.card: Betweenness centrality measures a node's or edge's share of shortest paths between other points in a network. When several shortest paths exist, their contribution is divided. This highlights potential intermediary positions that simple neighbor counts miss, while remaining a model of routes rather than a measurement of actual message traffic.

evidence.note: Checked shortest-path splitting and node/edge definitions; hypothetical flow is not claimed to be the route all real information follows.

concepts.label: Betweenness centrality
concepts.learning_takeaway: Measure how much shortest-path traffic passes through a node or edge rather than simply counting its immediate contacts.

relations.note: Shortest-path mediation is a specific way to analyze positions in social-network representations, distinct from describing the network or counting direct ties.

concepts.card: A bias facing uses a narrow strip of fabric cut on the bias to finish a curved edge. The strip can be shaped to follow the curve without the bulk of a wider facing. Its usefulness comes from how the fabric direction allows the finish to conform.

evidence.note: NMSU describes narrow bias strips shaped to curves and their use to reduce visible or heavy facings.

concepts.label: Bias facings
concepts.learning_takeaway: Finish a curved fabric edge using a narrow strip whose bias orientation allows it to conform to the curve.

relations.note: A bias facing is a specific sewn curved-edge finish within garment construction.

concepts.card: Bicameralism organizes a legislature into two chambers. In the United Kingdom, the Commons and Lords normally both pass a bill before it becomes law, but the Parliament Acts create specified exceptions. The example shows that two chambers need not possess equal or unrestricted blocking powers.

evidence.locator: Opening and Bills subject to the Parliament Acts
evidence.note: UK Parliament's opening describes two-house agreement and exceptions; the card confines the mechanics to the UK and does not universalize its unequal powers across all bicameral systems.

concepts.label: Bicameralism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand two-chamber lawmaking through the qualified Commons–Lords example.

relations.note: The Parliament Acts page directly explains the two chambers' ordinary role through the statutory exceptions that modify it.

concepts.card: Binary search exploits an ordered collection instead of inspecting every entry. It repeatedly narrows the range that could contain a requested key. SQLite's row lookup illustrates the payoff: search effort grows logarithmically with the number of records, rather than in proportion to the entire table.

evidence.note: Checked sorted-key requirement and logarithmic comparison with a scan; the card avoids the source's illustrative numerical speed estimate as a universal benchmark.

evidence.locator: Definition; Note on run time and ordered linked lists
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: SQLite's query-planner examples connect ordered binary searches with covering indexes, which avoid an additional lookup in the original table.

concepts.label: Binary search
concepts.learning_takeaway: Exploit sorted keys to find a record with logarithmic rather than full-scan search effort.

relations.note: SQLite's query-planner examples connect ordered binary searches with covering indexes, which avoid an additional lookup in the original table.

concepts.card: Biochemical oxygen demand measures the oxygen microorganisms consume while breaking down organic material under specified conditions. A high demand can help explain why a water body loses oxygen even when it initially contains plenty. The measure concerns consumption, rather than simply the oxygen concentration at one moment.

evidence.note: USGS defines microbial oxygen use during aerobic decomposition and its relationship to organic loading and depleted dissolved oxygen.

concepts.label: Biochemical oxygen demand
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use microbial oxygen consumption as an indicator of biodegradable organic loading.

relations.note: The distinction separates the amount of dissolved oxygen present from biological demand that consumes it.

concepts.card: A bipartite graph divides its vertices into two groups with edges only between groups. This is equivalent to coloring the vertices with two colors without same-colored neighbors. An odd cycle prevents such a division, while graphs containing no odd cycles permit it.

evidence.locator: Bipartite Graph -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3
evidence.note: Two vertex classes with only cross-class edges are equivalent to two-colorability and absence of odd cycles.

concepts.label: Bipartite graph
concepts.learning_takeaway: Two vertex classes with only cross-class edges are equivalent to two-colorability and absence of odd cycles.

relations.note: Bipartite structure supplies a concrete graph-theoretic constraint that can be tested independently of a drawing.

concepts.card: Briefly heating vegetables before freezing can slow or stop enzymes that would otherwise degrade flavor, color and texture during storage. This blanching step protects quality, but its duration depends on the vegetable and its size. Too little or too much heating can undermine the intended result.

evidence.note: NCHFP explains enzyme inactivation/quality preservation and the vegetable/size-dependent harms of under- and overblanching.

concepts.label: Blanching vegetables before freezing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain a brief heat treatment as a way to slow enzyme-driven quality loss during frozen storage.

relations.note: Both explain enzyme-mediated changes in food, but blanching uses heat before frozen storage while enzymatic browning describes a particular reaction after tissue exposure.

concepts.card: Blocking shapes a knitted piece and evens its fabric using moisture, sometimes with steam. The method should suit the yarn and its care instructions. Testing a swatch first helps reveal how the material responds before trying to bring a finished garment to its intended dimensions.

evidence.note: Knit Picks explains shaping/evening, wet/spray/steam methods, yarn-care dependence and a test on the gauge swatch.

concepts.label: Blocking knitted fabric
concepts.learning_takeaway: Set a knitted piece’s dimensions and even its fabric using a method suited to the yarn.

relations.note: Blocking is a post-knitting shaping and finishing practice applied to the loop-based fabric, rather than a stitch-forming technique.

concepts.card: A monatomic body-centered cubic crystal has atoms at a cube’s corners and one at its center. Sharing corner atoms with neighboring cells gives two atoms per conventional cell. Each atom has eight nearest neighbors, illustrating how the arrangement determines local coordination.

evidence.locator: 10.6 Lattice Structures in Crystalline Solids; inspected passage indices 29, 30 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idp78313376; fs-idm23808480
evidence.note: A cubic cell with one central atom has two atoms per cell and eight nearest neighbors.

concepts.label: Body-centered cubic structure
concepts.learning_takeaway: A cubic cell with one central atom has two atoms per cell and eight nearest neighbors.

relations.note: The source classifies BCC as one of the crystalline arrangements of metals.

concepts.card: Body plethysmography measures lung volumes, including air that remains after a person breathes out as fully as possible. Testing takes place in an enclosed booth. This adds information beyond the air a person can blow through a spirometer, helping distinguish different aspects of lung function.

evidence.locator: Lung volume test; Body plethysmography procedure
evidence.note: MedlinePlus’s lung-volume test description includes the enclosed booth, total capacity and remaining air after full expiration.

concepts.label: Body plethysmography
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish measuring residual lung volume from measuring only air that can be exhaled.

relations.note: The two procedures assess different aspects of lung function: exhaled flow/volume versus volumes including retained air.

concepts.card: Hemoglobin releases oxygen more readily when its surroundings become more acidic. This pH-dependent change in oxygen affinity is the Bohr effect. It helps connect local chemical conditions with oxygen unloading, rather than treating hemoglobin as a container that releases oxygen at one fixed rate.

evidence.locator: Oxygen Dissociation from Hemoglobin, pH paragraph
evidence.note: OpenStax explicitly states that lower pH promotes oxygen dissociation and higher pH inhibits it.

concepts.label: Bohr effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why lower pH promotes oxygen unloading from hemoglobin.

relations.note: The Bohr effect concerns acidity changing oxygen affinity; the Haldane effect concerns oxygenation changing carbon-dioxide carriage.

concepts.card: Bolting is a crop’s shift into flowering earlier than the grower wants. In cool-season vegetables, heat or long days can help trigger it, depending on the crop and its history. Once reproductive growth begins, the quality of leaves or roots harvested for food can decline.

evidence.note: UMN explains premature flowering in cool-season crops, heat/daylength influences and losses of edible quality.

concepts.label: Bolting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize premature flowering as a shift that can reduce the edible quality of a leafy or root crop.

relations.note: Daylength response provides one possible timing influence on flowering, but bolting is a crop-development outcome rather than photoperiodism itself.

concepts.card: A financial bond is a debt security: investors lend money to an issuer under specified payment terms. Those terms typically cover interest and repayment of principal at maturity. The issuer can default, so a contractual promise to repay differs from a guarantee of receiving the money.

evidence.locator: What are bonds?; What are the benefits and risks?
evidence.note: Checked debt, issuer payments, maturity and default against Investor.gov; interest is qualified as typical rather than universal. The approved financial-debt identity remains separate from chemical bonding, but that cross-domain contrast is not used as an unsupported explanatory claim in this card.

concepts.label: Bond (finance)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Treat a bond as an issuer's debt promise to pay specified interest and principal, with default still possible.

relations.note: Investor.gov explicitly lists interest-rate risk among the risks of bonds and explains the effect on an older bond's resale value.

concepts.card: The first Borel–Cantelli lemma links a sum of event probabilities with what happens over an infinite sequence. If that sum is finite, only finitely many of the events occur with probability one. An endless list of possible events therefore need not produce endlessly many actual occurrences.

evidence.locator: Borel-Cantelli Lemma -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3
evidence.note: If event probabilities have a finite sum, infinitely many occurrences have probability zero.

concepts.label: Borel–Cantelli lemma
concepts.learning_takeaway: If event probabilities have a finite sum, infinitely many occurrences have probability zero.

relations.note: The lemma turns bounds on individual event probabilities into a statement about an entire infinite sequence.

concepts.card: The Borsuk–Ulam theorem guarantees that a continuous map from an n-dimensional sphere to n-dimensional Euclidean space gives the same output at some antipodal pair. For an ordinary sphere, any two continuous real-valued measurements therefore agree simultaneously at a pair of opposite points.

evidence.locator: Borsuk-Ulam Theorem -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2
evidence.note: A continuous map from an n-sphere to n-dimensional space identifies some antipodal pair.

concepts.label: Borsuk–Ulam theorem
concepts.learning_takeaway: A continuous map from an n-sphere to n-dimensional space identifies some antipodal pair.

relations.note: Both results impose global constraints on continuous data assigned to spheres, but assert different conclusions and retain different dimensional conditions.

aliases: United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference
concepts.card: The Bretton Woods Conference in 1944 combined negotiations over exchange-rate stability with plans for new international institutions. The IMF would support countries facing payments imbalances, while a reconstruction bank had a different task. The resulting system linked adjustable national currencies to a dollar convertible into gold.

evidence.locator: Creation of the Bretton Woods System, main account
evidence.note: Checked distinct institutional roles, adjustable rates and dollar-gold link; the conference is separate from the institutions and the later fully operating monetary system.

concepts.label: Bretton Woods Conference
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how 1944 negotiations combined adjustable exchange-rate commitments with new institutions for payments support and reconstruction.

relations.note: Federal Reserve History identifies the conference's reconstruction institution as the precursor of what became the World Bank Group; not every later group member was created there.

concepts.card: For unpolarized light striking an ideal nonabsorbing dielectric interface, Brewster’s angle makes the reflected light fully linearly polarized. The angle depends on the refractive-index ratio. This helps explain why rotating polarized sunglasses changes the glare seen from surfaces such as water or glass.

evidence.locator: 1.7 Polarization; inspected passage indices 26, 27, 28, 29 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1172100528765; fs-id1172100781361; fs-id1172098530951; fs-id1172100513646
evidence.note: At a particular dielectric reflection angle, reflected light is fully polarized.

concepts.label: Brewster’s angle
concepts.learning_takeaway: At a particular dielectric reflection angle, reflected light is fully polarized.

relations.note: Reflection can produce polarized glare; transmission through a polarizer then depends on its angle to that polarization.

concepts.card: Broadbalk compares wheat grown under different nutrient treatments across many years. An unfertilized strip maintained since 1843 provides a persistent reference against which fertilized plots can be read. The experiment shows how a long-lived control helps separate treatment effects from the changing background of agricultural seasons.

evidence.note: Rothamsted states the nutrient-treatment purpose and unfertilized control strip maintained since 1843.

concepts.label: Broadbalk Wheat Experiment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use a persistent untreated comparison to interpret crop responses to fertilizer over many years.

relations.note: Broadbalk and Park Grass are separate long-term Rothamsted experiments, useful for comparing arable nutrient studies with permanent-grassland treatment histories.

concepts.card: The Brooklyn Bridge’s suspension design changed from iron to steel to reduce dead load. Its main cables bundle thousands of galvanized steel wires, while stiffening trusses were intended to limit deck oscillations. The bridge combines flexible suspension with structural elements designed to control unwanted movement.

evidence.locator:
Brooklyn Bridge | ASCE
; inspected passage indices 7, 10, 11 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-8; paragraph-11; paragraph-12
evidence.note: Steel suspension cables reduced dead load while trusses were designed to resist deck oscillations.

concepts.label: Brooklyn Bridge
concepts.learning_takeaway: Steel suspension cables reduced dead load while trusses were designed to resist deck oscillations.

relations.note: ASCE identifies the project as a bridge and describes its suspension and stiffening systems.

concepts.card: Brouwer’s fixed-point theorem states that every continuous map from a closed finite-dimensional ball into itself leaves at least one point fixed. The map may move most points dramatically. Continuity and keeping the whole image inside that same ball are essential conditions of the claim.

evidence.locator: Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3
evidence.note: Every continuous self-map of a closed finite-dimensional ball leaves at least one point fixed.

concepts.label: Brouwer fixed-point theorem
concepts.learning_takeaway: Every continuous self-map of a closed finite-dimensional ball leaves at least one point fixed.

relations.note: The theorem gives a global consequence of continuity and domain shape, linking an explicit mapping problem with topology.

concepts.card: Brown v. Board of Education rejected state-imposed racial segregation in US public education under equal protection. The Court treated separate schooling as inherently unequal, rather than asking only whether physical facilities matched. The decision challenged a legal framework of separation, although implementing desegregation required further proceedings and resistance persisted.

evidence.locator: Brown v. Board of Education case summary
evidence.note: The US Courts educational account supports the public-education holding and later compliance/resistance discussion; state-imposed and public preserve constitutional scope without claiming immediate practical integration or a rule covering every private activity.

concepts.label: Brown v. Board of Education
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore the constitutional rejection of state-mandated racial segregation in public education.

relations.note: Brown illustrates the possibility of departing from precedent: Cornell's stare decisis entry expressly connects it with rejection of Plessy's separate-but-equal rule, while the court account supplies the education holding.

concepts.card: Buffers with nearly the same pH can tolerate very different additions of acid or base. Buffer capacity depends on how much of the conjugate pair is present. Increasing both components together can raise capacity while approximately preserving their ratio-dependent initial pH.

evidence.locator: 14.6 Buffers; inspected passage indices 38 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm103629216
evidence.note: Buffers with equal pH can resist different acid loads because their total concentrations differ.

concepts.label: Buffer capacity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Buffers with equal pH can resist different acid loads because their total concentrations differ.

relations.note: The source defines buffer capacity and compares buffers with equal pH but different component concentrations.

concepts.card: A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, or an analogous weak-base pair. Added strong acid or base is converted into weaker species, limiting the pH change. This resistance has limits: a buffer does not keep its pH fixed under unlimited additions.

evidence.locator: 14.6 Buffers; inspected passage indices 7, 8, 38 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm127493136; fs-idp41915456; fs-idm103629216
evidence.note: A weak conjugate pair consumes modest additions of strong acid or base; the finite component amounts determine buffer capacity.

concepts.label: Buffer solution
concepts.learning_takeaway: A weak conjugate acid-base pair consumes small additions of strong acid or base.

relations.note: The same section defines capacity as the finite amount of added acid or base a buffer can accommodate.

concepts.card: Bumpless transfer avoids an abrupt commanded-output jump when switching from manual to automatic control. One implementation lets the automatic controller track the manual signal and adjust its internal state before taking over, aligning the two outputs at the switching moment.

evidence.locator: Bumpless Control Transfer Between Manual and PID Control; inspected passage indices 1, 11, 15, 16, 17, 19 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-12; paragraph-16; paragraph-17; paragraph-18; paragraph-20
evidence.note: Track the active manual signal internally before switching to automatic control to avoid a sudden output jump.

concepts.label: Bumpless transfer
concepts.learning_takeaway: Track the active manual signal internally before switching to automatic control to avoid a sudden output jump.

relations.note: The cited MathWorks example uses a PID controller’s tracking mode to achieve manual-to-automatic bumpless transfer; this is an implementation example, not a claim that all bumpless transfer requires PID.

concepts.card: Buon fresco paints onto freshly applied wet plaster. The wall’s preparation and the painter’s timing are therefore inseparable: the surface must still be suitable when the pigment is applied. Work proceeds in manageable fresh sections rather than treating the entire wall as an indefinitely available canvas.

evidence.note: Wet-plaster process and daily finishing-plaster work are explained.

concepts.label: Buon fresco
concepts.learning_takeaway: Painting into freshly applied wet plaster makes the timing of plaster preparation part of the painting process.

relations.note: The National Gallery describes painting onto wet plaster as a painting process.
The daily plaster section follows directly from working on a fresh surface.

concepts.card: Burnside’s lemma counts distinct objects when symmetries make some appearances equivalent. For a finite group acting on a finite set, count the objects fixed by each symmetry and average those counts. The answer is the number of orbits, avoiding the mistake of treating every rotated appearance as new.

evidence.locator: Cauchy-Frobenius Lemma -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2
evidence.note: Count symmetry classes by averaging the number of objects fixed by each group action.

concepts.label: Burnside’s lemma
concepts.learning_takeaway: Count symmetry classes by averaging the number of objects fixed by each group action.

relations.note: The lemma turns symmetry operations into a concrete counting method; equivalence classes are generated by the specified group action.

concepts.card: A cadential six-four contains the notes of a tonic triad with its fifth in the bass, yet commonly functions as part of a dominant arrival. Before the following dominant chord, its pitch content and its harmonic role therefore point in different analytical directions.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 16.3 explicitly identifies I6/4 preceding V and its dominant function; commonly avoids asserting that every second-inversion tonic is a cadential six-four.

concepts.label: Cadential six-four chord
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why an inverted tonic sonority can perform a dominant function.

relations.note: This sonority illustrates how harmonic function can differ from a chord's apparent tonic pitch content.

concepts.card: A caesura is a pause within a line of verse. It can divide the line’s movement without ending the line itself, making an internal break audible or meaningful. Attending to caesuras distinguishes the rhythm of a sentence from the poem’s outer line boundaries.

evidence.note: Internal pause definition supports the distinction from line ending.

concepts.label: Caesura
concepts.learning_takeaway: A pause within a poetic line can divide its movement without coinciding with the line ending.

relations.note: The comparison separates an internal pause from syntax continuing across a line break.
The glossary identifies a pause within a poetic line.

concepts.card: A canal lock raises or lowers a vessel by changing the water level inside an enclosed chamber. Water enters or leaves through controlled passages while gates retain it. At Panama, gravity supplies the water movement, turning a difference in elevation into a controlled transfer between levels.

evidence.locator: Design Of The Locks; inspected passage indices 15, 16, 17, 18 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-16; paragraph-17; paragraph-18; paragraph-19
evidence.note: Describes vessel lifting by water, gravity-fed culverts, filling/draining valves, and retaining gates.

concepts.label: Canal lock
concepts.learning_takeaway: Controlled filling or draining changes a chamber’s water level to move floating vessels between elevations.

relations.note: The vessel remains afloat as the chamber level changes, connecting the lock mechanism with buoyant support.

concepts.card: Candidate-understanding repair offers a possible interpretation and asks the original speaker to confirm or correct it. Repeating a guessed phrase with questioning intonation can make the proposed solution explicit. The task differs from simply asking for clarification: the speaker can often resolve the trouble with a short confirmation.

evidence.locator: Results, restricted offer definition and response patterns, pp. 4–5
evidence.note: Checked proposed interpretation and short-confirmation tendency; no assumption that the candidate is correct or confirmation is always sufficient.

concepts.label: Candidate-understanding repair
concepts.learning_takeaway: Offer a possible interpretation of the prior message and ask the original speaker to confirm or correct it.

relations.note: The study's restricted-offer category explicitly proposes a candidate understanding and invites confirmation, distinguishing it from both request types.

concepts.card: A scriptural canon identifies writings recognized as authoritative within a religious tradition. The Catholic list of biblical books provides one specific example. Studying a canon means asking which texts belong to the collection and how that authority is understood, without assuming every community recognizes the same boundaries.

evidence.note: Catholic canon paragraph supplies a concrete authoritative collection.

concepts.label: Canon (scriptural collection)
concepts.learning_takeaway: A religious community identifies a bounded set of authoritative texts; the Catholic list illustrates one particular canon rather than every tradition’s collection.

relations.note: The cited Catholic teaching connects its recognized scriptures through a particular practice of interpretation.

concepts.card: Unicode can represent the same abstract character in different ways, such as a precomposed accented letter or a letter followed by a combining accent. Canonical equivalence identifies these alternatives as fundamentally equivalent. Normalization allows software to compare their representations consistently.

evidence.note: Checked the combining-sequence example and equivalence definition; no assumption that every similarly drawn character is canonically equivalent.

concepts.label: Canonical equivalence in Unicode
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize a precomposed accented character and its decomposed sequence as the same abstract character.

relations.note: Canonical equivalence supplies one precisely defined basis for normalization; grouping it as a facet distinguishes the equivalence relation from the transformation algorithm.

concepts.card: Canonical Huffman coding determines the actual codewords from ordered symbol lengths. Codes of equal length receive consecutive values, with shorter codes preceding longer ones. DEFLATE uses these rules so a decoder can reconstruct the codebook from lengths rather than receiving every codeword explicitly.

evidence.note: Checked both ordering rules and reconstruction sufficiency; this concerns representing a codebook, not choosing optimal lengths.

concepts.label: Canonical Huffman coding
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reconstruct a Huffman codebook from ordered code lengths using deterministic code assignment.

relations.note: RFC 1951 section 3.2.2 gives additional ordering rules for Huffman codes and explains reconstruction from code lengths.

concepts.card: Capability-based security represents authority with an unforgeable ticket for a particular object. Presenting the ticket demonstrates permission to access that object. This organizes protection around what a principal possesses, rather than asking every object to maintain a list of all principals allowed to use it.

evidence.note: Checked unforgeable object-specific authority and ticket-versus-list distinction; no claim that an ordinary copyable identifier is a secure capability.

concepts.label: Capability-based security
concepts.learning_takeaway: Represent authority with unforgeable object-specific tickets that a principal presents to obtain access.

relations.note: The paper's glossary contrasts ticket-oriented capabilities with object-centered access-control lists; this is a comparison, not an equivalence or prerequisite.

concepts.card: The Carnot cycle is an ideal reversible heat-engine cycle operating between two thermal reservoirs. Its efficiency sets an upper bound for engines working between those temperatures. Real irreversibilities reduce performance, making the cycle a reference limit for comparison rather than a promise about a practical machine.

evidence.locator: 4.5 The Carnot Cycle; inspected passage indices 5, 6, 16, 17 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1167585127729; fs-id1167584870646; fs-id1167585020408; fs-id1167584673103
evidence.note: A reversible cycle sets the maximum heat-engine efficiency between two specified thermal reservoirs.

concepts.label: Carnot cycle
concepts.learning_takeaway: A reversible cycle sets the maximum heat-engine efficiency between two specified thermal reservoirs.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies Carnot efficiency as the upper limit for heat engines between the same reservoirs.

concepts.card: Cascade control nests a fast inner feedback loop inside a slower outer one. The outer controller sets the inner loop’s target, while the inner loop helps reject local disturbances before they spread through the plant. Speed separation matters; stacking two controllers does not ensure this benefit.

evidence.locator: Designing Cascade Control System with PI Controllers; inspected passage indices 3, 4, 5 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-4; paragraph-5; paragraph-6
evidence.note: A fast inner loop rejects local disturbances while a slower outer loop commands its setpoint.

concepts.label: Cascade control
concepts.learning_takeaway: A fast inner loop rejects local disturbances while a slower outer loop commands its setpoint.

relations.note: The source provides a specific multi-loop feedback architecture within control engineering.

concepts.card: In the Cascadia Subduction Zone, the Juan de Fuca Plate descends beneath North America. Scraped-off material helps build coastal ranges, while deeper processes support the Cascade volcanic arc inland. The region shows how one convergent boundary can produce distinct landscape features at different distances.

evidence.note: NPS’s Cascadia section links the descending Juan de Fuca Plate, coastal accreted material and inland volcanic chain.

concepts.label: Cascadia Subduction Zone
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain the paired coastal and volcanic ranges produced by the descending Juan de Fuca Plate.

relations.note: Cascadia is a particular geographic example of the broader subduction process.

concepts.card: Castling moves a king and rook in one turn, but permission depends on more than empty squares. Moving the king or the relevant rook permanently loses that castling right. Pieces between them or attacks on the king's starting, crossing or destination square can temporarily prevent it.

evidence.note: FIDE 3.8.2 distinguishes forfeited rights from temporary obstruction; the attacked-square restriction concerns the king's route, not every square the rook crosses.

concepts.label: Castling
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish permanent loss of castling rights from temporary obstacles.

relations.note: FIDE explicitly defines castling as a king-and-rook move within the chess movement rules.

concepts.card: Catalan numbers appear when counting ways to triangulate a regular polygon with fixed vertices using noncrossing diagonals. The same sequence arises in tree-enumeration problems. Such repeated appearances suggest a useful strategy: translate one counting problem into another structure whose possibilities are already understood.

evidence.locator: Catalan Number -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 4, 5 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-5; paragraph-6
evidence.note: The same integer sequence counts polygon triangulations and related recursive combinatorial structures.

concepts.label: Catalan numbers
concepts.learning_takeaway: The same integer sequence counts polygon triangulations and related recursive combinatorial structures.

relations.note: Polygon triangulation is a bounded counting example within the broader idea of decomposing surfaces into triangles.

concepts.card: An impact makes a tennis racket both recoil and rotate. At a particular supporting point, those motions can cancel. The corresponding impact location is its center of percussion. Adding the hand's mass shifts this relationship, so a freely suspended racket does not reproduce every playing condition.

evidence.note: Cross's Centre of percussion section defines conjugate supporting and impact points and the hand-mass shift; this is not a universal fixed spot on every racket.

concepts.label: Center of percussion in a tennis racket
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how recoil and rotation can cancel motion at a particular supporting point.

relations.note: Cross distinguishes cancellation of recoil and rotation from the separate vibration-node explanation of the sweet spot.

concepts.card: Ruth Asawa’s 1965 lithograph Chair (TAM.1558-II) lets furniture emerge from patterned marks and from unmarked areas between them. Some chairs appear through the marks; others through their absence. The work offers a case for examining how positive and negative areas organize a composition.

evidence.locator: Object header, lines 61–68; gallery label, lines 78–79; medium, line 88; object number, line 98
evidence.note: Object header identifies the 1965 lithograph; the gallery label describes five patterned chairs and two additional negative-space chairs.

concepts.label: Chair by Ruth Asawa
concepts.learning_takeaway: In the 1965 lithograph Chair (TAM.1558-II), patterned marks and unmarked spaces both delineate chairs, making negative space an active part of the composition.

relations.note: The museum explicitly describes additional chairs outlined in negative space.

concepts.card: Chandra’s X-ray telescope uses four pairs of precisely shaped mirrors. X-rays that would penetrate an ordinary face-on mirror can reflect at grazing angles, so the optics resemble nested barrels. Extremely smooth, aligned, iridium-coated surfaces guide the radiation into sharp images of energetic cosmic environments.

evidence.locator:
Chandra :: About Chandra :: Telescope System
      ; inspected passage indices 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: content
evidence.note: Chandra’s four paired grazing-incidence mirror shells require precise shaping, polishing, iridium coating and alignment.

evidence.locator: Chandra X-ray Observatory; inspected passage indices 5, 22 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-6; paragraph-23
evidence.note: NASA identifies the purpose of Chandra’s X-ray images as studying exotic cosmic environments and the universe’s structure and evolution.

concepts.label: Chandra X-ray Observatory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Special paired mirrors allow Chandra to image high-energy X-rays that ordinary optical designs cannot focus.

relations.note: Both observatories use grazing-incidence X-ray mirrors; their distinct nested-mirror implementations offer a useful engineering comparison.

concepts.card: Chantale Cenerini describes documenting stories with Michif and Métis communities as work that can preserve language, family histories, and locally valued knowledge. Her account emphasizes learning each community's linguistic history first. A shared national identity does not mean every community uses the same language.

evidence.locator: §9.7, interview on local context and community stories
evidence.note: Checked first-person account and community-specific language histories; no universal claim about every Métis speaker or documentation project's outcome.

concepts.label: Chantale Cenerini
concepts.learning_takeaway: Learn from her account of documenting community stories while respecting distinct local Michif and Métis language histories.

relations.note: Cenerini's interview directly describes her story-recording work and its language-documentation and family-legacy purposes.

concepts.card: Chebyshev’s inequality bounds large deviations from a mean using variance. For a positive deviation threshold, the probability of reaching or exceeding it is at most the variance divided by the threshold squared. The bound applies without assuming a normal distribution, provided the variance is finite.

evidence.locator: Chebyshev Inequality -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3
evidence.note: Finite variance bounds large deviations from the mean without requiring a particular distribution shape.

concepts.label: Chebyshev’s inequality
concepts.learning_takeaway: Finite variance bounds large deviations from the mean without requiring a particular distribution shape.

relations.note: The source obtains Chebyshev’s inequality by applying Markov’s inequality to squared deviations.

concepts.card: A chemigram creates an image by manipulating photographic paper with chemicals and substances that resist them. Working in full light lets materials such as oils or varnishes shape the reaction. Chance and direct intervention can both influence marks without a camera recording an external scene.

evidence.note: Chemical manipulation, resists, full light and experimental chance are described.

concepts.label: Chemigram
concepts.learning_takeaway: Chemigrams manipulate photosensitive paper with resists and photographic chemicals in full light, allowing chemical interaction and chance to shape the image.

relations.note: Compare a chemical-resist image with an object-shadow image made through light exposure.

concepts.card: Chiasmus reverses the arrangement of paired elements into a crossing pattern. The effect depends on their order rather than simply on repeating a sound. When identical words recur in reverse order, the pattern takes the more specific form often called antimetabole.

evidence.note: Hirsch’s expanded definition distinguishes crossing structure from the identical-word subtype.

concepts.label: Chiasmus
concepts.learning_takeaway: A statement reverses the arrangement of paired elements, producing a crossing pattern that can sharpen contrast.

relations.note: Both reorganize repeated or paired elements, but crossing order differs from chaining adjacent boundaries.

concepts.card: Chimerism means that genetically distinct cell populations within one individual originated from different fertilized eggs. Mosaicism instead arises among descendants of a single fertilized egg. The distinction concerns the populations’ origins, even when both situations produce a body containing more than one cellular genome.

evidence.note: The NHGRI mosaicism narration explicitly contrasts chimerism from distinct zygotes with mosaicism from one zygote.

concepts.label: Chimerism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish cell populations derived from different zygotes from mosaicism within one zygote.
