relations.note: The shared glossary directly contrasts different-zygote cell origins with variation within one zygote’s descendants.

aliases: Civil service examinations in imperial China
concepts.card: Chinese imperial examinations linked literary and Confucian learning with entry into government. In the Song period, growing candidate numbers competed for limited posts, and most never became officials. This example exposes both a route to advancement and strong constraints on success.

evidence.note: The Song-specific discussion connects literary/Confucian examinations with fixed available posts, growing candidate numbers and widespread failure to obtain office.

concepts.label: Chinese imperial examinations
concepts.learning_takeaway: In the Song case, literary and Confucian examinations offered a route into government, but most candidates never became officials.

relations.note: The examination system helps explain the educational basis of scholar-official status.

concepts.card: Indian painted and printed cottons attracted overseas buyers because their colors endured washing and their designs could be adapted to different tastes. European demand encouraged imitation and restrictive import policies. A textile’s commercial history therefore reveals both shared fashions and competition between producers.

evidence.locator: Indian Painted and Printed Cottons, lines 145–148
evidence.note: Colorfast cottons, adapted designs, imitation and restrictions are discussed.

concepts.label: Chintz in global trade
concepts.learning_takeaway: Washable, colorfast Indian cottons were adapted to foreign tastes and prompted European restrictions and domestic imitation.

relations.note: Palampores give a particular form through which Indian painted cotton entered overseas markets.

concepts.card: The chlor-alkali process uses electrolysis of brine to produce chlorine and sodium hydroxide. Water participates in the electrode chemistry alongside dissolved ions. This makes the aqueous process different from simply decomposing molten sodium chloride, showing why the solvent matters to industrial electrochemistry.

evidence.locator: 17.7 Electrolysis; inspected passage indices 14, 15, 17, 18 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm37835104; fs-idm172416352; fs-idm194552416; fs-idm37680480
evidence.note: Electrolyzing brine produces chlorine and sodium hydroxide through competing electrode reactions.

concepts.label: Chlor-alkali process
concepts.learning_takeaway: Electrolyzing brine produces chlorine and sodium hydroxide through competing electrode reactions.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies sodium-chloride solution electrolysis as part of the chlor-alkali process.

concepts.card: Tempering chocolate encourages cocoa butter to form a suitable stable crystal structure. That preparation helps the finished chocolate set with gloss, a clean snap and useful contraction. Simply letting melted chocolate become cold does not necessarily produce the same arrangement of crystals or the same finish.

evidence.note: Callebaut explains precrystallizing cocoa butter into a stable structure and resulting shine, snap and contraction.

concepts.label: Chocolate tempering
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect controlled cocoa-butter crystallization with gloss, snap and contraction as chocolate sets.

relations.note: Tempering concerns the desired crystal structure, while fat bloom is a visible defect involving fat migration and surface crystallization.

concepts.card: Choosing a titration indicator means matching its color-change interval to the steep part of the pH curve near equivalence. An indicator that changes earlier can give a premature stopping signal; one suitable for a strong acid may fail for a weak acid.

evidence.locator: 14.7 Acid-Base Titrations; inspected passage indices 54, 55 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm188916592; fs-idm224614176
evidence.note: Match an indicator’s color-transition interval to the steep pH change near equivalence.

concepts.label: Choosing a titration indicator
concepts.learning_takeaway: Match an indicator’s color-transition interval to the steep pH change near equivalence.

relations.note: The source directly compares indicator intervals with the titration curve to select an endpoint indicator.

concepts.card: A choropleth map shades geographic areas according to an attribute such as a rate or ratio. The pattern lets readers compare regions, but large areas can attract disproportionate attention. Using appropriate normalized values helps prevent population size from masquerading as the phenomenon being compared.

evidence.locator: Opening; How choropleth maps work, lines 23 and 102–112
evidence.note: Rate/ratio mapping, normalization and area-size effects are discussed.

concepts.label: Choropleth mapping
concepts.learning_takeaway: Shading geographic areas by a rate or ratio reveals spatial comparisons while differing area sizes can influence visual attention.

relations.note: A method for encoding regional attributes is a specific map-design subject within cartography.
The source recommends normalization when comparing counts across areas with different populations or sizes.

concepts.card: Christian typological interpretation reads earlier scriptural people or events as anticipations of later ones. Catholic teaching uses this approach to connect the Testaments while also affirming the earlier texts’ intrinsic value. The interpretive link therefore does not require treating the earlier narrative as meaningless on its own.

evidence.note: Catechism paragraphs 128–130 connect anticipation with retained Old Testament value.

concepts.label: Christian typological interpretation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Earlier scriptural events are read as anticipations of later ones, while Catholic teaching also preserves the earlier texts’ intrinsic value.

relations.note: The cited teaching interprets relationships among texts within the Catholic scriptural collection.

concepts.card: A finite undirected graph’s chromatic polynomial counts its proper vertex colorings for any specified number of available colors. Adjacent vertices must receive different colors, and color names are distinguishable. Evaluating the polynomial answers many counting questions rather than only finding the fewest necessary colors.

evidence.locator: Chromatic Polynomial -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 3, 13 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-4; paragraph-14
evidence.note: Count proper vertex colorings for each palette size using a graph-associated polynomial.

concepts.label: Chromatic polynomial
concepts.learning_takeaway: Count proper vertex colorings for each palette size using a graph-associated polynomial.

relations.note: Bipartite graphs permit two-colorings; a chromatic polynomial asks how many proper colorings exist for a given palette.

concepts.card: Circumstantial moral luck concerns the unchosen situations that test a person's character. Someone placed in a brutal political environment may face choices another person never encounters. The philosophical problem is whether differing moral assessments are justified when the opportunity for wrongdoing itself depended on luck.

evidence.note: SEP's circumstantial-luck paragraph compares collaborators with imagined counterparts elsewhere; the card generalizes that structure without excusing atrocities or asserting that circumstances compel every action.

concepts.label: Circumstantial moral luck
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ask how unchosen situations expose people to different moral tests.

relations.note: Nagel's taxonomy in the entry expressly treats luck in one's circumstances as a kind of moral luck affecting assessment.

concepts.card: In US litigation, claim preclusion generally prevents repeating a cause of action after a final judgment on its merits. A losing plaintiff cannot simply sue the same defendant again on that claim; a winning plaintiff likewise cannot start another suit just to obtain additional recovery.

evidence.note: Cornell's res judicata overview and Bar and Merger examples support both losing and winning plaintiffs; generally avoids treating the brief account as an exhaustive jurisdiction-independent test.
The issue-specific definition supports the stated contrast with a repeated cause of action.

concepts.label: Claim preclusion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why a resolved cause of action generally cannot be litigated again.

relations.note: The res judicata entry expressly distinguishes claim preclusion from issue preclusion; the former concerns the cause of action, while the latter concerns a decided issue.

concepts.card: In Steve Reich's Clapping Music, rhythmic alignment changes through discrete rotations of a repeated pattern. One performer maintains the original pattern while the other moves to the next alignment on a measure's downbeat. Unlike Piano Phase, the transition does not require gradually speeding up.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 35.2 directly names the work and discrete-rotation contrast; do not describe its shifting as continuous tape-style drift.

concepts.label: Clapping Music
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear how discrete rhythmic rotations create changing alignments without a gradual tempo drift.

relations.note: The textbook identifies Clapping Music as a live-performance phase-shifting example using discrete rotations.

concepts.card: A simple clarinet model is a cylindrical pipe closed at one end, which supports an odd-harmonic sequence. Its next resonance is therefore near three times the fundamental, a musical twelfth higher. Real clarinets depart from the ideal cylinder, but the model explains their characteristic register jump.

evidence.note: UNSW explicitly compares closed and open pipes and cautions that bore, bell, mouthpiece and end corrections complicate real instruments; no exact all-register harmonic claim.

concepts.label: Clarinet overblowing at the twelfth
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare a clarinet's next register with a flute's octave using boundary conditions.

relations.note: The article directly applies the closed-pipe approximation to clarinet register behavior.

concepts.card: Wet clay shrinks as water between its particles leaves and the particles pack closer together. If different parts dry unevenly, they can shrink by different amounts and develop cracks as the piece stiffens. This drying change occurs before the separate transformations produced by firing in a kiln.

evidence.locator: Opening definition; differential drying and cracking
evidence.note: Digitalfire describes inter-particle water loss, packing, uneven drying and stress-driven cracks as clay becomes less plastic.

concepts.label: Clay drying shrinkage
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain shrinkage before firing through particle packing as inter-particle water leaves the clay.

relations.note: Drying shrinkage is a material behavior encountered between shaping clay and firing a pottery object.

concepts.card: Cliché-verre turns a drawing on a transparent plate into a photographic printing surface. Marks painted or scratched on glass control the light reaching sensitized paper beneath it. The result joins hand-made lines with photographic exposure rather than recording a scene through a camera lens.

evidence.note: Drawn/painted/scratched glass and contact exposure are described.

concepts.label: Cliché-verre
concepts.learning_takeaway: A drawn, painted or scratched glass plate acts as a negative for exposing light-sensitive paper.

relations.note: Both use direct light exposure on paper, but a drawn transparent matrix differs from objects casting contact shadows.

concepts.card: Cluny’s great Benedictine church combined monumental scale with rich decoration and elaborate liturgy. Its architecture made a community’s worship visible and spatially impressive. The example shows how monastic religious priorities could shape artistic patronage and building, alongside the disciplined routines of life within the abbey.

evidence.note: Large church, ornament and spectacular liturgy are explicit.

concepts.label: Cluny Abbey
concepts.learning_takeaway: Its monumental church and rich decoration show how an influential Benedictine community made elaborate worship visible in architecture.

relations.note: Cluny is the essay’s named example of monastic worship shaping architecture.

concepts.card: A coannular nozzle provides concentric outlets for two exhaust streams. In a turbofan, core flow leaves the central passage while fan air exits through a surrounding annulus. Their interaction affects thrust and noise, showing why the arrangement of outlets matters as well as the flow within them.

evidence.locator: Nozzles; inspected passage indices 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-3
evidence.note: Route engine-core and fan exhaust through concentric outlets to combine their flows.

concepts.label: Coannular exhaust nozzle
concepts.learning_takeaway: Route engine-core and fan exhaust through concentric outlets to combine their flows.

relations.note: NASA explicitly describes coannular nozzles as an arrangement used in turbofan engines.

concepts.card: Grand Pré preserves long agricultural land divisions alongside its coastal marsh reclamation works. The pattern records how settlers organized access and farming space, while dykes and drainage addressed water. Reading these features together distinguishes the geometry of landholding from the engineering that made cultivation possible.

evidence.note: Long divisions and separate marsh-drainage system are described.

concepts.label: Coastal strip-land division at Grand Pré
concepts.learning_takeaway: Long agricultural divisions along the coast preserve a settlement pattern alongside the separately maintained marsh-drainage system.

relations.note: The strip-land pattern is one preserved component of the named cultural landscape.

concepts.card: When winds move coastal surface water away, colder water can rise from below to replace it. This upwelling often brings nutrients into sunlit waters and supports high biological productivity. The process connects a change in water movement with conditions that can benefit marine food webs.

evidence.note: NOAA describes displaced surface water, rising cold nutrient-rich replacement and frequently high productivity/fishing grounds.

concepts.label: Coastal upwelling
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect offshore displacement of surface water with rising cold nutrient-rich water.

relations.note: Coastal upwelling is a circulation process linking the physical and biological parts of oceanography.

concepts.card: Coinsurance divides a covered cost by percentages between an insurer and the insured party. If coverage pays eighty percent, the other share remains with the policyholder. This differs from a deductible's initial threshold and a copayment's fixed charge for a covered service.

evidence.note: Checked percentage example and distinction among the three mechanisms; no claim about the exact ordering or combination of charges in a particular contract.

concepts.label: Coinsurance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Split a covered loss by percentages so the insured party retains part of each covered cost.

relations.note: The textbook directly contrasts percentage sharing with deductibles and fixed copayments within its cost-sharing discussion.

concepts.card: Colcas were Inka state storehouses for food, textiles and other goods collected from different regions. Their placement and construction could use natural airflow to help preserve supplies. Clusters of storehouses supported redistribution, including when harvests were poor or officials needed stored resources.

evidence.note: State collection, airflow preservation and redistribution are explicit.

concepts.label: Colca
concepts.learning_takeaway: Inka state storehouses combined regional collection and redistribution with storage designed to exploit natural airflow.

relations.note: Storage and accounting illuminate different material operations of the Inka state.

concepts.card: A collagraph builds a printing surface by attaching materials to a support. Their textures can hold or distribute ink that is then transferred to paper. The assembled surface functions as a matrix, which distinguishes the resulting print from a collage whose attached materials remain the finished image.

evidence.note: Attached materials, inking and transfer define the process.

concepts.label: Collagraph
concepts.learning_takeaway: Materials glued onto a support create a textured printing surface that can be inked and pressed onto paper.

relations.note: Both assemble materials, but collagraph construction prepares a matrix for another surface.
The printmaking guide describes the collagraph matrix and printing process.

concepts.card: Collective behavior involves group activity that is not governed through an established institution's rules. Crowds, dispersed publics, and shared fashions can take different forms. Studying these episodes does not require assuming that participants lose reason; sociological theories also examine coordination, interpretation, and newly developing norms.

evidence.note: Checked noninstitutionalized activity and variety of forms; no claim that all gatherings lack organization or have identical motives.

concepts.label: Collective behavior
concepts.learning_takeaway: Study noninstitutionalized group activity while distinguishing a shared gathering from a formally regulated organization.

relations.note: The collective-behavior chapter directly introduces emergent-norm theory as one framework for understanding these activities without assuming irrational crowds.

concepts.card: The Columbian Exchange names the movements of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and other regions after 1492. New crops changed diets, while disease and coercive colonial relationships brought devastating consequences. Exchange here describes connected transformations, not an equal bargain.

evidence.note: Post-1492 biological transfers, disease and unequal consequences support the account.

concepts.label: Columbian Exchange
concepts.learning_takeaway: Post-1492 transfers of plants, animals, people and disease reshaped societies across the Atlantic in unequal and often destructive ways.

relations.note: The movement of crops is one route from this exchange into the history of diets.

concepts.card: Cooling lava can contract and fracture into columns separated by polygonal joints. Seen from above, the cracks may resemble a honeycomb. Columnar jointing records a material response to cooling, distinguishing these fractures from a structure that necessarily formed through later faulting or folding.

evidence.note: USGS Shenandoah’s igneous-structures passage identifies cooling basalt, contraction and polygonal/honeycomb cracks.

concepts.label: Columnar jointing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect contraction during cooling with polygonal fractures in volcanic rock.

relations.note: Both structures preserve cooling history, but columns reflect contraction fractures while pillows reflect lava cooling in water.

concepts.card: At a common temperature, equilibrium constants follow the algebra of reaction equations. Reversing a reaction takes the reciprocal of its constant; multiplying coefficients raises the constant to that power. Adding reactions multiplies their constants, letting a difficult equilibrium be assembled from known ones.

evidence.locator: 13.2 Equilibrium Constants; inspected passage indices 97, 98, 99, 100 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm374944688; fs-idm328298096; fs-idm336251504; fs-idm351795744
evidence.note: Reverse, scale, or add reaction equations to derive the corresponding transformed equilibrium constants.

concepts.label: Combining equilibrium constants
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reverse, scale, or add reaction equations to derive the corresponding transformed equilibrium constants.

relations.note: The cited section applies these transformations to coupled equilibrium reactions.

concepts.card: Combustion analysis can determine the carbon and hydrogen content of a hydrocarbon sample. Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water, which are collected separately. Their measured masses reveal how much of each element was present and can establish the compound’s empirical formula.

evidence.locator: 4.5 Quantitative Chemical Analysis; inspected passage indices 36, 41 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idp91356704; fs-idm26289056
evidence.note: Infer elemental composition from measured carbon dioxide and water produced by complete combustion.

concepts.label: Combustion analysis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Infer elemental composition from measured carbon dioxide and water produced by complete combustion.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies combustion analysis as a gravimetric method.

concepts.card: Common ground consists of knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions participants take to be mutually shared. It gives them a starting point for coordination, but is updated as they communicate. Two people separately knowing the same fact is not automatically the same as recognizing it as shared between them.

evidence.note: Checked mutual-recognition requirement and updating; common ground is distinct from private knowledge and from the process that establishes it.

concepts.label: Common ground in communication
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use mutually taken-for-granted knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions as the shared basis for coordinated communication.

relations.note: The source explicitly defines common ground and explains how grounding updates it during interaction.

concepts.card: In a common-value auction, the object has the same underlying value to bidders, but they may estimate it differently. A jar of coins is a simple example. Winning can then reveal that one's estimate was unusually optimistic, so the information contained in winning matters for sensible bidding.

evidence.note: Checked shared value versus different estimates and winner information; real auctions can combine common and private components.

concepts.label: Common-value auction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish shared underlying value from bidders' differing information about that value.

relations.note: The Yale lecture introduces the winner's curse through its common-value coin-jar auction and explains conditioning on winning.

concepts.card: Community-led language reclamation begins with a community's own history and goals. Cenerini's Michif case explains that Métis communities do not all share one language, so a uniform national approach can miss local identities. Learning what people speak and value shapes which reclamation work makes sense there.

evidence.note: Checked the approved local-history/goals condition and multilingual-community qualification; no generic replacement of the baseline revitalization identity.

concepts.label: Community-led language reclamation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Let communities' own language histories and goals guide locally tailored reclamation work rather than assuming one shared language.

relations.note: Cenerini's local-history emphasis can guide the purposes of documentation; the link preserves the governance distinction instead of renaming generic revitalization.

concepts.card: Compatibility equivalence connects Unicode forms that may differ in presentation, such as a circled numeral and its ordinary digit. Compatibility normalization can fold these distinctions. That can help comparison, but blindly applying it may erase formatting or mathematical distinctions that matter in context.

evidence.note: Checked examples and the warning about lost semantic distinctions; compatibility folding is not declared safe for arbitrary text.

concepts.label: Compatibility equivalence in Unicode
concepts.learning_takeaway: Treat certain stylistic or presentation variants as equivalent while recognizing potentially meaningful distinctions lost by folding.

relations.note: Compatibility equivalence is a separately specified equivalence basis used by NFKC and NFKD, so it is grouped as a qualified normalization facet.

concepts.card: Two species competing for exactly the same limiting resources cannot indefinitely occupy the same niche under the competitive exclusion principle. Laboratory comparisons with Paramecium illustrate one competitor displacing another. Coexistence becomes more plausible when species differ in resource use, habitat or feeding time.

evidence.note: The OpenStax exclusion section presents same-niche competition and the Paramecium example, then explains resource partitioning as an avoidance route.

concepts.label: Competitive exclusion principle
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why competing for all the same limiting resources can prevent stable coexistence.

relations.note: Partitioning reduces the overlap in resource use on which competitive exclusion depends.

concepts.card: Two sounds have complementary distribution when they occur in nonoverlapping environments. That can help identify allophones, but it is not enough by itself: English /h/ and /ŋ/ also occupy different environments for many speakers. Phonetic similarity and broader patterns help determine whether sounds belong together.

evidence.locator: §4.4, Phones without contrastive distribution; Phonetic similarity
evidence.note: Checked h/ŋ counterexample and need for additional evidence; did not equate complementary distribution automatically with allophony.

evidence.locator: §4.1, The phonological units of spoken language
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source directly contrasts complementary distributions that do and do not justify grouping sounds as allophones of one phoneme.

concepts.label: Complementary distribution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize nonoverlapping sound environments without assuming this alone proves that the sounds share one phoneme.

relations.note: The source directly contrasts complementary distributions that do and do not justify grouping sounds as allophones of one phoneme.

concepts.card: Complete mediation requires checking authority for every access to every protected object. The requirement includes initialization, recovery, and maintenance, not only the usual operation path. A bypass can undermine an otherwise careful permission system, so identifying the source of each request is part of the problem.

evidence.note: Checked the every-access rule and exceptional operations; no unsupported advice to discard valid authorization caching without considering its correctness.

concepts.label: Complete mediation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Check authority for every access, including recovery and maintenance paths rather than only ordinary operation.

relations.note: Saltzer and Schroeder explicitly define complete mediation as an information-protection principle covering all access paths.

concepts.card: The Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory combined four instruments sensitive to different gamma-ray energies. It mapped radioactive aluminum across the Milky Way and provided evidence pointing toward distant origins for gamma-ray bursts. The mission demonstrates how high-energy observations can trace processes unavailable to ordinary visible-light surveys.

evidence.locator: CGRO; inspected passage indices 1 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2
evidence.note: Four complementary instruments surveyed gamma rays and mapped radioactive aluminum in the Milky Way.

concepts.label: Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Four complementary instruments surveyed gamma rays and mapped radioactive aluminum in the Milky Way.

relations.note: Mapping radioactive aluminum connects gamma-ray observations with radiation from unstable nuclei.

concepts.card: In Germany's concurrent legislative sphere, the Länder generally may legislate while the Federation has not exercised its power. Federal legislation can therefore change the space for state action. Article 72 also permits departures in specified fields, so concurrency does not mean either unrestricted coexistence or uniform federal exclusion.

evidence.note: Basic Law Articles 70–72, reinspected through all of Article 72, support the general rule and paragraph 3 exceptions; generally and specified fields avoid falsely absolute federal displacement.
The general federal-displacement rule has specified Land-departure exceptions; all of Article 72 was reinspected in source-raw/stage-b-german-competence.json.

concepts.label: Concurrent legislative powers in Germany
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how federal action can displace state legislative authority within a shared competence.

relations.note: Concurrent competence is a constitutional allocation of lawmaking authority between governmental levels, a specific example of the powers and structure a constitution defines.

concepts.card: Amnesty before South Africa's TRC was conditional, not automatic for politically connected violence. In a 1997 decision, Henry Khanyile's application failed because the committee found he had withheld relevant facts. The case shows why political context did not remove the requirement for full disclosure.

evidence.locator: 18 August 1997 statement; Khanyile and Tumahole decisions
evidence.note: The TRC's 18 August 1997 statement quotes the committee's section 20(1)(c) nondisclosure finding; the card reports its decision without asserting that disclosure alone guaranteed amnesty or retrying guilt independently.

concepts.label: Conditional amnesty in South Africa's TRC
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why political context alone did not guarantee amnesty without full disclosure.

relations.note: The statement is an actual Amnesty Committee decision within the TRC process and expressly applies its statutory full-disclosure condition.

concepts.card: Conditional expectation averages an integrable random quantity while retaining specified information, such as another variable’s value. The result can itself vary with that information rather than being one fixed number. Its mathematical definition preserves the appropriate averages over events recognizable from the conditioning information.

evidence.locator: Conditional Expectation -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 3 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-4
evidence.note: Average a random quantity while retaining the information supplied by another variable or sigma-algebra.

concepts.label: Conditional expectation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Average a random quantity while retaining the information supplied by another variable or sigma-algebra.

relations.note: This refines unconditional expected value by retaining specified information instead of averaging over it all.

concepts.card: A confidence and supply agreement allows one party to support another on specified parliamentary matters without forming a coalition government together. New Zealand's electoral authority distinguishes these arrangements from parties joining government. The distinction shows that keeping a government functioning need not mean sharing its entire program.

evidence.locator: Parties negotiate to form a government
evidence.note: The Electoral Commission's Parties negotiate section differentiates coalition membership from support on certain issues/laws; the card does not claim all agreements have identical terms or require support on every bill.

concepts.label: Confidence and supply agreement
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish supporting a government on specified matters from joining its coalition.

relations.note: The New Zealand MMP explanation discusses confidence and supply as one arrangement parties may negotiate when no party can govern alone, not an inevitable consequence of MMP.

concepts.card: Connecting concrete and abstract representations means explicitly showing how familiar examples correspond to symbols or general concepts. Without that bridge, learners may manipulate a formula yet struggle to apply it elsewhere. Comparing several representations can direct attention away from surface details toward the underlying relation.

evidence.note: Checked explicit mappings and risk of inert knowledge; transfer is a goal of the method, not an automatic outcome in every setting.

concepts.label: Connecting concrete and abstract representations
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explicitly map familiar objects or examples onto abstract symbols so knowledge can transfer beyond surface features.

relations.note: The guide's mapping between examples and abstract symbols complements, but is not identical to, coordinating words and pictures.

concepts.card: Constituency tests investigate which words behave together as a unit inside a sentence. Replacing a group with a pronoun or moving it can supply evidence for a phrase. Different tests offer complementary clues, so a sentence's visible sequence alone need not reveal its internal structure.

evidence.note: Checked replacement and movement methods and unit interpretation; no single test is presented as infallible or every sequence as a constituent.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Constituency tests supply evidence about phrase units, while structural ambiguity shows how different arrangements of those units can change interpretation.

concepts.label: Constituency tests
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine replacement and movement evidence to identify word groups that behave as sentence units.

relations.note: Constituency tests supply evidence about phrase units, while structural ambiguity shows how different arrangements of those units can change interpretation.

concepts.card: Constitutive moral luck concerns traits and dispositions shaped partly by factors people did not choose, including inheritance and upbringing. If those traits influence action, judging someone's character also raises a question about control. The issue is responsibility for who one has become, not merely what happens afterward.

evidence.note: SEP's constitutive-luck paragraphs identify genes, caregivers and peers, and connect dispositions with action; partly avoids a deterministic claim that character or conduct is wholly unchosen.

concepts.label: Constitutive moral luck
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine responsibility for dispositions shaped partly by unchosen development and inheritance.

relations.note: The source explicitly classifies luck in character and dispositions as constitutive moral luck, extending the control problem to agents as well as actions.

concepts.card: Construct validity asks whether a measure actually captures the concept it is intended to represent. A procedure can produce consistent scores yet miss its intended target. The challenge is therefore more than repeatability: it is connecting an observable measurement to the psychological idea being studied.

evidence.note: Section 2.3 defines construct validity and separates validity from reliability; the card does not assert that surface plausibility or one correlation settles the question.

concepts.label: Construct validity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ask whether an operational measure captures the intended psychological concept.

relations.note: The source explicitly contrasts measuring the intended construct with merely obtaining consistent results; observer agreement is one specified form of that consistency.

concepts.card: A constructed treatment wetland uses wetland plants, soils and associated microorganisms as part of an engineered water-treatment system. Water-quality improvement depends on these natural processes working within a designed setting. The vegetation is therefore part of the treatment approach, not merely decoration around a pond.

evidence.note: EPA’s opening definition identifies treatment systems using vegetation, soils and microbial communities to improve water quality.

concepts.label: Constructed treatment wetland
concepts.learning_takeaway: Treat wastewater with deliberately arranged vegetation, soils and microbial processes.

relations.note: Both approaches use vegetation and surrounding ecological processes for water-quality goals, but a treatment wetland and a streamside buffer have different layouts and roles.

concepts.card: Germany's constructive vote of no confidence requires the Bundestag to elect a successor Chancellor by a majority of its members while seeking the incumbent's dismissal. Opposition must therefore agree on a replacement, not merely on rejection. Article 67 also requires forty-eight hours between motion and election.

evidence.note: Basic Law Article 67 supplies majority membership, successor election, dismissal request and waiting period; the institutional consequence follows those express conditions and is bounded to Germany.

concepts.label: Constructive vote of no confidence
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why Germany requires choosing a successor while removing the Chancellor.

relations.note: Compare Germany's constitutional replacement requirement with New Zealand's negotiated support arrangements. Both concern parliamentary support for government, but one is a removal procedure and the other an interparty agreement.

concepts.card: Convergent evolution produces similar features in separate evolutionary lineages. Bird and bat wings both serve flight, but their wing structures arose independently. Their underlying forelimbs still share ancestry, showing that the answer depends on which feature and evolutionary level a comparison is examining.

evidence.note: Berkeley connects analogous wings with convergent evolution while distinguishing homologous forelimbs.

concepts.label: Convergent evolution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain similar functions that evolved separately rather than being inherited from a shared ancestor.

relations.note: Contrasting wing function with forelimb ancestry makes convergence and biological homology distinguishable without making them mutually exclusive at every level.

concepts.card: A conversational acknowledgment gives brief evidence that a listener is following or understanding, often without taking the speaking turn. Responses such as yeah or a head nod can serve this function. Their role is feedback within coordination, rather than necessarily endorsing the truth of everything the speaker says.

evidence.note: Checked brief verbal/gestural evidence and turn status; understanding is not equated with agreement or complete comprehension of every detail.

concepts.label: Conversational acknowledgment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Provide brief verbal or gestural evidence of understanding, often without taking over the speaking turn.

relations.note: The grounding chapter explicitly lists acknowledgments and head nods as positive evidence of understanding, generally without taking a turn.

concepts.card: A conversational implicature is an interpretation suggested by context rather than guaranteed by the sentence's truth. Hearing that a customer sighed might suggest annoyance, yet the speaker can add that the customer was relieved. This cancellability helps distinguish an implicature from a necessary entailment.

evidence.note: Checked context dependence and cancellation without contradiction; the card does not say a sigh always implies annoyance.

concepts.label: Conversational implicature
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a contextually suggested conclusion from a necessary implication by checking whether it can be cancelled.

relations.note: The source directly contrasts the cancellable anger interpretation with the necessary breath entailment of sighing.

concepts.card: Conversational turn-taking coordinates who speaks and when. Experiments with conversation fragments show that listeners can anticipate turn endings, supporting accounts that involve preparation before silence arrives. Such laboratory tasks isolate useful cues, but do not establish how every transition is managed in natural conversation.

evidence.note: The abstract and experiments report button-press anticipation with conversation fragments; the introduction distinguishes anticipation ability from proof of use in every natural exchange. The card now states the observed ability and the limited inference, while retaining the turn-completion framework.

concepts.label: Conversational turn-taking
concepts.learning_takeaway: Coordinate alternating speakers partly by anticipating possible turn endings rather than waiting only to react after silence.

relations.note: The research paper explicitly relates turn anticipation to possible completion points called transition-relevance places.

concepts.card: Coordinating graphics with verbal explanations helps learners connect what an image shows with the process being described. Relevant labels can sit close to the visual elements they explain. Decorative or overly detailed pictures may distract instead, so the principle concerns meaningful integration rather than adding images indiscriminately.

evidence.note: Checked near-element labels, relevant graphics, and distracting-detail caveat; no visual/verbal learning-style categories are implied.

concepts.label: Coordinating graphics and verbal explanations
concepts.learning_takeaway: Place relevant verbal explanations alongside the visual elements they explain so learners can connect representations.

relations.note: The guide links visual/verbal integration with connections between representations, while the second method specifically connects concrete examples to abstract ideas.

concepts.card: Stressed corals can lose the symbiotic algae living in their tissues, leaving them pale or white. This bleaching also removes an important food source. A bleached coral is not necessarily dead, but prolonged stress makes recovery harder and can ultimately lead to death.

evidence.note: NOAA explains stress-driven expulsion of symbiotic algae, loss of color and food, possible recovery and death if stress persists.

concepts.label: Coral bleaching
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish stress-driven loss of symbiotic algae from immediate coral death.

relations.note: Bleaching shows what can happen when a coral’s beneficial partnership with algae is disrupted.

concepts.card: The Coriolis force appears when motion is described from a rotating reference frame. A path can seem to bend sideways because the observer’s coordinate system is turning. An inertial-frame description accounts for the same motion without assigning this apparent force a separate physical interaction.

evidence.locator: 6.3 Centripetal Force; inspected passage indices 44, 50 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1165039268847; fs-id1165039316978
evidence.note: A rotating frame describes apparent trajectory bending through an inertial force absent from the inertial-frame account.

concepts.label: Coriolis force
concepts.learning_takeaway: A rotating frame describes apparent trajectory bending through an inertial force absent from the inertial-frame account.

relations.note: The source explicitly contrasts rotating-frame Coriolis descriptions with inertial-frame accounts.

concepts.card: A countersubject is recurring counterpoint that accompanies a fugue's subject. Its identity matters: the composer brings back recognizable accompanying material when the subject returns, rather than inventing completely different counterpoint each time. The same countersubject can appear in different voices as the texture changes.

evidence.note: Fugue Analysis defines consistent accompaniment and identifies one countersubject in alto and soprano; no requirement that every fugue have one is imposed.

concepts.label: Countersubject
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify recurring counterpoint accompanying successive subject entries.

relations.note: The source defines countersubject specifically within its fugue analysis and contrasts it with nonrecurring accompaniment.

concepts.card: A covalent network solid contains atoms joined in an extended web of covalent bonds. Disrupting that network requires breaking bonds, rather than merely separating intact molecules. Such solids often have high melting temperatures; diamond illustrates the hardness that extensive covalent bonding can produce.

evidence.locator: 10.5 The Solid State of Matter; inspected passage indices 14 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm59353248
evidence.note: A continuous covalent-bond network helps explain the hardness and high melting temperatures of diamond-like solids.

concepts.label: Covalent network solid
concepts.learning_takeaway: A continuous covalent-bond network helps explain the hardness and high melting temperatures of diamond-like solids.

relations.note: The passage explicitly attributes network-solid properties to the connected covalent bonds between its atoms.

concepts.card: Cover crops are grown primarily to keep living vegetation on the soil and provide conservation benefits, rather than as the main harvested crop. Their roots and residues can reduce erosion and add organic matter. Timing and management determine how those functions fit around the farm’s other crops.

evidence.note: NRCS defines seasonal vegetative cover rather than cash crops and identifies erosion reduction, organic matter and soil-structure benefits.

concepts.label: Cover crops
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a crop grown for soil cover and ecosystem functions from one grown primarily for harvest.

relations.note: Cover crops supply living cover, while no-till changes soil disturbance and residue handling; they can serve complementary but distinct soil-management functions.

concepts.card: A covering index contains every column a particular query needs, including its output columns. The database can answer that query from the index without looking up matching rows in the original table. Whether an index covers a query therefore depends on that query's requested information.

evidence.note: Checked search-plus-output coverage and eliminated table lookup; an index can cover one query without covering every query.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: This index design changes how a database retrieves selected columns; it is an implementation facet rather than a synonym for the database itself.

concepts.label: Covering index
concepts.learning_takeaway: Include search and output columns in an index so a query need not consult the original table.

relations.note: This index design changes how a database retrieves selected columns; it is an implementation facet rather than a synonym for the database itself.

concepts.card: Creep is deformation that accumulates under sustained loading over time. In metals and ceramics at elevated temperatures, it can become important even below the usual yield stress. Components such as turbine blades must therefore be assessed for service duration and temperature, not only their initial deformation.

evidence.locator: Chapter 10: Creep, Fracture, and Fatigue; inspected passage indices 68, 69, 71 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-69; paragraph-70; paragraph-72
evidence.note: Time-dependent deformation can accumulate at elevated temperature even below a material’s usual yield stress.

concepts.label: Creep (materials)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Time-dependent deformation can accumulate at elevated temperature even below a material’s usual yield stress.

relations.note: Creep emphasizes sustained load and time, while fatigue emphasizes repeated loading; the sources treat these as different failure concerns.

concepts.card: For a displaced linear spring–mass system released from rest, critical damping returns it toward equilibrium as quickly as possible without oscillation. It marks the threshold between oscillatory and nonoscillatory response; simply adding more damping makes the return slower rather than always improving the result.

evidence.locator: 15.5 Damped Oscillations; inspected passage indices 18, 19 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1167131215180; fs-id1167131503759
evidence.note: Tune the linear damping threshold for rapid nonoscillatory return to equilibrium.

concepts.label: Critical damping
concepts.learning_takeaway: Tune the linear damping threshold for rapid nonoscillatory return to equilibrium.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies critical damping as the threshold regime within damped harmonic motion.

concepts.card: A fluid’s critical point marks the end of the liquid–vapor coexistence boundary. As it is approached, the distinction between the two phases disappears. Above the critical temperature, applying more pressure cannot produce a separate liquid phase, although the fluid can become dense.

evidence.locator: 10.4 Phase Diagrams; inspected passage indices 40 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm114606944
evidence.note: At the end of liquid-vapor coexistence, the liquid-gas boundary disappears and pressure alone cannot liquefy hotter gas.

concepts.label: Critical point of a fluid
concepts.learning_takeaway: At the end of liquid-vapor coexistence, the liquid-gas boundary disappears and pressure alone cannot liquefy hotter gas.

relations.note: The source explains the disappearance of the liquid–vapor boundary as the transition to supercritical fluid behavior.

concepts.card: Crop rotation changes the crops grown in a field through a planned sequence over time. This can interrupt recurring pest associations and diversify how the field is used. It is a preventive management practice, rather than simply moving an existing pest after it has become a problem.

evidence.note: Identifies crop rotation as a way to prevent pest problems within IPM.
Defines planned crop sequence over time on the same field and reduced pest pressure as a possible benefit.

concepts.label: Crop rotation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Disrupt recurring crop-pest associations by changing the crop grown in a field over time.

relations.note: EPA explicitly includes rotation among preventive practices within integrated pest management.

concepts.card: A crystal vacancy is an unoccupied position where an atom or ion normally belongs in a lattice. It differs from an interstitial defect, where a particle occupies a gap between regular positions. Both disturb an otherwise repeating internal arrangement of particles.

evidence.locator: 10.5 The Solid State of Matter; inspected passage indices 24 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm62566768
evidence.note: A missing atom at a regular lattice site is a structural defect distinct from an interstitial impurity.

concepts.label: Crystal vacancy
concepts.learning_takeaway: A missing atom at a regular lattice site is a structural defect distinct from an interstitial impurity.

relations.note: The solid-state section explicitly describes vacancies as defects in a crystalline solid’s repeating pattern.

concepts.card: A spinning baseball can experience a sideways aerodynamic force that bends its path. NASA's simplified curveball model links the curvature to spin, speed and air density. It treats the path as a circular arc when drag and the resulting changes in the force are neglected.

evidence.note: NASA Aerodynamic Force gives the spinning-ball force and explicitly states the approximation; retain model qualification rather than declaring every real pitch a circular arc.

concepts.label: Curveball aerodynamics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect spin-generated sideways force with a curved pitch trajectory.

relations.note: NASA explicitly explains the curveball through aerodynamic force acting on a spinning baseball.

concepts.card: Cyanotype uses light-sensitive iron salts to produce a characteristic blue image. Exposure and washing make the image visible on a prepared surface. Because the process can record objects placed directly on paper, it can join photographic chemistry with close observation of a specimen’s shape.

evidence.note: Iron-salt chemistry and washing are in a05; Atkins supplies the contact-specimen application.
Directly arranged algae establish the specimen application.

concepts.label: Cyanotype
concepts.learning_takeaway: Light acts on iron-salt-coated paper, and washing develops the characteristic blue image.

relations.note: Atkins used cyanotype contact images to record algae specimens.

concepts.card: In a weakly damped spring–mass system, oscillations lose energy and their amplitude declines. A common low-speed model makes the damping force proportional to velocity and opposite to motion. Under that model, the oscillating displacement fits inside a shrinking exponential envelope.

evidence.locator: 15.5 Damped Oscillations; inspected passage indices 7, 9, 10, 12 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1167131080334; fs-id1167131181569; fs-id1167129966801; fs-id1167131498071
evidence.note: Dissipation removes oscillator energy so its amplitude declines rather than continuing indefinitely.

concepts.label: Damped harmonic motion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Dissipation removes oscillator energy so its amplitude declines rather than continuing indefinitely.

relations.note: The source contrasts weakly damped oscillation with critical and overdamped responses as damping increases.

concepts.card: Darshan concerns the devotional encounter of seeing a deity, commonly through an image. The visual interaction can be central to puja rather than merely decorative. Debates about internet worship make this emphasis especially visible by asking how an encounter changes when the image is mediated online.

evidence.locator: Opening; online shrine discussion, lines 56 and 82
evidence.note: The case study identifies visual interaction and internet-mediated puja.

concepts.label: Darshan
concepts.learning_takeaway: Seeing a deity’s image can be a devotional encounter; visual presence matters in temples and in debates over online worship.

relations.note: Darshan is presented as a common visual dimension of puja.
The case study identifies devotional visual encounter within Hindu practice.

concepts.card: Dasymetric mapping uses additional information to redistribute an aggregate quantity within reporting areas. Population can be allocated away from places identified as uninhabited. The method replaces a uniform-density assumption with a distribution informed by ancillary data, so the result depends on that information.

evidence.note: Ancillary data refine within-zone population allocation.

concepts.label: Dasymetric mapping
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ancillary information reallocates aggregate population away from uninhabited areas instead of assuming uniform density within census boundaries.

relations.note: Compare uniform reporting-area shading with redistribution informed by supplementary spatial information.

concepts.card: The de Broglie wavelength associates a wave with a particle’s momentum: larger momentum means shorter wavelength. Electrons as well as photons obey this relationship. It provides a bridge between particle motion and wave behavior, helping explain why matter can produce diffraction patterns.

evidence.locator: 6.5 De Broglie’s Matter Waves; inspected passage indices 6, 7, 8, 9 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: list-00001; fs-id1163711990811; fs-id1163712336118; fs-id1163712430653
evidence.note: The matter-wave discussion and Equation 6.54 give wavelength as Planck’s constant divided by momentum and connect matter waves with diffraction.

concepts.label: de Broglie wavelength
concepts.learning_takeaway: Relate particle momentum to matter-wave wavelength, extending wave behavior beyond photons.

relations.note: The two subjects approach wave-particle behavior from complementary directions: light transfers energy discretely, and matter exhibits wavelength-dependent behavior.

concepts.card: A dead position ends a chess game because neither player could checkmate through any possible sequence of legal moves. This is stronger than saying that checkmate seems unlikely or cannot be forced: even cooperative play by the opponent would not make mate possible.

evidence.note: FIDE 5.2.2 quantifies over any legal sequence; the cooperative-play explanation unpacks that condition rather than adding a material-count rule.

concepts.label: Dead position in chess
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize a draw where neither side can ever deliver legal checkmate.

relations.note: Both end the game as a draw, but stalemate concerns present legal moves while dead position concerns impossibility of future mate.

concepts.card: Psychological studies sometimes conceal their precise purpose because knowing it could change participants' responses. That creates an ethical tension between informative behavior and informed participation. The cited ethics account limits deceptive procedures and requires a later explanation of the purpose, data use and reasons for concealment.

evidence.note: Section 2.4 explains response distortion and debriefing, with ethical limits; the card attributes this account and does not treat scientific convenience as sufficient permission for harmful deception.

concepts.label: Deception in psychological research
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine the tension between realistic responses and participants' knowledge of a study's purpose.

relations.note: The source directly connects permissible use of deception with a subsequent full debriefing rather than treating concealment as an unrestricted research tool.

concepts.card: DEFLATE is a lossless compressed-data format combining two techniques. Repeated byte strings become LZ77-style length-and-distance references, while literals and references are represented with Huffman codes. Data is organized into blocks, which can use fixed codes, transmitted code tables, or no compression.

evidence.note: Checked the combination and three valid block types; not described as an Internet standard because RFC 1951 is informational.

concepts.label: DEFLATE
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine LZ77 references and Huffman-coded symbols inside a lossless block format.

relations.note: The RFC abstract and section 2 expressly state that DEFLATE combines the LZ77 algorithm with Huffman coding.

concepts.card: A deformation retract continuously moves a space onto one of its subspaces, ending with that subspace’s points fixed. A stronger version keeps those points fixed throughout the movement. This distinction separates the final result of the deformation from what happens during every intermediate stage.

evidence.locator: Deformation Retract -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-4; paragraph-5; paragraph-6; paragraph-7
evidence.note: A continuous deformation moves a space onto a subspace, with a stronger version fixing that subspace throughout.

concepts.label: Deformation retract
concepts.learning_takeaway: A continuous deformation moves a space onto a subspace, with a stronger version fixing that subspace throughout.

relations.note: The definition constructs a deformation retract using a homotopy.

concepts.card: A cue-only delayed judgment of learning asks someone to estimate future recall after time away from the material, using a cue without the answer visible. The delay reduces reliance on immediate familiarity. The cited guide treats this as promising for allocating study, while noting limited classroom evidence.

evidence.note: Recommendation 6a, printed pp. 23–24, describes the cue-only delayed judgment procedure: delay after study, target answer absent and prospective recall judgment. The guide rates classroom evidence as limited; the narrower label retains the same selected facet and reserved ID.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Both approaches use information to guide subsequent learning, but a learner's delayed recall estimate is distinct from the broader formative use of assessment evidence.

concepts.label: Cue-only delayed judgments of learning
concepts.learning_takeaway: After a delay, use only a cue to judge future recall so immediate familiarity is less misleading.

relations.note: Both approaches use information to guide subsequent learning, but a learner's delayed recall estimate is distinct from the broader formative use of assessment evidence.

concepts.card: The Ottoman devshirme forcibly recruited Christian boys for conversion, education and state service. Some entered military units, while others pursued administrative roles. The system linked coercive removal from families with the state’s attempt to train personnel whose careers depended on the ruler.

evidence.note: Recruitment, conversion, schooling and military/administrative destinations are explicit.

concepts.label: Devshirme
concepts.learning_takeaway: The Ottoman state forcibly gathered Christian boys, converted and educated them, and assigned them to military or administrative service.

relations.note: Devshirme supplied some recruits to the Janissaries while also serving other state roles.

concepts.card: Diagnostic sensitivity asks: among people who have the target condition, how often is the test positive? A highly sensitive test misses fewer affected people. This is different from asking whether a particular positive result means disease, which requires a probability conditioned on the test result.

evidence.note: NCI defines sensitivity as positive-test probability given cancer and separately defines predictive value in the reverse conditional direction.

concepts.label: Diagnostic sensitivity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read sensitivity as the chance of a positive test among people who have the target condition.

relations.note: Sensitivity conditions on disease status, while positive predictive value conditions on a positive test.

concepts.card: Diagnostic specificity asks: among people without the target condition, how often is the test negative? Higher specificity means fewer false positives in that group. It complements sensitivity, but neither quantity alone tells a patient the probability of disease after receiving a positive result.

evidence.note: NCI defines specificity as negative-test probability without cancer and distinguishes it from sensitivity and positive predictive value.

concepts.label: Diagnostic specificity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read specificity as the chance of a negative test among people without the target condition.

relations.note: Sensitivity and specificity describe test behavior in different disease-status groups; they are complementary rates, not interchangeable names.

concepts.card: Dick Fosbury's lasting influence came from the high-jump technique bearing his name. He won Olympic gold in 1968, but his legacy extended beyond that result: the Fosbury Flop transformed how the event was approached. Olympedia distinguishes this technical influence from his relatively brief competitive prominence.

evidence.note: Olympedia biography supports 1968 gold, technique and enduring influence; the card does not invent biomechanical details absent from this source.

concepts.label: Dick Fosbury
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine an athlete whose enduring influence came from a new jumping style.

relations.note: The biography identifies Fosbury's innovation and Olympic result specifically with the high-jump event.

concepts.card: A diffraction grating uses many regularly spaced lines or openings to combine light waves by interference. Their contributions reinforce at selected angles, producing narrow bright maxima. Different wavelengths reinforce at different angles, allowing a grating to separate light into a spectrum for analysis.

evidence.locator: 4.4 Diffraction Gratings; inspected passage indices 5, 7, 8 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1172100770948; fs-id1172100664530; fs-id1172100887164
evidence.note: Many regularly spaced slits produce narrow interference maxima that separate light by wavelength.

evidence.locator: 4.5 Circular Apertures and Resolution; inspected passage indices 5 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1172102062471
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected passage establishes the alternate example, field identity, or alias used in the takeaway.

concepts.label: Diffraction grating
concepts.learning_takeaway: Many regularly spaced slits produce narrow interference maxima that separate light by wavelength.

relations.note: The grating is an optical instrument exploiting interference to reveal wavelength composition.

concepts.card: Aquatic organisms use oxygen dissolved in water, which is different from the oxygen chemically bound inside water molecules. Microorganisms decomposing organic matter can consume this available oxygen. If consumption outpaces replenishment, oxygen levels fall and conditions can become difficult for other aquatic life.

evidence.note: USGS’s BOD account distinguishes dissolved available oxygen and describes microbial decomposition consuming it with ecological consequences.

concepts.label: Dissolved oxygen in water
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish biologically available dissolved oxygen from the oxygen bound inside water molecules.

relations.note: Biochemical oxygen demand measures an oxygen-consuming process that can lower the dissolved-oxygen concentration.

concepts.card: Replicated-log consensus lets machines agree on an ordered command history despite crash failures and unreliable communication. Raft-style protocols preserve safety under delays and partitions, but remain available only while a suitable majority can communicate. Agreement here concerns replicated commands, not every form of collective decision-making.

evidence.note: Sections 2 and 5 distinguish safety under non-Byzantine communication failures from availability requiring an operational communicating majority. The card gives a Raft-style example, not a theorem about every consensus protocol.

concepts.label: Replicated-log consensus under crash faults
concepts.learning_takeaway: Make non-Byzantine replicas agree on ordered commands, with availability requiring a communicating majority.

relations.note: The bounded crash-fault replicated-log problem is a specific coordination problem within distributed systems, with the failure model made explicit.

concepts.card: Dante’s Divine Comedy uses terza rima to link successive three-line stanzas. A rhyme introduced in the middle of one tercet becomes the surrounding rhyme in the next, with a final line completing the sequence at a canto’s close. Form carries continuity across local divisions.

evidence.note: The glossary explains Dante’s interlocking tercets and closing line.

concepts.label: Divine Comedy
concepts.learning_takeaway: Dante’s interlocking terza rima connects successive tercets, while a final line completes each canto’s rhyme sequence.

relations.note: The glossary explicitly identifies Dante’s use of the interlocking rhyme scheme.

concepts.card: A divisional structure places several functions together around a product, market, service, or region. Each division can coordinate its own activities and take clearer responsibility for its segment. The tradeoff is that divisions may become isolated, with duplicated systems and weaker coordination across the whole organization.

evidence.note: Checked grouping basis and divisional isolation; did not claim that geographic and product divisions must use identical arrangements.

concepts.label: Divisional organizational structure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Place several functions together within product, market, or regional divisions to concentrate accountability locally.

relations.note: OpenStax explicitly describes divisions as groupings of functional departments and contrasts their local coordination with functional silos.

concepts.card: DNA metabarcoding examines a mixed sample for traces of multiple species. Broadly targeted primers amplify DNA fragments, and high-throughput sequencing reads the resulting mixture. The approach turns one pooled sample into a multispecies assessment rather than a test focused on only one organism.

evidence.note: USGS defines metabarcoding through nonspecific primers, PCR, high-throughput sequencing and identifying multiple species in a pooled sample.

concepts.label: DNA metabarcoding
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify multiple species from a pooled DNA sample using broad primers and sequencing.

relations.note: The glossary presents metabarcoding as a multispecies analysis of a pooled DNA sample, making it an editorial application link to environmental-DNA investigation.

concepts.card: DNA methylation adds small chemical tags to particular places on DNA. These marks can change how proteins interact with the molecule and whether nearby genes are used. The underlying DNA sequence stays the same, while its activity can change.

evidence.note: The epigenomics explanation describes methyl groups attached to DNA bases, changed DNA–protein interactions and altered gene use without sequence rewriting.

concepts.label: DNA methylation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how methyl tags influence DNA–protein interactions without rewriting the DNA sequence.

relations.note: Both are epigenomic marks, but methylation tags DNA directly while histone modification tags its packaging proteins.

concepts.card: The doctrine of double effect distinguishes harm intended as a means from harm foreseen as a side effect of pursuing a good end. Its defenders also require proportionality and attention to avoiding harm. Merely saying a bad result was unintended does not make it permissible.

evidence.note: SEP sections 1 and 3 support the intention/foresight distinction, proportionality and harm minimization; attribution to defenders avoids presenting a contested doctrine as settled morality.

concepts.label: Doctrine of double effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish intending harm as a means from foreseeing it as a side effect.

relations.note: The entry explicitly warns that intended versus foreseen harm is a different distinction from doing versus allowing harm; neither distinction should be substituted for the other.

concepts.card: Doing harm and allowing harm distinguish bringing about a harmful outcome from failing to prevent it. Philosophers dispute their moral significance. Rachels's paired cases compare deliberate drowning with deliberately withholding rescue, testing whether the distinction alone can explain a difference in blame.

evidence.note: SEP sections 1–2 present Rachels's cases and objections to both their comparability and generalization; the card treats the cases as a test, not proof that killing and letting die are always equivalent.

concepts.label: Doing versus allowing harm
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate causing versus permitting harm from intention and from moral verdicts.

relations.note: The entry uses driver and bystander trolley variants to examine whether doing/allowing explains moral judgments, and records challenges to that explanation.

concepts.card: In a double-blind study, participants and the relevant researchers do not know which group each participant belongs to. Concealing assignments helps limit both participant expectations and experimenter expectations. It is a protection against those influences, not a substitute for sound sampling, measurement or comparison groups.

evidence.note: Section 2.3 defines concealed assignment for researchers and participants; the final limitation follows the chapter's separate design requirements and avoids claiming that blinding alone demonstrates causation.

concepts.label: Double-blind study
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare controlling participant expectations with controlling researcher expectations.

relations.note: Double blinding is directly introduced as controlling both experimenter and participant expectations, so its relation to expectancy bias is stated rather than inferred.

concepts.card: When doubling is allowed in backgammon, a player offers it at the start of their own turn, before rolling. The opponent can decline and lose at the old value, or accept. Acceptance gives that player the cube and the exclusive right to offer the next redouble.

evidence.note: USBGF Doubling supports own-turn timing, before rolling, refusal cost and ownership. When allowed preserves format exceptions such as the separately discussed Crawford game; this is descriptive scoring, not advice to gamble.

concepts.label: Doubling cube
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how accepting a double transfers the right to offer the next redouble.

relations.note: The federation presents the cube as the game's mechanism for offering and accepting increased stakes.

concepts.card: A cyclist riding in another rider's wake can encounter less aerodynamic resistance and use less energy to maintain speed. The leading rider can also gain a smaller benefit. Road-racing groups exploit this shared airflow, although position and spacing affect how much shelter each rider receives.

evidence.note: Exploratorium explains follower and leader advantages and spacing dependence; avoid exporting its numerical savings to all speeds, terrains or formations.

concepts.label: Drafting in cycling
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect riding in another cyclist's wake with reduced aerodynamic effort.

relations.note: The museum's Aerodynamics and Drafting explanation explicitly applies wake airflow to road cycling.

concepts.card: Drawboring deliberately offsets peg holes in a mortise-and-tenon joint. Driving a wooden peg through them pulls the pieces tightly together. A tapered metal drawbore pin can first test the fit, but the temporary pin and the wooden peg securing the finished joint have different roles.

evidence.note: Lee Valley explains offset holes drawing the joint tight and distinguishes temporary tapered test pins from final wooden pegs.

concepts.label: Drawboring
concepts.learning_takeaway: Pull a mortise-and-tenon joint tight by driving a peg through intentionally offset holes.

relations.note: Drawboring is a specific way to tighten and secure a mortise-and-tenon assembly.

concepts.card: Drip irrigation delivers water through small outlets placed near individual plants. In the inspected hydroponic example, a hose system supplies nutrient solution at plant bases instead of sending a continuous stream down a channel. The delivery arrangement targets the root area rather than wetting an entire surface uniformly.

evidence.note: UMN’s drip-system passage describes hoses and small holes/outlets located at each plant base, contrasted with nutrient-film channels.

concepts.label: Drip irrigation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Deliver water or nutrient solution near individual plants through controlled small outlets.

relations.note: Localized delivery through outlets is a particular irrigation method within the broader application of water to plants.

concepts.card: After contract bridge's opening lead, the declarer's partner lays their hand face up as dummy. The declarer chooses which cards to play from both partnership hands. This creates a distinctive information pattern: defenders can see one opposing hand, but not the declarer's concealed cards.

evidence.note: ACBL Play supports timing, exposed dummy and declarer's control; the information consequence is directly entailed, without claiming defenders see each other's hands.

concepts.label: Dummy in bridge
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why one partnership hand becomes visible and is played by declarer's instructions.

relations.note: The play instructions define dummy as a specific role within the declaring partnership.

concepts.card: Duplicate bridge compares results from players holding the same deal of cards. A weak hand is therefore judged against what others achieved with that weak hand, rather than against opponents lucky enough to receive stronger cards. The format reduces the influence of the deal's initial luck.

evidence.note: ACBL Duplicate Bridge supports identical deals and comparison against the field; reduces rather than eliminates chance, without claiming every duplicate scoring system is identical.

concepts.label: Duplicate bridge
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand comparison against other players holding the same cards.

relations.note: ACBL presents duplicate as a bridge format in which the same deals are played at multiple tables.

concepts.card: A dyad is a two-person social group. Its existence depends directly on both participants: when one leaves, no two-person group remains. This gives the relationship a different structure from a larger group, where some members can continue interacting after another person withdraws.

evidence.note: Checked two-member dependence; not claimed that all social consequences or obligations disappear when a dyad ends.

concepts.label: Dyad (social group)
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why a two-person group depends on both members' continued participation and cannot outlast either member's departure.

relations.note: OpenStax explicitly contrasts Simmel's two-member and three-member groups by withdrawal and the continuing relationships available.

concepts.card: A dynamic Huffman block in DEFLATE carries descriptions of its own coding tables before the compressed data. The descriptions encode code lengths, including repeated lengths. Fixed-code blocks avoid that table description, creating a format-level choice between predetermined codes and block-specific ones.

evidence.note: Checked transmitted lengths and repeated-length symbols; no unsupported claim that dynamic blocks always compress better.

concepts.label: Dynamic Huffman blocks in DEFLATE
concepts.learning_takeaway: Transmit block-specific code lengths rather than always using the format's fixed Huffman tables.

relations.note: RFC 1951 sections 3.2.6–3.2.7 define fixed and dynamic Huffman block types within DEFLATE.

concepts.card: In the E. coli Long-Term Evolution Experiment, researchers replayed evolution using bacteria from different points in one population’s history. Later samples were more likely to evolve aerobic citrate use. The result showed how earlier genetic changes could enable a later innovation, making evolutionary history experimentally testable.

evidence.note: The 2008 primary abstract reports replay experiments from different generations and a higher probability of aerobic citrate use in later clones, supporting historical contingency under the experiment’s oxic conditions.

concepts.label: E. coli Long-Term Evolution Experiment
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how revived archived populations let researchers test whether prior mutations enabled a later innovation.

relations.note: Replaying different inherited genetic backgrounds links this experiment to genetics through the effect of prior changes on a later trait.

concepts.card: The Eads Bridge relied on deep pneumatic caissons to place mid-river piers on solid rock. This enabled a major Mississippi rail crossing, but construction brought serious human costs, including deaths from caisson disease. The case joins structural innovation with the hazards of working below a river’s surface.

evidence.locator:
Eads Bridge | ASCE
; inspected passage indices 4, 5, 6 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-5; paragraph-6; paragraph-7
evidence.note: Pneumatic caissons established deep river foundations for a major rail crossing, with serious construction hazards.

concepts.label: Eads Bridge
