concepts.learning_takeaway: Pneumatic caissons established deep river foundations for a major rail crossing, with serious construction hazards.

relations.note: ASCE explicitly describes the Eads Bridge as a major railroad crossing and explains its foundations.

concepts.card: An ecofact is a natural remain that provides archaeological evidence, such as an animal bone or plant seed associated with human activity. Its importance comes from what it can reveal about past lives, even though people did not manufacture it as an artifact.

evidence.locator: What is an Archeologist?, ecofacts definition
evidence.note: Natural remains and seed/bone examples distinguish ecofacts from manufactured artifacts.

concepts.label: Ecofact
concepts.learning_takeaway: Unmanufactured remains such as seeds and animal bones can be archaeological evidence of human resource use.

relations.note: Associations establish why an unmanufactured remain is evidence of human activity.
The NPS explicitly includes ecofacts among the evidence archaeologists study.

concepts.card: In this research-methods sense, ecological validity concerns how well findings apply to ordinary settings. Unobtrusive observation of people in their usual surroundings can improve realism, but sacrifices experimental control. A realistic setting helps the applicability question without automatically answering every question about cause and effect.

evidence.note: Section 2.2's naturalistic-observation discussion supports realism, generalization and control tradeoffs; retain this cited sense rather than treating all uses of ecological validity as interchangeable.

concepts.label: Ecological validity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Assess how closely a research setting represents real-world behavior.

relations.note: Real-world applicability and accurate measurement of an intended construct are different validity questions; the comparison is a learning bridge, not a claim that one guarantees the other.

concepts.card: Economic signaling uses observable actions or credentials to convey information about less visible qualities. A prospective worker's qualifications may help an employer infer preparation or persistence. The signal does not remove all uncertainty; it offers evidence about something the employer cannot fully observe before hiring.

evidence.note: Checked credential-as-signal example and remaining uncertainty; not claimed that a credential perfectly measures ability or always forms a separating equilibrium.

concepts.label: Signaling in economics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use observable credentials or actions to convey information about otherwise hidden qualities.

relations.note: The source's credential and employer-investigation examples support distinguishing information supplied by the informed party from screening initiated by the less-informed party.

concepts.card: Economy of mechanism asks security designers to keep protection mechanisms small and simple. Hidden access paths may escape notice during normal use, so extra complexity makes careful examination harder. The aim is a design whose safeguards can be understood and checked, rather than complexity mistaken for protection.

evidence.note: Checked the simplicity and unnoticed-access-path rationale; not a claim that the shortest possible system is always safest.

concepts.label: Economy of mechanism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Keep protection mechanisms small and simple to make hidden access paths easier to examine.

relations.note: Saltzer and Schroeder directly identify economy of mechanism as a foundational protection-design principle and explain its error-detection rationale.

concepts.card: Organisms can alter the physical environment that other species use. Beavers, for example, build dams that create aquatic habitats and change local living conditions. Ecosystem engineering draws attention to these habitat modifications, extending the study of species interactions beyond who eats whom.

evidence.note: The NPS Wolves and Beaver passage explicitly calls beavers ecosystem engineers and describes dams creating aquatic habitat.

concepts.label: Ecosystem engineering
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how organisms change physical habitat for other species, using beaver dams.

relations.note: Physical habitat modification by organisms is an ecological interaction connecting species with the environment they create.

concepts.card: Edge embeddedness counts how many common neighbors the two ends of a tie share. Mutual contacts create a social setting around the relationship and may make misconduct more visible. A local bridge has zero embeddedness, connecting people without that immediate shared-neighbor context.

evidence.note: Checked shared-neighbor count and zero case; mutual friends are not claimed to ensure trust or prevent all misconduct.

concepts.label: Edge embeddedness
concepts.learning_takeaway: Count the mutual neighbors of a connected pair to describe the social context surrounding their tie.

relations.note: The chapter directly equates zero embeddedness with the local-bridge condition and discusses mutual neighbors' reputational role.

concepts.card: An efficiency wage can exceed the worker's reservation wage because pay changes behavior as well as cost. In the labor-discipline model, a more valuable job encourages effort and makes departure less attractive. A firm weighs the wage bill against the amount of effective work it obtains.

evidence.locator: Section 6.7 Wages, effort, and profits in the labour discipline model, Figure 6.6 and efficiency wages definition; Section 6.4 Employment rents
evidence.note: Checked explicitly as a model, not a universal wage law; distinct from a statutory minimum wage or a claim that raising any wage always pays for itself.

concepts.label: Efficiency wage
concepts.learning_takeaway: Pay above the reservation wage when the induced effort and reduced turnover can justify the extra wage cost.

relations.note: The model uses the value at risk from losing a job to connect wages with effort; this applies the employment-rent mechanism to wage setting.

concepts.card: Heating egg white unfolds proteins and allows them to connect with one another. The resulting network traps water, changing a flowing liquid into a firmer structure. Too much heating can make that network rubbery, showing how the same molecular process can produce very different cooking textures.

evidence.note: Exploratorium describes heat unfolding egg-white proteins, intermolecular bonds, trapped water and rubberiness after excessive heating.

concepts.label: Egg protein coagulation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why a liquid egg becomes a network that traps water as it is heated.

relations.note: Eggs can stabilize food in different ways: heat-linked protein networks versus yolk emulsifiers separating fat droplets.

concepts.card: The Eiffel Tower was originally intended to last only twenty years after its exhibition role. Scientific experiments, especially radio transmission, gave it a continuing technical purpose and helped preserve it. The structure’s history shows how repurposing infrastructure can change the value and lifetime of an engineering project.

evidence.locator: Eiffel Tower information : facts, height in feet, weight, ...; inspected passage indices 3, 7, 8 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-4; paragraph-8; paragraph-9
evidence.note: Radio experiments gave an originally temporary exhibition structure a continuing technical role.

concepts.label: Eiffel Tower
concepts.learning_takeaway: Radio experiments gave an originally temporary exhibition structure a continuing technical role.

relations.note: The official monument reference identifies the structure as a tower and documents its later communications use.

concepts.card: The Train scene in Philip Glass's Einstein on the Beach provides a concrete example of additive process. A five-chord progression gradually lengthens as each chord receives more subdivisions. Musical change comes from stretching the allotted duration of recurring harmonies rather than continuously introducing new chords.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 35.1 describes the named scene, five chords and added subdivisions; the claim is limited to that example, not the entire opera.

concepts.label: Einstein on the Beach
concepts.learning_takeaway: Observe a five-chord progression expanding through added subdivisions.

relations.note: The source explicitly recommends the Train scene as an example of additive growth in chord duration.

concepts.card: Wind sets surface water in motion, and friction passes some movement into deeper layers. Earth’s rotation deflects those layers as their speeds decrease, producing the turning pattern called an Ekman spiral. It describes changing current direction with depth, rather than a single uniform flow beneath the wind.

evidence.note: NOAA explains downward momentum transfer through friction, decreasing speed and successive Coriolis deflection.

concepts.label: Ekman spiral
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why a wind-driven current changes direction and weakens with depth.

relations.note: The Ekman spiral is a specific physical-oceanography pattern linking wind, friction and rotation.

concepts.card: The elaboration likelihood model distinguishes persuasion through evaluating a message's arguments from persuasion through peripheral cues. A buyer might compare safety evidence or respond to a celebrity endorsement. The model connects these routes with the audience's motivation and effort in processing the message.

evidence.note: Section 12.3, Figure 12.15 and central/peripheral route paragraphs, support argument evaluation, endorsement cues and processing effort; the card identifies a model rather than an exhaustive settled binary for all persuasion.

concepts.label: Elaboration likelihood model
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare evaluating an argument with responding to peripheral cues.

relations.note: The model concerns how a persuasive message is processed; foot-in-the-door concerns the sequence of requests. Their comparison distinguishes explanatory route from influence procedure.

concepts.card: A material’s elastic limit marks the stress beyond which unloading leaves permanent deformation. It is different from elastic modulus, which measures stiffness within the elastic range. A material can therefore deform easily yet recover substantially, or be stiff while tolerating less recoverable strain.

evidence.locator: 12.4 Elasticity and Plasticity; inspected passage indices 7, 8, 9 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1163709757929; fs-id1163709667701; fs-id1163713071188
evidence.note: Distinguish recoverable deformation from permanent shape change when stress exceeds a material’s elastic limit.

concepts.label: Elastic limit
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish recoverable deformation from permanent shape change when stress exceeds a material’s elastic limit.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies elastic modulus and elastic limit as different parameters governing elastic behavior.

concepts.card: Rocks beside a locked fault can deform as plate movement continues. When the fault slips, stored elastic strain is released and the rocks rebound toward a less-deformed shape. Elastic rebound theory connects gradual stress buildup with the sudden energy release of many earthquakes.

evidence.note: USGS’s Reid account describes progressive deformation, locked-fault strain and sudden release/rebound inferred from the 1906 earthquake.

concepts.label: Elastic rebound theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain earthquakes as sudden release of strain accumulated while rocks deform elastically.

relations.note: Slow-slip events provide a contrast to the abrupt strain-release picture, showing that fault displacement can unfold over different timescales.

concepts.card: Electrolysis uses an external electrical supply to drive a redox reaction that would not proceed spontaneously in that direction. Recharging a battery is one example: electrical work pushes its discharge chemistry backward, restoring some of the chemical state that can later deliver energy.

evidence.locator: 17.7 Electrolysis; inspected passage indices 6, 9, 12 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm133590080; fs-idm174200080; fs-idp152393360
evidence.note: An imposed voltage drives an otherwise nonspontaneous redox transformation.

concepts.label: Electrolysis
concepts.learning_takeaway: An imposed voltage drives an otherwise nonspontaneous redox transformation.

relations.note: The electrolysis section explicitly lists electroplating as a use of externally driven electrolytic cells.

concepts.card: Electrons possess intrinsic angular momentum called spin. Measuring its projection along a chosen axis gives two possible values, conventionally called spin up and spin down. These labels refer to the measurement axis; they do not describe a continuous range of classical orientations within the atom.

evidence.locator: 8.3 Electron Spin; inspected passage indices 6, 7, 8, 11 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1170902277768; fs-id1170902065387; fs-id1170903866542; fs-id1170903793199
evidence.note: Electrons have intrinsic half-integer angular momentum with two measured projections along a chosen axis.

concepts.label: Electron spin
concepts.learning_takeaway: Electrons have intrinsic half-integer angular momentum with two measured projections along a chosen axis.

relations.note: The source uses the Stern–Gerlach silver-atom result as evidence of the two electron-spin projections.

concepts.card: Electroplating deposits metal onto a conducting object by reducing dissolved metal ions at its surface. In one silver-plating setup, the object serves as cathode while a silver anode supplies metal. Current, voltage, and solution composition influence the coating’s quality.

evidence.locator: 17.7 Electrolysis; inspected passage indices 21, 22, 23, 24 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm182126896; fs-idm52313424; fs-idm104543584; fs-idm28358112
evidence.note: Reduction deposits a metal coating on a conducting cathode while process conditions control coating quality.

concepts.label: Electroplating
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reduction deposits a metal coating on a conducting cathode while process conditions control coating quality.

relations.note: The source explicitly describes electroplating as a use of electrolytic cells.

concepts.card: Elizabeth Peyton compares the immediacy of monotype with the dense revisions possible in her paintings. A plate’s workable pigment gives the print process a limited window for adjustment. Her account shows how choosing a medium also changes the time and manner in which an image can be developed.

evidence.locator: Peyton’s comparison of painting and monotype, lines 26–28
evidence.note: The interview discussion contrasts revised paintings with the monotype working window.

concepts.label: Elizabeth Peyton
concepts.learning_takeaway: Peyton contrasts densely revised paintings with the time-limited immediacy of monotype, where a plate can be manipulated only while its pigment remains workable.

relations.note: Peyton’s account explicitly discusses how this process affects her work.

concepts.card: Removing dams from the Elwha River restored connections between upstream habitat and the sea. The project reopened routes used by migrating fish and allowed sediment to move again. It demonstrates that river restoration can involve reconnecting processes across a whole watershed, not only repairing one riverbank.

evidence.note: NPS describes the dams’ barriers to fish and sediment and the restoration through dam removal.

concepts.label: Elwha River restoration
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how removing dams reconnects fish migration and sediment movement.

relations.note: Reconnecting fish movement and sediment transport makes the Elwha project an ecological case linking organisms with physical processes.

concepts.card: Emergent norm theory explains crowd behavior through guidelines that participants develop in unfamiliar situations. People bring prior expectations, interact, and may accept new ways of acting as circumstances change. The theory treats crowds as more than irrational masses, while leaving questions about how norms spread and gain acceptance.

evidence.note: Checked explanatory status and the source's unresolved acceptance/spread questions; the theory is not presented as a universally established causal law.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source explicitly makes changing and newly established norms central to the emergent-norm account of crowds.

concepts.label: Emergent norm theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain crowd conduct through locally developing guidelines in unfamiliar situations rather than assuming all crowds act irrationally.

relations.note: The source explicitly makes changing and newly established norms central to the emergent-norm account of crowds.

concepts.card: Employment rent is the value of keeping a job above the worker's next-best alternative, after considering its benefits and costs. Losing that surplus makes dismissal consequential. In the labor-discipline model, this can influence effort and retention, connecting wage setting to something beyond the minimum pay a worker would accept.

evidence.locator: Section 6.4 Employment rents; Section 6.7 Wages, effort, and profits in the labour discipline model
evidence.note: Checked job-versus-alternative surplus and model-based effort/retention channels; no blanket claim that fear of dismissal explains all work motivation.

concepts.label: Employment rent
concepts.learning_takeaway: Measure the value of holding a job above the worker's next-best alternative, making job loss consequential.

relations.note: CORE explicitly links employment rents to staying with a firm and incentives to provide effort, then develops the efficiency-wage model.

concepts.card: ENCODE, the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements, investigates the working parts of the genome. Its research includes epigenomic maps from different cell types, helping distinguish the DNA sequence a cell carries from the regions it uses. A shared genome can support different cellular patterns of activity.

evidence.locator: How are researchers exploring the epigenome?
evidence.note: NHGRI states that ENCODE catalogs working genomic parts and includes cell-type epigenomic maps; the same fact sheet explains differentiated cells and altered marks.

concepts.label: ENCODE
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish identifying functional genomic elements from merely obtaining a DNA sequence.

relations.note: Histone marks are one kind of epigenomic information that makes ENCODE’s cell-type maps useful for studying differential genome use.

concepts.card: The open cells exposed at wood’s end grain can draw adhesive away from a joint’s interface. Excessive penetration leaves voids and helps explain why a simple end-to-end butt bond can be weak. Joint geometry matters because increasing useful bonded area can change how loads pass between pieces.

evidence.locator: Density and Porosity, p. 10–6; End-Grain Joints, pp. 10–16 to 10–17
evidence.note: USDA describes end-grain porosity, overpenetration/bond-line voids and the increased area achieved by scarf/finger arrangements.

concepts.label: End-grain gluing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect end-grain porosity with adhesive overpenetration and weak butt-joint behavior.

relations.note: Adhesive penetration at end grain is a specific material-and-joint problem within woodworking.

concepts.card: Mitochondria retain their own genetic material, divide in a bacteria-like way and have surrounding membranes consistent with an engulfed ancestor. These clues support endosymbiotic origins from once-independent cells. The broad ancestry is well supported even while details of the earliest host–partner sequence remain debated.

evidence.note: OpenStax discusses mitochondrial genomes, fission-like division, membranes and unresolved ordering relative to the host nucleus.

concepts.label: Endosymbiotic theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use organelle genomes, division and membranes as evidence of ancestry from once-independent cells.

relations.note: Organelle similarities and shared ancestry offer a molecular/cellular setting for the ancestry reasoning introduced by biological homology.

concepts.card: Organisms leave genetic traces in water, sediment and other surroundings through shed cells and biological material. Environmental DNA sampling uses those traces to investigate which organisms may be present. It can reveal a species without requiring researchers to catch or directly observe that organism.

evidence.note: The USGS EDNA definition lists environmental samples and genetic material shed by organisms; this supports indirect detection.

concepts.label: Environmental DNA
concepts.learning_takeaway: Detect organisms through genetic traces in environmental samples without having to capture them.

relations.note: Metabarcoding is one way to analyze mixed environmental DNA for multiple species.

concepts.card: Cutting an apple exposes its tissues to oxygen, allowing enzymes to drive browning reactions. Changing conditions such as acidity can slow the process. The color change therefore connects damage to plant cells with chemical activity, rather than being explained solely by the fruit drying out.

evidence.note: ACS’s explanatory section connects exposed apple tissue, oxygen, enzymes and the slowing effect of acidity.

concepts.label: Enzymatic browning
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a cut fruit surface, oxygen and enzyme activity with a change in color.

relations.note: Both topics concern food-quality changes mediated by enzymes, while acidifying an exposed surface and heat-blanching before freezing are different interventions.

concepts.card: Epistemic closure asks whether competent deduction preserves knowledge. On a common formulation, someone who retains knowledge of a premise and comes to believe its consequence by competent deduction knows that consequence. This is not a claim that people automatically know every implication of everything they know.

evidence.note: SEP section 1 rejects unqualified entailment closure and gives the competent-deduction principle with continued premise knowledge; the card presents a formulation within a disputed debate.

concepts.label: Epistemic closure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Investigate whether competent deduction from known premises preserves knowledge.

relations.note: Knowledge preservation under inference is a specific epistemological question; the closure entry and the broad account of cognitive success support this placement without implying universal acceptance of closure.

concepts.card: A safe belief would not easily have been false: in nearby possible circumstances where the person holds it, it remains true. This proposed condition on knowledge differs from asking what the person would believe if the claim were false. What counts as nearby is itself contested.

evidence.note: SEP section 5.2 gives the nearby-worlds formulation and discusses vagueness of nearness; the card avoids treating safety as a settled necessary or sufficient condition.

concepts.label: Epistemic safety
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ask whether a belief could easily have been false in nearby circumstances.

relations.note: The source explicitly distinguishes safety's nearby true beliefs from sensitivity's response to falsity, noting that the two modal conditions are not equivalent.

concepts.card: A sensitive belief tracks a counterfactual question: if the claim were false, would the person stop believing it? A mirage-based belief may fail because the same appearance would persuade without water. Sensitivity has been proposed as a condition on knowledge, but its adequacy is disputed.

evidence.note: SEP section 5.1 states the counterfactual and desert-water example, then discusses limitations; the card does not equate sensitivity with safety or endorse it as sufficient for knowledge.

concepts.label: Epistemic sensitivity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ask whether someone would stop believing a claim if it were false.

relations.note: Section 5.2 explicitly contrasts sensitivity with safety and explains why counterfactual contraposition does not make them equivalent.

concepts.card: Epistemicism treats vagueness as a limit of knowledge rather than an absence of precise boundaries. There is, on this view, an exact cutoff between a heap and a non-heap, although we cannot identify it. Statements remain true or false even when their status is inaccessible.

evidence.note: SEP section 3.2 describes hidden sharp boundaries and preservation of bivalence; on this view makes the controversial account explicit rather than reporting it as a discovered linguistic fact.

concepts.label: Epistemicism about vagueness
concepts.learning_takeaway: Consider the view that vague categories have sharp boundaries we cannot know.

relations.note: The article presents epistemicism among responses to sorites, preserving classical bivalence while denying that every adjacent pair must share the same status.

concepts.card: Epistrophe repeats a word or phrase at the ends of successive units. Different statements arrive at the same verbal destination, giving their sequence a recurring point of emphasis. Its placement distinguishes it from anaphora, where the repetition appears at the beginning instead.

evidence.note: End repetition is contrasted with anaphora in the glossary.

concepts.label: Epistrophe
concepts.learning_takeaway: Repeating words at successive phrase or stanza endings gives the sequence a recurring point of arrival.

relations.note: The two devices distinguish where repeated wording occurs.

concepts.card: Equal-interval classification divides an attribute’s numeric range into classes of the same width. It emphasizes comparable steps in value, but does not guarantee equal numbers of places in each class. A strongly uneven dataset may therefore leave some map classes sparsely populated.

evidence.note: Equal-width intervals and uneven class occupancy follow the stated method.

concepts.label: Equal-interval map classification
concepts.learning_takeaway: Dividing an attribute’s numeric range into equal-width intervals emphasizes value differences rather than equalizing the number of mapped places.

relations.note: Equal-width numerical classes are a specific decision in representing attributes on maps.
Equal-width values and equal-count classes solve different classification problems.

concepts.card: Wood exchanges moisture with the air around it. Its equilibrium moisture content is the point at which it is neither gaining nor losing moisture under those conditions. Because temperature and relative humidity matter, wood does not have one universally correct moisture level for every room or season.

evidence.note: USDA Chapter 4 defines EMC by no net gain/loss and relates it to surrounding temperature and relative humidity.

concepts.label: Equilibrium moisture content of wood
concepts.learning_takeaway: Relate a wood component’s stable moisture level to its surrounding air rather than one universally dry state.

relations.note: Sorption hysteresis adds moisture-history dependence to the environmental conditions that determine a wood specimen’s EMC.

concepts.card: Eric Mazur's work on Peer Instruction helped redesign introductory physics lectures around students' reasoning. In the reported courses, learners answered conceptual questions individually, discussed their explanations, and voted again. The case makes a teaching method inspectable through its sequence of activities rather than a lecturer's reputation alone.

evidence.note: Checked coauthorship and course design; did not attribute every result solely to discussion because other course elements also changed.

concepts.label: Eric Mazur
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how a physicist's course redesign made individual commitments and peer reasoning part of lectures.

relations.note: The coauthored paper directly documents Mazur's implementation of Peer Instruction and describes its question/discussion/revote sequence.

concepts.card: For a small object launched outward from an isolated spherical body, escape velocity is the minimum initial speed that permits escape without further thrust. Ignoring atmospheric drag, it depends on the body’s mass and starting distance, not the projectile’s mass in this ideal model.

evidence.locator: 13.3 Gravitational Potential Energy and Total Energy; inspected passage indices 27, 30, 42, 46 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1168326809119; fs-id1168329319252; fs-id1168329151238; fs-id1168329060634
evidence.note: Under ideal gravitational assumptions, sufficient initial speed permits escape without further propulsion.

concepts.label: Escape velocity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Under ideal gravitational assumptions, sufficient initial speed permits escape without further propulsion.

relations.note: The source derives escape speed by comparing kinetic energy with gravitational potential energy.

concepts.card: Eternalism holds that past and future objects exist as well as present ones. An object can belong to reality without occupying the present moment. The disagreement with presentism concerns what exists, rather than whether past events are now occurring or can presently be observed.

evidence.locator: 6 Presentism, Eternalism, and the Growing Block Theory
evidence.note: SEP Time section 6 separates ontological existence from temporal location and includes past and future objects. The card avoids an extra spatial analogy and does not claim past events are happening at the present time.

concepts.label: Eternalism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish existing from being present when considering past and future objects.

relations.note: Section 6 explicitly defines eternalism as a way of opposing presentism's restriction of existence to present objects.

concepts.card: An ideal straight, slender column can lose stability and bend sideways under axial compression. Euler’s pinned-end model makes the critical load proportional to elastic modulus and second moment of area, and inversely proportional to length squared. The result assumes linear elasticity and correctly specified end conditions.

evidence.locator: Chapter 8: Beam Bending, Buckling, and Torsion; inspected passage indices 225, 230, 231, 236, 237, 238, 239, 240, 241, 242 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-226; paragraph-231; paragraph-232; paragraph-237; paragraph-238; paragraph-239; paragraph-240; paragraph-241; paragraph-242; paragraph-243
evidence.note: An ideal slender elastic column loses stability at a load controlled by stiffness, length, and end constraints.

concepts.label: Euler column buckling
concepts.learning_takeaway: An ideal slender elastic column loses stability at a load controlled by stiffness, length, and end constraints.

relations.note: The source’s Euler critical-load formula explicitly depends on the cross-section’s second moment of area.

concepts.card: For a polyhedron with sphere-like topology, the number of vertices minus edges plus faces equals two. This is the genus-zero case of the Euler characteristic. The condition matters: a surface with a handle changes the topological count, so the formula is not universal for all polyhedra.

evidence.locator: Polyhedral Formula -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 3 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-4
evidence.note: States the vertex-edge-face formula for genus-zero polyhedra.

evidence.locator: Euler Characteristic -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 3 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-4
evidence.note: Explicitly connects the polyhedral formula with the genus-zero Euler characteristic.

concepts.label: Euler’s polyhedron formula
concepts.learning_takeaway: For a sphere-like polyhedron, vertices minus edges plus faces equals two.

relations.note: The Euler-characteristic reference explicitly identifies the polyhedral formula as its genus-zero special case.

concepts.card: Sweat cools the body when it evaporates from the skin and carries heat into the surrounding air. Producing liquid alone is not the whole cooling mechanism. The response works alongside changes in skin blood flow as part of the body’s feedback control of temperature.

evidence.note: The homeostasis passage links increased sweating, skin blood flow and heat removed as sweat evaporates.

concepts.label: Evaporative cooling by sweating
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why sweat cools the body when it evaporates from the skin.

relations.note: Sweating is an effector response in the cited temperature-regulation feedback example.

concepts.card: A feature’s current job need not be the reason it originally evolved. Exaptation describes a trait co-opted for a use that did not originally shape it by natural selection. Feathers possibly selected for insulation before flight illustrate the distinction between origin and later function.

evidence.note: Berkeley defines co-option and presents insulation-first feathers as a possible historical example.

concepts.label: Exaptation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a trait’s present use from the selective context in which it arose.

relations.note: Comparing exaptation with convergence separates a change of function in an inherited feature from the independent evolution of similar functions.

concepts.card: A researcher's expectations can influence how ambiguous observations are scored. Someone who knows which participants received an intervention may interpret borderline responses in its favor. Concealing group assignments from the scorer helps reduce this route of bias, without guaranteeing that every other source of error disappears.

evidence.note: Section 2.3's test-scoring example motivates observer blinding; helps reduce avoids the textbook's stronger implication that blinding alone removes all alternative explanations.

concepts.label: Experimenter expectancy bias
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how a researcher's expectations can shape interpretation of ambiguous responses.

relations.note: The source introduces researcher blinding to address experimenter expectations and then defines double blinding as concealing assignment from participants as well.

concepts.card: The exponential distribution models waiting times between events in a positive constant-rate Poisson process. Its probability density decreases as the waiting time grows. It is memoryless: having already waited does not change the distribution of the additional time until the next event.

evidence.locator: Exponential Distribution -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 4 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-5
evidence.note: Model waiting times between events of a constant-rate Poisson process with a continuous memoryless law.

concepts.label: Exponential distribution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Model waiting times between events of a constant-rate Poisson process with a continuous memoryless law.

relations.note: The source derives exponential waiting times from the Poisson event model.

concepts.card: An eye is an internal space in a connected Go group. Two genuine, separate eyes can keep a group safe: an opponent cannot fill both in one move, and occupying the first would be self-capture rather than capturing the surrounding stones.

evidence.locator: Life and death and the concept of eyes
evidence.note: BGA Life and death and self-capture examples support two-eye safety; genuine eyes prevents confusing superficial holes with the protected spaces in the rule explanation.

concepts.label: Eyes in Go
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why two separate internal spaces protect a group from capture.

relations.note: The guide explains eye-based survival through internal liberties and the prohibition on noncapturing self-capture.

concepts.card: A monatomic face-centered cubic structure places atoms at cube corners and face centers. Shared boundaries leave four atoms per conventional cell, with twelve nearest neighbors around each atom. The arrangement can also be described as cubic close packing, using an ABC layer sequence.

evidence.locator: 10.6 Lattice Structures in Crystalline Solids; inspected passage indices 31, 32 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idp30613264; fs-idp4268832
evidence.note: Corner and face atoms form a close-packed cubic structure with four atoms per conventional cell.

concepts.label: Face-centered cubic structure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Corner and face atoms form a close-packed cubic structure with four atoms per conventional cell.

relations.note: The source explicitly contrasts ABC cubic close packing with AB hexagonal close packing.

concepts.card: Faded worked examples gradually turn a demonstrated solution into a problem the learner completes. Early steps may remain visible while later steps are removed. As expertise develops, learners supply more of the solution themselves, creating a transition from studying a model to carrying out the procedure independently.

evidence.note: Checked direction of fading and expertise-dependent increase in responsibility; not merely shortening an explanation arbitrarily.

concepts.label: Faded worked examples
concepts.learning_takeaway: Gradually remove later solution steps so learners supply more of the solution as expertise develops.

relations.note: The guide explicitly describes fading by retaining early steps and requiring progressively more later steps from learners.

concepts.card: Fahrenheit 451 follows a book-burning fireman whose allegiance changes as he begins reading. Its major sections end in increasingly expansive fires, while a community of readers preserves books through memory. An editorial reading connects these elements with the vulnerability of cultural memory.

evidence.note: Fireman’s change, three escalating fires and memorizing community are described.

concepts.label: Fahrenheit 451
concepts.learning_takeaway: The book-burning fireman’s changing allegiance is structured through expanding fires and a counter-community that preserves books by memory.

relations.note: The NEA guide compares imagined worlds as a means of exposing familiar social flaws.

concepts.card: Fail-safe defaults make lack of permission the starting point for access decisions. A system grants access only when a rule explicitly permits it. If a permission rule is missing or incomplete, the design tends to deny access instead of accidentally creating an unprotected opening.

evidence.note: Checked allow-by-rule versus exclusion-list design; fail-safe here concerns authorization defaults, not every conceivable hardware failure.

concepts.label: Fail-safe defaults
concepts.learning_takeaway: Deny access unless a permission rule explicitly allows it so missing rules tend to fail closed.

relations.note: The protection paper explicitly names permission-based default denial as a security design principle.

concepts.card: Network Rail describes a fail-safe response in which a failed track circuit normally indicates occupancy. Trains can be stopped even when none is present because reliable clearance is lost. This favors a restrictive signal over uninterrupted service while the section’s status is uncertain.

evidence.locator: Track circuits explained; inspected passage indices 8, 9, 10, 12 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-9; paragraph-10; paragraph-11; paragraph-13
evidence.note: Many circuit failures are treated as occupied track, prioritizing safe train separation over uninterrupted service.

concepts.label: Fail-safe track-circuit signalling
concepts.learning_takeaway: Many circuit failures are treated as occupied track, prioritizing safe train separation over uninterrupted service.

relations.note: The operator explains this fail-safe occupied response as a behavior of track circuits.

concepts.card: In the fake-barn case, Henry happens to see a real barn in a landscape full of convincing facades. His belief is true and apparently justified, yet could easily have been mistaken. The example challenges whether accurate perception alone guarantees knowledge in a systematically deceptive environment.

evidence.note: SEP section 4's Barn County passage supplies Henry, the real barn and facades; apparently and challenges preserve the evaluative character of the knowledge verdict.

concepts.label: Fake-barn case
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how a deceptive environment can undermine otherwise accurate perception.

relations.note: The source presents Barn County as a challenge to the no-false-lemmas repair because Henry's belief need not involve inference from a false premise.

concepts.card: Fangyan is a Han-era collection of regional words associated with the scholar Yang Xiong. By recording different expressions and pronunciations across places, it preserved evidence about linguistic diversity. Later scholars used that material to infer earlier dialect groupings, showing how a vocabulary work can become historical evidence.

evidence.locator: §10.5, Dialectology: Then and now, Yang Xiong paragraph
evidence.note: Checked regional vocabulary, Yang Xiong attribution, and later scholarly use; no unverified precise date or exhaustive dialect classification is asserted.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The methods chapter describes later inferences about earlier dialect groups from Fangyan, linking the particular work to historical language study.

concepts.label: Fangyan
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how a Han-era collection of regional words preserves evidence used to infer earlier dialect groupings.

relations.note: The methods chapter describes later inferences about earlier dialect groups from Fangyan, linking the particular work to historical language study.

concepts.card: Faraday’s laws connect electrical charge with the amount of material transformed during electrolysis. Charge gives the number of transferred electrons; the balanced electrode reaction gives how many electrons each converted ion requires. Equal charge can therefore deposit different amounts of different metals.

evidence.locator: 17.7 Electrolysis; inspected passage indices 27, 28, 29 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm90272368; fs-idm90332432; fs-idm371971168
evidence.note: Convert transferred electric charge into deposited material using the reaction’s electron stoichiometry.

concepts.label: Faraday’s laws of electrolysis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Convert transferred electric charge into deposited material using the reaction’s electron stoichiometry.

relations.note: The electrolysis section derives stoichiometric material calculations from the charge transferred in the electrode reaction.

concepts.card: John Ashbery’s Farm Implements and Rutabagas in a Landscape places Popeye characters inside a sestina. Recurring end-words produce comic surprises while domestic unease persists beneath them. The poem demonstrates how a demanding inherited form can accommodate cartoon familiarity, melancholy and playful resistance to its own constraints.

evidence.note: The glossary describes the Popeye cast, comic recurrence and domestic pathos.

concepts.label: Farm Implements and Rutabagas in a Landscape
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ashbery places Popeye characters in a sestina whose repeated words produce comic surprises alongside domestic unease.

relations.note: The glossary names the poem as a playful use of the sestina form.

concepts.card: Under fixed conditions, each successive half-life of a first-order reaction removes half the reactant still present. The half-life depends on the rate constant, not the starting concentration. Equal time intervals therefore produce equal fractional losses rather than equal amounts disappearing.

evidence.locator: 12.4 Integrated Rate Laws; inspected passage indices 70, 72, 74, 75 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm99562880; fs-idp162624; fs-idp123084256; fs-idm124479504
evidence.note: First-order half-life depends on the rate constant rather than the initial reactant concentration.

concepts.label: First-order reaction half-life
concepts.learning_takeaway: First-order half-life depends on the rate constant rather than the initial reactant concentration.

relations.note: The integrated-rate section explicitly contrasts the concentration-independent first-order half-life with other orders.

concepts.card: In a first-price sealed-bid auction, bidders submit offers privately, the highest bidder wins, and the winner pays their own bid. The bid therefore helps determine both the chance of winning and the payment if successful. That payment rule differs from a second-price auction.

evidence.note: Checked sealed submission, highest-bid winner and own payment; no unqualified optimal-bidding formula or revenue comparison is asserted.

concepts.label: First-price sealed-bid auction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Submit bids privately and let the highest bidder win while paying their own bid.

relations.note: The Yale lecture directly compares highest-bid allocation with own-bid versus second-highest-bid payment rules.

concepts.card: A flat-felled seam wraps one fabric edge within a folded edge and secures the assembly flat with stitching. The enclosed raw edges and additional stitching produce a durable finish familiar from jeans and other hard-wearing garments. Its flattened construction distinguishes it from a French seam’s enclosed ridge.

evidence.note: Supports folded enclosure, stitching flat, durability and jeans use.
Supports the contrast with enclosing one seam inside another.

concepts.label: Flat-felled seam
concepts.learning_takeaway: Create an enclosed-edge seam that is folded down and secured flat with visible stitching.

relations.note: The connection compares two genuinely different enclosed-edge constructions rather than counting synonymous finishes.

concepts.card: Florence Nightingale used mortality data to argue for changes in military health care after the Crimean War. Her campaign involved checking inconsistent records and communicating results through writing and the Rose Diagram. The example joins data reconstruction with making statistical evidence understandable to a broader audience.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Rose Diagram; mortality dataset reconstruction
evidence.note: The historical research article describes seven months of dataset checking, the sanitary-reform campaign and collaboration with Martineau using prose and the Rose Diagram.

concepts.label: Florence Nightingale
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how checking mortality records and explaining them visually supported sanitary reform.

relations.note: Using population mortality evidence to campaign for sanitary reform is a specific historical example of public-health reasoning.

concepts.card: Focalization concerns how a narrative selects or restricts information in relation to what characters or narrators can know. It differs from identifying who speaks. A story may remain close to one character’s knowledge even when someone else supplies the narrative voice.

evidence.note: Information restriction and separation from narrative voice are explained.

concepts.label: Focalization
concepts.learning_takeaway: The information a narrative reveals can be limited by a character’s knowledge without making that character the speaker.

relations.note: Narrator participation and limits on available information are separate analytical questions.

concepts.card: FOIA segregability means an exempt passage does not necessarily justify withholding an entire record. Federal agencies must consider partial disclosure and release reasonably separable nonexempt portions after redaction. The practical question is what can still be disclosed without revealing the information protected by a valid exemption.

evidence.note: 5 USC 552(a)(8)(A)(ii) and the final paragraph of (b) require reasonable segregation and partial release; reasonably and valid exemption preserve limits rather than promising every document has releasable fragments.

concepts.label: FOIA segregability
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why an exempt passage need not justify withholding the entire record.

relations.note: The statute itself imposes partial-disclosure and segregation duties within FOIA, tying the mechanism directly to the federal records-access regime.

concepts.card: The foot-in-the-door technique begins with a small request before asking for something larger. In Freedman and Fraser's study, people who first accepted a small sign or petition were more likely to accept a large yard sign. This was an experimental tendency, not guaranteed compliance.

evidence.note: Section 12.3 describes the 1966 sign/petition comparison; the final sentence preserves probabilistic scope and avoids presenting a guaranteed method of controlling another person.

concepts.label: Foot-in-the-door technique
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore the qualified finding that a small request can precede increased agreement to a larger one.

relations.note: Compare a request-sequencing procedure with a model of message processing. Both concern persuasion, but the cited section does not make one an instance of the other.

concepts.card: Passing in Othello is compulsory when you cannot legally outflank an opposing disc, but forbidden when a legal move is available. Your opponent may therefore move twice in succession. If neither player can move, the game ends even when some squares remain empty.

evidence.note: World Othello rules 2 and 8 support mandatory pass, prohibition of voluntary pass and early ending; no claim that every pass immediately ends play.

concepts.label: Forced passing in Othello
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish being unable to move from choosing to pass strategically.

relations.note: The official game rules define passing entirely through legal outflanking moves.

concepts.card: A formal organization specifies official relationships, responsibilities, and reporting lines. Its chart shows how work is supposed to be coordinated and who is accountable for particular duties. That planned structure may differ from the informal network of people others actually consult to get things done.

evidence.note: Checked planned versus emergent relationships; formal structure is not treated as a complete description of everyday behavior.

concepts.label: Formal organization
concepts.learning_takeaway: Specify official roles, reporting lines, and responsibilities so work has an explicit coordination structure.

relations.note: The source explicitly contrasts officially defined formal relationships with emergent informal ties and their practical influence.

concepts.card: Formative assessment uses evidence during learning to improve what happens next. An instructor may identify a misconception and adjust teaching, while a learner redirects study. The defining feature is this feedback purpose: even information from a final exam can later be used formatively in another course.

evidence.note: Checked ongoing feedback and later formative use of summative information; low stakes is typical rather than a necessary definition.

evidence.locator: What is it?; distinction from teaching for mastery
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Mastery learning uses checks and corrective support to guide progression, providing a specific comparison with formative assessment's broader feedback purpose.

concepts.label: Formative assessment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use evidence during learning to adjust teaching and study, with purpose mattering more than a test's format.

relations.note: Mastery learning uses checks and corrective support to guide progression, providing a specific comparison with formative assessment's broader feedback purpose.

concepts.card: The Forth railway bridge uses a double-cantilever arrangement to carry trains across an estuary. Its design followed abandonment of an earlier scheme after the Tay Bridge collapse. Large steel spans and shipping clearance show how a railway crossing must also accommodate the waterway beneath it.

evidence.locator:
Firth of Forth Railway Bridge | ASCE
; inspected passage indices 6, 9, 10 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-7; paragraph-10; paragraph-11
evidence.note: A double-cantilever design carried railway spans across the Forth after an earlier proposal was abandoned.

concepts.label: Forth Bridge
concepts.learning_takeaway: A double-cantilever design carried railway spans across the Forth after an earlier proposal was abandoned.

relations.note: ASCE identifies the structure as a railway bridge and explicitly describes its double-cantilever design.

concepts.card: Forward secrecy limits the damage from later compromise of a long-term key. In an appropriate protocol mode, revealing that key after a handshake does not reveal the earlier session key. The guarantee depends on conditions such as erasing session secrets; it does not cover every pre-shared-key mode.

evidence.locator: Appendix E.1, Forward secret with respect to long-term keys
evidence.note: Checked compromise timing, erased session-key condition, and PSK-only exception; secrecy is not promised after the session key itself is exposed.

concepts.label: Forward secrecy
concepts.learning_takeaway: Keep earlier session keys safe after later long-term-key compromise, subject to the protocol's mode and key-erasure assumptions.

relations.note: RFC 8446 Appendix E explicitly defines forward secrecy relative to long-term keys and names a PSK mode that lacks it.

concepts.card: Foundation species help build the physical setting of a community. Kelp forms underwater forests, while reef-building corals create habitats used by many other organisms. Their importance comes from shaping the environment that supports the community, rather than simply being another species within it.

evidence.note: OpenStax’s Foundation Species passage identifies kelp forests and coral habitat construction as community-shaping examples.

concepts.label: Foundation species
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect habitat structure supplied by organisms with the communities that depend on it.

relations.note: Habitat construction by foundation species can be compared with ecosystem engineering, while avoiding an assertion that the two categories are identical.

concepts.card: When a new population begins with only a few colonists, its genetic frequencies can differ markedly from the source population. The founder effect arises because those founders are a small sample. Their descendants may inherit unusual frequencies without the variants offering any local advantage.

evidence.note: The Berkeley founder-effect section describes colonization by a few individuals and altered genetic variation/frequencies through sampling.

concepts.label: Founder effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how a few colonists can establish unrepresentative genetic frequencies.

relations.note: Founding a population from a small sample is a specific demographic route to drift, distinct from survival after a population crash.

concepts.card: Foxconn appears in The Economy's historical iPhone example as a contract assembler within a wider supply chain. Components came from several other firms and countries, while Apple coordinated the product. The case distinguishes assembling a finished device from producing all its parts or owning the consumer-facing product.

evidence.note: Checked case framing and component/assembly distinction; did not assert that Foxconn currently assembles every Apple device or that assembly captures all product value.

concepts.label: Foxconn
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how contract assembly fits into a larger value chain whose components and product ownership sit elsewhere.

relations.note: The inspected textbook directly relates Foxconn's assembly role to Apple's historical product supply chain.

concepts.card: Fracture toughness describes a material’s resistance to extension of an existing crack. In linear-elastic fracture mechanics, crack growth can become unstable when stress intensity reaches the appropriate critical value. This connects material resistance with flaw size and loading, rather than treating applied stress alone as sufficient.

evidence.locator: Chapter 10: Creep, Fracture, and Fatigue; inspected passage indices 142, 143, 144, 145 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-143; paragraph-144; paragraph-145; paragraph-146
evidence.note: Compare crack-tip loading with a material’s resistance to crack extension.

concepts.label: Fracture toughness
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare crack-tip loading with a material’s resistance to crack extension.

relations.note: The source states the fracture condition by comparing applied stress intensity with the material’s critical toughness.

concepts.card: Frame alignment connects a movement's interpretations and goals with potential participants or allied groups. Shared concerns may be bridged, emphasized, extended, or transformed to support cooperation. The concept focuses on how people understand an issue and their relationship to it, rather than only counting the movement's resources.

evidence.note: Checked the four named alignment processes and audience/goal connection; not reduced to organizational merger alone or asserted as a guarantee of recruitment.

concepts.label: Frame alignment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a movement's interpretations and goals with prospective participants or allied groups to support coordinated action.

relations.note: Comparing interpretive alignment with resource acquisition distinguishes two ways the source analyzes collective organizing.

concepts.card: The Framingham Heart Study follows community participants over time, with repeated examinations and later generations joining the research. It connected factors such as blood pressure and cholesterol with future cardiovascular disease. Its long view shows how risk can be studied before illness becomes apparent.

evidence.note: NHLBI describes repeated cohort examinations, multigenerational participation and identification of cardiovascular risk factors including pressure and cholesterol.

concepts.label: Framingham Heart Study
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how repeated examinations across generations established patterns of cardiovascular risk.

relations.note: Population follow-up can identify prevention targets, linking this specific study with public health’s community-level focus.

concepts.card: The US Freedom of Information Act lets people request existing federal agency records, subject to specified exemptions. It does not require an agency to create new records, conduct research or answer a questionnaire. The right therefore concerns access to recorded information rather than a general government research service.

evidence.locator: What is the FOIA?; What can I ask for?
evidence.note: FOIA.gov's definition and What can I ask for? support agency-record scope, exemptions and no new-research obligation; people avoids incorrectly limiting requesters to US citizens.

concepts.label: Freedom of Information Act (United States)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand access to existing federal agency records subject to specified exemptions.

relations.note: FOIA concerns access to agency records; the Sunshine Act concerns observation of covered agency meetings. Their comparison distinguishes two transparency mechanisms with different scopes and exceptions.

concepts.card: A French cleat hangs a fixture using two matching beveled strips: one attached to the wall and one to the object. Their opposing slopes engage to carry the load while allowing a flexible storage layout. Secure anchoring and suitable load distribution remain part of the system.

evidence.note: Lee Valley’s workshop account describes wall strips, opposing fixture bevels, movable storage and added cleats for heavier objects.

concepts.label: French cleat
concepts.learning_takeaway: Support a removable wall fixture with two mating beveled strips.

relations.note: The paired wooden strips apply shaped joinery to mounting movable fixtures rather than permanently joining board ends.

concepts.card: A French seam encloses raw fabric edges inside a second seam. The first pass joins the fabric with wrong sides together; after turning, another pass hides that initial allowance. This creates a tidy enclosed finish, useful when exposed edges would show through a sheer fabric.

evidence.note: BERNINA’s original tutorial defines two-part edge enclosure, wrong-sides-first sequencing and usefulness for sheer fabrics.

concepts.label: French seam
concepts.learning_takeaway: Enclose raw fabric edges inside a second seam rather than leaving them exposed to fray.

relations.note: Both enclose raw edges, but a French seam contains the first seam within a second while a flat-felled seam is secured down flat.

concepts.card: Fresco a secco applies paint to a dry plaster surface. That distinction separates it from buon fresco, where painting takes place while the plaster is wet. Comparing the methods shows why the condition of the wall matters alongside the pigments and the image itself.

evidence.note: Dry-versus-wet plaster distinction is explicit.

concepts.label: Fresco a secco
concepts.learning_takeaway: Fresco a secco applies paint to a dry plaster surface, contrasting with buon fresco on wet plaster.

relations.note: The National Gallery distinguishes dry-plaster painting as another wall-painting method.
The glossary directly contrasts painting on dry plaster with painting on wet plaster.

concepts.card: Functional fixedness restricts thinking about an object to its usual purpose. In Duncker's candle problem, seeing a box only as a container can obscure its use as a candle support. Overcoming that restriction requires reconsidering what the available materials can do.

evidence.note: Section 7.3, Duncker problem and Figure 7.10, support the box's alternative use; the prose avoids repeating the source's apparent typo about using fixedness to overcome the problem.

concepts.label: Functional fixedness
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how an object's conventional use can hide an alternative solution.

relations.note: The source expressly describes functional fixedness as a kind of mental set: a familiar use constrains the attempted solution.

concepts.card: A functional organizational structure groups people by expertise, such as production, marketing, or finance. It supports specialization and clear reporting within departments. The same boundaries can create silos, making cross-department decisions slower or encouraging units to compete for resources instead of coordinating their work.

evidence.note: Checked specialization/reporting benefits and coordination costs; these are potential tendencies, not guaranteed outcomes in every firm.

concepts.label: Functional organizational structure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Group specialists by expertise while recognizing the risk that departmental boundaries hinder coordination.

relations.note: The source contrasts expertise-based departments with divisions that contain several functions around products or markets.

concepts.card: Gaia repeatedly measured stellar positions, distances, motions, and brightness to construct a detailed three-dimensional view of the Milky Way. Its catalog treats stars as moving objects rather than fixed points on a sky map, providing evidence for the Galaxy’s structure, origin, and history.

evidence.locator: ESA; inspected passage indices 7, 8, 10 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-8; paragraph-9; paragraph-11
evidence.note: Repeated positional measurements build a three-dimensional map of stellar distances and motions.

concepts.label: Gaia mission
concepts.learning_takeaway: Repeated positional measurements build a three-dimensional map of stellar distances and motions.

relations.note: ESA explicitly connects Gaia’s positional and velocity measurements with the reconstruction of stellar motions.

concepts.card: In the gambler’s ruin model, two players transfer one unit after each independent fair coin toss until one has everything. With finite starting funds, absorption eventually occurs with probability one. The player starting with less has a greater chance of losing everything despite fair odds.

evidence.locator: Gambler's Ruin -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 3 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-4
evidence.note: Even a fair finite-bankroll game eventually absorbs one player, with ruin odds depending on starting capital.

concepts.label: Gambler’s ruin
concepts.learning_takeaway: Even a fair finite-bankroll game eventually absorbs one player, with ruin odds depending on starting capital.

relations.note: The changing bankroll is a one-dimensional random walk stopped at either boundary; the source’s unit transfers supply the model.

concepts.card: A backgammon loser who has not removed any checkers suffers a gammon, worth twice the doubling cube's value under standard scoring. If that loser also has a checker on the bar or in the winner's home board, the loss is instead a triple-value backgammon.

evidence.note: USBGF Gammons and Backgammons supports the two scoring conditions; standard scoring qualification leaves room for the separately selected optional Jacoby rule.

concepts.label: Gammon
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why losing before bearing off any checker doubles the game's value.

relations.note: USBGF explicitly describes Jacoby as an optional rule changing when gammon and backgammon multipliers count.

concepts.card: For a compact smooth two-dimensional surface without boundary, the Gauss–Bonnet theorem links total Gaussian curvature to its Euler characteristic: the curvature integral equals two pi times that number. Changing the shape can redistribute curvature while leaving this topologically determined total unchanged.

evidence.locator: Gauss-Bonnet Formula -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 4, 5 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-5; paragraph-6
evidence.note: For a compact boundaryless surface, total Gaussian curvature is fixed by its Euler characteristic.

concepts.label: Gauss–Bonnet theorem
concepts.learning_takeaway: For a compact boundaryless surface, total Gaussian curvature is fixed by its Euler characteristic.

relations.note: The source explicitly equates total Gaussian curvature with two pi times the Euler characteristic.

concepts.card: Gaussian curvature is the product of the two principal curvatures at a surface point. Matching nonzero signs give a positive product; opposite signs give a negative one. This is an intrinsic geometric quantity, independent of the coordinates chosen to describe the surface.

evidence.locator: Gaussian Curvature -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 13, 21, 23 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-14; paragraph-22; paragraph-24
evidence.note: A surface has an intrinsic curvature determined by its two principal curvatures.

concepts.label: Gaussian curvature
concepts.learning_takeaway: A surface has an intrinsic curvature determined by its two principal curvatures.

relations.note: The Gauss–Bonnet formula relates integrated Gaussian curvature to Euler characteristic.

concepts.card: Some inherited disorders appear earlier or become more severe in successive generations. Genetic anticipation can arise when unstable repeated DNA sequences expand during transmission. Differences between relatives alone do not establish it: researchers consider the disorder’s genetic cause and patterns across several generations.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus connects anticipation with earlier/more severe manifestations and repeat expansion, while warning that ordinary variation among relatives has other causes.

concepts.label: Genetic anticipation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect expanding repeat sequences with earlier or more severe inherited disease in some families.

relations.note: Contrasting anticipation with variable expressivity prevents ordinary differences among affected relatives from being mistaken for a generational expansion pattern.

concepts.card: Nearby positions on a chromosome tend to travel together from parent to offspring. Recombination during the formation of eggs or sperm can separate them, but closer markers are less likely to be split. Genetic linkage turns patterns of joint inheritance into clues about chromosome organization.

evidence.note: NHGRI linkage describes neighboring loci and recombination-dependent joint inheritance; the map definition links proximity to co-inheritance.

concepts.label: Genetic linkage
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect physical proximity on a chromosome with the likelihood of joint inheritance.

relations.note: Linkage mapping uses the co-inheritance pattern described by genetic linkage to infer marker order.

concepts.card: Genetic linkage mapping follows how markers are inherited together across generations. Markers that are rarely separated by recombination are generally closer together on a chromosome. Comparing inheritance patterns lets researchers infer relative order and position, rather than directly reading a physical sequence of DNA bases.

evidence.note: The inspected NHGRI Genetic Map definition specifically identifies linkage maps, co-inheritance, relative marker order and location.

concepts.label: Genetic linkage mapping
concepts.learning_takeaway: Infer marker order from joint inheritance rather than directly measuring physical DNA length.

relations.note: This mapping method applies the proximity-dependent co-inheritance relationship described by genetic linkage.

concepts.card: For some genes, the copy inherited from one parent is active while the other copy is largely switched off. Genomic imprinting establishes this parent-of-origin pattern through epigenetic regulation. It shows why inheriting a gene copy and using that copy are different questions.

evidence.note: The imprinting section identifies maternal-only and paternal-only expression for a small subset of genes and says the epigenome distinguishes their copies.

concepts.label: Genomic imprinting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain parent-of-origin gene expression without a difference in the inherited DNA sequence.

relations.note: Parent-of-origin expression is a specific inheritance-related phenomenon within the study of genetics.

concepts.card: The genus of a closed connected surface counts handles when the surface is orientable and cross-caps when it is not. A sphere has orientable genus zero, while a torus has genus one. The definition distinguishes kinds of holes rather than measuring physical size.

evidence.locator: Genus -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 3 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-4
evidence.note: Count handles or cross-caps to distinguish closed surfaces with different topology.

concepts.label: Genus of a surface
concepts.learning_takeaway: Count handles or cross-caps to distinguish closed surfaces with different topology.

relations.note: The source directly gives the relation between surface genus and Euler characteristic.

concepts.card: In Riemannian geometry, a geodesic is a locally length-minimizing path. In a plane it is straight; on a sphere it follows a great circle. Local shortestness matters: continuing along a great circle far enough need not give the shortest route between its endpoints.

evidence.locator: Geodesic -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3
evidence.note: Locally shortest paths depend on the surface metric; great circles play this role on a sphere.

concepts.label: Geodesic
concepts.learning_takeaway: Locally shortest paths depend on the surface metric; great circles play this role on a sphere.

relations.note: Geodesics add metric information to the study of spaces; topology alone does not fix lengths or shortest paths.

concepts.card: A geographic buffer marks a zone within a chosen distance of a feature. It is useful for proximity questions, but distance alone does not say how someone can travel there. A circular zone around a facility can therefore differ from its reachable area along roads.

evidence.note: Buffer comparison distinguishes geometric proximity from network travel.

concepts.label: Geographic buffer
concepts.learning_takeaway: A fixed-distance zone measures proximity around a feature but does not by itself model roads, barriers or travel time.

relations.note: A network service area can answer the accessibility question that a simple buffer leaves open.

concepts.card: The geometric distribution describes how long repeated independent trials with a fixed positive success probability take to produce a first success. Some conventions count preceding failures from zero; others count trials from one. Keeping that convention explicit prevents an otherwise correct formula from being shifted by one.

evidence.locator: 4.4 Geometric Distribution; inspected passage indices 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: list-00001; list-00002
evidence.note: Explains independent fixed-probability trials and failure-count versus trial-count conventions.

evidence.locator: Geometric Distribution -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 3, 4 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-4; paragraph-5
evidence.note: Confirms memorylessness and the alternative zero- and one-based definitions.

concepts.label: Geometric distribution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Model repeated independent trials until success, distinguishing conventions that count trials or preceding failures.

relations.note: The source explicitly states that the geometric distribution is the discrete memoryless distribution.

concepts.card: George Town’s religious buildings, quarters and shophouses preserve the layered history of a trading port. Malay, Chinese, Indian and European influences appear within the same urban setting. The city shows how repeated commercial contact can leave enduring patterns in architecture and communal organization.

evidence.note: Trading-port history and named cultural influences are documented.

concepts.label: George Town, Penang
concepts.learning_takeaway: Religious buildings, ethnic quarters and shophouses show how a trading port accumulated Malay, Chinese, Indian and European influences.

relations.note: The port’s built environment records cultural exchange through settlement patterns.

concepts.card: Germany's eternity clause makes certain constitutional amendments inadmissible, including changes affecting the federal division into Länder and principles protected by Articles 1 and 20. This differs from merely requiring a large majority: Article 79 sets substantive limits that the ordinary two-thirds amendment procedure cannot override.

evidence.note: Basic Law Article 79(2)–(3) distinguishes two-thirds votes from inadmissible amendments; including avoids claiming that the examples exhaust the clause, and no universal claim about all constitutions is made.

concepts.label: German eternity clause
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a difficult amendment from a constitutionally inadmissible amendment.

relations.note: The clause exemplifies a constitutional limit on the power to amend basic governmental rules; the Basic Law provision and general constitution account support that editorial placement.

concepts.card: The Gettier problem asks why some justified true beliefs still seem not to be knowledge. A person can reason from a justified but false premise to a conclusion that happens to be true for an unrelated reason. The success is accidental despite the apparent justification.

evidence.note: SEP section 3's Smith/Jones disjunction case supports justified false premise, valid inference and accidental truth; some and seem preserve the philosophical status of the counterexample judgment.

concepts.label: Gettier problem
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why a justified belief can be accidentally true yet fail to count as knowledge.

relations.note: Gettier cases are directly formulated as counterexamples to the traditional tripartite analysis, separating justified truth from nonaccidental knowledge.

concepts.card: A ghazal joins relatively autonomous couplets through a shared rhyme-and-refrain pattern. Formal recurrence connects lines whose thoughts may remain distinct. This combination allows unity without continuous narrative, and it creates particular challenges when poets translate or adapt the form into another language.

evidence.note: Couplet autonomy, shared scheme and translation/adaptation challenges are explicit.

concepts.label: Ghazal
concepts.learning_takeaway: Autonomous couplets share a rhyme-and-refrain pattern, joining formal unity with discontinuity of thought.

relations.note: The Academy explains the ghazal through its couplets and poetic rhyme-refrain structure.
The glossary describes Ali’s advocacy for retaining the form’s constraints in English.

concepts.card: Gideon v. Wainwright established the right to appointed counsel for indigent defendants in state felony trials. After Gideon was denied a lawyer, the Supreme Court held that the Sixth Amendment guarantee applies to states through the Fourteenth Amendment. The case concerns fair criminal proceedings, not universal publicly funded legal representation.

evidence.note: US Courts Facts and Reasoning support Florida felony prosecution, indigence, denial and incorporation; the card confines its claim to state felony trials rather than all civil disputes or every minor offense.

concepts.label: Gideon v. Wainwright
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect an indigent defendant's denied lawyer with the right to appointed counsel in state felony trials.

relations.note: The case summary explicitly records Gideon's state habeas petition challenging his detention after the denial of counsel, before his later Supreme Court petition.

concepts.card: A giornata is the section of fresh finishing plaster prepared for a day’s fresco painting. Its size follows what the painter expects to complete while that surface remains workable. The division turns a large wall painting into a sequence of time-sensitive working areas.

evidence.note: A day’s fresh plaster and painting capacity are described.

concepts.label: Giornata
concepts.learning_takeaway: A fresco painter prepares fresh finishing plaster in daily working sections sized to what can be painted while the surface remains workable.

relations.note: Daily plaster sections are part of the wet-plaster fresco workflow.

concepts.card: Benjamin Franklin's glass armonica uses glass bowls of different sizes mounted on a spinning axle. A player's touch sustains their vibration through friction, much as a damp finger can make a glass rim sing. The instrument turns that small physical effect into a playable arrangement of pitches.

evidence.locator: Why does rubbing your finger around the rim of a wine glass make a note?
