relations.note: The entry identifies circumstantial luck as one form of moral luck, involving which situations a person happens to face rather than only how an action ends.

concepts.card: The Morris worm spread across the early Internet in 1988 and disrupted computers and services without destroying their files. Its impact illustrates that availability can fail even when stored data remains intact. The incident also prompted organized response efforts, including an early computer emergency response team.

evidence.locator: Main history, propagation and operational impact paragraphs
evidence.note: Checked year, self-propagation, absence of file destruction, service disruption and response-team consequence; no detailed exploit instructions or precise uncertain damage totals.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The FBI's account of disruption without file destruction provides a concrete case for considering service availability within computer protection.

concepts.label: Morris worm
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how self-propagating code disrupted network services without destroying stored files in the 1988 incident.

relations.note: The FBI's account of disruption without file destruction provides a concrete case for considering service availability within computer protection.

concepts.card: A mortise-and-tenon joint fits a projecting end of one piece into a matching recess in another. Close-fitting faces provide contact for bonding, while the shoulders seat against the receiving piece. The arrangement connects shape and fit with joint performance, rather than relying on an end-to-end butt connection alone.

evidence.note: The original WOOD instruction defines projection/recess, glue surface and shoulder contact as components of the fitted joint.

concepts.label: Mortise-and-tenon joint
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a fitted projection, its matching recess and seated shoulders with a strong wooden joint.

relations.note: This is a specific geometric method of joining wooden components within woodworking.

concepts.card: A person can have genetically different groups of cells that all descend from the same fertilized egg. This is mosaicism: a change arising during development is inherited by that cell’s descendants. Its effects depend on the variant and which cells carry it.

evidence.note: NHGRI defines genetically distinct populations from one zygote and explains post-fertilization variants and variable consequences.

concepts.label: Mosaicism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish genomic differences arising within descendants of one fertilized egg from chimerism.

relations.note: Mosaicism and chimerism can both involve different cell genomes, but their cell populations have different developmental origins.

concepts.card: Mulching covers the soil surface with a chosen material. The layer can slow evaporation, reduce light available to weeds and alter soil temperature. Those effects depend on the material, so a gardener’s choice of covering changes more than the appearance of the bed.

evidence.note: UMN explains surface cover, moisture conservation, weed-light restriction and material-dependent thermal effects.

concepts.label: Mulching
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how a surface covering changes evaporation, weed growth and soil temperature.

relations.note: A mulch layer is a specific gardening intervention affecting root-zone conditions.

concepts.card: A multi-column index orders records using several fields together. In SQLite's fruit example, indexing fruit and state lets the database locate California oranges directly instead of first finding all oranges and rejecting other states. Column order determines how that combined ordering can be used.

evidence.note: Checked combined conditions and ordered index columns; no blanket guarantee that any column order accelerates every query.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Composite ordering is a particular database access structure; the fruit-and-state example supports the concrete retrieval mechanism.

concepts.label: Multi-column index
concepts.learning_takeaway: Order index entries by several columns so combined constraints avoid filtering unrelated intermediate matches.

relations.note: Composite ordering is a particular database access structure; the fruit-and-state example supports the concrete retrieval mechanism.

concepts.card: Musical diminution shortens the rhythmic values of a motive or phrase, commonly by halving every duration. The pitch sequence can remain recognizable while the idea unfolds faster. Some uses of the term are less exact, referring more generally to a passage rewritten with shorter note values.

evidence.note: Section 11.2.3 supports both exact halving and the broader usage; commonly prevents treating halving as an exceptionless definition.

concepts.label: Musical diminution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish proportional rhythmic shortening from changing only some durations.

relations.note: The textbook defines diminution in direct contrast with augmentation's usual doubling of durations.

concepts.card: Phase shifting changes the alignment of repeated musical patterns. One part can retain its timing while another gradually runs ahead, or a performer can jump directly to the next rotation. Reich's Piano Phase and Clapping Music demonstrate these different ways of reorganizing the same recurring material.

evidence.note: Section 35.2 explicitly contrasts gradual speeding in Piano Phase with discrete rotations in Clapping Music; no claim that both works require continuous tempo drift.

concepts.label: Musical phase shifting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare gradual desynchronization with discrete shifts of a repeated pattern.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly identifies Piano Phase as a live-performance application of Reich's phase-shifting process.

concepts.card: Mutualism is an interaction between species in which both participants benefit. Ants attending Karner blue butterfly larvae provide protection and receive carbohydrate-rich secretions in return. Examining what each partner gains turns a vague picture of cooperation into a testable account of a biological exchange.

evidence.note: OpenStax explicitly defines mutual benefit and supplies the ant–butterfly exchange used here.

concepts.label: Mutualism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize interspecific exchanges in which both partners benefit, as in ant-tended butterfly larvae.

relations.note: Mutualism is a particular interspecific interaction studied at ecology’s community level.

concepts.card: An N-of-1 trial compares intervention and control periods repeatedly within the same person, often in randomized order. This can reveal an individual response that a group average obscures. It works best when effects can change or fade between periods, rather than permanently carrying into later comparisons.

evidence.note: UK guidance describes randomized multiple crossovers within individuals and limits for slow-onset or long-lasting interventions.

concepts.label: N-of-1 trial
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare interventions repeatedly within one person rather than assuming a group average fits everyone.

relations.note: Washout periods can reduce carryover between the repeated intervention/control periods used in this design.

concepts.card: Narrative eventfulness concerns how a change becomes significant, surprising or unusual within a story’s context. Merely changing state is not enough for this stronger sense. Characters, narrators or readers interpret the change against expectations, so the same occurrence can acquire different importance in different settings.

evidence.note: Type-II events depend on relevance, unexpectedness and interpretation.

concepts.label: Narrative eventfulness
concepts.learning_takeaway: A change becomes especially eventful when interpreted as significant or unexpected against a story’s cultural and situational expectations.

relations.note: Significant interpreted changes can contribute to why a narrative is worth telling.

concepts.card: Narrative levels describe the relationship between an act of telling and the story world it presents. A character who begins another story can introduce a further level. The model tracks these thresholds, including relationships that exist even without an obvious frame tale.

evidence.note: Narrating acts, embedded stories and distinction from framing are explicit.

concepts.label: Narrative levels
concepts.learning_takeaway: A character’s act of telling can establish a further story level, creating nested relations between narration and narrated worlds.

relations.note: Frame stories use embedding, but the handbook explains why narrative levels cover a wider analytical relationship.

concepts.card: Narrative paralepsis supplies information that exceeds a particular text’s established focalization norm. The exception is defined against the work’s own pattern of disclosure. Identifying it therefore requires attention to narrative coherence rather than a universal rule about what a narrator could plausibly know.

evidence.note: Paralepsis and text-specific informational norms are explicitly defined.

concepts.label: Narrative paralepsis
concepts.learning_takeaway: A narrative can reveal information beyond its established focalization norm; identifying this excess depends on the particular text.

relations.note: Paralepsis is an alteration of the informational norm established by focalization.

concepts.card: Offering a narrator the chance to review an interview before public release can connect historical access with informed participation. The Oral History Association recommends building this opportunity into the process when possible, alongside clear expectations about preservation, access and the project’s timetable.

evidence.note: Preparation 3 recommends consent and possible pre-release approval.

concepts.label: Narrator review in oral history
concepts.learning_takeaway: Giving narrators an opportunity to review an interview before release connects historical access with consent and the terms of participation.

relations.note: Pre-release review is a recommended part of planning an oral-history project.

concepts.card: Natural-breaks classification groups similar values and places boundaries near larger gaps in the data. The resulting classes can reveal internal clusters, but their thresholds depend on the particular dataset. Maps classified separately this way may therefore be difficult to compare directly through their legends.

evidence.note: Dataset-specific groups and comparison limits are explicitly stated.

concepts.label: Natural-breaks map classification
concepts.learning_takeaway: Grouping similar values and separating large gaps creates dataset-specific classes that may hinder direct comparisons across maps.

relations.note: Data-dependent class boundaries are a specific decision in representing attributes on maps.
Both classify mapped values, but natural breaks follows data gaps rather than equalizing class counts.

concepts.card: The Neapolitan chord is a major chord built on the lowered second scale degree. In classical tonal analysis it commonly appears in first inversion and serves a predominant function. Its distinctive chromatic color therefore has a directional role, helping prepare the approach to dominant harmony.

evidence.note: Section 20.1 names flat II, most-common first inversion and predominant function; major quality follows the uppercase chord notation, not a claim that every flat-II sonority has this function.

concepts.label: Neapolitan chord
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize the flattened-supertonic major chord as a chromatic predominant.

relations.note: The Neapolitan's predominant role contrasts with the cadential six-four's dominant role, despite both often occurring near a cadence.

concepts.card: Negative space is the area around or between depicted forms that helps shape a composition. In Ruth Asawa’s 1965 lithograph Chair, unmarked gaps suggest chairs among patterned marks. These spaces show how an image can describe an object through areas left open.

evidence.locator: Object header, lines 61–68; gallery label, lines 78–79; medium, line 88; object number, line 98
evidence.note: Object header identifies the 1965 lithograph; the gallery label describes five patterned chairs and two additional negative-space chairs.

concepts.label: Negative space
concepts.learning_takeaway: Unmarked areas around or within depicted forms can describe an object, as blank chair shapes do in Ruth Asawa’s 1965 lithograph Chair (TAM.1558-II).

relations.note: The museum label identifies negative-space chairs in the work catalogued as the 1965 lithograph Chair (TAM.1558-II).

concepts.card: A networked team structure organizes work around flexible connections among task-focused teams. Teams may initially be assigned, then find additional collaborators and resources as the work develops. The distinctive feature is this evolving task arrangement, rather than treating every informal workplace friendship as an organizational design.

evidence.note: Checked the approved task-team distinction from informal organization and the wider organic orientation; no claim that reporting responsibilities vanish.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source explicitly lists networked team structure among organizational designs and describes teams forming useful links after initial assignment.

concepts.label: Networked team structure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Coordinate task-focused teams through flexible relationship networks rather than relying primarily on fixed reporting lines.

relations.note: The source explicitly lists networked team structure among organizational designs and describes teams forming useful links after initial assignment.

concepts.card: Under simple elastic beam bending, fibers on one side are stretched while those on the other are compressed. The neutral axis marks where the axial bending stress changes sign and becomes zero. Finding it helps locate the regions where tensile or compressive failure may begin.

evidence.locator: 4.2: Stresses in Beams; inspected passage indices 68, 70, 72 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: section_1; section_2
evidence.note: A bending beam has a zero-axial-stress line between tensile and compressive regions.

concepts.label: Neutral axis in beam bending
concepts.learning_takeaway: A bending beam has a zero-axial-stress line between tensile and compressive regions.

relations.note: The moment-of-area reference explicitly measures distance from the neutral axis to evaluate bending resistance.

concepts.card: The neutral theory of molecular evolution emphasizes mutation and genetic drift in explaining much genetic variation. When alternative gene versions do not differ in fitness, chance can change their frequencies. This does not mean all variation is neutral or that natural selection is unimportant.

evidence.note: Berkeley emphasizes mutation and drift and defines the illustrative neutral alternatives as having no difference in fitness. It explicitly rejects claims that all variation is neutral or selection is unimportant.

concepts.label: Neutral theory of molecular evolution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate neutral genetic variation and drift from the claim that all evolution is nonadaptive.

relations.note: Neutral theory assigns a major explanatory role to genetic drift for variants with no fitness difference, rather than introducing a different drift mechanism.

concepts.card: During the Panic of 1907, the New York Clearing House supported member banks with loans and later loan certificates. Trust companies outside its membership initially lacked that access. The case shows how an institution can provide collective liquidity while its eligibility boundary leaves other connected institutions exposed.

evidence.note: Checked member/nonmember distinction and timing; support is not represented as unlimited insurance for every institution or proof of solvency.

concepts.label: New York Clearing House
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how membership-based mutual liquidity support helped some banks while initially excluding distressed trust companies.

relations.note: The historical account explicitly describes clearing-house support, membership restrictions and loan certificates during the Panic of 1907.

concepts.card: New Zealand's MMP system gives parties two routes to parliamentary eligibility: at least five percent of the party vote or an electorate victory. The alternative route means a party below the percentage threshold can still qualify through local success. These are New Zealand's rules, not universal MMP requirements.

evidence.locator: Political parties try to win party votes and electorate votes
evidence.note: The Electoral Commission explicitly states the five-percent or electorate-seat alternatives; the card does not claim an exact seat entitlement or apply the threshold to other countries.

concepts.label: New Zealand MMP threshold
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore two alternative routes to eligibility for proportional representation.

relations.note: The official page locates the threshold within New Zealand's MMP allocation and explains it alongside separate party and electorate votes.

concepts.card: The no-false-lemmas condition proposes repairing justified true belief by excluding beliefs inferred from false premises. It blocks some Gettier examples, but deceptive perceptual environments pose a further challenge. A belief can apparently be accidentally true without having been inferred from any false proposition.

evidence.note: SEP section 4 states the proposed fourth condition and noninferential counterexamples; the card does not claim the repair is accepted or sufficient.

concepts.label: No-false-lemmas condition
concepts.learning_takeaway: Evaluate the proposed repair that knowledge cannot be inferred from false premises.

relations.note: The entry expressly develops no false lemmas as an attempted additional condition for solving the Gettier problem, then presents objections.

concepts.card: No-till farming establishes crops while limiting soil disturbance and retaining previous plant residues at the surface. Planting directly into that cover differs from turning the whole field before sowing. The practice changes both how soil is worked and how residues remain part of the growing environment.

evidence.locator: Residue and Tillage Management, No Till
evidence.note: NRCS states limits on soil disturbance, year-round residue retention and direct planting into the residue.

concepts.label: No-till farming
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reduce soil disturbance by establishing crops without full-width tillage.

relations.note: Retaining residue through reduced disturbance differs from growing a seasonal cover crop, though both address soil cover.

concepts.card: Joining two normalized Unicode strings does not guarantee that the result stays normalized. A combining mark at the boundary may need reordering or composition with the preceding text. Software can therefore need to normalize the join even when both original pieces were already normalized.

evidence.note: Checked concatenation versus substring behavior; the claim is limited to joins and does not say every concatenation changes normalization.

concepts.label: Normalization across string concatenation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recheck normalization at concatenation boundaries because joining normalized strings can require reordering or composition.

relations.note: UAX 15 section 1.4 explicitly explains normalization's failure to be closed under concatenation and shows boundary examples.

concepts.card: Normalizing a count divides it by a relevant denominator before mapping it. Cases per resident, for example, answer a different question from total cases. The choice helps distinguish prevalence from population size, although the denominator must fit the comparison the map is intended to make.

evidence.note: Dividing counts by appropriate totals supports rate-based comparison.

concepts.label: Normalization for choropleth maps
concepts.learning_takeaway: Dividing a count by a relevant denominator distinguishes prevalence or intensity from the size of a region’s population.

relations.note: Normalization is a specific preparation choice for meaningful choropleth comparisons.

concepts.card: Normative social influence draws people toward a group's position because acceptance matters. Someone may publicly give an answer they privately doubt to avoid ridicule or fit in. Agreement in this case need not mean believing the group has better information about the question.

evidence.locator: Why conform? normative versus informational influence
evidence.note: Section 12.4 distinguishes fitting in from information-based conformity and notes public agreement without private acceptance in Asch's setting; the card allows rather than requires private disagreement.

concepts.label: Normative social influence
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish joining a group to gain acceptance from believing its answer is correct.

relations.note: The text explicitly contrasts acceptance-seeking with trusting the group's information, identifying two different motivations for conformity.

concepts.card: Numerical identity means being one and the same thing; qualitative identity means being alike in qualities. The distinction matters for change: a persisting object can remain the same object while its features alter. Similarity of appearance alone does not settle whether two descriptions pick out one thing.

evidence.note: SEP Identity Over Time section 1 distinguishes one object from exact resemblance and connects persistence with qualitative change; the card does not assume the controversial converse identity-of-indiscernibles principle.

concepts.label: Numerical and qualitative identity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish being one and the same object from being perfectly alike.

relations.note: The introduction moves directly from numerical/qualitative identity to Leibniz's Law, exposing the need to explain how qualitative change fits identity through time.

concepts.card: NuSTAR uses high-energy X-rays to study regions around black holes, exploding stars, and active galaxies. Its observations have helped estimate black-hole spin, illustrating how radiation from an object’s surroundings can carry information about the object itself.

evidence.locator: NuSTAR; inspected passage indices 5 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-6
evidence.note: High-energy X-ray observations reveal black-hole dynamics and enabled a precise spin measurement.

concepts.label: NuSTAR
concepts.learning_takeaway: High-energy X-ray observations reveal black-hole dynamics and enabled a precise spin measurement.

relations.note: The mission description explicitly identifies black-hole dynamics and spin measurements as results of NuSTAR observations.

concepts.card: Nutrient-film technique moves a shallow stream of nutrient solution through channels containing plant roots. The solution circulates back toward a reservoir while roots retain access to air. The arrangement differs from deeply immersing the whole root system, and depends on keeping that moving supply available.

evidence.note: UMN describes shallow continuous flow through channels, return circulation and the root-zone arrangement.

concepts.label: Nutrient-film technique
concepts.learning_takeaway: Circulate a shallow nutrient stream past roots while retaining access to oxygen.

relations.note: The channel-and-shallow-flow arrangement is a specific hydroponic system described in the source.

concepts.card: An oasis settlement joins habitation and agriculture to a dependable local water supply within an arid region. At Al Ain, irrigation works and settlement remains record this relationship over time. Water management helps explain how settled life could persist in an otherwise demanding desert landscape.

evidence.note: Al Ain links irrigation and sustained desert settlement.

concepts.label: Oasis settlement
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reliable managed water lets settled agriculture and habitation persist within desert landscapes, as archaeological evidence at Al Ain illustrates.

relations.note: The named archaeological landscape preserves evidence of the settlement-water relationship.

concepts.card: The observer's paradox in sociolinguistics is that researchers want to study how people speak when they are not being observed, yet must observe them to collect evidence. A recording or unfamiliar interviewer can change self-monitoring, so natural rapport helps but cannot guarantee completely unmonitored speech.

evidence.note: Checked observation/self-monitoring tension and absence of a foolproof elicitation method; not equated with experimenter expectancy or socially desirable answers generally.

concepts.label: Observer's paradox in sociolinguistics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize that systematically recording everyday speech may change the very speech researchers want to observe.

relations.note: The methods chapter explicitly identifies the observer's paradox as a central difficulty in obtaining vernacular speech through interviews.

concepts.card: When seawater absorbs carbon dioxide, chemical reactions increase hydrogen ions and reduce the availability of carbonate ions. Ocean acidification can therefore make building some shells and skeletons more difficult. The change concerns a shift in ocean chemistry, not a claim that seawater has become acidic in everyday terms.

evidence.note: NOAA explains CO2 uptake, increased hydrogen ions, reduced carbonate availability and effects on calcifying organisms.

concepts.label: Ocean acidification
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect absorbed atmospheric CO2 with more hydrogen ions and less available carbonate.

relations.note: Acidification and bleaching are distinct pressures on marine organisms: carbonate chemistry versus loss of coral symbiotic algae.

concepts.card: Shelley’s Ode to the West Wind adapts terza rima into five units resembling sonnets. Interlocking tercets lead into closing couplets, joining forward movement with repeated moments of closure. The poem offers a specific case of reshaping an inherited rhyme pattern for a different design.

evidence.note: Five sonnet-like sections, tercets and closing couplets are described.

concepts.label: Ode to the West Wind
concepts.learning_takeaway: Shelley adapts interlocking tercets into five sonnet-like units, each closing with a couplet.

relations.note: The glossary names Shelley’s poem as an adaptation of this rhyme form.

concepts.card: An offside position is judged when a teammate plays or touches the ball, but position alone is not an offence. Penalization requires the specified involvement in active play. A player receiving the ball directly from a goal kick, throw-in or corner kick commits no offside offence.

evidence.note: IFAB Law 11.1–11.3 fixes the position assessment at the teammate play/touch and separately requires active involvement. Direct goal-kick, throw-in and corner-kick receipt are the stated exceptions; no exhaustive geometry or contact-point nuance is asserted.

concepts.label: Offside in association football
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish occupying an offside position from committing an offside offence.

relations.note: IFAB identifies offside as Law 11 within association football's Laws of the Game.

concepts.card: Ofuda are shrine tablets of paper or wood bearing a kami’s or shrine’s name. Commonly placed on a household altar, they are understood by practitioners to extend sacred protection into the home. The object links domestic veneration with the shrine from which it was received.

evidence.note: Named paper/wood tablets, household placement and attributed protection are explicit.

concepts.label: Ofuda
concepts.learning_takeaway: A shrine tablet bearing a kami or shrine name supports veneration in the home, extending a visit into domestic religious life.

relations.note: Jinja Honcho describes ofuda as a shrine-related form of domestic kami veneration.

concepts.card: Omamori are small protective amulets associated with shrines and particular requests, such as seeking good fortune or avoiding danger. Often carried in bags, they are understood to hold a kami’s presence. Their portability connects a shrine visit with a person’s ordinary movements and concerns.

evidence.note: Personal requests, attributed kami presence and carrying in bags are described.

concepts.label: Omamori
concepts.learning_takeaway: A portable shrine amulet is often selected for a particular request and carried as an expression of a kami’s protection.

relations.note: The source contrasts portable personal amulets with tablets commonly placed on household altars.

concepts.card: Elizabeth Bishop’s One Art moves from small misplaced things toward more intimate loss within a villanelle’s returning lines. An editorial reading hears the repeated assurance becoming harder to sustain. The poem offers a way to examine how formal repetition can expose strain as well as control.

evidence.note: The poem supports the sequence of losses; l12 explicitly identifies the villanelle form.
Names One Art as a villanelle with refrain variation.

concepts.label: One Art
concepts.learning_takeaway: Bishop’s villanelle moves from small losses toward personal loss; an editorial reading hears increasing strain in its repeated assurance.

relations.note: The Academy’s glossary identifies One Art as a villanelle that varies its refrains.

concepts.card: An open repair request signals that something in the previous message was unclear without identifying the troublesome part. A brief Huh? is one example. Because the speaker receives little information about the problem, resolving it may require repeating or reformulating more of the earlier utterance.

evidence.locator: Results, Three basic types recur in all languages, pp. 4–5
evidence.note: Checked unspecified trouble and qualified longer/repeated response tendency; not treated as interchangeable with a targeted question.

concepts.label: Open repair request
concepts.learning_takeaway: Request help with an unclear message without specifying which part caused difficulty.

relations.note: The repair study explicitly defines open requests as one of three functionally distinct other-initiated repair types and describes their response patterns.

concepts.card: Open security design keeps protection from depending on attackers being ignorant of how the mechanism works. Specific keys or passwords remain secret instead. This separation allows the design to be examined by reviewers without assuming that publishing its structure necessarily defeats the protection.

evidence.note: Checked public mechanism versus secret key; openness is not claimed sufficient for security or a reason to disclose credentials.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source explicitly contrasts open mechanisms with protected keys; cryptographic protocols offer a concrete setting for exploring that distinction.

concepts.label: Open security design
concepts.learning_takeaway: Keep protection dependent on guarded keys rather than secrecy of the mechanism, enabling public review.

relations.note: The source explicitly contrasts open mechanisms with protected keys; cryptographic protocols offer a concrete setting for exploring that distinction.

concepts.card: Neo-Impressionists placed separate colored strokes beside one another in the hope that they would interact in the viewer’s perception. They sought effects different from physically mixing pigments beforehand. Understanding optical mixing here means examining an artistic strategy and its historical ambitions, rather than assuming literal pigment fusion.

evidence.note: The Met explains the artists’ optical-mixture aim and separated strokes.

concepts.label: Optical mixing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Neo-Impressionists separated colored strokes in the hope that their interaction in the viewer’s eye would produce more vibrant effects than physically mixed pigments.

relations.note: The essay presents Seurat’s painting as a major demonstration of the separated-color approach.

concepts.card: An oral-history lead-in records basic context at the start of a session: who is speaking, when and where it happens, and the intended subject. Appropriate names or pseudonyms preserve identification while avoiding unnecessary exposure, such as stating a private home address.

evidence.note: Interviewing 2 specifies contextual identifiers and cautions about residential addresses.

concepts.label: Oral-history interview lead-in
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recording participant names or pseudonyms, date, setting and proposed subject preserves the interview’s context for future users.

relations.note: A recorded lead-in is a specific interviewing practice within oral history.

concepts.card: An organic organizational structure gives people more room to coordinate and make decisions as circumstances change. Authority is less tightly concentrated, and work relies less exclusively on fixed routines. The idea describes a flexible design orientation, rather than simply naming the friendships that arise inside any workplace.

evidence.note: Checked design flexibility versus informal relationships; an organic structure is not assumed to have no responsibilities, hierarchy or rules.

concepts.label: Organic organizational structure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distribute decisions and rely on adaptive coordination when work and circumstances change quickly.

relations.note: OpenStax explicitly contrasts organic flexibility and distributed decisions with mechanistic hierarchy and standardization.

concepts.card: Organizational formalization describes how explicitly roles, duties, and accountability are defined. A highly formalized system spells them out closely; a looser one relies more on relationships that emerge through work. Formalization is a matter of degree, distinct from whether an organization has any structure at all.

evidence.note: Checked degree of definition and contrast with emergent coordination; formalization is not equated with the existence of a formal organization chart alone.

concepts.label: Organizational formalization
concepts.learning_takeaway: Specify roles, responsibilities, and accountability to different degrees instead of leaving all coordination to emergent relationships.

relations.note: The organizational-design chapter explicitly identifies formalization as one of the dimensions managers consider when arranging structure.

concepts.card: An orientable surface admits a consistent choice of orientation across its tangent planes. That choice can vary continuously as you move across the surface. A Möbius strip shows what can go wrong: its half-twist prevents a locally chosen side from remaining globally consistent.

evidence.locator: Orientable Surface -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2
evidence.note: Defines orientability through continuously chosen tangent-space structure.

evidence.locator: Möbius Strip -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2
evidence.note: Defines the half-twisted Möbius band as one-sided and nonorientable.

concepts.label: Orientable surface
concepts.learning_takeaway: Local tangent-space orientations can be chosen continuously across an orientable surface.

relations.note: The Möbius strip’s stated nonorientability provides the concrete contrast for the abstract continuous-orientation definition.

concepts.card: Original order preserves the arrangement a record creator used, when that order can be established and remains meaningful. Keeping the sequence may reveal how an office or person worked. Rearranging everything by a modern subject scheme can erase those functional connections.

evidence.note: Creator arrangement and evidential relationships support the principle.

concepts.label: Original order in archives
concepts.learning_takeaway: Preserving a creator’s record sequence can retain evidence of how the records functioned, rather than replacing it with a modern subject arrangement.

relations.note: Creator-based grouping and internal arrangement preserve different relationships among records.

concepts.card: An oscillator’s quality factor describes how sharply it responds near resonance. With light damping, oscillations persist and the resonance peak is narrow; stronger damping broadens it. A tuned radio circuit uses a narrow response to select one frequency while reducing its response to nearby ones.

evidence.locator: 15.6 Forced Oscillations; inspected passage indices 16 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1167131421041
evidence.note: Light damping produces narrow resonance curves and high frequency selectivity; the tuned-radio example applies this qualitative relation.

evidence.locator: 15.5 Damped Oscillations; inspected passage indices 9 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1167131181569
evidence.note: Weak damping lets oscillations persist while their amplitude gradually decreases.

concepts.label: Oscillator quality factor
concepts.learning_takeaway: Lower damping produces a narrower resonant response and more selective frequency discrimination.

relations.note: The source introduces quality factor through the width and damping of resonant oscillator responses.

concepts.card: Othello changes the ownership of pieces already on the board. A player places a disc to bracket an uninterrupted line of opposing discs, then flips those discs to their color. The winner has more discs when neither player can make a legal move.

evidence.note: Official outflanking and ending rules support placement, flipping and the final majority; the game need not fill all sixty-four squares.

concepts.label: Othello
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how a placement changes ownership of intervening discs.

relations.note: A lack of outflanking moves determines both forced passes and the eventual end of the game.

concepts.card: Other-initiated repair occurs when a listener signals trouble with someone else's message and the original speaker helps resolve it. The response may repeat words, clarify a missing detail, or confirm an interpretation. This creates a collaborative detour aimed at restoring understanding so the conversation can proceed.

evidence.locator: Introduction; Materials and Methods, repair-sequence definition
evidence.note: The paper defines trouble source, repair initiator and repair solution. Repair may require more than one attempt; reported brief durations are averages in the sampled corpus. The card describes the collaborative aim without guaranteeing a brief or immediately successful outcome.

evidence.locator: Opening; Grounding in Conversation; contribution model
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Repair makes a breakdown explicit, while grounding also includes routine evidence of understanding; the two sources support their connection without making them equivalent.

concepts.label: Other-initiated conversational repair
concepts.learning_takeaway: Signal trouble with another speaker's message so the original speaker can repeat, clarify, or confirm it.

relations.note: Repair makes a breakdown explicit, while grounding also includes routine evidence of understanding; the two sources support their connection without making them equivalent.

concepts.card: The cochlea can produce very quiet sounds when its sensory hair cells respond to stimulation. An otoacoustic-emission test records these responses through a probe in the ear canal. Weak or absent emissions need careful interpretation because outer- or middle-ear problems can also obstruct the returning sound.

evidence.note: The hearing-test source describes cochlear hair-cell responses and warns that blockage or middle-ear problems can prevent emissions from being recorded.

concepts.label: Otoacoustic emissions
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use tiny cochlear sounds as evidence about inner-ear function while considering transmission blockages.

relations.note: Middle-ear assessment can help interpret an emission result because sound must pass through that pathway to be recorded.

concepts.card: The Otto cycle idealizes a spark-ignition piston engine through compression, rapid heat addition, expansion, and heat rejection. Heat is added and removed at fixed volume in the model. The enclosed area on its pressure–volume diagram represents net work, after accounting for work spent compressing the gas.

evidence.locator: Ideal Otto Cycle; inspected passage indices 2, 3, 4 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-3; paragraph-4; paragraph-5
evidence.note: A simplified spark-ignition engine cycle converts heat into net work represented by enclosed pressure-volume area.

concepts.label: Otto cycle
concepts.learning_takeaway: A simplified spark-ignition engine cycle converts heat into net work represented by enclosed pressure-volume area.

relations.note: The NASA reference presents the thermodynamic cycle as an explanation of an engine producing work from heat.

concepts.card: Overdiagnosis occurs when testing finds a real condition that would never have caused symptoms or harm during a person’s life. The finding is not necessarily a false-positive result. Detecting it can still expose someone to unnecessary investigations or treatment, so more diagnoses need not mean better health.

evidence.note: NCI describes screen-detected cancers that would never become clinically apparent and ensuing harms from diagnosis/treatment.

concepts.label: Overdiagnosis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish detecting a real condition from finding one that would ever have harmed the patient.

relations.note: Overdiagnosis changes which cases are counted, while lead time changes when the survival clock begins; they are separate screening biases/harms.

concepts.card: An overlong UTF-8 sequence uses more bytes than the encoding permits for a character. Accepting such sequences can make one character appear in multiple byte patterns. Security checks may reject a forbidden normal encoding yet overlook an invalid alternative that a later parser interprets identically.

evidence.note: Checked invalidity and the bypass mechanism; no actionable exploit procedure or claim that all parsers accept such sequences.

concepts.label: Overlong UTF-8 encodings
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reject longer-than-permitted encodings so alternate byte sequences cannot bypass character-based security checks.

relations.note: RFC 3629 sections 3 and 10 explicitly prohibit invalid overlong sequences and describe their parser-security consequences.

concepts.card: A palampore is a large Indian painted cotton textile often used as a bedcover or hanging. Many export examples arrange abundant flowers around a central tree. Their designs show how makers shaped local techniques and motifs for the tastes of distant buyers.

evidence.locator: Indian Painted and Printed Cottons, line 147
evidence.note: Large painted cottons, central-tree patterns and European-market adaptation are explicit.

concepts.label: Palampore
concepts.learning_takeaway: Indian hand-painted cotton bedcovers commonly organized luxuriant flowers around a central tree and were tailored to European markets.

relations.note: The museum presents palampores within the overseas trade in Indian painted cottons.

concepts.card: The Panic of 1907 spread through trust companies that were important lenders but largely outside New York's clearing-house support network. Runs on their deposits disrupted wider market liquidity. The episode shows how vulnerability can grow at institutional boundaries, rather than remaining confined to the first troubled bank.

evidence.note: Checked trust-company importance, runs and liquidity propagation; no claim that one cause alone explains the entire worldwide crisis.

concepts.label: Panic of 1907
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace how runs on institutions outside the main clearing-house support network disrupted wider financial-market liquidity.

relations.note: Federal Reserve History explicitly explains the clearing house's membership boundary and its role in supporting some institutions during the panic.

concepts.card: A pantoum repeats lines in new positions across successive stanzas. The words return, but their neighbors and grammatical connections can change. Following those shifts shows how a fixed pattern of recurrence can generate new meanings without requiring every repeated line to be rewritten.

evidence.note: Repeated lines move between stanza positions and change context.

concepts.label: Pantoum
concepts.learning_takeaway: Lines recur in new stanza positions, so changing context and punctuation can shift their meaning.

relations.note: Both use recurrence, but pantoum line recycling differs from the villanelle’s paired refrains.
The Academy presents the pantoum as a poetic form organized by recurring lines.

concepts.card: Machine-made paper often has fibers preferentially aligned in one direction, called its grain. Folding across that direction can produce uneven creases, and moisture from adhesive causes greater expansion across the grain. These directional differences matter when arranging folds and glued parts in bookbinding.

evidence.note: Cornell’s preservation tutorial describes machine-aligned fibers, cross-grain fold puckering and larger moisture expansion across grain.

concepts.label: Paper grain direction in bookbinding
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect aligned paper fibers with easier folding along the grain and unequal expansion when adhesive wets the sheet.

relations.note: Grain direction is a specific material consideration when folds and glued paper elements are assembled in bookbinding.

concepts.card: Paris law estimates fatigue-crack growth in an intermediate growth regime. Crack advance per loading cycle follows an empirical power of the stress-intensity range. The fitted constants depend on the material and conditions, and the law does not describe every near-threshold or final rapid-fracture stage.

evidence.locator: Chapter 10: Creep, Fracture, and Fatigue; inspected passage indices 204, 210, 211, 212, 213 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-205; paragraph-211; paragraph-212; paragraph-213; paragraph-214
evidence.note: In the middle growth regime, an empirical power law links crack advance per cycle to stress-intensity range.

concepts.label: Paris law for fatigue crack growth
concepts.learning_takeaway: In the middle growth regime, an empirical power law links crack advance per cycle to stress-intensity range.

relations.note: The cited section explicitly presents Paris law as a model of fatigue-crack growth.

concepts.card: Park Grass has studied grassland responses to fertilizer and liming since the nineteenth century. Its long record is not a single unchanging protocol: later liming subplots and changes in harvesting affect comparisons. Reading the experiment requires the treatment and measurement history alongside the hay-yield numbers.

evidence.locator: Study description; Liming design; Harvest methods
evidence.note: The e-RA dataset describes the experiment’s 1856 origin, 1965 liming subplots, hay yields and historical harvesting changes affecting comparability.

concepts.label: Park Grass Experiment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Interpret a long-term grassland experiment in light of treatment design and changes in measurement methods.

relations.note: Both experiments offer long records, but the inspected Park Grass design is a distinct grassland/liming study rather than another name for Broadbalk wheat plots.

concepts.card: The Parliament Act 1911 followed the Lords' rejection of the 1909 budget. It replaced their veto over most Commons public bills with delay, while excluding bills extending Parliament beyond five years. The 1949 Act shortened that delay, showing how legislative power shifted between the chambers.

evidence.locator: Why were the Parliament Acts brought into force?; Bills not subject to the Parliament Acts
evidence.note: UK Parliament history and Bills not subject sections support the 1909 conflict, qualified veto reduction, exclusion of extensions beyond five years and 1949 shortening. This is not a rule for every bill or all changes to parliamentary duration.

concepts.label: Parliament Act 1911
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect the 1909 budget conflict with replacing most Lords vetoes by delay.

relations.note: The official explanation sets the Act within normal Commons–Lords agreement and specifies circumstances where one chamber's consent can be bypassed.

concepts.card: Parliamentary sovereignty is the UK's principle that Parliament is the supreme legal authority and can make or repeal laws. One Parliament cannot generally prevent a later Parliament from changing its legislation. Institutional reforms may constrain how power is exercised without, in this account, extinguishing that legal principle.

evidence.locator: Opening and Developments affecting Parliamentary sovereignty
evidence.note: UK Parliament's sovereignty page states supremacy, future repeal and reforms; generally and in this account preserve the official explanation's legal qualifications and avoid denying practical political constraints.

concepts.label: Parliamentary sovereignty
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore Parliament's legal supremacy in the UK and its relationship with institutional reforms.

relations.note: The official page presents sovereignty as a central principle of the UK's partly written, uncodified constitution, directly connecting principle and constitutional form.

concepts.card: Some greenhouse cucumber varieties can form seedless fruit without pollination, an example of parthenocarpy. Pollinating those varieties may instead introduce seeds. The case separates fruit development from seed production, while reminding growers that a pollination rule useful for one cucumber type may not fit another.

evidence.note: UMN’s cucumber passage specifically identifies parthenocarpic greenhouse varieties, fruit without pollination and possible seed production if pollinated.

concepts.label: Parthenocarpy
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish fruit formation without pollination in selected cucumber varieties from ordinary pollination-dependent fruit set.

relations.note: The cucumber case contrasts fruit formation without pollination with fruit crops that need pollen from a compatible partner.

concepts.card: Password salting adds a separate value when a password is hashed for storage. Different salts help prevent equal passwords from routinely producing equal stored hashes. A suitable password-hashing scheme also makes each guess costly; salting and computational expense address different parts of an offline guessing attack.

evidence.note: Checked salt collision minimization, stored salt/hash pair, and cost factor; no claim that salt alone makes weak passwords safe.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: NIST's salted password-hashing process applies cryptographic transformations to password storage rather than encrypting a message for later reading.

concepts.label: Password salting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Add per-password salt before costly hashing to prevent shared passwords from routinely producing identical stored hashes.

relations.note: NIST's salted password-hashing process applies cryptographic transformations to password storage rather than encrypting a message for later reading.

concepts.card: Patronage-based surplus distribution returns cooperative benefits in proportion to members' transactions with the cooperative. This differs from distributing returns solely according to invested capital. The cooperative principles also allow surplus to support reserves, development, or other approved purposes, so member payouts are not the only permitted use.

evidence.note: Checked transaction basis, alternative surplus uses and limited capital compensation; not every cooperative must distribute all surplus this way.

concepts.label: Patronage-based surplus distribution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Allocate cooperative surplus in proportion to member transactions rather than only in proportion to invested capital.

relations.note: The International Cooperative Alliance's third principle explicitly lists transaction-proportional member benefit among ways to allocate cooperative surplus.

concepts.card: Paul Signac helped develop and promote Neo-Impressionism through both artistic practice and theoretical writing. His later exploration of watercolor extended his investigation of color into a different medium. The case shows a movement continuing through explanation and experiment after the death of its leading innovator, Seurat.

evidence.note: The essay describes Signac’s writing, continuing role and watercolor experimentation.

concepts.label: Paul Signac
concepts.learning_takeaway: Signac helped carry Neo-Impressionism forward through theoretical writing and through watercolor experiments that extended its investigation of color.

relations.note: The essay places Signac’s artistic and theoretical work within the movement’s investigation of separated color.

concepts.card: A negative eDNA test may mean the assay was inhibited, not that the species was absent. Substances such as humic acids can interfere with PCR. An internal positive control helps reveal this problem by checking whether DNA amplification succeeds inside the tested sample.

evidence.note: USGS defines inhibited samples, names humic acids and describes internal positive controls detecting inhibition or false negatives.

concepts.label: PCR inhibition in eDNA samples
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why a negative molecular detection can reflect assay inhibition rather than species absence.

relations.note: Inhibition is a specific limitation of interpreting environmental-DNA tests; it concerns assay performance rather than the biological absence of a species.

concepts.card: Pectin molecules can form a network that gives fruit spreads their gel structure. Setting conditions depend on the pectin formulation: conventional types rely on appropriate sugar and acid, while other types can work with little or no sugar. Substituting one formulation blindly can therefore change the result.

evidence.note: UMN defines the pectin mesh and distinguishes formulation-specific sugar/acid needs and low/no-sugar products.

concepts.label: Pectin gelation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain fruit-spread setting as a network whose requirements depend on the kind of pectin used.

relations.note: Pectin gel formation can be compared with syneresis, where a gel later releases liquid; no claim is made that every pectin gel will weep.

concepts.card: A pedal point holds one note while surrounding harmonies change. It begins as a chord tone but can become a non-chord tone against later chords. Often heard in the bass, it can also appear higher up, creating continuity while its harmonic meaning shifts.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 10.8 supports changing harmonic status, frequent bass placement and upper-voice pedals; the card does not restrict the device to a literal organ pedal.

concepts.label: Pedal point
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear a held note change harmonic status while surrounding chords move.

relations.note: Both can sustain a note across a harmonic change, but the pedal persists across harmonies while a suspension has a prepared stepwise resolution.

concepts.card: Peer Instruction inserts conceptual questions into a lecture. Students first commit to individual answers, explain their reasoning to nearby peers, then answer again before the instructor explains. The sequence gives discussion a specific job: compare reasons and reconsider an answer, rather than simply listen to another mini-lecture.

evidence.note: Checked initial answer, discussion, second poll and instructor feedback; not claimed that all answers improve or that every peer-learning format follows this protocol.

concepts.label: Peer Instruction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Sequence an individual conceptual answer, peer explanation, a second vote, and instructor feedback during class.

relations.note: The paper directly describes structured peer explanation as the central collaborative activity within its classroom protocol.

concepts.card: Perceptual closure is the tendency to see a complete object from incomplete visual parts. Broken arcs can look like a circle rather than unrelated segments. The perceived whole therefore contains an organization that is not supplied by a continuous drawn outline.

evidence.note: Section 5.6, closure definition and Figure 5.29, explicitly contrast whole circles and rectangles with fragmented segments; this is a perceptual tendency, not a guarantee for any broken image.

concepts.label: Perceptual closure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how incomplete parts can be perceived as a complete object.

relations.note: Closure fills an incomplete whole, whereas good continuation favors smooth trajectories; comparing their illustrations prevents treating all visual grouping as one mechanism.

concepts.card: Chemist Percy Lavon Julian developed ways to obtain useful steroid compounds from plentiful plant materials. Working with soybean sterols helped make progesterone and other hormones more accessible. His work shows how changing a chemical starting material can reshape the practical scale of production.

evidence.locator: 1.1 Chemistry in Context; inspected passage indices 11 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idp139124096
evidence.note: Julian used plentiful plant sterols to make steroid compounds more accessible through chemical synthesis.

concepts.label: Percy Lavon Julian
concepts.learning_takeaway: Julian used plentiful plant sterols to make steroid compounds more accessible through chemical synthesis.

relations.note: Julian’s change of starting material is a documented example of chemistry altering the practical production of useful substances.

concepts.card: Repeated checking is not a safe route to a draw in shogi. Under the Japan Shogi Association's cited explanation, if continuous checks produce the same position four times, the player giving those checks loses. Ordinary repetition without continuous checking is treated differently.

evidence.locator: 連続王手の千日手というのは反則なのですか
evidence.note: The official Japanese FAQ supports the fourth-occurrence loss and distinguishes ordinary repetition; the broad Shogi card instead explains piece reuse.

concepts.label: Perpetual check in shogi
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare ordinary repetition with repeated checks that make the checking player lose.

relations.note: The Japan Shogi Association identifies this as shogi's special treatment of repetition by continuous check.

concepts.card: Peshat seeks a text’s plain or contextual sense by attending to how its words work within the surrounding passage. That does not make interpretation automatic. Commentators can disagree because their assumptions shape what they take to be the most straightforward reading.

evidence.note: Contextual sense and disagreement shaped by assumptions are discussed.

concepts.label: Peshat
concepts.learning_takeaway: A contextual reading asks what biblical words mean within their surrounding narrative, while commentators can disagree about that plain sense.

relations.note: The lesson contrasts contextual explanation with readings that draw further instructive meaning.

concepts.card: Phishing-resistant authentication binds the authentication process to the legitimate verifier or communication channel. An impostor cannot simply relay a captured output to sign in elsewhere. NIST therefore distinguishes cryptographic verifier binding from manually entered one-time codes, whose outputs can be relayed despite being temporary.

evidence.note: Checked channel/name binding and manually entered output limitation; no claim that user vigilance or a short-lived code alone provides phishing resistance.

concepts.label: Phishing-resistant authentication
concepts.learning_takeaway: Bind cryptographic authentication to the real verifier or channel so an impostor cannot relay a reusable output.

relations.note: The same NIST guideline separates verifier/channel binding from replay freshness, supporting a precise comparison of these protections.

concepts.card: A photogram places objects on light-sensitive paper and exposes it directly. In the process described here, opaque objects leave light areas while translucent ones can produce intermediate tones. The image records contact and light transmission rather than a camera’s view of a scene.

evidence.note: Opaque/translucent objects and tonal effects are explicit.

concepts.label: Photogram
concepts.learning_takeaway: In the described paper process, opaque objects leave light areas while translucent objects can yield intermediate tones during direct exposure.

relations.note: A photogram supplies a camera-free method within light-based image making.

aliases: Photographs of British Algae: Cyanotype Impressions
concepts.card: Anna Atkins’s Photographs of British Algae arranged specimens directly on sensitized paper to make cyanotype images. Botanical names accompanied the delicate traces. The project brings scientific identification together with the visual decisions involved in placing an individual specimen against the blue photographic field.

evidence.locator: Specimen making and handwritten labels, lines 10–12
evidence.note: Algae contact images, handwritten nomenclature and cyanotype book project are documented.

concepts.label: Photographs of British Algae
concepts.learning_takeaway: Anna Atkins arranged algae directly on sensitized paper for cyanotype images, combining botanical naming with the visual traces of individual specimens.

relations.note: The Met identifies cyanotype as the method used for the book’s specimen impressions.

concepts.card: Photogravure translates a photographic image into an intaglio printing plate. A light-sensitive gelatin resist helps produce etched recesses of differing depth, which hold varying amounts of ink. Those differences reproduce tonal variation through printing rather than through a conventional photographic paper image alone.

evidence.note: Gelatin resist, variable etching and ink-bearing tones are described.

concepts.label: Photogravure
concepts.learning_takeaway: A light-sensitive gelatin resist helps etch varying depths into a printing plate, whose ink-bearing recesses reproduce photographic tones.

relations.note: The V&A explains etched-plate transfer through a printing press.
The photographic resist controls the etched matrix used to print the image.

concepts.card: Plants can use the duration of light and darkness as a seasonal signal. Photoperiodism helps regulate events such as flowering or winter-bud formation, with different species responding differently. A plant’s calendar can therefore depend on day–night timing, rather than only on whether the weather is warm.

evidence.note: OpenStax describes photoperiod-dependent flowering/bud formation and different plant responses.

concepts.label: Photoperiodism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain seasonal plant responses through the duration of light and darkness rather than temperature alone.

relations.note: Seasonal light signals can influence flowering, while bolting is the crop-quality consequence of an early shift into reproductive growth.

concepts.card: Steve Reich's Piano Phase makes a repeating twelve-note pattern change through alignment rather than replacement. A second pianist gradually increases speed relative to the other part, causing the patterns to slip out of phase. The process lets different combinations emerge from recurring material.

evidence.note: Section 35.2 supports the twelve-note pattern and second pianist's gradual speed change; emergent combinations follow from changing alignment, without an unsupported claim about exact complete formal design.

concepts.label: Piano Phase
concepts.learning_takeaway: Follow two repeated patterns as one pianist gradually changes their alignment.

relations.note: The source explicitly presents the work as Reich's application of phase shifting to live pianists.

concepts.card: In a basic formulation, PID control combines three responses to error: proportional action responds to present error, integral action accumulates it, and derivative action responds to its rate of change. Adjusting their gains changes how a system approaches its target, including persistent offset, overshoot, and settling.

evidence.locator: What Is PID Control?; inspected passage indices 68, 70, 72, 74 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-69; paragraph-71; paragraph-73; paragraph-75
evidence.note: Combine present error, accumulated error, and error-rate feedback to regulate a system.

concepts.label: PID control
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine present error, accumulated error, and error-rate feedback to regulate a system.

relations.note: The anti-windup source explicitly examines a practical saturation problem in PID control.

concepts.card: When lava flows into water, its exposed surface cools rapidly, producing rounded forms known as pillow lava. These shapes can survive within ancient rock. Recognizing them helps geologists infer that molten rock once met water, rather than assuming every lava flow formed in open air.

evidence.note: USGS describes pillow basalts forming when lava enters water and is rapidly cooled from exposed sides, including preserved examples at Shenandoah.

concepts.label: Pillow lava
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize rounded lava forms as evidence of rapid cooling in water.

relations.note: Pillow forms illustrate how geologists use a rock’s preserved structure to infer its formation environment.

concepts.card: The ochre sea star, Pisaster ochraceus, feeds on mussels along rocky shores. By limiting mussels that would otherwise occupy much of the available surface, it helps other organisms retain space. This makes its feeding behavior a useful case of a predator shaping community diversity.

evidence.note: NPS names the sea star and California mussels and explains how predation prevents mussels from crowding out other intertidal species.

concepts.label: Pisaster ochraceus
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore why ochre sea-star predation on mussels helps preserve rocky-shore diversity.

relations.note: The named sea star provides the documented ecological example for the keystone-species concept.

concepts.card: Tar-derived pitch can feel solid and break under a quick hammer blow, yet flow over much longer times. The University of Queensland’s pitch-drop experiment demonstrates this contrast: material placed in a funnel slowly forms drops over years, with the flow rate affected by temperature.

evidence.locator: Pitch Drop experiment; inspected passage indices 4, 6, 8, 9, 11 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-5; paragraph-7; paragraph-9; paragraph-10; paragraph-12
evidence.note: Pitch may shatter under a quick blow yet flow extremely slowly over years.

concepts.label: Pitch (tar-derived material)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how tar-derived pitch can shatter under a quick blow yet flow extremely slowly over years.

concepts.card: Pitch is a sound's perceived highness or lowness. On a piano, moving right produces higher notes. For periodic musical tones, doubling the vibration frequency raises pitch by an octave, showing why musical intervals depend on frequency ratios rather than equal additions of hertz.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 1.1 supports keyboard direction; UNSW's pitch discussion supplies periodic-tone frequency and octave ratio. Keep this auditory meaning separate from material pitch.

evidence.locator: Pitch, frequency, harmonics and missing fundamental
evidence.note: Frequency ratios, including doubling for an octave, support the quantitative explanation.

concepts.label: Pitch (music)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Relate perceived high and low notes to their ordering on a keyboard.

relations.note: The UNSW pitch discussion explicitly uses a missing fundamental to show that perceived pitch can persist when the lowest-frequency component is absent.

concepts.card: A graph is planar if it can be drawn in a plane without edges crossing except at shared vertices. One messy drawing does not disprove planarity: another arrangement might remove the crossings. The distinction concerns the existence of a suitable drawing, not its first appearance.

evidence.locator: Planar Graph -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 4, 5 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-5; paragraph-6
evidence.note: Planarity means some crossing-free drawing exists, even if another drawing of the same graph crosses.

concepts.label: Planar graph
concepts.learning_takeaway: Planarity means some crossing-free drawing exists, even if another drawing of the same graph crosses.

relations.note: The dual-graph source starts from a planar graph together with a particular planar embedding.

aliases: Plaque with equestrian oba and attendants
concepts.card: This Benin brass palace plaque makes its ruler larger than the surrounding attendants. Size expresses rank within the composition rather than simply reproducing natural proportions. The mounted figure and accompanying people show how a particular court artwork can organize political relationships visually.

evidence.note: Equestrian ruler, attendants, palace context and hierarchical scale are documented.

concepts.label: Plaque with equestrian ọ́bà and attendants
concepts.learning_takeaway: The enlarged ruler and smaller attendants on this Benin brass palace plaque use relative size to make rank visible.

relations.note: The collection description explicitly explains relative size as an expression of status.

concepts.card: Pochoir applies color by hand through a stencil, without the mesh used in screen printing. Brushes can leave visible traces as pigment passes through the cut openings. The process combines a repeatable shape with variations created by the way each impression is colored.

evidence.note: Hand-brushed stencil without a screen and visible marks are described.

concepts.label: Pochoir
concepts.learning_takeaway: Brushing pigment through a stencil without a screen creates hand-colored impressions that can retain visible brush marks.

relations.note: The glossary distinguishes pochoir’s open stencil from the mesh-based screen-printing process.

concepts.card: A constant-rate Poisson process has independent event counts in nonoverlapping time intervals. For very short intervals, one-event probability is approximately proportional to duration, while multiple events become negligible by comparison. Random clusters can occur even though the model’s average event rate stays constant.

evidence.locator: Poisson Process -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-4; paragraph-5; paragraph-6
evidence.note: Model independent event counts in disjoint intervals at a constant rate.

concepts.label: Poisson process
concepts.learning_takeaway: Model independent event counts in disjoint intervals at a constant rate.

relations.note: The exponential-distribution reference identifies the waiting-time law corresponding to Poisson events.

concepts.card: A polder landscape is enclosed and drained land whose usability depends on water management. Dykes, canals and drainage works make fields and settlement possible, while requiring continued maintenance. Reclamation therefore creates a lasting relationship between the land’s apparent stability and the infrastructure that controls water.

evidence.note: Beemster’s reclaimed land and managed water network support the case.

concepts.label: Polder landscape
concepts.learning_takeaway: Draining and enclosing wet land creates inhabitable agricultural space that depends on a maintained network of dykes, canals and drainage.

relations.note: Beemster offers a named example of reclaimed land organized by a drainage and settlement grid.

concepts.card: A population bottleneck sharply reduces the number of individuals contributing genes to later generations. Chance can eliminate variants during that small-population period. Even if numbers subsequently rebound, the lost diversity need not return, as the history of heavily hunted northern elephant seals illustrates.

evidence.locator: Population bottlenecks; An example of a bottleneck
evidence.note: Berkeley defines bottlenecks and uses northern elephant seals to show numerical recovery with persistently reduced genetic variation.

concepts.label: Population bottleneck
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why rapid numerical recovery need not restore lost genetic diversity.

relations.note: A bottleneck is a demographic circumstance that magnifies genetic drift through a small surviving sample.

concepts.card: Positive predictive value is the probability of having a condition after a positive test. Even with unchanged sensitivity and specificity, it falls when the condition is rarer in the tested population. A positive result therefore gains meaning from both test performance and the starting prevalence.

evidence.note: NCI defines PPV and explicitly states that lower prevalence reduces PPV for given sensitivity and specificity.

concepts.label: Positive predictive value
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why a positive test is less convincing when the target condition is rare.

relations.note: The distinction shows why knowing sensitivity does not directly answer the question posed by a positive result.

concepts.card: Prasad connects offerings made to a deity with their later sharing among worshippers. In many pujas, food or other offerings move through this ritual sequence. Receiving and distributing them joins an individual act of devotion with a shared material practice within the community.

evidence.note: Offerings later shared with worshippers are explicit.

concepts.label: Prasad
concepts.learning_takeaway: Offerings made to a deity can later be shared among worshippers, connecting devotion with communal distribution.

relations.note: The case study locates the shared offerings in Hindu puja practice.
The case study presents shared offerings as a common element of puja.

concepts.card: The Pratimoksha is a code of Buddhist monastic discipline governing ordained practitioners. It extends beyond the basic ethical precepts shared with lay followers. Distinguishing these layers shows how common commitments coexist with more detailed obligations attached to a particular religious role.

evidence.note: Additional monastic code beyond shared precepts is explicit.

concepts.label: Pratimoksha
concepts.learning_takeaway: A monastic code adds extensive rules for ordained Buddhists beyond ethical precepts shared with lay followers.

relations.note: The source explains the code within the distinction between monastic and lay communities.

concepts.card: A Tibetan Buddhist prayer wheel contains rolls of written mantras within a rotating cylinder. Turning it joins repeated bodily motion with devotional text, even when the words remain enclosed. Wheels range from handheld objects to larger stationary installations, giving the practice several material forms.

evidence.note: Enclosed mantra rolls, rotation and handheld/stationary forms are described.

concepts.label: Prayer wheel
concepts.learning_takeaway: A rotating cylinder encloses written mantras, joining textual devotion with repeated physical motion in Tibetan Buddhist practice.

relations.note: The prayer wheel supplies a tradition-specific example of textual and material Buddhist practice.

concepts.card: An author can reasonably believe each carefully researched claim in a book while admitting that the book probably contains an error. Combining all the individual beliefs conflicts with that admission. The preface paradox tests how rational confidence in particular claims fits with recognition of one's fallibility.

evidence.note: SEP section 4 explains Makinson's author case and its conflict with agglomeration; the card preserves rational belief rather than recasting every assertion as knowledge or certainty.

concepts.label: Preface paradox
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine believing each researched claim while reasonably expecting some mistake in the whole book.

relations.note: The source connects both paradoxes through agglomeration while distinguishing the preface's ordinary recognition of fallibility from a numerical probability-acceptance rule.

concepts.card: A prefix-free code gives each symbol a bit string that is never the beginning of another symbol's complete code. A decoder follows bits until it reaches a symbol, then starts again. Variable-length messages can therefore be separated into codewords without additional boundary markers.

evidence.note: Checked the binary-tree leaves and symbol-by-symbol decoding; prefix-free does not mean every possible bit string is a valid codeword.

concepts.label: Prefix-free code
concepts.learning_takeaway: Decode concatenated codewords unambiguously because no codeword is another codeword's prefix.

relations.note: The RFC's prefix-coding explanation directly introduces Huffman coding as a frequency-based construction of such codes.

concepts.card: A preliminary injunction provides court-ordered protection before final judgment. In US federal practice, the cited test considers likely success, likely irreparable harm, competing hardships and the public interest. The question is whether interim relief is justified while the dispute remains unresolved, not whether the applicant has already won.

evidence.note: Cornell's Winter factors and Rule 65 discussion support the four considerations and interim role; federal qualification avoids treating varying state procedures as identical.

concepts.label: Preliminary injunction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore temporary relief before final judgment and why irreparable harm matters.

relations.note: Contrast temporary relief pending resolution with an adjudication without trial when material facts do not require a factfinder; the procedures answer different questions despite possible pretrial timing.

concepts.card: A prepared piano changes its sound through objects placed beneath or between its strings. John Cage used such physical alterations to expand the instrument's available timbres. The keys remain a familiar interface, while the altered vibrating system produces sounds unlike those of an unprepared grand piano.

evidence.note: John Cage Trust explains objects placed among a grand piano's strings and the resulting transformed instrument; no invented preparation materials or exact acoustic mechanism is specified.

concepts.label: Prepared piano
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear how objects placed between piano strings transform its available timbres.

relations.note: The Trust explicitly connects its prepared-piano samples with materials used for Cage's Sonatas and Interludes.
