concepts.card: Prequestioning asks learners questions before they encounter new material. This can activate relevant knowledge and direct attention to what they need to learn. The cited guide cautions that selective reading may neglect material not covered by the questions, and its classroom evidence for this recommendation was limited.

evidence.note: Checked pre-exposure timing, attention rationale, nonquestioned-material risk, and the guide's low-evidence classification rather than asserting a universal benefit.

concepts.label: Prequestioning
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ask questions before exposure to focus study, while preserving attention to material the questions do not cover.

relations.note: Questions before exposure differ from retrieving already studied material; contrasting them prevents all uses of quizzes being treated as one testing mechanism.

concepts.card: Presentism holds that only temporally present objects exist. Merely past or future objects are excluded from its inventory of reality, though abstract entities may fall outside time. The claim concerns existence itself, not simply which events people can currently observe or remember.

evidence.locator: 6 Presentism, Eternalism, and the Growing Block Theory
evidence.note: SEP Time section 6 defines presentism and explicitly distinguishes temporal presence from spatial presence and timeless abstract objects; no claim that the past never occurred.

concepts.label: Presentism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore the thesis that only temporally present objects exist.

relations.note: The source directly opposes presentism to eternalism, which includes objects at past and future times in what exists.

concepts.card: Pressure thrust is the force contribution from a difference between nozzle-exit and ambient pressure. With uniform exit pressure, it equals that difference times exit area, alongside momentum-flow thrust. Equal pressures remove this term, but need not remove the engine’s remaining thrust.

evidence.locator: Specific Impulse; inspected passage indices 4 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-5
evidence.note: A nozzle’s exit-pressure mismatch contributes force in addition to exhaust momentum flux.

concepts.label: Pressure thrust
concepts.learning_takeaway: A nozzle’s exit-pressure mismatch contributes force in addition to exhaust momentum flux.

relations.note: The thrust equation separates exhaust momentum flow from pressure force, clarifying what contributes to a jet engine’s propulsive force.

concepts.card: A principal–agent problem arises when one party depends on another's action or attributes, but their interests differ and a contract cannot fully guarantee the desired result. Employers may value effort that is hard to verify. The framework separates who wants the outcome from who controls the relevant behavior.

evidence.note: Checked conflicting interests and unverifiable action; principal-agent relationships also cover hidden attributes, so the concept is not reduced to moral hazard alone.

concepts.label: Principal–agent problem
concepts.learning_takeaway: Analyze conflicting interests when one party relies on another's behavior or attributes that contracts cannot fully guarantee.

relations.note: CORE explicitly defines principal-agent relationships in terms of behavior or attributes not guaranteed in a binding contract.

concepts.card: The sociolinguistic principle of accountability requires counting all occasions when a variant could occur, not only the instances that attract attention. Ten examples in one setting may represent a lower usage rate than eight in another. The relevant denominator makes comparisons across speaking contexts interpretable.

evidence.note: Checked eligible alternatives and count-versus-rate distinction in the source table; no rate inferred without the opportunity denominator.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The quantitative-analysis section explicitly names this denominator rule as a foundation of variationist sociolinguistic analysis.

concepts.label: Principle of accountability in sociolinguistics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Count every eligible variant to form a denominator instead of counting only the interesting pronunciation.

relations.note: The quantitative-analysis section explicitly names this denominator rule as a foundation of variationist sociolinguistic analysis.

concepts.card: Least privilege gives each user or program only the authority needed for its job. If an error or misuse occurs, fewer permissions limit what can be damaged. The principle also reduces the number of privileged components that must be examined when investigating an unexpected access path.

evidence.note: Checked minimum necessary authority, limiting damage, and reducing privileged interactions; least privilege is not a guarantee that permitted actions are harmless.

concepts.label: Principle of least privilege
concepts.learning_takeaway: Give each program and user only necessary permissions to limit accidents and the code requiring trust.

relations.note: Saltzer and Schroeder explicitly list least privilege among the basic design principles for protecting information in computer systems.

concepts.card: A private-value auction models each bidder's valuation as personal: learning that someone else values the object highly does not change one's own value. It is an idealized case. A house, for example, may mix personal enjoyment with resale concerns that introduce a common-value component.

evidence.note: Checked independence of personal value from others' valuations and mixed housing example; private value is not equated with secret bidding.

concepts.label: Private-value auction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Model each bidder's value as personal and unaffected by learning others' valuations, an idealized limiting case.

relations.note: The lecture explicitly contrasts the two limiting valuation models and uses housing to illustrate mixtures between them.

concepts.card: Proactive interference occurs when older learning gets in the way of remembering newer information. After changing phone numbers, you might keep giving the old number automatically. The direction matters: an established memory is obstructing access to its more recently learned replacement.

evidence.note: OpenStax 8.3 defines old-to-new interference and gives the phone-number example; this concerns retrieval competition, not proof that the new memory was erased.

concepts.label: Proactive interference
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how an older memory can obstruct recall of newly learned information.

relations.note: The source explicitly distinguishes the two forms by whether older or newer information interferes.

concepts.card: The problem of closeness challenges the line between intended means and foreseen side effects. A harmful result may be so closely connected with an agent's chosen means that calling it unintended seems artificial. The difficulty is classifying the action without already assuming the moral verdict.

evidence.note: SEP section 4.2 identifies closely connected harms, and 4.3 raises evaluation-driven descriptions; the card presents a criticism rather than declaring that every intention distinction collapses.

evidence.locator: Sections 4.2 The Problem of Closeness and 4.3 The Side Effect Effect
evidence.note: The closely connected harm problem and normative influence on action descriptions together support the classification concern.

concepts.label: Problem of closeness in double effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine when a harmful side effect seems inseparable from the agent's chosen means.

relations.note: The entry names the problem of closeness as a criticism of double effect's distinction between intended means and merely foreseen harms.

concepts.card: The problem of temporary intrinsics asks how one persisting object can have incompatible intrinsic properties at different times. A metal plate may change from round to square. Explaining that change requires an account of what it means to possess a property at a time.

evidence.note: SEP Identity Over Time sections 2.3–2.4 use the plate's shape change and discuss competing solutions; the card does not infer that ordinary change is logically impossible.

concepts.label: Problem of temporary intrinsics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ask how one persisting object can possess incompatible intrinsic properties at different times.

relations.note: The section explicitly frames the temporary-intrinsics problem through Leibniz's Law: identity and differing properties require explaining the temporal qualification.

concepts.card: Procedural memory is expressed in skilled actions, such as balancing on a bicycle or driving. Practice can improve performance even when a person cannot fully describe the knowledge guiding it. This distinguishes remembering how to do something from consciously reporting facts or past events.

evidence.note: OpenStax Long-Term Memory defines implicit procedural skill and contrasts reportable explicit memories; not every component of driving is claimed unconscious.

concepts.label: Procedural memory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish remembering how to perform a skill from verbally recalling its instructions.

relations.note: Molaison's preserved improvement despite impaired new declarative memory provides a concrete comparison between performance-based and consciously reportable remembering.

concepts.card: Puja is a Hindu form of worship that can bring a devotee into a ritual encounter with a deity. Images, visual attention and offerings often participate in the encounter. Practices vary with the deity and community, and pujas can occur at home, in temples or elsewhere.

evidence.note: Visual encounter, offerings, varied locations and contextual diversity are explicit.

concepts.label: Puja
concepts.learning_takeaway: Offerings and visual interaction with deity images are common elements of Hindu puja; practices vary with the deity and community.

relations.note: The case study explicitly identifies puja as a form of Hindu worship while emphasizing variation.
The case study identifies visual interaction with an image as a common element of puja.

concepts.card: Pulmonary surfactant helps the lungs remain expanded so air sacs can participate in breathing. Premature newborns may have too little, allowing lung collapse and making breathing much harder. The example connects a substance within the lung with the mechanical ability to keep air spaces open.

evidence.note: NHLBI identifies inadequate surfactant as a cause of neonatal respiratory distress, lung collapse and increased work of breathing.

concepts.label: Pulmonary surfactant
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect surfactant deficiency with air-sac collapse and difficult breathing in premature newborns.

relations.note: Surfactant concerns lung mechanics, while spirometry measures aspects of breathing performance; the link is a learning comparison, not a claim that neonatal surfactant deficiency is diagnosed by spirometry.

concepts.card: A pulse oximeter shines light through tissue to estimate blood oxygen saturation. A small sensor can provide this information without drawing arterial blood. The reading is an estimate, however, and factors including poor circulation, cold skin or skin pigmentation can affect its accuracy.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus describes the optical sensor and estimated oxygen saturation; its listed limitations include poor circulation, cold skin and darker skin pigmentation.

concepts.label: Pulse oximetry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Estimate blood oxygen saturation from light passing through tissue.

relations.note: Skin pigmentation is one specifically documented limitation of the broader optical measurement method.

concepts.card: Pure-tone audiometry measures the quietest tones a person can detect at different pitches. Through headphones, sounds are presented while the listener signals when they hear them. The resulting pattern separates sensitivity across frequencies, rather than reducing hearing to a single yes-or-no ability.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus describes pure-tone presentation at varied pitches/volumes and the listener’s response to the softest audible sound.

concepts.label: Pure-tone audiometry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Map the quietest tones a person detects at different frequencies.

relations.note: Pure-tone detection and eardrum movement are complementary but distinct types of hearing-test evidence.

concepts.card: Qibla is the direction toward Mecca used in Muslim prayer. It coordinates worshippers’ orientation across very different locations. A mosque’s mihrab indicates that direction, but the niche and the direction are different things: one is an architectural marker of the other.

evidence.locator: Summary and prayer preparation, lines 149 and 156
evidence.note: Mecca orientation and the indicating mihrab are described.

concepts.label: Qibla
concepts.learning_takeaway: A shared orientation toward Mecca organizes Muslim prayer; a mosque’s mihrab indicates this direction rather than being the direction itself.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies the mihrab as a marker of the prayer direction.

concepts.card: Quantile classification places roughly equal numbers of mapped features in each class. This spreads observations across the legend, but nearby values can fall on opposite sides of a class boundary. Conversely, quite different values may share a class when the data are unevenly distributed.

evidence.note: Equal-count grouping and separation/combination caveats are explicit.

concepts.label: Quantile map classification
concepts.learning_takeaway: Putting equal numbers of geographic features in each class can separate close values or combine widely different values.

relations.note: Equal-count numerical classes are a specific decision in representing attributes on maps.
Compare grouping by numbers of features with grouping by equal numeric intervals.

concepts.card: Quantum tunneling allows a particle’s wave state to extend through a finite potential barrier higher than its total energy. Some amplitude can emerge beyond the barrier even when a classical particle would turn back. The transmission probability depends on the barrier’s width, height, and particle energy.

evidence.locator: 7.6 The Quantum Tunneling of Particles through Potential Barriers; inspected passage indices 7, 9, 15, 16 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1170902689053; fs-id1170901605351; fs-id1170901769645; fs-id1170903049760
evidence.note: A quantum state can transmit through a finite barrier that forbids passage at the same classical energy.

concepts.label: Quantum tunneling
concepts.learning_takeaway: A quantum state can transmit through a finite barrier that forbids passage at the same classical energy.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies scanning tunneling microscopy as an application of barrier tunneling.

concepts.card: A quotient group replaces a group’s individual elements with cosets of a normal subgroup. Multiplying those cosets gives a new group whose elements each represent an entire collection of original elements. The construction organizes selected distinctions into classes while retaining an algebraic operation.

evidence.locator: Quotient Group -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 3 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-4
evidence.note: Cosets of a normal subgroup become group elements, collapsing selected distinctions while preserving an operation.

concepts.label: Quotient group
concepts.learning_takeaway: Cosets of a normal subgroup become group elements, collapsing selected distinctions while preserving an operation.

relations.note: For finite groups, the quotient-group source connects the sizes of groups and cosets with Lagrange’s group theorem; the quotient construction itself need not be finite.

concepts.card: Raft manages a replicated log by electing a leader that receives commands and sends entries to followers. Its design separates leader election, log replication, and safety rules. This decomposition was chosen to make the protocol easier to understand while preserving agreement when machines stop or become disconnected.

evidence.note: Checked leader role and design decomposition; failure language excludes arbitrary malicious behavior and does not promise availability during every partition.

concepts.label: Raft consensus algorithm
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate leader election, log replication, and safety to make a replicated-log consensus algorithm easier to understand.

relations.note: The Raft paper explicitly presents the algorithm as a solution to consensus for a replicated log under non-Byzantine failures.

concepts.card: Moist air rising over a mountain cools and can release precipitation on the windward side. After crossing the summit, descending air warms and becomes drier. This rain-shadow effect helps explain why nearby places on opposite sides of a mountain can have sharply different rainfall.

evidence.locator: Windward precipitation and leeward drying mechanism
evidence.note: NOAA’s Hawaii explanation connects windward ascent/cooling/precipitation with leeward descent/warming/drying.

concepts.label: Rain shadow
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace contrasting mountain rainfall through rising moist air and descending dry air.

relations.note: Comparing a mountain’s lifting effect with atmospheric-river moisture transport separates where vapor arrives from how terrain can release it as precipitation.

concepts.card: Ramp metering uses entrance-ramp signals to regulate freeway entry. Breaking up merging platoons can reduce sudden mainline braking and improve traffic flow. Metering also creates waiting queues, so its design must account for ramp storage and effects on adjacent streets.

evidence.locator: About Ramp Metering; inspected passage indices 12, 16, 17 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: contenttext
evidence.note: Regulate freeway entry to break up merging platoons and reduce flow breakdown.

concepts.label: Ramp metering
concepts.learning_takeaway: Regulate freeway entry to break up merging platoons and reduce flow breakdown.

relations.note: The ramp-management handbook explicitly links metering success with containing and managing the resulting ramp queues.

concepts.card: A ramp meter can protect freeway flow while allowing its waiting queue to spill into nearby streets. Queue detectors and available storage therefore matter. Increasing the release rate can relieve the ramp but worsen freeway conditions, making queue management a balance between connected parts of the road system.

evidence.locator: Ramp Management and Control Handbook | Chapter 10 Planning and Design Considerations; inspected passage indices 72, 73, 107, 108, 109 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-73; paragraph-74; paragraph-108; paragraph-109; paragraph-110
evidence.note: Balance freeway entry control with finite ramp storage so queued vehicles do not block adjacent streets.

concepts.label: Ramp-queue spillback management
concepts.learning_takeaway: Balance freeway entry control with finite ramp storage so queued vehicles do not block adjacent streets.

relations.note: The handbook explicitly treats queue management as a design and operational concern for ramp metering.

concepts.card: A Ramsey number gives the smallest vertex count that forces either a clique of one chosen size or an independent set of another in any simple undirected graph. The party analogy treats vertices as people and edges as mutual acquaintance.

evidence.locator: Ramsey Number -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3
evidence.note: Find when every sufficiently large graph must contain a chosen clique or independent-set pattern.

concepts.label: Ramsey number
concepts.learning_takeaway: Find when every sufficiently large graph must contain a chosen clique or independent-set pattern.

relations.note: Ramsey numbers express an unavoidable-pattern question using graph vertices and edges.

concepts.card: A random walk builds a path from successive randomly chosen steps. The allowed directions, step lengths, and surrounding space define the model. Walks on a line, a plane, or a lattice can behave differently, so specifying the rules matters as much as calling the motion random.

evidence.locator: Random Walk -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 3 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-4
evidence.note: Repeated random steps form paths whose behavior changes with dimension and allowed movement.

concepts.label: Random walk
concepts.learning_takeaway: Repeated random steps form paths whose behavior changes with dimension and allowed movement.

relations.note: The Markov-chain reference explicitly names a simple random walk as an example.

concepts.card: A randomized controlled trial uses chance to assign participants to an intervention or comparison group. Comparing outcomes helps separate the intervention’s effects from differences that might influence who receives it. Randomization is a design tool; clear follow-up and careful analysis are still needed for a trustworthy result.

evidence.note: Supports chance assignment and comparing experimental and control outcomes.
Supports the qualification that randomization alone does not remove analysis or missing-outcome concerns.

concepts.label: Randomized controlled trial
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use chance-based assignment and a comparison group to assess an intervention’s effects.

relations.note: Concealing forthcoming assignments protects the random allocation process against selective enrollment.

concepts.card: Raft randomizes election timeouts so followers are less likely to start competing elections simultaneously. After a split vote, candidates wait for new randomized timeouts before trying again. Spreading their attempts helps one candidate obtain a majority before others begin another round.

evidence.note: Checked probabilistic reduction, retry timing, and majority election; not presented as a deterministic deadline guarantee.

concepts.label: Randomized election timeouts
concepts.learning_takeaway: Spread election starts probabilistically so competing candidates are less likely to repeatedly split votes.

relations.note: Raft section 5.2 explicitly uses randomized election timeouts to reduce and resolve split votes.

concepts.card: Rashi’s biblical commentary often proceeds verse by verse, noticing questions raised by the wording. His stated approach joins attention to contextual meaning with selected interpretive stories that help settle textual difficulties. The combination shows why plain reading and inherited commentary need not be mutually exclusive.

evidence.note: Verse-by-verse questions and the peshat/selected-aggadah combination are explicit.

concepts.label: Rashi
concepts.learning_takeaway: His verse-by-verse commentary combines attention to plain meaning with selected interpretive stories that address textual difficulties.

relations.note: The inspected lesson and quoted commentary explicitly connect Rashi’s method with peshat.

concepts.card: Ravishing DisUnities collected English ghazals under Agha Shahid Ali’s editorship, with poems differing in their fidelity to the inherited form. The anthology makes adaptation visible across writers. Its variety lets readers compare what happens when autonomous couplets and recurring verbal patterns are maintained or loosened.

evidence.note: The anthology and differing fidelity of its contributions are described.

concepts.label: Ravishing DisUnities: Real Ghazals in English
concepts.learning_takeaway: This anthology assembled English ghazals with varying fidelity to the inherited form, making formal adaptation visible across poets.

relations.note: The glossary explicitly credits Ali with assembling the anthology.

concepts.card: The Rayleigh criterion conventionally treats two point sources as just resolved when one diffraction maximum meets the other’s first minimum. For an ideal circular aperture much wider than the wavelength, increasing aperture size or shortening wavelength reduces the corresponding angular separation.

evidence.locator: 4.5 Circular Apertures and Resolution; inspected passage indices 9, 11, 12, 13 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1172101945964; fs-id1172099490776; fs-id1172101788340; fs-id1172101918383
evidence.note: Compare overlapping diffraction patterns to estimate when two point sources are just resolvable.

concepts.label: Rayleigh criterion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare overlapping diffraction patterns to estimate when two point sources are just resolvable.

relations.note: The source explicitly formulates the criterion as a diffraction limit on angular resolution.

concepts.card: Reaction order describes how a measured reaction rate depends on concentration. Doubling a reactant with order two multiplies its contribution to the rate by four. Orders can be zero, fractional, or negative, and do not generally follow the balanced equation’s coefficients.

evidence.locator: 12.3 Rate Laws; inspected passage indices 8, 9, 70, 71, 72 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idp18257184; fs-idm115903376; fs-idp9200128; fs-idm178764304; fs-idm284144576
evidence.note: Reaction orders are experimentally determined concentration exponents and need not match balanced-equation coefficients.

concepts.label: Reaction order
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reaction orders are experimentally determined concentration exponents and need not match balanced-equation coefficients.

relations.note: Initial-rate comparisons are explicitly used to infer reaction orders in the same section.

concepts.card: A reaction quotient summarizes a mixture’s current composition using products and reactants raised to their stoichiometric powers. Comparing it with the equilibrium constant predicts which reaction direction will dominate. Unlike the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature, the quotient changes as the mixture reacts.

evidence.locator: 13.2 Equilibrium Constants; inspected passage indices 6, 9, 43 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idp120703584; fs-idm352046000; fs-idm377606544
evidence.note: Compare the current reaction quotient with its equilibrium value to predict net reaction direction.

concepts.label: Reaction quotient
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare the current reaction quotient with its equilibrium value to predict net reaction direction.

relations.note: The source explicitly uses comparison of Q and K to predict the direction toward chemical equilibrium.

concepts.card: Carrying a disease-associated genetic variant does not always mean developing the condition. Reduced penetrance describes this incomplete appearance among people with the variant. Genetic background, environment and lifestyle may contribute, making a family’s inheritance pattern harder to interpret than a simple all-or-nothing prediction.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus defines penetrance as the proportion with signs and identifies incomplete expression and probable multifactorial causes.

concepts.label: Reduced penetrance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why not everyone carrying a disease-associated variant develops that condition.

relations.note: Penetrance asks whether a condition appears, while expressivity asks how its manifestations differ among affected people.

concepts.card: Reduplication repeats part or all of a linguistic form to express a grammatical or meaning contrast. In Halq'eméylem, one pattern derives meanings such as being disposed to an action. English salad-salad provides a different example: repetition can emphasize a prototypical instance rather than simply pluralizing something.

evidence.note: Checked repeated form, Halq'eméylem disposition example and English prototypicality; meanings of reduplication vary by construction and language.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source explicitly lists reduplication among morphological processes beyond affixation and supplies the two contrasting language examples.

concepts.label: Reduplication
concepts.learning_takeaway: Repeat all or part of a linguistic form to express a grammatical or meaning contrast.

relations.note: The source explicitly lists reduplication among morphological processes beyond affixation and supplies the two contrasting language examples.

concepts.card: A reference group supplies a standard people use to compare themselves with others. It need not be a group they actually belong to: admired athletes or an older sibling's friends may serve that role. Several reference groups can matter at once and convey competing expectations.

evidence.note: Checked comparison versus membership and multiple competing groups; no assumption that a reference group is necessarily beneficial or deliberately chosen.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source explicitly links reference groups with comparisons that guide behavior and establish social norms.

concepts.label: Reference groups
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish groups used as comparison standards from groups someone actually joins.

relations.note: The source explicitly links reference groups with comparisons that guide behavior and establish social norms.

concepts.card: A regulatory sandbox permits supervised testing of an innovation within defined limits. The UK's Financial Conduct Authority typically uses small, time-limited trials with real consumers. Acceptance does not remove authorization requirements or exempt a firm from national law, distinguishing controlled experimentation from unrestricted permission to operate.

evidence.locator: What the Regulatory Sandbox offers; tests; tools
evidence.note: FCA sections on offers, tests and tools support real consumers, scale/duration limits, authorization and inability to waive national law; the specific mechanics remain attributed to this regulator's program.

concepts.label: Regulatory sandbox
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish supervised, limited testing from exemption from regulation.

relations.note: Compare time-limited regulatory testing with automatic statutory expiry: both impose a time boundary, but a sandbox limits a trial while a sunset provision ends legal authority unless renewed.

concepts.card: Relative identity proposes that asking whether two things are the same requires specifying the kind of thing: the same what? On Geach's view, things might be the same under one classification but different under another. This contested proposal challenges treating identity as a single unqualified relation.

evidence.note: SEP Identity Over Time section 1 attributes sortal-relative identity to Geach and contrasts it with absolute identity; proposes and contested prevent endorsing it as standard logic.

concepts.label: Relative identity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore the proposal that identity must answer same what rather than identity without qualification.

relations.note: Compare ordinary numerical identity with a proposal that identity must be qualified by a sortal. This is a competing analysis, not another name for qualitative similarity.

concepts.card: Fluid travels in opposite directions through neighboring limbs of the kidney’s loop of Henle. The descending limb allows water to leave, while the thick ascending limb moves salt outward without water following. These differences help build the medullary concentration gradient used to recover water.

evidence.locator: Descending Loop; Ascending Loop; Countercurrent Multiplier System
evidence.note: The descending/thick-ascending passages support unequal water permeability, active salt reabsorption and the opposing-flow arrangement.

concepts.label: Renal countercurrent multiplication
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how opposite flows and unequal permeability build a medullary concentration gradient.

relations.note: The gradient-building arrangement supports the water recovery that ADH-regulated collecting-duct channels permit.

concepts.card: The kidney’s incoming arteriole responds directly to pressure changes. Rising pressure stretches its smooth muscle, which contracts and increases resistance; falling pressure permits relaxation. This local myogenic response helps stabilize renal blood flow without requiring a fresh instruction from nerves or circulating hormones.

evidence.note: OpenStax’s renal myogenic mechanism identifies the afferent arteriole, stretch-induced contraction, lower-pressure relaxation and intrinsic autoregulation.

concepts.label: Renal myogenic autoregulation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how pressure-induced contraction of an afferent arteriole stabilizes renal flow.

relations.note: Both contribute to renal autoregulation, but the myogenic response senses vessel stretch while tubuloglomerular feedback senses tubular conditions.

concepts.card: Reduced pressure at the kidney can trigger renin release and a cascade producing angiotensin II. This constricts vessels and stimulates aldosterone, which promotes sodium retention; water retention then supports blood volume. The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system connects circulation with the kidney’s handling of salt and water.

evidence.note: OpenStax describes renal renin release, angiotensin II vasoconstriction and aldosterone-mediated sodium/water retention.

concepts.label: Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect reduced renal pressure with vasoconstriction and sodium retention through a hormonal cascade.

relations.note: Comparing this volume-retaining cascade with atrial natriuretic peptide shows hormonal responses acting in opposing directions.

concepts.card: Repetitive narration recounts more than once an event that happened once. The repetition belongs to the telling, not to the occurrence. Separating those counts distinguishes several accounts of one event from a story in which similar events happen repeatedly.

evidence.note: Frequency taxonomy defines multiple tellings of one occurrence.

concepts.label: Repetitive narration
concepts.learning_takeaway: A single event can be recounted more than once, allowing repeated tellings rather than repeated occurrences to structure a narrative.

relations.note: Both can represent one occurrence, but only repetitive narration tells it several times.

concepts.card: Replay-resistant authentication makes a recorded earlier exchange insufficient for another successful login. Fresh challenges, nonces, or appropriately checked one-time outputs can demonstrate that an exchange is current. A reusable password alone lacks that property because the same secret is presented again each time.

evidence.note: Checked replay definition, freshness mechanisms, and password contrast; one-time outputs require proper verification rather than automatic safety from their name.

concepts.label: Replay-resistant authentication
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use freshness challenges or one-time outputs so recording a past authentication does not enable successful reuse.

relations.note: NIST distinguishes freshness against replay from binding authentication to the legitimate verifier against phishing; neither property is treated as a synonym for the other.

concepts.card: A replicated log records commands in a shared order across machines. In Raft, a leader sends entries to followers and uses log information to identify disagreements. Committed entries can then drive deterministic state machines, separating the agreement on history from execution of that history.

evidence.note: Checked ordered commands, leader replication, and committed execution; temporary follower differences are not incorrectly denied.

concepts.label: Replicated log
concepts.learning_takeaway: Retain an ordered command history across replicas and repair disagreements before applying committed entries.

relations.note: The Raft paper connects consistent replicated logs to ordered execution by replicated state machines.

concepts.card: A replicated state machine keeps several machines consistent by giving them the same ordered commands. If each replica executes those commands deterministically, their states and outputs match. The difficult coordination work is agreeing on the log despite failures, rather than independently guessing what state each machine should hold.

evidence.note: Checked same order and determinism conditions; replicas do not stay identical merely because software is copied onto them.

concepts.label: Replicated state machine
concepts.learning_takeaway: Execute the same ordered commands deterministically on several replicas to obtain matching states and outputs.

relations.note: Section 2 of the Raft paper explicitly implements replicated state machines using a replicated log of deterministic commands.

concepts.card: A seller's reputation can make future business depend on how current customers are treated. Passing off a poor-quality product may earn money now but lose repeat customers and recommendations later. This gives buyers a reason to consider the seller's ongoing stake, alongside the product they can inspect.

evidence.note: Checked short-term versus future-business incentives and repeat-customer mechanism; reputation is not treated as proof that a product is good.

concepts.label: Reputation in markets
concepts.learning_takeaway: Make future business valuable enough that sellers have a reason to preserve buyers' trust.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly discusses reputation together with guarantees, warranties and service contracts as responses to buyers' quality uncertainty.

concepts.card: Research debriefing explains a study after participation, especially when its purpose was concealed. Participants receive an honest account of the research question, the use of their data and why deception was used. The explanation helps restore information that the study deliberately withheld during the task.

evidence.note: Section 2.4 explicitly requires a full explanation after deceptive studies, including purpose, data use, reasons and further information; the card does not promise that explanation erases any harm.

concepts.label: Research debriefing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why concealed research purposes must be explained after deceptive studies.

relations.note: The ethics passage makes debriefing a requirement following deception and specifies the information participants should receive.

concepts.card: Resource mobilization theory explains social movements partly through their ability to obtain time, money, and participants. Grievances alone do not describe the practical work of organizing transport, meetings, or sustained action. The perspective directs attention to the resources and connections that make collective efforts possible.

evidence.note: Checked resource definitions and organizing examples; no claim that more money automatically guarantees movement success or that interpretation is irrelevant.

concepts.label: Resource mobilization theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain collective organizing partly through acquiring time, money, and people rather than grievances alone.

relations.note: Resource mobilization concerns practical capacity, whereas frame alignment concerns shared interpretations and goals; the source presents both as distinct movement perspectives.

concepts.card: Species can reduce direct competition by using different foods, different parts of a habitat or different feeding times. Resource partitioning separates their ecological niches even when they live nearby. The key distinction is how resources are used, rather than simply how many species are present.

evidence.note: The resource-partitioning paragraph names different resources, habitat areas and feeding times as ways to minimize direct competition.

concepts.label: Resource partitioning
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how different food, places or feeding times can reduce direct competition.

relations.note: The exclusion discussion introduces resource partitioning as a way species avoid complete niche overlap.

concepts.card: When metabolism makes the blood too acidic, increased ventilation can remove more carbon dioxide. This shifts the carbonic-acid balance and helps raise pH toward its usual range. Respiratory compensation can limit the disturbance, but it does not itself remove the underlying metabolic cause.

evidence.locator: Respiratory Regulation of Acid-Base Balance, paragraphs on CO2 removal
evidence.note: The respiratory-regulation section connects increased rate/depth of breathing, CO2 loss, lower carbonic acid and upward pH adjustment.

concepts.label: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect increased ventilation with lower carbon dioxide and partial correction of low blood pH.

relations.note: An arterial blood gas sample measures both carbon dioxide and pH, the quantities needed to examine this compensation mechanism.

concepts.card: A restricted repair request identifies a particular part of a message that needs clarification. Asking Who? narrows the trouble to a person reference instead of rejecting the whole utterance. This gives the original speaker a more focused task, such as specifying the missing identity or repeating that component.

evidence.locator: Results, Three basic types recur in all languages, pp. 4–5
evidence.note: Checked targeted slot and request format; unlike a restricted offer, it does not already supply a proposed interpretation for confirmation.

concepts.label: Restricted repair request
concepts.learning_takeaway: Target a specific missing or unclear component so the original speaker can give a focused clarification.

relations.note: The study explicitly defines restricted requests through targeted specification or clarification of a component of the prior turn.

concepts.card: Retroactive interference occurs when newer learning makes older information harder to recall. After learning a replacement address, you might struggle to recover the previous one. The direction reverses proactive interference: what was learned later now obstructs access to what was learned earlier.

evidence.note: OpenStax 8.3 defines new-to-old interference and depicts new and old email addresses; harder to recall does not assert permanent erasure.

concepts.label: Retroactive interference
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how later learning can obstruct access to older information.

relations.note: The chapter presents retroactive and proactive interference as opposite directions of interference between old and new learning.

concepts.card: Reviewability is a communication medium's ability to leave messages available for the recipient to inspect again. Written or recorded messages can support checking details that ordinary unrecorded speech leaves behind only briefly. This changes the effort needed for grounding, and differs from the sender's ability to revise before sending.

evidence.locator: Grounding Changes with the Medium, constraint 7
evidence.note: Checked recipient reinspection versus sender revisability; ordinary speech is qualified as unrecorded, and no medium is assumed perfectly persistent.

concepts.label: Reviewability of communication
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use persistent messages that an addressee can revisit, changing the need and cost of repetition during coordination.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly identifies reviewability as a medium constraint that changes available grounding techniques and their costs.

concepts.card: Rhythmic augmentation stretches a musical idea in time while preserving its relative durations. A motive in quarter notes might return in half notes, with every value doubled. This differs from simply adding notes at the end: the existing pattern itself occupies more time.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 11.2.3 defines usual proportional doubling; the contrast with extension is supported by 11.2.6. Preserve the registered rhythmic-augmentation control.

concepts.label: Rhythmic augmentation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize a motive whose durations expand proportionally while its pitch pattern remains recognizable.

relations.note: The text explicitly presents diminution as the opposite temporal transformation to augmentation.

concepts.card: A riparian forest buffer places trees, shrubs or other perennial vegetation beside water. The strip can filter runoff, stabilize banks and shade aquatic habitat. Its effectiveness depends on site conditions and continuity, so the presence of a few trees alone does not guarantee the same conservation benefit everywhere.

evidence.note: USFS defines streamside perennial buffers, identifies runoff filtering/bank stability/shade and lists site, landscape and continuity factors affecting effectiveness.

concepts.label: Riparian forest buffer
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect streamside vegetation with filtering runoff, stabilizing banks and shading aquatic habitat.

relations.note: A buffer changes habitat and runoff conditions, while benthic bioassessment can provide evidence of biological conditions in receiving waters.

concepts.card: Risk pooling combines many people's uncertain losses so premiums can fund the claims that actually occur. An individual may face a large bill even when the group's average loss is manageable. How people are grouped and priced matters, especially when their risks differ or are privately known.

evidence.note: Checked shared premiums and average loss example; pooling is not said to remove all correlated or catastrophic risk.

concepts.label: Risk pooling
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine many uncertain individual losses into a shared pool funded by premiums.

relations.note: The insurance example moves from pooled losses to premiums based on expected claims and distinguishes actuarially fair pricing.

concepts.card: The Rochdale Pioneers pooled scarce resources to sell basic goods through a cooperative shop in 1844. Customers became members, gained a democratic voice, and shared in profits connected with their custom. The case links retail trust and access to goods with a different arrangement of ownership and control.

evidence.note: Checked date, pooled resources, membership and profit sharing; not claimed to be the first cooperative activity anywhere in history.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The International Cooperative Alliance explicitly presents the Rochdale society as an influential prototype of the modern cooperative.

concepts.label: Rochdale Pioneers
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how pooling resources, honest retailing, democratic membership, and shared profits formed an influential cooperative model.

relations.note: The International Cooperative Alliance explicitly presents the Rochdale society as an influential prototype of the modern cooperative.

concepts.card: Role conflict occurs when obligations associated with different roles pull in incompatible directions. A parent may need to collect a sick child while an employer expects work on a deadline. The problem concerns competing roles, rather than only having too many demands inside one role.

evidence.note: Checked cross-role incompatibility and parent/work example; preserved the existing identity and distinction from role strain.

concepts.label: Role conflict
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish incompatible obligations between different roles from excessive demands within one role.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly contrasts parent-worker role conflict with strain arising from demands within a single role.

concepts.card: A role-set is the array of role relationships attached to a particular social status. Being a student, for example, involves more than one expectation or relationship. The concept differs from simply listing all the separate statuses a person holds, such as student, worker, and family member.

evidence.note: Checked Merton's single-status role-set definition; did not imply that having several attached roles necessarily creates conflict.

concepts.label: Role-set
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize that one social status can carry several distinct role relationships and expectations.

relations.note: A role-set organizes expectations attached to one status, while role conflict concerns incompatible demands; the concepts address different structural and experiential questions.

concepts.card: Role strain arises when the demands inside a single role become difficult to satisfy together. Parenting, for example, includes care, organization, transport, and guidance. A person can experience that pressure without also holding a conflicting job role, which distinguishes strain from conflict between separate roles.

evidence.note: Checked single-role pressure and multiple parenting duties; preserved the prior card's sense rather than merging it with role conflict.

concepts.label: Role strain
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize competing or excessive demands within a single role even without a clash between separate roles.

relations.note: The source explicitly defines within-role strain and contrasts it with incompatible obligations across multiple roles.

concepts.card: A rollback journal saves original database content before a transaction overwrites it. If the transaction must be undone, the saved content can restore the earlier state. This differs from SQLite's write-ahead-log mode, which preserves the main database while appending new changes elsewhere.

evidence.note: Checked old-versus-new content distinction and restoration purpose; not described as a permanent historical audit log.

SQLite WAL section 2 contrasts saved original pages in rollback mode with appended changed pages in SQLite's WAL file; section 2.1 describes later checkpoint transfer. This is an implementation-specific comparison, not a generic claim about every WAL design.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The saved-original-content mechanism is a concrete way SQLite realizes atomic commit in rollback mode; WAL provides a contrasting mechanism.

concepts.label: Rollback journal
concepts.learning_takeaway: Preserve old database content before overwrite so an uncompleted transaction can be undone.

relations.note: The saved-original-content mechanism is a concrete way SQLite realizes atomic commit in rollback mode; WAL provides a contrasting mechanism.

concepts.card: A dwarfing rootstock can limit an apple tree’s size while its scion determines the fruit variety. If a buried scion forms its own roots, the rootstock’s dwarfing influence can be lost. Tree size therefore depends partly on which root system supports the grafted shoot.

evidence.note: UMN explains rootstock control of size and warns that scion rooting above a buried graft union can defeat dwarfing.

concepts.label: Rootstock dwarfing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why the same apple variety can grow to different sizes on different rootstocks.

relations.note: This is a specific growth consequence of choosing the root system in a grafted tree.

concepts.card: In US criminal law, lenity favors the defendant when a statute remains ambiguous. It concerns interpreting a penal law's reach, rather than deciding whether evidence proves the conduct. Its rationale includes reserving the definition of crimes and punishments to lawmakers instead of judicial expansion.

evidence.note: Cornell's definition and separation-of-powers rationale support criminal-law ambiguity and legislative responsibility; remains ambiguous avoids suggesting every initial uncertainty immediately triggers the rule.

concepts.label: Rule of lenity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore construing unresolved criminal-law ambiguity in a defendant's favor.

relations.note: Lenity concerns ambiguity in a criminal law's meaning; the prosecution's burden concerns evidentiary proof of guilt. The sources support this distinction without treating them as interchangeable safeguards.

concepts.card: The Rule of Saint Benedict organizes monastic life around shared obligations, including manual labor, reading and communal prayer. Repetition gives the day a religious structure. Its influence came through adoption by communities, turning a written rule into a recurring pattern of work, worship and collective discipline.

evidence.note: Rule, repeated prayer, labor, reading and broad adoption are described.

concepts.label: Rule of Saint Benedict
concepts.learning_takeaway: A monastic rule organizes manual labor, reading and communal prayer into a repeated rhythm of shared life.

relations.note: The essay presents the rule as widely adopted within western European monastic life.

concepts.card: Sakichi Toyoda's loom work connects a named invention history with jidoka. Toyota describes looms that stopped automatically when yarn broke or ran out, reducing the need for constant watching. The lesson is a design response to abnormal conditions, rather than automation understood only as continuous unattended operation.

evidence.locator: Roots of Ideas, How did the idea of Jidoka come about?
evidence.note: Checked yarn-related stopping and historical lineage; no claim that the loom independently diagnosed or repaired the cause.

concepts.label: Sakichi Toyoda
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect his self-stopping loom experiments with the later manufacturing principle of detecting abnormalities at their source.

relations.note: Toyota directly traces jidoka's origin to Sakichi Toyoda's self-stopping loom developments.

concepts.card: The Salisbury convention restrains the House of Lords from voting down government bills promised in an election manifesto. It helps an elected government advance its announced program even without a Lords majority. This convention concerns how a chamber exercises its powers, rather than a new statutory voting procedure.

evidence.note: UK Parliament's Salisbury section states manifesto-bill restraint and lack of a Lords majority; describing it as a convention distinguishes the source's separate account of statutory Parliament Acts procedures.

concepts.label: Salisbury convention
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore restraint by the Lords toward government bills promised in an election manifesto.

relations.note: Compare a political convention limiting opposition to manifesto bills with a statutory route around Lords consent; both affect inter-chamber relations but operate through different mechanisms.

concepts.card: Utah’s Sand Hollow Reservoir stores water at the surface while also allowing it to infiltrate the underlying Navajo Sandstone aquifer. Monitoring showed recharge rates changing over time, with clogging and hydraulic conditions among the likely influences. The site illustrates why recharge performance must be measured after construction.

evidence.locator: Sand Hollow case, infiltration rates and monitoring
evidence.note: USGS describes the reservoir’s dual purpose, infiltration to Navajo Sandstone and changing recharge rates with likely clogging/gradient influences.

concepts.label: Sand Hollow Reservoir
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why engineered recharge performance can change as gradients and clogging evolve.

relations.note: Sand Hollow is the inspected field example of deliberately recharging an aquifer through surface-basin infiltration.

concepts.card: Sangha names the Buddhist community, sometimes specifically monastics and sometimes a wider community including lay followers. Monastics and laity can sustain reciprocal relationships: teaching and guidance flow one way, while food and other material support flow the other. The term’s boundaries depend on context.

evidence.note: Variable scope and reciprocal teaching/material support are explicit.

concepts.label: Sangha
concepts.learning_takeaway: Buddhist monastics and lay followers sustain reciprocal relationships of material support and teaching, although the term’s boundaries vary.

relations.note: The monastic discipline helps distinguish ordained obligations within the community.

concepts.card: Matera’s Sassi developed through cave dwellings, churches and workshops integrated with ravines and a limestone plateau. Building and excavation worked with the terrain’s existing forms. The settlement illustrates how an inhabited landscape can grow by adapting geological spaces rather than replacing them with an entirely separate urban grid.

evidence.note: Cave spaces, varied uses and adaptation to the limestone terrain are described.

concepts.label: Sassi of Matera
concepts.learning_takeaway: Cave dwellings, churches and workshops developed with the ravines and limestone plateau instead of replacing their topography.

relations.note: Both offer rock-adapted settlement cases, with different geology and historical uses.

concepts.card: A scanning tunneling microscope brings a sharp conducting tip extremely close to a biased conducting sample. Electrons tunnel across the gap, and current changes strongly with tip–surface separation. Monitoring that current while scanning reveals atomic-scale structure through electronic behavior rather than ordinary reflected-light imaging.

evidence.locator: 7.6 The Quantum Tunneling of Particles through Potential Barriers; inspected passage indices 65, 66 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1170902851400; fs-id1170901616105
evidence.note: Use the strong gap-dependence of tunneling current to map a conducting surface with atomic detail.

concepts.label: Scanning tunneling microscopy
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use the strong gap-dependence of tunneling current to map a conducting surface with atomic detail.

relations.note: The source explicitly states that the tunneling phenomenon underlies scanning tunneling microscopy.

concepts.card: Screening is an effort by the less-informed side of a transaction to learn relevant hidden characteristics. A buyer may have a mechanic inspect a used car, or an employer may check references. This reverses the initiative in signaling, where the better-informed party supplies an observable indication.

evidence.note: Checked mechanic inspection, employer inquiries and direction of initiative; did not import unsupported contract-menu claims from inaccessible Nobel pages.

concepts.label: Screening in economics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Let a less-informed party investigate or set requirements to learn hidden characteristics before a transaction.

relations.note: The inspected examples distinguish the investigator's effort to gather information from the informed party's presentation of a signal.

concepts.card: Scribing to fit transfers the contour of an existing surface onto a new workpiece. A cabinet panel beside an uneven wall, for example, can be marked to match that wall’s profile. The method handles irregularity directly instead of assuming that every surrounding surface is straight.

evidence.locator: Transferring wall contours onto a panel
evidence.note: Lee Valley describes transferring contours and specifically copying an old irregular wall profile onto a cabinet panel.

concepts.label: Scribing to fit
concepts.learning_takeaway: Fit a new component to an irregular existing surface by transferring its contour onto the workpiece.

relations.note: The contrast separates copying an encountered contour from reusing dimensions already stored on a story stick.

concepts.card: A Secchi disk uses a contrasting black-and-white target to assess water clarity. It offers a simple visual way to compare how readily something can be seen through water. Clarity matters because it influences how much light can reach submerged plants and other photosynthetic organisms.

evidence.note: EPA identifies the black-and-white Secchi target for visual clarity measurement and explains ecological importance through underwater light.

concepts.label: Secchi disk
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use a simple black-and-white visual target to assess water clarity.

relations.note: The visual clarity measure responds to water’s light-obscuring properties, but is not asserted to be numerically identical to turbidity.

concepts.card: For a reaction whose rate is proportional to one reactant’s concentration squared, the half-life depends on the starting concentration. As the mixture becomes more dilute, consuming half of what remains takes longer. A half-life alone cannot determine its rate constant without concentration information.

evidence.locator: 12.4 Integrated Rate Laws; inspected passage indices 83, 88 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm67735584; fs-idm75571200
evidence.note: For a single-reactant second-order law, lower initial concentration produces a longer half-life.

concepts.label: Second-order reaction half-life
concepts.learning_takeaway: For a single-reactant second-order law, lower initial concentration produces a longer half-life.

relations.note: The source directly contrasts this second-order behavior with first-order half-life.

concepts.card: A second-price sealed-bid auction gives the item to the highest bidder but charges the second-highest bid. The allocation rule resembles a first-price auction, while the payment rule differs. Also called a Vickrey auction, it separates the winning offer from the amount the winner actually pays.

evidence.note: Checked highest-versus-second-highest distinction; truthful bidding is not asserted without its private-value assumptions.

concepts.label: Second-price sealed-bid auction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Award the item to the highest bidder but charge the second-highest submitted bid.

relations.note: The lecture explicitly names Vickrey auctions and contrasts their payment rule with first-price sealed bidding.

concepts.card: Seismic tomography infers structures inside Earth from seismic information. Its models can address targets ranging from fault zones to the whole planet, but their usefulness depends on data quality, geographic coverage and uncertainty. A tomographic image is therefore an interpreted model, not a direct photograph underground.

evidence.note: The USGS-hosted 2024 review abstract identifies interior-structure applications and explicitly discusses inversion, coverage, data quality and uncertainty quantification.

concepts.label: Seismic tomography
concepts.learning_takeaway: Treat inferred Earth-interior structure as a model constrained by coverage, data quality and uncertainty.

relations.note: Inferring hidden Earth structure from measurements is a geologic investigation method, with the cited model/uncertainty qualifications retained.

concepts.card: Seki is mutual survival in Go without each group having two independent eyes. Neighboring groups share a shortage of liberties, and either player's attempt to capture can allow the opponent to capture first. Leaving the position alone therefore preserves both sides' stones.

evidence.locator: Seki: a kind of local stalemate
evidence.note: BGA's seki examples support mutual stand-off and shortage of liberties; no universal territory-scoring rule is added because rulesets differ.

concepts.label: Seki
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize mutual survival when either attack would allow the opponent to capture.

relations.note: The guide introduces seki as an exception to the simple expectation that a group lacking two eyes will die.

concepts.card: Self-efficacy is a person's belief that they can carry out a particular task. In Bandura's account, this belief helps shape the challenges people attempt and their persistence after setbacks. Believing an outcome is valuable differs from believing one has the capability to achieve it.

evidence.note: Section 10.1 defines task-specific capability beliefs and attributes their motivational role to Bandura; the card does not equate confidence with actual skill or guarantee success.

concepts.label: Self-efficacy
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish believing one can complete a task from valuing its reward.

relations.note: Capability beliefs answer whether one can perform a task, whereas intrinsic motivation concerns satisfaction in doing it; the chapter supports both premises without identifying them.

concepts.card: Self-explanation asks learners to produce their own account of why an idea or solution works. The aim is to connect steps to causes, principles, or reasons rather than merely say them aloud. The IES guide encourages explanatory questions and feedback instead of treating repetition of an answer as understanding.

evidence.note: Checked deep causal/logical explanations and think-aloud guidance; simple verbatim repetition is not equated with the explanatory process, without claiming that repetition has no other learning use.

concepts.label: Self-explanation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Generate one's own causal or logical explanations during study rather than merely repeating the presented answer.

relations.note: Explaining why steps work can complement studying a worked solution; the guide treats explanation generation and displayed examples as different instructional supports.

concepts.card: Some fruit varieties cannot reliably set fruit using their own pollen and need a different compatible variety nearby. Hybrid plums provide an example, whereas some European plums are self-compatible. Planning pollination therefore requires matching varieties, not merely counting the number of trees in the garden.

evidence.note: UMN explicitly contrasts self-incompatible hybrid plums with self-compatible European plums and identifies specific compatible pollenizer varieties.

concepts.label: Self-incompatibility in fruit crops
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why some fruit trees need pollen from a different compatible variety to crop well.

relations.note: Variety compatibility is a practical planning issue in fruit gardening, rather than a rule that all gardens need two trees of every kind.

concepts.card: The self-reference effect is a relative memory advantage for information connected to oneself. Material considered in personally relevant terms can be remembered better than less self-relevant material. It is studied as an influence on encoding, linking what information means to a person with later remembering.

evidence.note: OpenStax Encoding defines the relative advantage and places it after semantic-processing experiments; can avoids an exceptionless guarantee or an instructional prescription.

concepts.label: Self-reference effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Investigate why relating information to oneself can improve later remembering.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly introduces self-reference as an effect on encoding and subsequent memory.

concepts.card: Semantic compositionality explains how unfamiliar expressions can be understood from familiar parts and the way they are combined. It applies to sentences and to complex words. Knowing each piece is not enough on its own: different structures can organize the same pieces into different meanings.

evidence.note: Checked parts-plus-combination definition and complex-word application; not claimed to solve every idiom or contextual interpretation.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The compositionality chapter explicitly applies its principle to multi-morphemic words as well as sentences, linking meaning combination to morphology.

concepts.label: Semantic compositionality
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how a novel expression's meaning depends on its parts and how those parts are combined.

relations.note: The compositionality chapter explicitly applies its principle to multi-morphemic words as well as sentences, linking meaning combination to morphology.

concepts.card: A sentence entails another when the first cannot be true while the second is false. If someone sighed, for example, they emitted a breath. Adding a denial of the entailed claim produces a contradiction, unlike a merely suggested interpretation that the speaker can cancel.

evidence.note: Checked the truth-condition test and sigh/breath example; entailment is separated from plausible but defeasible inferences.

concepts.label: Semantic entailment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Test whether one sentence being true necessarily makes another true by looking for contradiction under denial.

relations.note: The source explicitly contrasts contradiction under denied entailments with the cancellability of implicatures using the sigh example.

concepts.card: Senet used a thirty-square board in ancient Egypt. Its imagery became more than decoration: during the New Kingdom, the game's passage through marked hazards was associated with the deceased person's journey toward the afterlife. Surviving game boxes connect recreation with funerary belief.

evidence.locator: Senet; Why is this game important?
evidence.note: The Met's Senet and importance sections support thirty squares, New Kingdom association and funerary objects; avoid presenting reconstructed detailed rules as certain.

concepts.label: Senet
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect an Egyptian board race with New Kingdom beliefs about the afterlife.

relations.note: The museum documents double-sided game boxes carrying senet on one side and Twenty Squares on the other.

concepts.card: With prolonged stimulation, a continuing sensory input can become less noticeable even while it remains present. OpenStax describes this as sensory adaptation. The change highlights a gap between continuing stimulation and conscious experience, helping explain why an initially prominent feature of the surroundings can fade from awareness.

evidence.note: OpenStax's perception section explicitly describes reduced notice during continued stimulation; this phenomenological card does not assert a particular receptor mechanism or equate every attention lapse with adaptation.

concepts.label: Sensory adaptation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish continuing sensory stimulation from reduced conscious notice over time.

relations.note: Reduced notice of sustained input differs from missing a visible unexpected event while concentrating on another task.

concepts.card: Separation of privilege requires more than one independent authority for a protected action. Splitting the necessary keys between different people, programs, or organizations means a single accident or breach need not suffice. It is different from merely assigning one powerful user a more complicated password.

evidence.note: Checked independent keys and separate responsibility; the comparison distinguishes multiple authorities from complexity of one credential.

concepts.label: Separation of privilege
concepts.learning_takeaway: Require independently held authorities so one error or compromised party cannot alone unlock a protected action.

relations.note: Separating required authorities and minimizing each participant's authority are distinct security design choices described in the same source.

concepts.card: In Sestina: Altaforte, Ezra Pound adopts the voice of a troubadour-warrior praising combat. The poem’s end-words recur in changing contexts. An editorial reading hears that recurrence intensifying the speaker’s fervor, while keeping the dramatic persona distinct from the poet.

evidence.note: The glossary identifies speaker, war praise and changing end-word effects.

concepts.label: Sestina: Altaforte
concepts.learning_takeaway: Pound adopts a troubadour-warrior’s voice and recurring end-words; an editorial reading hears their repetition intensifying the monologue’s praise of combat.

relations.note: The glossary explicitly uses this poem to demonstrate the sestina’s recurring end-words.

concepts.card: In laboratory redback-spider observations, second males that were cannibalized mated longer, and longer mating was associated with more paternity. This offers a possible reproductive explanation for a behavior that risks death. The evidence concerns a small experimental sample, not a guaranteed outcome for every male.

evidence.note: The case specifies second males, longer mating among cannibalized males, a positive mating-duration/paternity association and ten matings.

concepts.label: Sexual cannibalism in redback spiders
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore why a mating behavior that risks death can still correlate with increased paternity.

relations.note: The case illustrates the sexual-selection question of reproductive benefit despite a survival cost, without making every death adaptive.

concepts.card: A trait can improve success in obtaining mates while making survival harder. Sexual selection explains why conspicuous ornaments or risky mating behavior can spread despite such costs. The relevant outcome is contribution to the next generation, not simply how long an individual stays alive.

evidence.note: Berkeley contrasts mating success with survival costs and describes conspicuous ornaments and risky redback mating behavior.

concepts.label: Sexual selection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish mating success from survival when explaining conspicuous or risky traits.

relations.note: Redback sexual cannibalism offers a documented case for examining reproductive success despite a survival cost.

concepts.card: A shabad is a Sikh hymn sung or recited as a source of guidance and inspiration. Hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib are understood as divine teaching. Their use in worship and ordinary life connects the scripture’s words with memory, sound and repeated devotional practice.

evidence.note: Hymns, divine-word understanding and worship/everyday recitation are described.

concepts.label: Shabad
concepts.learning_takeaway: Sung or recited Sikh hymns are understood as divine teaching, joining scriptural words with everyday devotion.

relations.note: The source identifies shabads as hymns within this scripture.

concepts.card: Sharpening a blade can leave a thin wire edge, or burr, along the cutting edge. An unwanted burr may feel sharp initially but break away during use, leaving a rougher edge. Honing removes this fragile remnant, so forming an edge and finishing it are distinct parts of sharpening.

evidence.note: Tormek’s official answer describes wire-edge formation, breakoff during use and removal through honing.

concepts.label: Sharpening burr
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize the fragile wire edge left by sharpening and why it must be removed from a finished cutting edge.

relations.note: An unwanted sharpening burr is a particular edge condition addressed during the broader edge-refinement process.

concepts.card: Shibam’s tall mud-brick houses concentrate urban life within a compact defensive settlement. The surrounding floodplain supplied agricultural resources and building material. Its architecture is therefore tied to the landscape beyond the walls, combining dense habitation with dependence on nearby water and land.

evidence.note: Tower houses, defensive density and floodplain resources are described.

concepts.label: Shibam
concepts.learning_takeaway: Tall mud-brick houses combine dense defensive settlement with the floodplain resources that supplied agriculture and building material.

relations.note: Compare two earthen settlements whose distinct forms address collective habitation and defense.

concepts.card: Under the cited professional shogi impasse procedure, both kings have entered enemy territory and neither mating prospects nor further captures remain. Rooks and bishops count five points; other nonking pieces count one. Both players having at least twenty-four points leads to a draw and replay.

evidence.locator: 持将棋の規定はどうなっていますか
evidence.note: The Japan Shogi Association FAQ specifies professional play, both kings entering enemy territory, no mating prospect or further captures, and at least 24 points each. Amateur 27-point and declaration procedures are not generalized.

concepts.label: Shogi impasse
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore material counting when neither advanced king can plausibly be mated.

relations.note: The official FAQ describes material-count adjudication as a shogi procedure and distinguishes professional from amateur variants.

concepts.card: Signal detection theory separates sensory evidence from the criterion for reporting a signal. With evidence quality held fixed, lowering the criterion can increase both hits and false alarms; raising it can reduce both. Better sensitivity and greater willingness to answer yes are different changes.

evidence.note: Heeger’s Information and Criterion discussion and Figures 2–4 distinguish changing a criterion along one ROC from changing evidence quality. The revised card explicitly holds information fixed for the criterion tradeoff and makes no clinical recommendation.
Separates information quality and decision criterion, and shows the hit/false-alarm tradeoff.

concepts.label: Signal detection theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore detecting a target among noise when expectations and task goals influence reports.

relations.note: A fifty-percent detection threshold summarizes responses, while signal detection theory distinguishes evidence quality from the criterion behind those responses.

concepts.card: A signed social network records whether a relationship is positive or negative, rather than only whether a tie exists. This allows friendship and antagonism to appear in the same representation. Researchers can then examine configurations such as shared enemies or incompatible alliances, while recognizing that two signs simplify richer relationships.

evidence.note: Checked positive/negative interpretation and modeling simplification; no claim that all real relations fit a complete friend-or-enemy classification.

concepts.label: Signed social network
concepts.learning_takeaway: Represent both friendly and antagonistic relations with edge signs instead of recording only whether a relationship exists.

relations.note: The source introduces signed relationship graphs specifically as the representation used to investigate structural balance.

concepts.card: Silicon can protect itself with a thin surface layer of silicon dioxide. This passivation changes how the underlying material reacts with its surroundings. When hot, strong aqueous base removes the oxide, exposed silicon can react, illustrating the importance of surface chemistry to bulk behavior.

evidence.locator: 18.3 Structure and General Properties of the Metalloids; inspected passage indices 26 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm38894288
evidence.note: A thin oxide layer protects silicon; removing that layer changes its chemical reactivity.

concepts.label: Silicon passivation
concepts.learning_takeaway: A thin oxide layer protects silicon; removing that layer changes its chemical reactivity.

relations.note: Passivation concerns a protective surface layer, while zone refining removes bulk impurities; the same source supports this comparison.

concepts.card: Simultaneous contrast occurs when a color’s appearance changes with the colors beside it. The same painted area may therefore seem different in another setting. Comparing adjacent combinations shows that color is perceived relationally, rather than as an isolated property experienced identically in every composition.

evidence.note: The glossary defines appearance influenced by surrounding colors.

concepts.label: Simultaneous contrast
concepts.learning_takeaway: A color can look different because of the colors immediately surrounding it.
