relations.note: Neighbor-dependent color appearance is a specific phenomenon examined in color theory.
The glossary distinguishes neighboring-color effects from afterimage effects across time.

concepts.card: Singulative narration tells once what happened once. Its defining feature is the relation between occurrences and tellings, not the length of the passage. A long account can still be singulative if it represents a single occurrence one time.

evidence.note: The frequency definition establishes the one-occurrence/one-telling relation.

concepts.label: Singulative narration
concepts.learning_takeaway: A telling can represent one occurrence once, providing the baseline relation against which other narrative frequencies are compared.

relations.note: Compare one occurrence told once with several occurrences gathered into one telling.

concepts.card: Under the British Go Association's AGA-style rule, a player cannot make a play that recreates a board position previously created by that player. This reaches beyond immediate ko recapture, preventing longer repeating cycles such as triple ko from continuing indefinitely.

evidence.note: The precise BGA same-player formulation and triple-ko motivation are retained; this is not asserted to describe every international superko variant.

concepts.label: Situational superko
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare a whole-game repetition ban with the immediate ko restriction.

relations.note: BGA describes its superko restriction as preventing triple ko and other repeated positions beyond the basic local cycle.

concepts.card: A skin graft moves a piece of detached skin onto a wound that needs coverage. For the graft to survive, it must gain a blood supply from the receiving area. Successful placement therefore depends on biological attachment and nourishment, not merely covering the wound’s surface.

evidence.locator: What is a skin graft?; Risks—graft take
evidence.note: The NHS explanation defines transferred skin and describes new blood-vessel supply as part of graft take, with possible failure.

concepts.label: Skin grafting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why transferred skin must acquire blood supply from its new wound bed.

relations.note: Both practices transfer living tissue, but medical skin grafting depends on revascularization while horticultural grafting joins plant parts with different roles. This is an explicitly editorial cross-domain comparison, not equivalence.

concepts.card: Pulse oximeters estimate oxygen saturation using light, and skin pigmentation is one factor that can affect the result. A displayed number should therefore not be treated as equally exact in every person or circumstance. Understanding this limitation separates a convenient estimate from an infallible measurement.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus lists darker pigmentation among factors affecting pulse-oximetry accuracy and describes its light-based method.

concepts.label: Skin pigmentation and pulse oximetry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize skin pigmentation as one factor that can make an optical oxygen estimate inaccurate.

relations.note: Pigmentation-related error is a documented measurement limitation within pulse oximetry, not a second method for measuring oxygen.

concepts.card: Not all fault slip occurs as a sudden earthquake rupture. In Cascadia, slow-slip events produce deformation over longer periods and are observed through precise position measurements together with unusual seismic signals. They reveal movement on the plate boundary that the ordinary locked-then-breaking picture leaves incomplete.

evidence.note: The USGS review describes geodetic transient deformation, associated seismic signals and slower, prolonged slip in Cascadia.

concepts.label: Slow-slip events
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish prolonged transient fault slip from the rapid rupture of ordinary earthquakes.

relations.note: The Cascadia review supplies a named setting where slow-slip behavior has been observed and studied.

concepts.card: An S–N curve links repeated stress amplitude with the number of cycles a test specimen survives before failure. Some materials show an endurance-limit plateau, while others do not. Reading the curve requires the loading conditions, so one fatigue-life value cannot describe every service situation.

evidence.locator: 6.5: Fatigue; inspected passage indices 73, 74 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: section_2
evidence.note: Relate cyclic stress amplitude to measured fatigue life, recognizing that not every material has an endurance limit.

concepts.label: S–N curve
concepts.learning_takeaway: Relate cyclic stress amplitude to measured fatigue life, recognizing that not every material has an endurance limit.

relations.note: The reference explicitly presents S–N diagrams as measured descriptions of the fatigue process.

concepts.card: Snapshot isolation gives a transaction a stable view of data while other transactions may commit changes. SQLite's WAL readers keep seeing their earlier snapshot until they start a new transaction. A stable snapshot describes visibility; by itself, that description does not establish every system's serializability guarantees.

evidence.note: Checked the stable-view example and preserved the reviewer's distinction from serializable snapshot isolation; no universal serializability claim.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: SQLite's isolation documentation explicitly states that WAL mode exposes snapshot isolation to readers and explains the unchanged read view.

concepts.label: Snapshot isolation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Give a read transaction a stable historical view while later commits remain invisible until it restarts.

relations.note: SQLite's isolation documentation explicitly states that WAL mode exposes snapshot isolation to readers and explains the unchanged read view.

concepts.card: Social desirability bias can make self-reports reflect how people want to appear rather than what they actually do or believe. A respondent might underreport drinking to seem more acceptable. This is one possible source of inaccurate survey answers, alongside memory errors and other influences.

evidence.note: Section 2.2's surveys paragraph explicitly separates lying, misremembering and answers intended to look good; the card does not diagnose every inaccurate response as deliberate dishonesty.

concepts.label: Social desirability bias
concepts.learning_takeaway: Consider why answers about behavior may reflect a wish to appear acceptable.

relations.note: Social desirability concerns the participant's presentation of an answer, whereas experimenter expectancy concerns the researcher's interpretation; contrasting them separates two locations where measurement can be distorted.

concepts.card: Social norms are shared expectations about conduct. Some are written and formally enforced, while others are learned through observation and everyday reactions. A person's behavior can follow a norm even without an official watching, because approval, disapproval, and anticipated consequences also help sustain expectations.

evidence.note: Checked formal/informal expectations and social reactions; norms are distinguished from ideals and from a claim that everyone always complies.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The social-reality chapter explicitly defines institutionalization through establishing conventions or norms within society.

concepts.label: Social norms
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize shared expectations for conduct, including unwritten rules learned by observing others and their consequences.

relations.note: The social-reality chapter explicitly defines institutionalization through establishing conventions or norms within society.

concepts.card: A sociolinguistic corpus brings together records of language use so patterns can be studied beyond one person's conversation. Collections may include interviews, letters, or other speech and writing. Which speakers and contexts are represented matters when interpreting a pattern as characteristic of a wider community.

evidence.note: Checked collection types and representative sampling concern; a corpus is not automatically representative or restricted to interviews.

concepts.label: Sociolinguistic corpus
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine recordings across a relevant speaker sample so community patterns can be distinguished from individual habits.

relations.note: The source describes collections of interviews as sociolinguistic corpora while also allowing written and other recorded material.

concepts.card: A sociolinguistic interview gathers speech for studying variation. Tasks such as reading passages, pronouncing word pairs, and casual conversation can elicit different levels of self-monitoring. Researchers tailor the format to their question; an interview seeking natural conversation need not use every traditional task.

evidence.note: Checked traditional tasks and the source's tailoring caveat; not all sociolinguistic interviews are formal question lists or identical protocols.

evidence.locator: §10.7, Labov comparison of casual speech and reading
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The methods chapter explicitly designs interview tasks to elicit varying self-monitoring and compare contextual styles.

concepts.label: Sociolinguistic interview
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare speech across tasks that elicit different levels of self-monitoring, or collect natural conversation.

relations.note: The methods chapter explicitly designs interview tasks to elicit varying self-monitoring and compare contextual styles.

concepts.card: Sogdian merchants established communities along Eurasian trade networks rather than merely passing through them. These dispersed settlements helped goods, languages, religions and artistic practices circulate. Their history shows how sustained social connections could make merchants influential cultural intermediaries.

evidence.note: Dispersed communities and transmission of cultural practices are explicit.

concepts.label: Sogdian merchant diasporas
concepts.learning_takeaway: Sogdian commercial communities also transmitted religious traditions, artistic practices and languages through their dispersed trading networks.

relations.note: Sogdian trading communities operated within the Silk Road networks described by the museum.

concepts.card: Strong shaking can make loose, water-saturated sediment lose much of its supporting strength. During soil liquefaction, ground that previously carried buildings or other loads can deform and fail. The hazard depends on the material and water conditions, not just the earthquake’s size.

evidence.note: USGS defines loss of strength in saturated sediment during shaking and illustrates damage to supported structures.

concepts.label: Soil liquefaction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how shaking can make loose water-saturated sediment lose supporting strength.

relations.note: Earthquake energy release and liquefaction concern different steps: the shaking source and a susceptible ground material’s response.

concepts.card: A soil tensiometer uses a water-filled tube, a porous ceramic tip and a gauge to assess soil-water tension. It measures how tightly the soil holds water, not simply the fraction of soil volume occupied by water. That distinction matters when judging how hard roots must work to extract moisture.

evidence.note: UMN explains tension as extraction energy and describes the tensiometer’s water-filled tube, ceramic tip and gauge.

concepts.label: Soil tensiometer
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish how tightly soil holds water from the amount of water it contains.

relations.note: Water-availability measurements can inform irrigation decisions, while variable-rate irrigation concerns varying delivery across zones; no automatic control connection is assumed.

concepts.card: Cage's Sonatas and Interludes, composed in 1946–48, uses a prepared piano whose strings are altered by inserted materials. The John Cage Trust later supervised samples made with the work's actual preparation materials, linking the composition's identity to a particular physically modified sound source.

evidence.note: The Trust gives dates, work title and supervised sampling using actual preparation materials; no unsupported list of objects or formal analysis of the cycle is added.

concepts.label: Sonatas and Interludes
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a particular Cage cycle with reproducible preparations altering piano sound.

relations.note: The official description explicitly identifies the work's piano preparations as the basis for its supervised sampled sounds.

concepts.card: Song scholar-officials joined literary cultivation with government service. Their education helped define elite status, while their duties could include criticizing a ruler’s conduct. The role therefore linked political participation with a learned ideal of responsibility that could place officials in tension with authority.

evidence.note: Literary education, service and criticism of rulers are described.

concepts.label: Song scholar-officials
concepts.learning_takeaway: Literary education and service linked elite prestige with duties that could include criticizing rulers’ policies.

relations.note: Examinations connect the scholar-official role with the cultivation and testing of learning.

concepts.card: The sorites paradox turns tiny changes into a puzzle about vague categories. If one grain is not a heap, and adding one grain never makes the difference, repeated additions seem to imply that no heap is possible. Plausible small steps produce an unacceptable conclusion.

evidence.note: SEP opening and section 2 supply the grain-addition chain; the card identifies the conflict without asserting that the tolerance premise is true or resolving vagueness by definition.

concepts.label: Sorites paradox
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how apparently harmless small changes can generate a contradiction about vague categories.

relations.note: The entry presents epistemicism as one response to the sorites paradox, locating a sharp but unknowable boundary rather than accepting every small-step premise.

concepts.card: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission addressed abuses associated with apartheid through separate work on human-rights violations, reparations and rehabilitation, and amnesty. Its committee structure shows that truth-finding, assistance to victims and decisions about perpetrators' amnesty were related tasks, rather than one undifferentiated act of forgiveness.

evidence.note: The official TRC introduction identifies the post-apartheid mandate and three committees; the card describes institutional tasks rather than claiming universal reconciliation or automatic forgiveness.

concepts.label: South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare truth-finding, reparations and amnesty as separate parts of a post-apartheid process.

relations.note: The official site identifies the Amnesty Committee as one of the Commission's three components, directly locating amnesty decisions within its wider mandate.

concepts.card: The South Sea Bubble linked speculation in company shares with British government debt. The Bank of England's history describes limited trading but a dramatic stock-price rise after the company received part of the national debt in 1720. The episode contrasts share prices with actual trading activity.

evidence.note: The 1720 entry reports limited trading, involvement in national debt, a dramatic share-price rise and a crash. The card's closing comparison does not establish intrinsic value or assign the crash a single cause.

concepts.label: South Sea Bubble
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine how national-debt conversion and expectations drove a company's stock boom despite limited trading activity.

relations.note: The Bank's history explicitly describes the South Sea Company challenging its role as government banker and national-debt holder.

concepts.card: Span of control concerns how many people report directly to a manager. A narrow span gives each manager fewer direct reports and can accompany more layers of hierarchy. Choosing the span is therefore part of balancing supervision and coordination, not simply choosing an impressive management title.

evidence.note: Checked fewer direct reports in narrow spans; no universal optimal number or guaranteed performance advantage is claimed.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source treats supervisory span as a design consideration affecting hierarchy, making it a specific variable within organizational design.

concepts.label: Span of control
concepts.learning_takeaway: Choose how many people report directly to a manager, affecting oversight and the number of hierarchy layers.

relations.note: The source treats supervisory span as a design consideration affecting hierarchy, making it a specific variable within organizational design.

concepts.card: A spanning tree keeps every vertex of a finite connected graph while using just enough edges to preserve connectivity without cycles. For n vertices it has n minus one edges. Different choices can connect the same graph, so a network may have many spanning trees.

evidence.locator: Spanning Tree -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3
evidence.note: A connected graph can be reduced to a cycle-free set of edges that still reaches every vertex.

concepts.label: Spanning tree
concepts.learning_takeaway: A connected graph can be reduced to a cycle-free set of edges that still reaches every vertex.

relations.note: The source explicitly gives the matrix-tree theorem as a way to count a graph’s spanning trees.

concepts.card: Spatial autocorrelation asks whether nearby places tend to have similar or dissimilar measured values. A test combines the values with a definition of spatial relationships. It can distinguish clustering, dispersion or an absence of detected pattern, without by itself explaining what caused the arrangement.

evidence.note: Moran’s I discussion combines attributes and spatial relationships to assess patterns.

concepts.label: Spatial autocorrelation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Nearby locations can have similar or dissimilar measured values; testing the pattern uses both attributes and spatial relationships.

relations.note: A mapped pattern can motivate a spatial test, but visual shading alone is not that test.

concepts.card: Species counterpoint teaches melodic combination through restricted rhythmic relationships. Exercises can place one, two, three or four notes against a note in another voice. The cited textbook focuses on two voices, while noting that a longer college course may extend the method to four.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 30.1 explicitly describes rhythmic ratios, its two-voice focus and up to four voices in a semester course. No uninspected claim of a staged educational or coordination benefit remains.

concepts.label: Species counterpoint
concepts.learning_takeaway: Learn how controlled note ratios organize practice in combining independent melodies.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly presents species counterpoint as a method for learning contrapuntal composition.

concepts.card: Specific impulse compares rocket thrust with propellant weight-flow rate, using standard gravity to convert from mass flow. Its units are seconds, but it is not the engine’s burn duration. A higher value means more impulse per unit propellant, rather than necessarily a larger thrust force.

evidence.locator: Specific Impulse; inspected passage indices 14, 16, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-15; paragraph-17; paragraph-23; paragraph-24; paragraph-25; paragraph-26; paragraph-27; paragraph-28; paragraph-29
evidence.note: Defines total and specific impulse, the standard-gravity conversion, time units, and comparison of propellant use.

concepts.label: Specific impulse
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare thrust per propellant weight-flow rate, rather than thrust alone, when evaluating rocket propulsion.

relations.note: The source defines specific impulse by dividing total impulse by propellant weight.

concepts.card: Spirometry records how much air a person can blow out and how quickly it leaves the lungs. A forceful breath into a measuring device produces information about airflow and volume. It is one part of lung-function assessment, rather than a single test that identifies every breathing disorder.

evidence.locator: Common lung function tests; Spirometry procedure
evidence.note: MedlinePlus describes forceful expiration into a spirometer and measurement of exhaled amount and speed.

concepts.label: Spirometry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Measure both the amount and speed of exhaled air to investigate lung function.

relations.note: Spirometry’s exhaled airflow/volume measurements contrast with the total and residual lung-volume information from body plethysmography.

concepts.card: Spit bite aquatint applies acid directly with a brush to an aquatinted plate. The local treatment allows tonal passages that resemble washes rather than relying only on an evenly timed bath. The resulting printed marks connect painterly handling with an intaglio process.

evidence.note: Direct brushed acid and wash-like tones are stated.

concepts.label: Spit bite aquatint
concepts.learning_takeaway: Applying acid directly with a brush to an aquatinted plate allows the printmaker to create wash-like tonal passages.

relations.note: The glossary explicitly identifies spit bite as a way of working an aquatinted plate.

concepts.card: Spitzer’s original cryogenic design cooled its telescope assembly to about five kelvin using liquid helium. Suppressing the observatory’s own infrared emission helped prevent its thermal glow from interfering with observations of relatively cold cosmic objects.

evidence.locator: Spitzer Space Telescope; inspected passage indices 7, 14, 16 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-8; paragraph-15; paragraph-17
evidence.note: Liquid-helium cooling suppressed the infrared telescope’s own heat during its original cryogenic mission.

concepts.label: Spitzer Space Telescope
concepts.learning_takeaway: Liquid-helium cooling suppressed the infrared telescope’s own heat during its original cryogenic mission.

relations.note: Herschel provides another documented infrared observatory with cryogenically cooled instruments, enabling comparison of thermal observing strategies.

concepts.card: SQL lets a program describe the data it wants rather than prescribe every retrieval step. The database's query planner chooses an execution strategy, such as scanning a table or using an index. The same requested result can therefore be produced through different underlying algorithms.

evidence.note: Checked declarative query semantics and planner alternatives; the description is about querying, not every SQL operation or implementation.

concepts.label: SQL
concepts.learning_takeaway: Describe desired query results declaratively while a database planner chooses how to find them.

relations.note: SQLite's query-planner overview explicitly explains SQL's declarative role and the database engine's choice of retrieval algorithm.

concepts.card: SQLite embeds a transactional SQL database engine inside an application. It reads and writes ordinary files without a separate database server process, and a complete database can occupy one file. That design makes a database library useful where an application would otherwise manage its own file format.

evidence.locator: About SQLite, first two main paragraphs
evidence.note: Checked in-process operation, absent separate server, and single-file storage; no claim that transient journal files never exist.

concepts.label: SQLite
concepts.learning_takeaway: Embed a transactional database directly in an application without a separate database server process.

relations.note: SQLite's About page directly states that it is an embedded, serverless SQL database engine and discusses its application-file-format role.

concepts.card: Stalemate is a drawn chess position in which the player to move has no legal move and their king is not in check. The distinction from checkmate is crucial: immobilizing the opponent does not win if no attack on the king accompanies that immobilization.

evidence.note: FIDE 5.2.1 supports side-to-move, absence of any legal move, no check and immediate draw; immobility of one piece alone is insufficient.

concepts.label: Stalemate
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish having no legal move from being checkmated.

relations.note: The laws define stalemate as one of chess's game-ending draw conditions.

concepts.card: In US federal court, standing ordinarily requires a concrete, particularized injury that is actual or imminent, linked to the challenged conduct and likely to be redressed by a favorable decision. Disagreeing with a policy is therefore different from showing the personal stake needed to bring the lawsuit.

evidence.note: Cornell's federal-standing section gives injury, causation and likely redressability; the jurisdiction is explicit and ordinarily avoids implying this short statement exhausts every standing doctrine.

concepts.label: Standing to sue
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a concrete, redressable legal injury from disagreement with government policy.

relations.note: Standing concerns a party's ability to bring suit; amicus participation lets a nonparty offer a brief under court rules. The comparison separates initiating litigation from contributing to its consideration.

concepts.card: When starch is heated with water, its granules absorb water and swell, thickening the mixture. This gelatinization helps give sauces and puddings their texture. It is a change in the hydrated starch structure, distinct from simply dissolving a sweetener or cooling a gelatin dessert.

evidence.note: The pastry text defines heat-and-water-driven swelling and thickening and names sauces/puddings as examples.

concepts.label: Starch gelatinization
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain thickening when starch granules absorb water and swell during heating.

relations.note: Gelatinization during heating and starch reassociation during storage are distinct stages in starch-based food structure.

concepts.card: After starch has been cooked, its molecules can associate again and develop more ordered structures during storage. This retrogradation changes the starch matrix and can affect texture and digestibility. It is a later rearrangement, distinct from the initial water uptake and swelling of heated starch granules.

evidence.note: Supports chain reassociation and ordering during storage and effects on structure and digestibility.
Supports initial water uptake/swelling during heating, used as the explicit comparison.

concepts.label: Starch retrogradation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish molecular re-ordering during storage from the initial swelling of starch during cooking.

relations.note: The comparison separates initial heat-driven granule swelling from later chain reassociation.

concepts.card: Stare decisis promotes consistency by directing courts to follow precedent. In the cited US account, vertical precedent comes from higher courts; horizontal precedent concerns a court's own earlier decisions. The Supreme Court can overrule its precedents, so continuity does not make every prior ruling permanent.

evidence.note: Cornell distinguishes horizontal and vertical precedent, cites the US Supreme Court’s limits on stare decisis and gives Brown as an example. The revised card does not imply lower courts may disregard binding higher-court precedent.

concepts.label: Stare decisis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare following a higher court with following one's own prior decisions.

relations.note: Cornell explicitly uses Brown's rejection of the separate-but-equal precedent as an example showing that stare decisis is not absolute.

concepts.card: Staystitching adds a permanent row of stitches to an individual fabric piece before assembly. Placed within the seam allowance, it helps keep vulnerable curves or bias edges from stretching during handling. It stabilizes the cut shape, rather than serving as the seam that joins two pieces together.

evidence.locator: What is it?; When to staystitch
evidence.note: ASG defines single-layer pre-assembly stabilization within the allowance, especially at curved/bias areas, and states the stitches remain in the garment.

concepts.label: Staystitching
concepts.learning_takeaway: Stabilize an individual cut fabric edge before handling and assembly stretch it out of shape.

relations.note: Staystitching stabilizes a cut edge before assembly; understitching controls a facing after its seam has been sewn.

concepts.card: Steam bending uses heat and moisture to make suitable wood more flexible. The piece is shaped and then restrained while it cools and dries, helping it retain the curve. Moisture changes later can still alter that shape, so bending success involves both forming and conditioning the material.

evidence.locator: Principles of Plasticizing and Bending; Fixing the Bend
evidence.note: USDA Chapter 19 describes heat/moisture plasticization, restraint during cooling/drying and later moisture-dependent curvature changes.

concepts.label: Steam bending
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use heat and moisture to soften wood, then retain a curved shape while it cools and dries.

relations.note: Steam bending is a wood-shaping process whose success depends on the material’s moisture and heat response.

concepts.card: Stellar parallax measures distance from a star’s apparent shift as Earth changes position in its orbit. Nearby stars shift more than distant ones against the background. Knowing the observing baseline turns this tiny angular change into a geometric measurement rather than an estimate based on stellar brightness.

evidence.locator: 19.2 Surveying the Stars; inspected passage indices 11, 12, 16, 17 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1165721912109; fs-id1165721391551; fs-id1165721903599; fs-id1165722097273
evidence.note: Earth’s orbital baseline turns tiny annual angular shifts into geometric stellar-distance measurements.

concepts.label: Stellar parallax
concepts.learning_takeaway: Earth’s orbital baseline turns tiny annual angular shifts into geometric stellar-distance measurements.

relations.note: Parallax reflects changing viewpoint, whereas proper motion reflects a star’s changing sky position over time; they must be separated in astrometry.

concepts.card: Proper motion is a star’s persistent angular drift across the sky over time. It differs from motion toward or away from us measured by radial velocity. Combining proper motion, distance, and radial velocity lets astronomers reconstruct the star’s actual movement through space.

evidence.locator: ESA; inspected passage indices 1, 2, 5 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3; paragraph-6
evidence.note: Separate stars’ long-term angular motion from line-of-sight velocity to reconstruct motion through space.

concepts.label: Stellar proper motion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate stars’ long-term angular motion from line-of-sight velocity to reconstruct motion through space.

relations.note: ESA explicitly describes combining these measurements from Gaia to determine stellar motion.

concepts.card: Stereographic projection maps a sphere, apart from its projection pole, onto a plane. Draw a line from the pole through a surface point and continue it to the plane. The construction turns spherical positions into planar coordinates using the geometry of similar triangles.

evidence.locator: Stereographic Projection -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3
evidence.note: Project from a sphere’s pole onto a plane to translate spherical locations into planar coordinates.

concepts.label: Stereographic projection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Project from a sphere’s pole onto a plane to translate spherical locations into planar coordinates.

relations.note: Projection coordinates can depict routes on a sphere, but the geodesic source makes clear that intrinsic shortest paths depend on the surface metric.

concepts.card: The Stern–Gerlach experiment sent ground-state silver atoms through a nonuniform magnetic field and produced two separated bands. A classical picture allowing every magnetic orientation would predict a continuous spread. The result reveals quantized angular-momentum projections associated with the atoms’ unpaired electron spin.

evidence.locator: 8.3 Electron Spin; inspected passage indices 26, 27 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1170902163294; fs-id1170903720942
evidence.note: A nonuniform magnetic field splits a silver-atom beam into two bands rather than a classical continuum.

concepts.label: Stern–Gerlach experiment
concepts.learning_takeaway: A nonuniform magnetic field splits a silver-atom beam into two bands rather than a classical continuum.

relations.note: The source explicitly interprets the two bands in terms of the unpaired electron’s spin projections.

concepts.card: Stirling numbers of the second kind count ways to divide distinct objects into a fixed number of nonempty, unlabeled groups. Three objects can form two groups in three ways. Membership matters, but swapping the order in which the groups are listed does not create another partition.

evidence.locator: Stirling Number of the Second Kind -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-3
evidence.note: Count partitions of a labeled set into a fixed number of nonempty unlabeled blocks.

concepts.label: Stirling numbers of the second kind
concepts.learning_takeaway: Count partitions of a labeled set into a fixed number of nonempty unlabeled blocks.

relations.note: Set partitions distinguish individual objects, while integer partitions distinguish summand sizes; comparing them prevents conflating two different counting problems.

concepts.card: A story stick carries a project’s important dimensions as full-size marks on one physical strip. The marks preserve their relationship to one another and provide a reusable layout reference. Transferring those positions can reduce the need to repeatedly reinterpret a list of separate numerical measurements.

evidence.note: WOOD’s explanation defines a strip bearing critical full-scale dimensions and a visual representation of the project.

concepts.label: Story stick
concepts.learning_takeaway: Preserve project dimensions together on a physical reference rather than repeatedly translating separate numbers.

relations.note: A story stick preserves designed positions, while scribing transfers an existing irregular contour; both are layout aids with different inputs.

concepts.card: Ireland's citizens' assembly recruitment combines chance with demographic balancing. Randomly invited households may nominate an adult applicant; members are then selected using demographic information so the group broadly resembles society. The resulting mini-public is intended to be diverse, rather than simply comprising whoever volunteers first.

evidence.locator: How are members selected?; recruitment method
evidence.note: The official FAQ's recruitment paragraphs describe random household invitations, one adult nominee and stratified selection among applicants; intended and broadly avoid claiming perfect representativeness or eliminating nonresponse effects.

concepts.label: Stratified sortition for citizens’ assemblies
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how lottery recruitment and demographic stratification produce an intended mini-public.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies stratified selection as the membership-recruitment procedure for Irish citizens' assemblies, connecting mechanism and deliberative body.

concepts.card: William Morris’s Strawberry Thief was produced using indigo-discharge printing. Its motif was inspired by thrushes stealing fruit in his garden. The V&A connects the method with crisp outlines, offering a technical context for examining the pattern’s printed detail.

evidence.note: The V&A identifies the indigo-discharge method and garden-thrush inspiration, then discusses the crisp outlines enabled by that method.

concepts.label: Strawberry Thief
concepts.learning_takeaway: Morris used indigo-discharge printing for Strawberry Thief, a textile pattern inspired by fruit-stealing thrushes in his garden.

relations.note: The workshop’s documented indigo facilities provide context for the design’s described indigo-discharge method.

concepts.card: A stress intensity factor describes the strength of an elastic crack-tip stress field. In opening mode, it depends on applied stress, crack size, and geometry. Two components carrying similar nominal stress can therefore face different crack-tip loading if their flaws differ in size or shape.

evidence.locator: Chapter 10: Creep, Fracture, and Fatigue; inspected passage indices 139, 140, 141 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-140; paragraph-141; paragraph-142
evidence.note: Combine applied stress, crack size, and geometry to characterize loading near a crack tip.

concepts.label: Stress intensity factor
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine applied stress, crack size, and geometry to characterize loading near a crack tip.

relations.note: The source explicitly compares stress intensity with fracture toughness to describe a crack-extension threshold.

concepts.card: Piano octaves are often tuned slightly wider than a strict two-to-one frequency ratio. Stiff strings have upper partials sharper than ideal harmonics. Matching the upper note to a lower string's second partial can reduce audible beating, making a mathematically exact octave a poor practical match.

evidence.note: UNSW FAQ gives stretched second partials and beat-eliminating tuning; often and can avoid prescribing one exact stretch for every piano or register.

concepts.label: Stretch tuning
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain slightly widened piano octaves through the inharmonicity of stiff strings.

relations.note: The FAQ explicitly explains stretched tuning as a response to stiffness-induced inharmonicity in struck piano strings.

concepts.card: The strong triadic closure property is an idealized rule: if someone has strong ties to two others, those two must have at least some tie between them. It permits deductions about network structure. The source explicitly warns that real social networks need not satisfy this rule everywhere.

evidence.note: Checked strong-to-two condition, either-strength closing edge, and explicit nonuniversality; the conditional model is not described as an observed social law.

concepts.label: Strong triadic closure property
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use an explicitly idealized rule that two strong neighbors must also have some tie to derive network consequences.

relations.note: The source introduces the named property as a formal, deliberately stronger version of the qualitative triadic-closure tendency.

concepts.card: Structural ambiguity occurs when the same words allow different internal groupings. In I saw someone with a telescope, the telescope may be the instrument used for seeing or something the other person possessed. The difference comes from phrase attachment, without requiring a word to acquire another meaning.

evidence.note: Checked both telescope attachments and distinction from lexical ambiguity; no claim that every ambiguous expression has exactly two parses.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The telescope example illustrates why semantic composition depends on how parts are grouped, not only on the meanings of individual words.

concepts.label: Structural ambiguity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Derive different interpretations from alternative phrase attachments while keeping the words unchanged.

relations.note: The telescope example illustrates why semantic composition depends on how parts are grouped, not only on the meanings of individual words.

concepts.card: Structural balance studies patterns of friendly and antagonistic ties. In its basic signed-triangle model, triangles with one or three positive edges count as balanced. Other combinations represent proposed tensions, such as being friends with two people who dislike each other; the model simplifies real relationships deliberately.

evidence.note: Checked the one-or-three-positive rule for the basic model; not confused with weaker balance variants or asserted as universal human behavior.

concepts.label: Structural balance in social networks
concepts.learning_takeaway: Model consistency of positive and negative ties by distinguishing balanced triangles from potentially conflicting configurations.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly develops structural balance by assigning positive and negative signs to network edges and examining triangle configurations.

concepts.card: Structural holes are gaps between groups that do not otherwise interact closely. Someone whose connections span such a gap may obtain information from different circles or broker their contact. The position can offer opportunities, but it can also create conflicting expectations and incentives to preserve the gap.

evidence.note: Checked informational/brokerage opportunities and competing incentives; correlations with success are not recast as guaranteed causal rewards.

concepts.label: Structural holes
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize opportunities for brokerage where otherwise weakly connected groups hold different information.

relations.note: The chapter connects brokerage across structural holes with boundary-spanning ties, while distinguishing a network position from how emotionally close a relationship is.

concepts.card: A stupa is a Buddhist structure that can house sacred relics and texts and serve as a focus of veneration. Forms range from small objects to monuments. Moving around a stupa in circumambulation connects the physical structure with an embodied devotional practice.

evidence.note: Relics/texts, varied scale and circumambulation are described.

concepts.label: Stupa
concepts.learning_takeaway: A structure housing sacred relics or texts provides a focus of Buddhist veneration, often approached through circumambulation.

relations.note: The source identifies stupas as Buddhist devotional structures.
The source identifies stupas as Buddhist relic repositories and objects of veneration.

concepts.card: Style shifting is a change in how a speaker uses linguistic variants across situations. Labov's New York study compared casual speech with reading aloud and found systematic differences in variant frequencies. Such shifts show that describing someone's language with one unchanging social label misses variation within that person's usage.

evidence.locator: §10.7, Labov comparison of casual speech and reading
evidence.note: Checked contextual frequencies and named study; not claimed that every speaker changes in an identical direction or amount.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The methods and social-status chapters explicitly connect interview contexts and Labov's casual-speech/reading comparisons to style shifting.

concepts.label: Style shifting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Observe speakers changing variant frequencies with speaking context rather than assigning one fixed style to each class.

relations.note: The methods and social-status chapters explicitly connect interview contexts and Labov's casual-speech/reading comparisons to style shifting.

concepts.card: Subak is a Balinese institution through which farmers coordinate irrigation and related obligations. Water temples connect these collective arrangements across terraced watersheds. The system joins agricultural management with ritual organization, showing how distributing water can depend on shared institutions as well as physical channels.

evidence.note: Farmer collectives, temple networks and coordinated irrigation are explicit.

concepts.label: Subak
concepts.learning_takeaway: Balinese farmer collectives coordinate irrigation across terraced watersheds through institutions centered on water temples.

relations.note: The landscape contains the temples, waterways and terraces through which subak institutions operate.

concepts.card: Suberogation is a proposed category of morally bad but permissible conduct, conceived as a counterpart to good actions beyond duty. Ingratitude is sometimes offered as an example, but both the examples and the category are disputed. Badness and prohibited wrongdoing need not be treated as identical.

evidence.note: SEP section 2 describes the proposed mirror category, contested ingratitude example and difficulty identifying clear cases; proposed and sometimes preserve its disputed status.

concepts.label: Suberogation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Consider the disputed category of bad yet morally permitted conduct.

relations.note: The source introduces suberogation by asking whether supererogation has a mirror image, then examines why the suggested symmetry is controversial.

concepts.card: Successive contrast occurs when an afterimage from a previously viewed color affects the appearance of a color seen afterward. The relationship unfolds across time, rather than between neighboring patches viewed together. What the viewer has just looked at becomes part of the next color experience.

evidence.note: The glossary explicitly identifies afterimage influence on a subsequently viewed color.

concepts.label: Successive contrast
concepts.learning_takeaway: An afterimage from a color seen first can alter the appearance of a color viewed afterward.

relations.note: Afterimage-dependent color appearance is a specific phenomenon examined in color theory.
The source contrasts temporal afterimage influence with spatially adjacent color influence.

concepts.card: Sugar-lift etching begins with a water-soluble drawing that is covered by a resistant ground. Water dissolves the drawing and lifts the covering above it, exposing those areas for further work. The method lets drawn marks determine where the plate can subsequently be etched.

evidence.note: Soluble drawing, varnish ground and lifting sequence are described.

concepts.label: Sugar-lift etching
concepts.learning_takeaway: A water-soluble sugar drawing beneath a varnish ground lifts away in water, exposing drawn areas for etching, often after aquatint.

relations.note: The lift-ground method prepares exposed areas for etching.

concepts.card: In US federal civil procedure, summary judgment can resolve a claim without trial when no genuine dispute of material fact remains and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. It does not authorize choosing between competing evidence that a reasonable factfinder could resolve differently.

evidence.note: Cornell's Rule 56 section and favorable-to-nonmovant discussion support both conditions and the factual-dispute limitation; the card is explicitly federal and civil rather than a universal rule for all courts.

concepts.label: Summary judgment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand deciding a claim without trial when no material factual dispute requires resolution.

relations.note: Both may be considered before trial, but summary judgment adjudicates a claim or issue while a preliminary injunction supplies interim protection before final judgment.

concepts.card: A sunset provision makes a law, program or agency expire after a specified period unless renewed through the required legislative process. Instead of requiring a fresh decision to terminate it, the provision makes continuation depend on renewed approval. This changes the default when lawmakers take no action.

evidence.note: Cornell's sunset-law definition and two-year program example support automatic expiry and renewal; required legislative process avoids assuming every sunset uses identical review procedures.

concepts.label: Sunset provision
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand automatic expiration as a way to require renewed legislative approval.

relations.note: A sunset changes the default duration of legal authority; a sandbox bounds a supervised test. Their shared time limit is useful to compare without equating the institutional mechanisms.

concepts.card: Supererogation is morally good action beyond what duty requires. A costly rescue may be admired even when failing to undertake it would not violate an obligation. Whether such optional goodness forms a genuine category is disputed, because some ethical theories make every morally best action compulsory.

evidence.note: SEP opening and Definition discuss good-but-not-required acts, heroic examples and theories denying the category; costly rescue is an illustration, not a requirement that every supererogatory act be costly.

concepts.label: Supererogation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore the possibility of morally good actions that duty does not require.

relations.note: The entry explicitly distinguishes optional action beyond duty from imperfect duties, which remain binding while allowing discretion over fulfillment, and notes attempts to equate them.

concepts.card: Supervaluationism evaluates a vague statement across admissible ways of making its terms precise. A statement true under every such interpretation is supertrue; some borderline statements are neither supertrue nor superfalse. This permits truth-value gaps while preserving many classical logical laws, including excluded middle.

evidence.note: SEP section 3.3.1 defines admissible precisifications, supertruth and gaps while discussing retained classical laws; the card does not equate semantic indeterminacy with epistemic ignorance.

concepts.label: Supervaluationism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore evaluating a vague statement across admissible precise interpretations.

relations.note: The entry explicitly contrasts supervaluationism's semantic indeterminacy with epistemicism's unknown but sharp boundaries; this comparison explains their different treatments of borderline cases.

concepts.card: A surface triangulation represents a surface as triangles joined along compatible edges. This replaces an apparently continuous object with pieces that can be counted and assembled. The construction supports topological reasoning without requiring the triangles to preserve every original distance or angle.

evidence.locator: Triangulation -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2
evidence.note: Represent a surface by joined triangles so its topology can be studied combinatorially.

concepts.label: Surface triangulation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Represent a surface by joined triangles so its topology can be studied combinatorially.

relations.note: Counting vertices, edges, and faces in a triangulation supplies a concrete route to a surface’s Euler characteristic.

concepts.card: A surrogate endpoint is a measured indicator used in place of an outcome that matters directly to patients. Tumor shrinkage, for example, can be observed sooner than longer survival. The substitution is useful only to the extent that the indicator reliably reflects the benefit being sought.

evidence.note: NCI gives tumor shrinkage and biomarkers as faster substitutes for survival/quality-of-life endpoints and warns they are not always true indicators.

concepts.label: Surrogate endpoint
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a quickly measured biological indicator from a direct patient benefit.

relations.note: Endpoint choice is a specific trial-design decision: the measured comparison may concern a surrogate rather than a direct patient outcome.

concepts.card: A suspension carries a prepared note into a moment where it becomes an accented non-chord tone, then resolves downward by step. Its three stages are preparation, suspension and resolution. Labels such as 4–3 describe the changing interval above the bass rather than the note's absolute pitch.

evidence.note: Section 10.9 supports preparation, accent, downward step and numbered intervals; bass suspensions have a special reference voice, so the card uses the ordinary 4–3 example.

concepts.label: Suspension in tonal music
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace preparation, accented dissonance and downward stepwise resolution.

relations.note: A suspension is approached by the same note, whereas an appoggiatura is approached by leap; their accented tension does not make them identical.

concepts.card: Swarna-Sub1 adds temporary flood tolerance to a widely grown rice variety through the SUB1 breeding trait. It can survive periods of submergence that threaten ordinary crops, but longer floods still pose serious limits. The case shows why a tolerant variety is not an invulnerable one.

evidence.note: IRRI names Swarna-Sub1 and describes SUB1-enabled temporary submergence survival with sharply reduced performance in longer floods.

concepts.label: Swarna-Sub1
concepts.learning_takeaway: See flood tolerance as a bounded crop trait rather than an ability to survive indefinitely underwater.

relations.note: The two named rice varieties illustrate different breeding objectives: semidwarf crop architecture and temporary flood tolerance.

concepts.card: World Curling's 2024 report describes sweepers using pressure, brush angle and technique to influence a stone's distance and curl. Athletes test methods on different ice surfaces and disagree about some effects. The account documents evolving practice rather than establishing that every reported technique works equally well.

evidence.note: The 12 January 2024 governing-body report quotes athletes about pressure, angle, surface testing and disputed knifing effects. Claims are attributed to this historical practitioner account, not certified as universal controlled findings or current equipment legality.

concepts.label: Sweeping in curling
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore altering stone travel through work on the ice rather than touching the stone.

relations.note: The governing body's report describes sweeping as a technique within curling that changes the stone's travel through surface work.

concepts.card: A watery layer on a gel-like food can result from syneresis: the structure contracts and releases some of the liquid it held. Yogurt and sour cream offer familiar examples. The liquid separation reflects a change within the gel, rather than proving that water was added afterward.

evidence.note: K-State defines gel contraction and water release during storage, using yogurt and sour cream examples.

concepts.label: Syneresis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish water expelled by a contracting gel from water merely added to a food.

relations.note: Comparing gel formation with subsequent liquid expulsion gives two separate questions about food-gel structure.

concepts.card: SPRINT compared systolic-pressure targets below 120 and 140 mmHg in higher-risk adults aged fifty or older with initial systolic pressure at least 130 mmHg, excluding diabetes and prior stroke. Intensive treatment reduced cardiovascular events and deaths but increased some adverse effects; eligibility limits matter.

evidence.locator: Why was SPRINT important?; Key findings
evidence.note: NHLBI states the two targets, age fifty or older, initial systolic pressure at least 130 mmHg, additional cardiovascular risk, diabetes/prior-stroke exclusions, cardiovascular/death benefit and increased hypotension-related, electrolyte and kidney adverse effects.

concepts.label: Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial
concepts.learning_takeaway: Interpret a blood-pressure target comparison together with its enrollment limits and adverse effects.

concepts.card: Two notes can give rise to an additional difference tone at the difference between their frequencies. Called a Tartini tone in music, it can result from nonlinear interactions in an instrument or the hearing system. The extra perceived pitch need not be one of the two notes originally played.

evidence.note: UNSW discusses difference-frequency combination tones and multiple possible nonlinear sources; can avoids attributing every case to one anatomical or instrumental mechanism.

concepts.label: Tartini tone
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify a difference tone produced by nonlinear interaction of two frequencies.

relations.note: A difference tone involves nonlinear frequency combination, whereas sympathetic resonance transfers energy into a compatible existing resonance; the comparison distinguishes two additional-sound phenomena.

concepts.card: TCP's congestion window limits how much unacknowledged data a sender injects into the network. It is separate from the receiver's advertised window, which reflects receiver-side capacity. The smaller limit constrains sending, so available space at the receiver does not by itself justify faster transmission.

evidence.note: Checked sender versus receiver limits and their minimum; congestion control is not equated with receiver flow control.

concepts.label: TCP congestion window
concepts.learning_takeaway: Limit unacknowledged sending with a network-congestion bound separate from the receiver's advertised capacity.

relations.note: RFC 5681 defines the congestion window and then uses it as the state variable adjusted by slow start.

concepts.card: TCP slow start probes how much data a connection can have outstanding by growing its congestion window as new data is acknowledged. Growth continues until a threshold or congestion changes the behavior. Despite its name, this phase can expand sending quickly rather than increasing by a fixed amount per round.

evidence.note: Checked growth per acknowledgment and threshold/congestion stopping conditions; avoided a rigid doubling claim dependent on acknowledgment behavior.

concepts.label: TCP slow start
concepts.learning_takeaway: Probe available network capacity by increasing outstanding data as acknowledgments arrive until a threshold or congestion intervenes.

relations.note: RFC 5681 section 3.1 defines slow start through acknowledgment-driven changes to the congestion window and its threshold.

concepts.card: Tea’s early expense in Britain made its storage and consumption a marker of status. Valuable supplies could be kept under lock. As imports expanded, tea became more widely available, showing how a once-exclusive luxury could become part of ordinary shopping and domestic routine.

evidence.note: High cost, guarded tea and expanding availability are discussed.

concepts.label: Tea as a British status good
concepts.learning_takeaway: Early expensive tea was guarded and consumed by elites; expanding imports helped transform it into a more widely accessible grocery.

relations.note: Changing tea consumption offers a specific case of food and drink acquiring new social meanings.

concepts.card: Tellability asks what makes a story worth telling in a particular situation. An unusual event may help, but audience, context and presentation also matter. A sequence can qualify as a narrative yet fail to interest its listeners or give them a reason to care.

evidence.note: Context, discourse and distinction from narrativity are explicit.

concepts.label: Tellability
concepts.learning_takeaway: What makes a story worth telling depends on audience, situation and presentation, not merely whether events occurred.

relations.note: The handbook connects noteworthy events with tellability while preserving contextual and presentational factors.

concepts.card: A temperature inversion occurs where air becomes warmer with height. Near the ground, warm air above cooler air can suppress mixing and trap pollution. Such inversions may form through nighttime surface cooling or warm-air advection above an existing cool layer.

evidence.note: NWS defines an inversion as air temperature increasing with height. Its near-ground examples describe nighttime surface cooling or warm-air advection, with a stable lid that can trap pollution.

concepts.label: Temperature inversion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how warmer air above cooler air can suppress mixing and trap near-surface pollution.

relations.note: The marine-cloud source places coastal stratus within stable atmospheric structure; comparison with inversions helps explain persistence and mixing limits without equating cloud and inversion.

concepts.card: A ball dropped onto a suitably supported racket can stop almost dead after striking a particular location. Cross explains this through matching effective masses: the ball transfers its energy to the racket instead of rebounding strongly. The same location behaves differently when the racket is moving.

evidence.note: Cross's Dead spot experiment supplies the support condition, effective-mass explanation and moving-racket contrast; avoid presenting this as an invariant no-rebound point in all strokes.

concepts.label: Tennis racket dead spot
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand an impact location where a stationary racket can absorb nearly all the ball's energy.

relations.note: Low rebound at a dead spot and reduced handle vibration at a sweet spot answer different questions about an impact.

concepts.card: Physicist Rod Cross distinguishes a tennis racket's vibration-node sweet spot from its center of percussion and point of fastest rebound. An impact at the vibration node removes that component of handle motion, but rotation and translation can still transmit forces to the hand.

evidence.note: Cross sections 1 and 3 expressly separate the vibration node, center of percussion and maximum rebound, with rotation/translation/vibration components. Attribution avoids treating one terminology choice as the only sense of sweet spot.

concepts.label: Tennis racket sweet spot
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a low-vibration impact location from the point of maximum rebound speed.

relations.note: The source directly compares a vibration-node sweet spot with the separate center-of-percussion concept.

concepts.card: A falling object reaches terminal velocity when fluid resistance balances its effective downward force. Its speed then stops increasing even though gravity still acts. In the simple skydiver model, faster motion produces more drag until the net force and acceleration both become zero.

evidence.locator: 6.4 Drag Force and Terminal Speed; inspected passage indices 19, 20, 21 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1165039119204; fs-id1165039111305; fs-id1165035706192
evidence.note: A falling object stops accelerating when its increasing drag balances its effective downward force.

concepts.label: Terminal velocity
concepts.learning_takeaway: A falling object stops accelerating when its increasing drag balances its effective downward force.

relations.note: Buoyant force can contribute to the fluid-force balance, although the cited skydiver approximation neglects its small contribution.

concepts.card: A terminus post quem is an earliest possible date for a deposit or event. In archaeology, the most recently introduced securely associated artifact can supply that bound. An old coin may circulate for years, so its minting need not date burial exactly.

evidence.note: TPQ row defines the lower bound from the latest-occurring artifact.

concepts.label: Terminus post quem
concepts.learning_takeaway: A deposit cannot predate its youngest securely associated object’s earliest possible date; this supplies a lower bound, not an exact deposition date.

relations.note: A lower bound and an assemblage estimate answer different dating questions.

concepts.card: Terza rima links three-line stanzas through interlocking rhyme: the middle rhyme of one stanza becomes the outer rhyme of the next. Each group thus reaches forward into another. The pattern creates continuity across stanza boundaries rather than treating every tercet as a closed unit.

evidence.note: Interlocking ABA BCB pattern is explicitly described.

concepts.label: Terza rima
concepts.learning_takeaway: The middle rhyme of one tercet becomes the outer rhyme of the next, chaining stanzas forward.

relations.note: The glossary identifies Dante’s poem as the major example of this interlocking form.
The glossary presents terza rima as an interlocking verse rhyme form.

concepts.card: Test–retest reliability asks whether a measure produces consistent results across repeated administrations. It evaluates stability over occasions, whereas inter-rater reliability evaluates agreement among observers. A repeatable score can still measure the wrong thing, so consistency alone does not establish the validity of its interpretation.

evidence.note: Section 2.3 distinguishes repeated-administration consistency from observer agreement and states that reliability does not entail validity; the card does not demand unchanged scores when the actual trait changes.

concepts.label: Test–retest reliability
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish stability across repeated measurements from agreement among observers.

relations.note: Both forms are explicitly listed in the same reliability passage, with different sources of variation being checked.

concepts.card: Holbein’s The Ambassadors presents two men with objects that invite close scrutiny, but a stretched skull disrupts the frontal view. Seen from an oblique position, the skull becomes recognizable. The painting makes a change in the viewer’s position part of encountering one of its key images.

evidence.locator: Portrait objects and skull, lines 102–104 and 122–123
evidence.note: Double portrait, displayed objects and viewpoint-dependent skull are described.

concepts.label: The Ambassadors
concepts.learning_takeaway: Holbein’s double portrait joins the sitters and their objects with a distorted skull whose recognition depends on moving to an oblique viewpoint.

relations.note: The gallery explains the skull through the specific distortion technique.

concepts.card: This penny token advertised a coffee house in London’s Exchange Alley through a list of goods and the image of a Turkish ruler. Coffee, chocolate and tea appeared together, showing how a small circulating object could advertise an establishment’s offerings and associations.

evidence.note: Penny token, place, listed drinks and ruler image are specified in the collection record.

concepts.label: The New Coffee House trade token
concepts.learning_takeaway: A penny token from Exchange Alley advertised coffee, chocolate, tea and other goods while associating the shop with a Turkish ruler.

relations.note: The token’s imagery and product list support an object-based inquiry into social and commercial life.

concepts.card: William Carlos Williams’s The Red Wheelbarrow breaks familiar compound words across short lines. An editorial reading treats those divisions as an invitation to slow down and attend to ordinary objects. The visible lineation supports that reading without making it the poem’s only possible effect.

evidence.note: Word divisions and line lengths are visible in the inspected poem excerpt.

concepts.label: The Red Wheelbarrow
concepts.learning_takeaway: Williams splits compound words across short lines; an editorial reading interprets that lineation as shaping pacing and attention.

relations.note: The glossary presents the poem’s word-spanning line breaks as a formal example of enjambment.

concepts.card: Janie recounts her life to Pheoby in Their Eyes Were Watching God, placing the novel’s events inside an act of retrospective telling. Hurston’s use of folklore and Black vernacular speech connects that structure with Janie’s developing voice and her struggle to speak for herself.

evidence.note: The framing conversation, folklore, idiom and emergence of voice are described.

concepts.label: Their Eyes Were Watching God
concepts.learning_takeaway: Janie’s retrospective telling to Pheoby frames a search for voice within a novel shaped by folklore and Black vernacular speech.

relations.note: Janie’s participation in the life she recounts offers an editorial example of this narrator relationship.

concepts.card: A thermocline is a layer where water temperature changes rapidly with depth, separating warmer surface water from colder water below. Its depth and strength vary with place and season. Recognizing the layer helps describe an ocean’s vertical structure instead of assuming its temperature is uniform.

evidence.note: NOAA defines the rapid-temperature-change zone beneath a warm mixed layer and describes seasonal/regional variation.

concepts.label: Thermocline
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize a depth interval where temperature drops rapidly below a warm mixed surface layer.

relations.note: Argo’s repeated temperature-versus-depth profiles provide a measurement approach for studying vertical structures such as thermoclines.

concepts.card: Temperature and salinity affect seawater density. In places where water becomes sufficiently cold and salty, it can sink and contribute to deep-ocean circulation, with other water moving to replace it. Thermohaline circulation highlights these density differences alongside the wind-driven motions visible at the surface.

evidence.note: NOAA describes cold, salty dense water sinking and helping drive deep circulation.

concepts.label: Thermohaline circulation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect temperature and salinity differences with density-driven deep-ocean flow.

relations.note: Comparing density-driven sinking with wind/friction-driven Ekman motion distinguishes two contributions to ocean circulation.

concepts.card: When ice within the ground thaws, the land can subside and form thermokarst depressions. Some fill with lakes or ponds; elsewhere, thaw can breach a basin’s edge and drain a lake. Warming can therefore produce both expanding water bodies and abrupt losses of surface water.

evidence.note: NPS defines thermokarst through ground-ice thaw/subsidence and explicitly describes lake formation/enlargement and drainage through breached banks.

concepts.label: Thermokarst
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use thaw-related ground subsidence to understand both lake formation and drainage.

relations.note: Landsat imagery is used in the inspected NPS study to monitor changing thermokarst-lake area.

concepts.card: Thin-film interference gives soap bubbles and oil films their changing colors. Light reflected from the film’s two boundaries travels different optical paths and may acquire different reflection phases. The waves then reinforce or cancel differently for different wavelengths, making thickness and surrounding materials matter.

evidence.locator: 3.4 Interference in Thin Films; inspected passage indices 6, 8, 10, 11 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1170903087288; fs-id1170902600773; fs-id1170903054004; fs-id1170902643736
evidence.note: Reflections at two film surfaces combine according to optical path length and reflection phase shifts.

concepts.label: Thin-film interference
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reflections at two film surfaces combine according to optical path length and reflection phase shifts.

relations.note: The film example connects optical wave interference with a visible everyday color pattern.

concepts.card: For a slender, uniform beam simply supported and loaded at its midpoint, an ideal three-point bending test links force and deflection. Linear-elastic, small-deflection beam theory predicts deflection proportional to load and span cubed, and inversely proportional to elastic modulus times second moment of area.

evidence.locator: Chapter 8: Beam Bending, Buckling, and Torsion; inspected passage indices 191, 197, 199, 201, 215, 216, 217 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-192; paragraph-198; paragraph-200; paragraph-202; paragraph-216; paragraph-217; paragraph-218
evidence.note: The small-angle Euler–Bernoulli derivation uses constant flexural rigidity EI; a simply supported beam with a midpoint load has maximum deflection PL³/(48EI).

evidence.locator: 4.2: Stresses in Beams; inspected passage indices 68, 72 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: section_1; section_2
evidence.note: The bending model treats shear as negligible for long slender beams and uses planar cross-sections with small rotations.

concepts.label: Three-point bending test
concepts.learning_takeaway: Load a simply supported beam at its center to relate deflection to material and cross-section stiffness.

relations.note: The inspected deflection formula explicitly contains the cross-section’s second moment of area and material elastic modulus.

concepts.card: Under FIDE rules, threefold repetition permits a draw claim rather than automatically ending play. The player to move may claim when the position has appeared for the third time, or record an intended move producing it and declare that intention to the arbiter before moving.

evidence.note: FIDE 9.2.1–2 supports current-position claims and intended-move claims recorded and declared to the arbiter before execution; 9.6.1 separately supplies the automatic fivefold contrast.

concepts.label: Threefold repetition
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain the claimable three-occurrence draw procedure, including the timing of a claim before a qualifying intended move.

relations.note: The rules distinguish a player's threefold claim from the automatic fivefold repetition draw.

concepts.card: Thrust vectoring redirects an engine’s exhaust so the propulsive force can change direction. This gives a vehicle another way to maneuver rather than keeping thrust along one fixed axis. NASA describes rectangular nozzle exits as one design approach that makes the exhaust flow easier to deflect.

evidence.locator: Nozzles; inspected passage indices 4 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-5
evidence.note: Deflect exhaust direction to change a vehicle’s thrust direction and maneuverability.

concepts.label: Thrust vectoring
concepts.learning_takeaway: Deflect exhaust direction to change a vehicle’s thrust direction and maneuverability.

relations.note: The nozzle reference explicitly connects redirected exhaust with greater aircraft maneuverability.

concepts.card: A Tibetan mandala can organize ritual space as a palace with a center and four directional gates. In the practitioner account described here, ritual objects occupy particular positions and the deity’s dwelling anchors orientation. The diagram therefore coordinates relationships rather than serving as decoration alone.

evidence.note: Palace, gates, ritual objects and central deity are explicit in the practitioner account.

concepts.label: Tibetan mandala palace plan
concepts.learning_takeaway: A central palace and directional gates organize ritual space and the practitioner’s relation to the represented deity.

relations.note: Compare two material forms through which Tibetan Buddhist practice connects objects, texts and ritual action.

concepts.card: Tidal forces arise because gravity differs across an extended object. The side nearer an attracting body is pulled more strongly than the far side. Comparing each part’s acceleration with the object’s center explains stretching, ocean-tide patterns, and potentially the disruption of stars passing too close.

evidence.locator: 13.6 Tidal Forces; inspected passage indices 6, 9, 28, 31 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1168328317120; fs-id1168327911126; fs-id1168325680556; fs-id1168328190636
evidence.note: Differences in gravitational pull across an extended object create stretching and tidal effects.

concepts.label: Tidal force
concepts.learning_takeaway: Differences in gravitational pull across an extended object create stretching and tidal effects.

relations.note: The same tidal-force section identifies synchronization as a long-term consequence of dissipative tidal deformation.

concepts.card: Tidal locking synchronizes a body’s rotation with its orbital motion through long-term tidal interactions and dissipation. Earth’s Moon therefore keeps roughly the same face toward Earth while still rotating. The fixed-looking lunar face reflects matched rotation and orbital periods, not absence of spin.

evidence.locator: 13.6 Tidal Forces; inspected passage indices 37 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1168325697191
evidence.note: Dissipative tidal deformation can synchronize an orbiting body’s spin with its orbital motion.

concepts.label: Tidal locking
concepts.learning_takeaway: Dissipative tidal deformation can synchronize an orbiting body’s spin with its orbital motion.

relations.note: The tidal-force section explicitly describes locking as a long-term consequence of tidal energy dissipation.

concepts.card: An Ottoman timar granted the right to collect revenue from a specified area in return for service. It supported its holder without a regular state salary. Because the grant could be revoked and did not automatically pass to heirs, it also limited independent hereditary power.

evidence.note: Revenue rights, service, revocation and noninheritance are described.

concepts.label: Timar
concepts.learning_takeaway: A revocable right to collect revenue supported Ottoman service personnel without making their assignments automatically hereditary.

relations.note: Compare two distinct imperial systems that linked service with reassigned revenue.

concepts.card: A titration’s equivalence point is the exact stoichiometric condition where the reacting amounts match the equation. Its end point is the observed signal used to stop measuring, such as a color change. A good method makes the difference between these two points small.

evidence.locator: 4.5 Quantitative Chemical Analysis; inspected passage indices 10 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idp43277952
evidence.note: Distinguish an observed end-point signal from the exact stoichiometric equivalence condition.

concepts.label: Titration end point and equivalence point
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish an observed end-point signal from the exact stoichiometric equivalence condition.

relations.note: The distinction applies to titrations generally and clarifies how acid–base titration measurements are interpreted.

concepts.card: TLS 1.3 is a protocol for establishing authenticated, encrypted communication. Its redesign removed static RSA and static Diffie–Hellman key exchange, so its public-key exchange modes provide forward secrecy. Other modes have different properties, and early data requires particular care about replay and weaker security guarantees.

evidence.note: Checked public-key scope and mode exceptions in sections 1.2, 2.2–2.3 and Appendix E; not every TLS 1.3 exchange is assigned identical guarantees.

concepts.label: TLS 1.3
concepts.learning_takeaway: Negotiate authenticated encrypted channels using a redesigned handshake that removes static public-key key exchange.

relations.note: RFC 8446 explicitly connects its public-key exchange redesign to forward secrecy and separately qualifies PSK and early-data modes.
