concepts.card: A fugue's answer is a subject entry associated with the dominant key. In a tonal answer, some intervals are changed to accommodate the movement between tonic and dominant. A real answer instead preserves the intervals, making tonal function and literal transposition different possible priorities.

evidence.note: Fugue Analysis defines answer, tonal modification and real preservation; associated with dominant leaves room for an answer beginning in tonic before moving there.

concepts.label: Tonal answer in fugue
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why a fugue answer alters intervals to navigate tonic and dominant.

relations.note: The answer is explicitly defined as a structural element of a fugue's subject-entry process.

concepts.card: When a rapidly spinning gyroscope experiences a torque perpendicular to its angular momentum, that vector turns rather than simply shrinking. In the slow-precession approximation, precession is much slower than the disk’s spin. This model explains a tilted top’s steady turning around the vertical.

evidence.locator: 11.4 Precession of a Gyroscope; inspected passage indices 6, 7, 17 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1165038331707; fs-id1165038198551; fs-id1165037997345
evidence.note: A perpendicular torque changes a spinning object’s angular-momentum direction instead of simply tipping it over.

concepts.label: Torque-induced gyroscopic precession
concepts.learning_takeaway: A perpendicular torque changes a spinning object’s angular-momentum direction instead of simply tipping it over.

relations.note: The passage explicitly models the torque-induced gyroscope case of precession and states the fast-spin approximation.

concepts.card: An ordinary torus is a surface with one handle, often pictured as a doughnut. It can also be constructed by identifying opposite edges of a rectangle without twists. This edge-gluing description makes the surface useful for representing two independently periodic coordinates.

evidence.locator: Torus -- from Wolfram MathWorld; inspected passage indices 1, 3 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-2; paragraph-4
evidence.note: Gluing opposite rectangle edges without twists creates a genus-one surface and models two periodic coordinates.

concepts.label: Torus
concepts.learning_takeaway: Gluing opposite rectangle edges without twists creates a genus-one surface and models two periodic coordinates.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies the ordinary torus as a genus-one surface.

concepts.card: Total impulse accumulates thrust over the duration of a burn. For constant thrust it is force multiplied by time; for varying thrust it is the area under the thrust–time curve. Engines with the same peak thrust can therefore deliver different total impulses if their firing histories differ.

evidence.locator: Specific Impulse; inspected passage indices 14, 15, 16, 17 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-15; paragraph-16; paragraph-17; paragraph-18
evidence.note: Integrate thrust over firing time to measure a propulsion system’s accumulated momentum delivery.

concepts.label: Total impulse
concepts.learning_takeaway: Integrate thrust over firing time to measure a propulsion system’s accumulated momentum delivery.

relations.note: The source normalizes total impulse by propellant weight to obtain specific impulse.

concepts.card: At an ideal nonabsorbing interface, total internal reflection occurs toward a lower-index medium at an incidence angle beyond the critical angle. Instead of a propagating refracted ray emerging, light is reflected back. The index ordering matters: increasing the angle at an arbitrary boundary is insufficient.

evidence.locator: 1.4 Total Internal Reflection; inspected passage indices 7, 10, 11 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1172100972304; fs-id1172100960831; fs-id1172100536074
evidence.note: Above the critical angle, light entering a lower-index boundary reflects back instead of transmitting.

concepts.label: Total internal reflection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Above the critical angle, light entering a lower-index boundary reflects back instead of transmitting.

relations.note: The source derives total internal reflection as a limiting consequence of refraction and Snell’s law.

concepts.card: In over-the-board chess, a player whose turn it is normally must move the first deliberately touched own piece that has a legal move. Announcing an intention to adjust a piece before touching it is different. Clearly accidental contact does not count as deliberate selection.

evidence.note: FIDE 4.2–4.5 restricts binding touch to the player having the move, prioritizes the first legally movable own piece, and distinguishes announced adjustment and clearly accidental contact.

concepts.label: Touch-move rule
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how deliberate touching commits a player when a legal move exists.

relations.note: FIDE's Act of Moving the Pieces regulates how a player's physical selection becomes binding.

concepts.card: Toyota's official production-system account combines just-in-time flow with jidoka, the practice of responding to abnormalities. One coordinates when work and parts are needed; the other helps prevent defects from continuing unnoticed. The case presents production as linked processes, rather than equating productivity only with machines running faster.

evidence.note: Checked the two-component account and distinct functions; the company's explanation is not treated as independent proof of superiority in every setting.

concepts.label: Toyota Motor Corporation
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how the company's production system joins abnormality detection with demand-coordinated flow rather than optimizing only machine speed.

relations.note: Toyota explicitly identifies jidoka as a central component of its own production system and explains its abnormality-stopping mechanism.

concepts.card: A track circuit uses the rails as part of an electrical path to detect whether a railway section is clear. In a basic relay-based arrangement, a train shunts current away from the relay. The wider signalling system uses this indication when deciding whether another train may proceed.

evidence.locator: Track circuits explained; inspected passage indices 2, 3, 6 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-3; paragraph-4; paragraph-7
evidence.note: A train shunts an electrical rail circuit so the signalling system detects occupied track.

concepts.label: Track circuit
concepts.learning_takeaway: A train shunts an electrical rail circuit so the signalling system detects occupied track.

relations.note: Network Rail explicitly explains how track-circuit failure can produce an occupied indication.

concepts.card: Transhumance moves herds and herders between seasonally useful pastures. A mountain summer grazing area and a lowland winter area function together through the route connecting them. Following that annual movement reveals a landscape organized around recurring mobility rather than one permanently occupied settlement.

evidence.note: Khinalig’s seasonal mountain/lowland system supports the explanation.

concepts.label: Transhumance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Seasonal movement between different pastures links otherwise separate places into a recurring system of herding and habitation.

relations.note: UNESCO describes the village, pastures and route as one transhumant cultural landscape.

concepts.card: TESS was designed to search bright stars across the sky for periodic dimming caused by planetary transits. Bright host stars make promising candidates easier to examine with other telescopes. Its survey strategy connects planet detection with follow-up studies of planetary masses, compositions, and atmospheres.

evidence.locator: The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite; inspected passage indices 7, 10, 11, 15 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-8; paragraph-11; paragraph-12; paragraph-16
evidence.note: An all-sky survey of bright stars makes transit discoveries practical targets for follow-up characterization.

concepts.label: Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite
concepts.learning_takeaway: An all-sky survey of bright stars makes transit discoveries practical targets for follow-up characterization.

relations.note: NASA explicitly states that TESS finds candidates through transit photometry.

concepts.card: A transition-relevance place is a point where a conversational turn could be complete and speaker change becomes possible. The current speaker may select someone, another participant may begin, or the speaker may continue. It is an opportunity for transition, rather than an automatic instruction that the turn must end.

evidence.locator: Introduction, turn-constructional units and allocation rules
evidence.note: Checked possible completion and optional transition; a pause is not automatically classified as a completed conversational turn.

concepts.label: Transition-relevance place
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize a possible completion point where another speaker may take over, although the current speaker can continue.

relations.note: The paper explicitly defines transition-relevance places and summarizes the three turn-allocation possibilities in the turn-taking model.

concepts.card: Trap cropping uses a more attractive planting to draw pests away from the crop being protected. The result depends on the pest, the plants and their arrangement. Extension examples include useful flea-beetle diversion and unsuccessful combinations, showing why companion-planting claims need evidence for the particular situation.

evidence.note: UMN describes trap cropping, a brassica flea-beetle example and a failed eggplant–potato combination.

concepts.label: Trap cropping
concepts.learning_takeaway: Redirect a pest toward a more attractive planting, while checking that the arrangement works for that pest and crop.

relations.note: Pest diversion is one specific management technique that can be considered within an evidence-led IPM strategy.

concepts.card: A travel-time service area shows locations reachable through a network within a specified travel cost. Roads, connections and restrictions shape its boundary, so it need not resemble a circle. The result describes accessibility under the model’s assumptions rather than simple straight-line proximity.

evidence.note: Network reachability and comparison with circular buffers are explicit.

concepts.label: Travel-time service area
concepts.learning_takeaway: A reachable area follows network paths and travel costs, so it need not match a circle drawn at a fixed distance.

relations.note: The source contrasts network accessibility with fixed-distance proximity.

concepts.card: A triad is a three-person social group. Adding the third member creates possibilities unavailable in a dyad, including two-against-one coalitions and a majority view. If someone withdraws, the remaining pair can still interact, so the group's relationships are not all dependent on one uninterrupted two-person bond.

evidence.note: Checked coalition and withdrawal distinctions; a remaining pair is not inaccurately called a three-person triad.

concepts.label: Triad (social group)
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how adding a third member permits coalitions and lets the group persist after one member leaves.

relations.note: The group-size chapter explicitly contrasts triads with dyads through coalition possibilities and survival of a remaining pair.

concepts.card: Triadic closure is the tendency for two people with a shared friend to become connected themselves. Meeting opportunities and social context can help such ties form. It is a pattern of network development, not a guarantee that every pair of friends-of-friends will eventually know each other.

evidence.note: Checked shared-neighbor tendency and distinction from a universal rule; no inevitability or fixed time scale is asserted.

concepts.label: Triadic closure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why two people sharing a friend are more likely to form a connection, without treating this as inevitable.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly develops the stronger formal closure property from the qualitative tendency and warns that the formal version is an extreme assumption.

concepts.card: A pure substance’s triple point is the pressure and temperature where three phases coexist in equilibrium. On water’s phase diagram, it is where the solid–liquid, liquid–vapor, and solid–vapor boundaries meet. Below that pressure, liquid water is not an equilibrium phase.

evidence.locator: 10.4 Phase Diagrams; inspected passage indices 12, 25, 40 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm105744432; fs-idm71881152; fs-idm114606944
evidence.note: The water and carbon-dioxide phase diagrams show three-phase coexistence and distinguish it from disappearance of the liquid–vapor boundary at the critical point.

concepts.label: Triple point
concepts.learning_takeaway: Three phases coexist at one pressure-temperature combination on a pure-substance phase diagram.

relations.note: The phase diagrams contrast a triple point, where three phases coexist, with a critical point, where the liquid–vapor distinction ends; this is a comparative learning bridge, not a hierarchy.

concepts.card: Trompe-l’oeil aims to make a painted representation appear to be the object itself. The term describes a potential illusion rather than realism alone: a viewer may momentarily mistake a depicted object for something physically present.

evidence.note: The glossary defines deceptive object-like representation.

concepts.label: Trompe-l’oeil
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trompe-l’oeil pictures an object so deceptively that viewers may take the painted representation for the object itself.

relations.note: Compare an illusion of an object’s presence with a distortion resolved by a special viewpoint.

concepts.card: Cells along a kidney tubule sense changes in the fluid and salt reaching them. Their local signals adjust resistance in the arteriole feeding the filter. Tubuloglomerular feedback therefore uses information downstream of filtration to help regulate how much new fluid is filtered.

evidence.note: The renal-flow passage identifies macula densa sensing of tubular conditions and local afferent-arteriole responses that change glomerular filtration.

concepts.label: Tubuloglomerular feedback
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace tubular salt delivery to local changes in afferent-arteriole resistance.

relations.note: Tubular sensing and direct vessel-wall stretch are two different inputs to renal autoregulation.

concepts.card: Tudor Londoners could buy prepared hot food from cookshops, especially when cramped homes lacked cooking facilities. Commercial ovens supplied ready-to-eat meals outside the household. The museum notes that evidence about the exact meals and their customers is limited, preserving uncertainty alongside the practical explanation.

evidence.note: The museum describes commercial ovens serving households without cooking facilities and explicitly notes limited evidence for exact menus and clientele.

concepts.label: Tudor London cookshops
concepts.learning_takeaway: Commercial ovens supplied hot ready-made food to city residents whose cramped homes lacked cooking facilities.

relations.note: Cookshops connect the history of meals with urban housing and commercial provision.

concepts.card: Turbidity describes water cloudiness associated with suspended particles and other material that interferes with light. Sediment or algae can reduce visibility and the light reaching underwater plants. Cloudy water is not automatically polluted, since some waters are naturally turbid, but the change can still matter ecologically.

evidence.note: EPA’s clarity account links suspended matter/algae, lower visibility and light available to aquatic plants, including naturally turbid waters.

concepts.label: Turbidity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect suspended matter with light scattering, absorption and reduced underwater visibility.

relations.note: A Secchi disk provides a visual clarity assessment, while turbidity describes the clouding property influencing underwater light.

concepts.card: Twenty Squares spread across the ancient Near East and was later imported into Egypt. Surviving boards reveal adaptation rather than simple copying: special squares on Near Eastern examples display rosettes, while Egyptian examples use hieroglyphs. A shared game could acquire a different visual language.

evidence.note: The Met explicitly reports geographic spread, import into Egypt and contrasting markings; no claim that all surviving boards preserve markings or identical rules.

concepts.label: Twenty Squares
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how an imported ancient game acquired Egyptian markings and visual conventions.

relations.note: The museum describes Egyptian boxes accommodating both games, making their material comparison explicit.

concepts.card: At the opening of Philip Glass's Two Pages, growth comes from adding repetitions whose final notes are progressively removed. A motive can therefore expand while newly added units become shorter. The cited analysis illustrates how repetition and subtraction can cooperate within an additive process.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 35.1 explicitly limits its Two Pages demonstration to the opening and labels the notation a transcription/analysis. The card does not assert that every section of the entire work follows the displayed process.

concepts.label: Two Pages
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore Glass's additive process through repetitions that successively omit final notes.

relations.note: The textbook analyzes the opening of Glass's Two Pages as an example of additive process, with shortening repetitions inside the expanding unit.

concepts.card: Indian Buddhist discussions of two truths distinguish conventional understanding from an ultimate perspective. Ordinary language and practices operate conventionally, while ultimate analysis asks how things really are. Buddhist schools interpret both levels and their relationship differently, so the distinction does not express one uniform doctrine across traditions.

evidence.note: SEP opening differentiates conventional and ultimate perspectives and explicitly warns that the schools can be radically opposed; the card avoids attributing one settled metaphysics or historical origin to all Buddhism.

concepts.label: Two truths in Indian Buddhist philosophy
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish conventional and ultimate truth while recognizing that Buddhist schools interpret the distinction differently.

relations.note: The distinction concerns perspectives on truth and knowledge, inviting comparison with epistemology's study of cognitive success without assimilating all Buddhist schools to a single Western theory.

concepts.card: Tympanometry changes air pressure in the ear canal and records how the eardrum responds. The resulting graph helps assess the mechanics of the eardrum and middle ear. It differs from asking someone whether they can hear a tone: movement and hearing threshold are separate measurements.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus describes a pressure-varying probe and eardrum-movement graphs, separately from behavioral audiometry.

concepts.label: Tympanometry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Assess middle-ear mechanics by measuring eardrum movement as pressure changes.

relations.note: Comparing mechanical eardrum response with a person’s detection of tones distinguishes two hearing-assessment questions.

concepts.card: An uncodified constitution lacks one consolidated constitutional text, not necessarily written rules. The United Kingdom's constitutional arrangements include many statutes alongside other sources. Calling the constitution unwritten can therefore mislead: the important distinction is whether its basic rules are collected in a single authoritative document.

evidence.locator: Parliamentary sovereignty and the UK constitution
evidence.note: UK Parliament's sovereignty page expressly describes the constitution as partly written and wholly uncodified; the card does not equate uncodified with informal, unenforceable or absent.

concepts.label: Uncodified constitution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish lacking a single constitutional document from lacking written constitutional rules.

relations.note: The page identifies uncodified as the form of the UK's constitution, while explaining that many constitutional rules are nevertheless written in statutes.

concepts.card: A pawn reaching its final rank need not become a queen. Underpromotion chooses a rook, bishop or knight instead. The new piece takes effect immediately, and the available choices do not depend on which pieces were captured earlier in the game.

evidence.note: FIDE 3.7.3.3–5 support all alternatives, immediate effect and independence from captured pieces; no unsupported tactical claim explains why a particular choice wins.

concepts.label: Underpromotion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize that promotion may choose a rook, bishop or knight instead of queen.

relations.note: FIDE's pawn-promotion rule explicitly permits the three non-queen choices described here.

concepts.card: Understitching secures a seam allowance to the facing on the inside of a garment. This encourages the seam to roll inward and helps prevent the facing from showing on the outside. It controls an already assembled edge, rather than stabilizing a loose pattern piece before sewing.

evidence.locator: Seam-allowance understitching; Tips for Applying Facings
evidence.note: NMSU describes pressing the allowance toward the facing, understitching and preventing the facing from rolling outside.

concepts.label: Understitching
concepts.learning_takeaway: Keep a facing from rolling to the garment’s outside by securing its seam allowance to the facing.

relations.note: These stitching operations differ in timing and purpose: control of an assembled facing versus stabilization of an unjoined cut edge.

concepts.card: A Unicode code point is a numbered position in the character space, rather than the bytes stored in a file. UTF-8 encodes valid scalar values with different byte lengths. Keeping the number separate from its encoding helps explain why counting bytes need not count characters.

evidence.note: Checked character-number terminology and variable-length storage; wording does not claim all code points are assigned characters or valid scalar values.

concepts.label: Unicode code point
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish the integer assigned to a character from the bytes used by an encoding.

relations.note: RFC 3629 explicitly distinguishes character numbers from the octet sequences used to encode them.

concepts.card: Unicode normalization gives equivalent text sequences a common representation. It decomposes characters, orders combining marks, and sometimes recomposes them. The chosen normalization form matters: canonical forms preserve distinctions that compatibility forms may remove, so normalization is more specific than simply making text look alike.

evidence.note: Checked decomposition, ordering, recomposition, and canonical versus compatibility behavior; normalization is not a general visual-similarity matcher.

concepts.label: Unicode normalization
concepts.learning_takeaway: Transform equivalent character sequences into a common binary representation through decomposition, ordering, and optional recomposition.

relations.note: UAX 15 sections 1.1–1.3 explicitly use canonical equivalence to define normalization forms and their transformations.

concepts.card: A unit cell is a repeating box used to describe a crystal lattice. Boundary points are shared with neighboring cells, so counting them requires fractions. A primitive cell contains one lattice point in total; a larger, nonprimitive cell contains more.

evidence.locator: Unit cell; inspected passage indices 8, 9 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-9; paragraph-10
evidence.note: Defines unit cell, primitive cell, and lattice-point multiplicity.

evidence.locator: 10.6 Lattice Structures in Crystalline Solids; inspected passage indices 10, 13 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm2181616; fs-idm15054992
evidence.note: Explains repetition and fractional counting of corner atoms in the simple cubic example.

concepts.label: Unit cell
concepts.learning_takeaway: Account for shared boundary atoms when identifying the repeating building block of a crystal.

relations.note: The crystallography references describe crystal repetition through unit cells.

concepts.card: A narrator can report events accurately yet interpret them poorly or evaluate them misleadingly. Unreliable narration therefore involves more than factual lying. Separating reporting, interpretation and judgment lets readers identify where an account becomes questionable and where it may remain dependable.

evidence.note: The source distinguishes reporting, interpreting and evaluating, including mixed reliability.

concepts.label: Unreliable narration
concepts.learning_takeaway: A narrator may report events accurately while interpreting or evaluating them misleadingly, so unreliability need not mean simple lying.

relations.note: The handbook explains the historical connection between unreliability and inferred norms of the work.

concepts.card: UTF-8 represents Unicode scalar values using one to four bytes. ASCII characters retain their familiar single-byte values, while other values use recognizable multibyte patterns. A character's assigned number and its encoded bytes are different things, which matters when counting or processing text.

evidence.note: Checked ASCII preservation, byte range, and distinction between scalar value and encoding; surrogate code points are not valid UTF-8 scalar values.

concepts.label: UTF-8
concepts.learning_takeaway: Encode Unicode scalar values in one to four bytes while preserving ASCII byte values.

relations.note: RFC 3629 sections 2–3 directly relate character numbers to their one-to-four-byte UTF-8 encodings.

concepts.card: Smelser's value-added theory analyzes collective behavior through a proposed combination of conditions, including structural strain, a shared interpretation, and a precipitating event. It asks what makes an episode possible and mobilizes action. The name refers to an explanatory sociological framework, rather than economic value added or a numerical prediction formula.

evidence.note: Checked named theory and selected conditions; qualification preserves that these are proposed explanatory requirements rather than a validated universal checklist.

concepts.label: Value-added theory of collective behavior
concepts.learning_takeaway: Analyze several proposed conditions for collective episodes, including strain, shared beliefs, and precipitating events.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly presents Smelser's conditions as a theoretical account of collective-behavior episodes.

concepts.card: A variable-area exhaust nozzle changes geometry to suit different engine operating conditions. Afterburning jet engines use adjustable converging-diverging passages to maintain useful flow conditions over a wider range. The moving structure adds weight, revealing a tradeoff between adaptable performance and the simplicity of a fixed nozzle.

evidence.locator: Nozzles; inspected passage indices 2 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: paragraph-3
evidence.note: Adjustable nozzle geometry trades extra weight for efficient operation across a wider airflow range.

concepts.label: Variable-area exhaust nozzle
concepts.learning_takeaway: Adjustable nozzle geometry trades extra weight for efficient operation across a wider airflow range.

relations.note: NASA’s afterburning-engine example uses a variable-geometry converging-diverging nozzle; this is a supported design connection, not a claim that every variable-area nozzle has that form.

concepts.card: People with the same genetic condition can have different signs, symptoms or severity. Variable expressivity describes that range of manifestations. It differs from reduced penetrance, which concerns whether the condition appears at all, and helps explain why affected relatives need not look clinically identical.

evidence.note: MedlinePlus distinguishes a range of manifestations from the proportion showing a disorder and describes differences among affected people.

concepts.label: Variable expressivity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish variation in a condition’s manifestations from whether it appears at all.

relations.note: The source treats presence of manifestations and range of manifestations as separate questions.

concepts.card: Variable-rate irrigation changes water delivery across a field using control zones and prescription maps. Those maps specify irrigation amounts, but soil and crop information must guide the prescription. The technology applies the planned pattern; it does not independently determine how much water a crop needs.

evidence.note: UMN describes control zones and prescription maps, then explicitly distinguishes spatial application from determining crop water need. Agronomic information and irrigation-scheduling tools are required to assign appropriate amounts.

concepts.label: Variable-rate irrigation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Match irrigation amounts to different areas of a field instead of assuming every area needs the same water.

relations.note: Spatially varied application is a specific control approach within irrigation rather than a second identity for irrigation as a whole.

concepts.card: Variationist sociolinguistics studies language as people use it, asking how social settings and linguistic environments influence variation. Instead of imagining one perfectly uniform speaker, it examines patterns across actual speech. A person may use the same variant at different rates when chatting casually and reading aloud.

evidence.note: Checked focus on usage, social/linguistic context, and casual-versus-reading example; no fixed speech stereotype is assigned to a social group.

evidence.locator: §10.7, Labov comparison of casual speech and reading
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The variationist introduction and social-status example explicitly study context-dependent variant frequencies, including systematic style shifting.

concepts.label: Variationist sociolinguistics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Analyze how linguistic and social conditions alter the probability of variants in language as actually used.

relations.note: The variationist introduction and social-status example explicitly study context-dependent variant frequencies, including systematic style shifting.

concepts.card: Venice developed as an urban system of islands and waterways within a lagoon. Buildings, canals and hydraulic interventions cannot be understood independently of that surrounding water. The site shows a city whose form emerged through a long, changing relationship between settlement and environmental management.

evidence.note: Island settlement, waterways and sustained hydraulic intervention are explicit.

concepts.label: Venice and its lagoon
concepts.learning_takeaway: Island settlements and canals form an urban system inseparable from the surrounding lagoon and centuries of hydraulic intervention.

relations.note: The connected city-lagoon system demonstrates a sustained relationship between settlement and environment.

concepts.card: Villa Savoye demonstrates how columns and floor slabs can separate a building’s structural support from the placement of walls. This permits a free plan and an independently arranged facade. The villa makes a design program visible through the relationships among support, enclosure and inhabited space.

evidence.locator: Pilotis, free plan and free facade, lines 13–14 and 43–52
evidence.note: Pilotis, free plan and independent facade are explained on the official site.

concepts.label: Villa Savoye
concepts.learning_takeaway: The villa demonstrates how columns and floor slabs can separate structure from wall placement, enabling a free plan and an independently organized facade.

relations.note: The named building provides a concrete architectural case connecting structure and spatial organization.

concepts.card: A villanelle uses five three-line stanzas and a final four-line stanza, with two alternating refrains that come together at the end. Repetition provides a stable structure, while the surrounding lines can change how each returning phrase is heard or understood.

evidence.note: Stanza pattern and alternating refrains are explicit.

concepts.label: Villanelle
concepts.learning_takeaway: Two refrains alternate through five tercets and join in a final quatrain, letting recurring words acquire different force.

relations.note: The Academy defines a structured poem through its stanza and refrain pattern.
The glossary identifies Bishop’s poem as a villanelle with variations in its refrains.

concepts.card: Virginia Apgar developed a standardized way to assess a newborn soon after birth. Observations of heart rate, breathing effort, muscle tone, reflex response and color were combined into one score. Her work turned several immediate clinical observations into a repeatable assessment of the transition outside the womb.

evidence.note: NLM identifies Apgar’s standardized newborn assessment and the five observations arising from obstetrical-anesthesia research.

concepts.label: Virginia Apgar
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how a rapid standardized assessment made newborn condition more consistently observable.

relations.note: Apgar’s standardized assessment and laboratory reference intervals invite comparison of two ways clinical observations are organized, without treating the score as a laboratory reference range.

concepts.card: A virtual organization uses communication technologies to connect dispersed expertise and activities beyond a single stable workplace. It can draw on remote teams or outsourced functions. The flexibility also creates coordination problems: limited interaction may weaken trust and leave participants feeling isolated from colleagues or the organization.

evidence.note: Checked dispersion, technology dependence and qualified trust/isolation risks; not every organization using remote work is asserted to be wholly virtual.

concepts.label: Virtual organization
concepts.learning_takeaway: Coordinate geographically dispersed expertise and outsourced activities through communication technologies, with trust and isolation challenges.

relations.note: OpenStax explicitly compares virtual structures with networked teams and distinguishes their geographical and technological organization.

concepts.card: A volcano’s surface can move as conditions change below it. Repeated GPS positions and tilt measurements help researchers infer changes in a magma reservoir’s depth or volume. Monitoring deformation turns small surface shifts into clues about an inaccessible system, while still requiring interpretation alongside other evidence.

evidence.note: USGS Mount St. Helens monitoring describes surface movement, GPS/tilt instruments and estimates of reservoir depth, volume and volume change.

concepts.label: Volcano ground-deformation monitoring
concepts.learning_takeaway: Infer subsurface magma changes from repeated measurements of surface movement.

relations.note: Kīlauea’s connected summit and rift activity offers a named case for thinking about subsurface magma movement, while the method’s cited demonstration is at Mount St. Helens.

concepts.card: Vulnerability changes bridge's rewards and risks: successful contracts can earn higher bonuses, while failed contracts can incur greater penalties. In duplicate bridge, the board determines which partnership is vulnerable. This differs from rubber bridge, where winning a game changes a partnership's vulnerability.

evidence.note: ACBL vulnerability definition supports premiums, undertrick penalties and the two different assignment methods; does not conflate vulnerable status with the strength of a hand.

concepts.label: Vulnerability in bridge
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how increased bonuses and penalties change a contract's stakes.

relations.note: ACBL describes vulnerability as a scoring status affecting bridge bonuses and penalties, then distinguishes its assignment in duplicate and rubber formats.

concepts.card: In SQLite, a WAL checkpoint transfers committed changes from the write-ahead log into the main database file. It is separate from reading, writing, or committing a transaction. SQLite can schedule checkpoints automatically or let applications control when they run to manage the accumulated log.

evidence.note: Section 2.1 defines SQLite's checkpoint transfer and automatic/application-controlled timing. No claim is made that all database checkpoints transfer pages from a log or run on each commit.

concepts.label: WAL checkpointing
concepts.learning_takeaway: In SQLite, move committed log content into the database as a separate operation from reading, writing, and committing.

relations.note: SQLite's WAL documentation names checkpointing as a distinct operation within its write-ahead-log mode; the facet link concerns that documented implementation.

concepts.card: Walden recounts Thoreau’s time living by Walden Pond and has inspired readers to reconsider conventional society. An editorial reading treats the account as an experiment in ways of living. That interpretation invites reflection without claiming to establish why the book’s influence has endured.

evidence.note: The NEA note identifies the cabin account and its influence on dissenting readers.

concepts.label: Walden
concepts.learning_takeaway: Thoreau’s account of life by Walden Pond invites an editorial reading of withdrawal from conventional society as an experiment in ways of living.

relations.note: The guide connects Walden with the philosophy of Bradbury’s book-preserving community.

concepts.card: William Morris’s Wandle has a pattern repeat measuring 98.4 by 44.5 centimeters, which the V&A calls his largest attempt. An editorial comparison asks how such a large repeating unit shapes a fabric’s composition beyond the scale of its individual motifs.

evidence.note: The V&A gives Wandle’s repeat as 98.4 by 44.5 cm and calls it Morris’s largest attempt; the composition question is editorial.

concepts.label: Wandle textile design
concepts.learning_takeaway: Wandle’s repeat measures 98.4 by 44.5 centimeters; the V&A identifies it as the largest Morris attempted.

relations.note: The named pattern illustrates why repeat scale matters when considering textile composition.

concepts.card: Warp threads need suitable, reasonably even tension while weaving. On a rigid-heddle loom, too little can let the raised reed fall, while too much can make changing positions difficult and strain the yarn. Good control means balancing the working tension, not simply making every thread as tight as possible.

evidence.locator: Even tension, PDF pp. 8–10; Helpful Hints—Tension, PDF p. 15
evidence.note: Ashford instructs checking equal tension and explains too-low/too-high tension effects on its rigid-heddle reed and yarn.

concepts.label: Warp tension
concepts.learning_takeaway: Balance a warp firmly enough to form the shed without unnecessarily straining the yarn and loom.

relations.note: Warp-tension control is a specific part of managing the thread set held by a loom during weaving.

concepts.card: A warranty promises specified repair or replacement if a product fails within agreed conditions. It reduces the need for buyers to verify every aspect of quality before purchase by assigning some consequences to the seller. Its protection depends on the actual terms, rather than the label alone.

evidence.note: Checked repair/replacement commitment and time qualification; no assertion that warranties eliminate hidden defects or cover every possible failure.

concepts.label: Warranties as quality assurance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Shift specified repair or replacement obligations to a seller so buyers need not verify every quality claim beforehand.

relations.note: The textbook presents warranties as an explicit response to quality uncertainty between buyers and sellers; the response is distinct from the information gap itself.

concepts.card: In a crossover study, the effects of one treatment period can persist into the next. A washout period leaves time without the intervention so those effects can diminish. Its usefulness depends on how long effects last; an arbitrary pause does not guarantee an uncontaminated comparison.

evidence.note: UK N-of-1 guidance describes a no-intervention interval intended to diminish previous effects and discusses long-lasting/carryover limitations.

concepts.label: Washout periods in crossover trials
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why effects from one treatment period can contaminate the next comparison.

relations.note: A washout interval is one design provision for the repeated within-person comparisons described in N-of-1 trials.

concepts.card: In We Real Cool, Gwendolyn Brooks repeatedly places the collective pronoun at line endings before the poem’s final reference to death. An editorial reading hears group bravado meeting a sudden limit. The formal pattern makes the relation between a shared voice and its ending available for interpretation.

evidence.note: Pronoun placement and final death reference are directly visible in the poem excerpt.

concepts.label: We Real Cool
concepts.learning_takeaway: Brooks places a collective pronoun at line endings; an editorial reading connects the recurring group voice with the poem’s final reference to death.

relations.note: The glossary uses the poem’s line endings to explore how syntax continues across verse boundaries.

concepts.card: Weak ties are less-close relationships, such as acquaintances, that may connect someone to information outside their usual circle. Close friends often know many of the same people. An acquaintance can therefore provide a different route, although a tie's usefulness depends on its network position rather than weakness alone.

evidence.note: Checked information access and the nonidentity of weak ties and local bridges; no claim that every acquaintance supplies novel information.

concepts.label: Weak ties
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why acquaintances can connect people to information outside densely connected close-friend circles.

relations.note: The chapter explicitly connects weak ties with local bridges while separating interpersonal tie strength from the mathematical edge property.

concepts.card: Western Christian monasticism organized disciplined religious life through withdrawal from ordinary worldly pursuits. It could take solitary or communal forms, while monasteries also provided hospitality, learning and artistic production. Withdrawal therefore did not necessarily mean a complete absence of relationships with surrounding society.

evidence.note: Solitary/communal forms and practical/cultural services are documented.

concepts.label: Western Christian monasticism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Withdrawal into disciplined religious life could take solitary or communal forms and also sustain learning, hospitality and artistic work.

relations.note: The Benedictine rule supplies a particularly influential program for communal monastic life.

concepts.card: William Labov's study of New York speech compared linguistic variation with occupation, education, and income. It also examined differences between casual speech and reading. The case shows how social categories become research variables and why contextual variation must be considered alongside differences between groups.

evidence.note: Checked the three social measures and two contexts; correlations are not described as proof that class causes a pronunciation.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The textbook explicitly presents Labov's study as an example of quantitative sociolinguistic analysis of social status and speaking style.

concepts.label: William Labov
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how occupation, education, and income were used to compare linguistic variant frequencies across social strata.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly presents Labov's study as an example of quantitative sociolinguistic analysis of social status and speaking style.

concepts.card: An open pipe behaves acoustically as though it extends slightly beyond its physical opening. The air's motion spreads outward before the pressure reflection develops, increasing the effective vibrating length. A resonance therefore occurs slightly lower than a simple model using only the measured tube length predicts.

evidence.note: UNSW End effects explains delayed reflection and effective length; slightly and simple model preserve the approximation rather than asserting one universal correction distance.

concepts.label: Wind-instrument end correction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why an open pipe resonates as though it were slightly longer.

relations.note: End corrections qualify ideal pipe predictions, including the simplified boundary-condition model used to explain clarinet register spacing.

concepts.card: The winner's curse can occur when the highest bidder also has an unusually high estimate of a shared uncertain value. Winning provides information about how optimistic that estimate was relative to others. Accounting for this selection before bidding differs from simply paying what one's initial estimate suggested.

evidence.note: Checked conditional-selection explanation; winning is not claimed to inevitably cause a loss when bidders already account for the effect.

concepts.label: Winner's curse
concepts.learning_takeaway: Condition an estimate on winning because the highest bid may reveal an unusually optimistic initial estimate.

relations.note: The lecture develops the winner's curse specifically through common-value bidding and the information revealed by winning.

concepts.card: Wood’s equilibrium moisture content can depend on whether it reached a humidity level by drying or by absorbing water. At the same temperature and relative humidity, the drying path can retain more moisture. This sorption hysteresis makes moisture history relevant even after equilibrium is reached.

evidence.note: USDA describes sorption isotherms at constant temperature and history-dependent equilibrium moisture content, with higher EMC on desorption than absorption at the same relative humidity.

concepts.label: Wood sorption hysteresis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why wood’s moisture history can matter even at the same temperature and relative humidity.

relations.note: The hysteresis passage describes path dependence of wood’s equilibrium-moisture relationship, a specific aspect of that property.

concepts.card: A worked example shows a solution path rather than asking a beginner to discover every step unaided. Studying examples alongside similar problems can focus attention on how the procedure works. The IES guide also notes that the appropriate amount of guidance changes as learners develop greater expertise.

evidence.note: Checked demonstrated solutions, alternating practice, and expertise qualification; no claim that worked examples should replace all problem solving.

concepts.label: Worked example
concepts.learning_takeaway: Study a demonstrated solution path before attempting comparable problems, especially while building initial expertise.

relations.note: The worked-example recommendation explicitly discusses gradually fading examples as expertise increases.

concepts.card: Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model treats temporary mental activity as more than a single storage box. A central executive coordinates specialized systems for verbal and visual-spatial material. The later addition of an episodic buffer illustrates that this is a developing explanatory model, not an immutable anatomical diagram.
